idea-plugin.name: IBM Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools
idea-plugin.description:
Easily and quickly modernize your enterprise Java applications using IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools (AMA Dev Tools) to use a modern Java runtime, the latest enterprise Java APIs, and current Java SE and Java EE / Jakarta EE versions.

AMA Dev Tools simplify and accelerate developer efforts to modernize legacy enterprise Java application code, including WebSphere Application Server traditional applications, to adopt current Java technologies and run on Liberty or Modernized Runtime Extension for Java (MoRE).

License

By downloading this plugin, you agree to the terms of IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools.

Features

Java runtime modernization

Analyze your legacy enterprise Java application and modernize it to use a more lightweight, flexible, and efficient runtime. Receive a prescriptive plan that describes the changes that are needed to modernize your application with a detailed assessment of complexity and required development effort. Use automation to quickly implement code and configuration changes. Migrate JAX-RPC services to JAX-WS services using automation and assistance with a source migration helper.

Java SE and Java EE / Jakarta EE upgrade

Identify changes required to upgrade Java code and automatically update the relevant application code. Receive a prescriptive plan that describes the changes that are needed to upgrade your application with a detailed assessment of complexity and required development effort. Use automation to quickly implement code changes.

Quick start

  1. Install IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools.
  2. Select the application project for modernization.
  3. Select and access available features from context menu.

Usage of IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools requires a valid access key or a migration plan from IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator.

Entitled usage of AMA Dev Tools is available to users of IBM Enterprise Application Runtimes (EAR) and IBM Modernized Runtime Extension for Java (MoRE).

Requirements

The requirements to use IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools features are:

Item Details
Java Java SE 17 or a later version
Maven Use Maven to build your application

For more information, see the documentation for IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools.

Support

If you want to report a problem or are looking for support options, see this documentation for IBM® Application Modernization Accelerator Developer Tools.

idea-plugin.name: BlendCharm
idea-plugin.description:
BlendCharm bridges PyCharm and Blender's extension system, giving you project scaffolding, hot-reload, debugging, manifest management, and integrated run configurations — without leaving the IDE.

  • Project Scaffolding: Create a fully structured Blender extension repository project and/or individual extensions.
  • Hot-Reload: File saves trigger automatic reloads with a configurable debounce.
  • Manifest Management: Manifest editor covers all standard fields, validates manifests against disk state on startup, and detects content drift.
  • Native debugging: Debug Blender extensions directly from the IDE.
  • Run Configurations:
    • Development — Launches Blender and loads your source extensions. Supports auto-install of active extensions and file-save triggered reload.
    • Distribution — Uses Blender to package the extension for distribution.
    • Validate — Uses Blender to validate the extension manifest against the Blender API.
  • Extension Lifecycle Management: Enable, disable, add, edit, reload, or mark extensions for deferred deletion without touching Blender directly.
  • SPDX License Catalog: Browse and select from the full SPDX license list directly in the manifest editor.

BlendCharm also supports IntelliJ IDE's with the Python plugin. BlendCharm currently only supports Blender extensions (4.2+), both add-on's and themes; legacy add-ons are not directly supported.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Prompt to track shared project settings in VCS: BlendCharm notifies when BlendCharmProjectSettings.xml is not under version control and prompts the user to add to VCS or explicitly ignore it.

Changed

  • Now built against IntelliJ Platform 2025.3 (build 253). The minimum supported IDE version is raised to 2025.3, and the upper build limit is removed so the plugin installs on newer IDEs as they release.

Fixed

  • Deleting a localized extension folder no longer logs an error: editing an extension's translation files and then deleting the extension folder within the same moment could trigger a background re-validation against the now-deleted folder, surfacing an "Accessing invalid virtual file" error in the log. Re-validation now treats a deleted extension as a no-op.
  • Stale BlendCharm run configurations are now cleared from non-BlendCharm projects: when a project that isn't configured for BlendCharm is opened, any leftover BlendCharm run configurations (e.g. carried in from a stale workspace.xml or a project that was once configured) are removed at startup instead of lingering in the run-config dropdown. Run configurations of other types are never touched.
  • Validating after an in-place Blender update now refreshes correctly: clicking Validate on the BlendCharm settings page after updating Blender in place (e.g. a 5.1.0 -> 5.1.1 hotfix) now writes the new version through and marks the installation valid, instead of leaving its status and version stale. Installations left in a bad state by this bug self-heal on the next validation pass.

idea-plugin.name: Guiced
idea-plugin.description:
Guiced is an IntelliJ IDEA plugin based on the JetBrains Guice plugin, providing full Google Guice and GuicedEE framework support for IntelliJ 2026+.

☕ Support this plugin: Buy me a coffee on Patreon

GuicedEE Framework Support

  • Create new GuicedEE projects with proper Maven dependencies
  • Generate module-info.java files with required dependencies
  • Create service loader implementations
  • Create various GuicedEE component templates:
    • Guice Modules
    • Lifecycle Hooks (Pre-Startup, Post-Startup, Pre-Destroy)
    • REST Services (with optional service class and DB session)
    • Router Configurations
    • Persistence / Database Modules
    • Cassandra Modules
    • MongoDB Modules
    • Redis Modules
    • HTTP Proxy Modules
    • WebSocket Channels, Message Receivers, and Hooks
    • RabbitMQ Connections, Consumers, and Publishers
    • Kafka Consumers
    • IBM MQ Consumers
    • Vert.x Startup and Configurators
    • Classpath Scanner SPIs
    • Cloud: Runtime Environment Providers, Service Registry Providers, Status Change Listeners
    • Consul and Consul Service Resolver support
  • Application templates for different use cases
  • Identify GuicedEE applications in the Services window
  • Recognise @VertxEventDefinition methods and classes as framework entry points so event-bus consumers are not flagged as unused

GuicedEE guice-core — Enhanced Google Guice

Upstream policy: this module tracks Google Guice releases. Changes are limited to modular descriptors, access-level fixes required by the module system, and the com.google.inject.gee SPI package. No behavioural changes are made to core Guice logic.

  • Full JPMS module — ships a real module-info.java (module com.google.guice) with explicit exports, requires, and uses directives
  • JDK 25 compatibility — access-level and reflection fixes so Guice runs cleanly on the module path without --add-opens hacks
  • Jakarta namespace — uses jakarta.inject and jakarta.annotation (not javax.*)
  • SPI-driven extensibility — six ServiceLoader-based SPIs let you register custom annotations for injection points, scopes, bindings, and naming without touching Guice source
  • Multibindings built-in — MapBinder, Multibinder, and OptionalBinder are included in the same module (no separate guice-multibindings artifact needed)
  • Drop-in replacement — all public Guice APIs remain unchanged; existing @Inject, @Provides, @Singleton, bind() EDSL code works as-is

Install via Maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.guicedee.modules.services</groupId>
    <artifactId>guice</artifactId>
</dependency>

SPI Extension Points (com.google.inject.gee)

Six SPIs loaded via java.util.ServiceLoader — declare uses in the Guice module and provides in your own module to extend Guice's annotation handling at runtime:

SPIPurpose
InjectionPointProviderRegister custom annotations that mark injection points (beyond @Inject)
InjectorAnnotationsProviderDeclare additional annotations that Guice should treat as injector annotations
BindScopeProviderProgrammatically bind custom scope annotations during module configuration
ScopeAnnotationProviderSupply annotation classes to be recognised as scope annotations (like @Singleton)
BindingAnnotationProviderSupply annotation classes to be recognised as binding annotations (like @Named)
NamedAnnotationProviderMap custom naming annotations to Guice's @Named, enabling alternative naming strategies

What Changed from Upstream

AreaChange
Module descriptorAdded module-info.java with full exports, requires, uses
Jakarta namespacejavax.inject → jakarta.inject, javax.annotation → jakarta.annotation
Access levelsWidened select internal access modifiers so packages work under strict JPMS enforcement
com.google.inject.geeNew package with 6 SPI interfaces for pluggable annotation handling
MultibindingsBundled into the core module instead of a separate artifact
Guice internalscom.google.inject.internal exported for framework-level consumers

Full Google Guice Support

  • Templates for creating Guice modules, providers, binding annotations, scope annotations, and method interceptors
  • Coding assistance: inspections, intentions, line markers, and navigation
  • Navigate between injection points and bindings (explicit bind() and JIT bindings)
  • 18 Guice-specific inspections for common mistakes
  • Intention actions to move bindings and scopes to class annotations
  • Works with both Google Guice and GuicedEE guice-core dependencies
  • SPI-driven injection point recognition — fields annotated with @Endpoint (REST Client) or @ConfigProperty (MicroProfile Config) are treated as injection points, with full implicit usage detection, gutter icons, and click-through navigation

  • Deterministic BOM resolution — GuicedEE BOMs no longer emit Maven 4 "Ignored POM import" model problems

idea-plugin.name: Jaspr | Dart Web Framework
idea-plugin.description:
Adds Jaspr framework support to JetBrains IDEs.

Jaspr is a web framework for Dart that lets you build type-safe, reactive web applications. This plugin integrates the Jaspr toolchain directly into your IDE.

Requires the Dart plugin and jaspr_cli.

Run Configuration

Run jaspr daemon directly from the IDE with graceful shutdown and Chrome lifecycle management.

Component Scopes

Inline code vision hints show whether a component renders on the server or the client, powered by the jaspr tooling-daemon.

HTML to Jaspr Conversion

Right-click any .html file and select Convert to Jaspr to generate the equivalent Dart component.

New Project Wizard

Create a new Jaspr project from scratch using the IDE's project wizard with full CLI integration.

Live Templates

Built-in templates for common patterns: stlessc, stfulc, jhtml, jtext, and more.

Advanced Tooling

Run jaspr clean and jaspr doctor from the Tools menu. Includes version mismatch notifications and console output formatting.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Dart/Melos workspace detection: the plugin now recognizes when a project is part of a Dart pub workspace or a Melos-managed monorepo, walking up from a member package to find the workspace root.
  • Automatic, idempotent injection of a delimited melos.scripts entry (in melos.yaml or the root pubspec.yaml) that runs jaspr daemon scoped to a package — merges safely alongside scripts the user or melos bootstrap already declared, without clobbering them.
  • New "Melos script" field in the Jaspr Run/Debug Configuration editor (dropdown of known scripts, editable) — when set, the daemon is launched via melos run <script> instead of directly, with all other run-configuration flags (port, mode, dart-defines, etc.) forwarded through.
  • New "Create Melos Script..." action under Tools → Jaspr, for registering an additional Jaspr app's script in a monorepo with more than one Jaspr package.
  • Proactive console warning when a run configuration has no "Melos script" set inside a detected workspace, before the daemon fails.

Fixed

  • Fixed project creation issue where generated files were not copied if the CLI failed on dependency constraints (e.g. pub get errors)[cite: 4].
  • Fixed failing unit/integration test suite.
  • Fixed --input and --dart-define-from-file paths being resolved against the workspace root instead of the target package directory when running via a Melos script, causing "Specified entry point ... does not exist" failures.

Changed

  • Added support and compatibility for IntelliJ IDEs version 2026.2.x.

Project Generator: Go to File → New → JSM Project, fill in the configuration, and generate your project.

More Information

Visit JSM Framework for documentation and examples.

idea-plugin.name: exida STIG
idea-plugin.description:
exida STIG brings the full exida STIG toolchain into your IntelliJ IDEA.

Copyright (C) 2026 exida & SAFETYGENCE. Author: Piotr Serwa.

STIG is a strongly typed modeling framework for efficiently authoring and reviewing specifications in mission-critical projects, including safety-related, security-related, and dependable systems.

It helps teams create structured, traceable engineering work and evidence supporting compliance activities for functional-safety standards such as ISO 26262 and IEC 61508, cybersecurity standards such as ISO/SAE 21434 and IEC 62443, and quality standards and process frameworks such as ISO 9001 and Automotive SPICE.

Its modular hierarchy and explicit ownership boundaries are designed to scale efficiently to large, distributed, multi-supplier programs involving 10,000+ people. Each team or supplier can own separate projects or modules while retaining integrated system-level links, automated checks, traceability, and reporting.

This plugin provides:

  • An automatic, live, rule-based checker that highlights model violations as you type.
  • All STIG libraries and Gradle tasks needed to work with your STIG projects directly from the IDE.
  • In-editor navigation across STIG model elements.
  • Shared GitHub reviews of released reports: a STIG Reviews tool window, source-linked findings, discussions and issue workflow actions without a pull request.
  • A bundled STIG Codex skill, installed with stigInstallSkill, that lets you collaborate with a Codex agent to co-author your STIG specifications or have the agent perform a structured review for you.

idea-plugin.name: Katalyst Support
idea-plugin.description:
Editor support for the Katalyst Kotlin backend framework.
Katalyst is annotation-free and discovers routes, middleware, websockets, exception handlers, services, components, repositories, tables, event handlers, schedulers, migrations, initializers and config loaders by convention at startup. This plugin teaches the IDE those conventions so it stops reporting framework entrypoints as unused (no more @Suppress("unused")), marks them with gutter icons, and warns when a function looks like an entrypoint but won't be discovered. Works in IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio.
idea-plugin.change-notes:

  • Aligned the vendored Katalyst discovery contract with framework 1.0.0-alpha04.
  • Internal: configuration-cache-safe build and tightened internal API visibility.
0.2.2
  • Scheduler: cron validation and inline English descriptions now recognize mixed named and positional arguments.
  • Scheduler: cron hints stay available for ScheduleConfig(...) based jobs, CronExpression("...") wrappers, named expression = ... arguments, and trailing-comma call layouts.
  • Scheduler: duplicate job-name validation now also reads ScheduleConfig(taskName = "...").
0.2.0
  • Scheduler: cron expressions are now shown in plain English inline (e.g. 0 0 2 * * ? → Every day at 02:00).
  • Scheduler: invalid cron expressions are flagged in the editor with the exact field error, instead of only failing at startup.
  • Scheduler: duplicate job names within a jobs { } block are flagged.
  • Events: warns when an EventHandler<T>'s eventType does not match its type argument (a handler wired to the wrong event).
0.1.4
  • Declare the Java-plugin dependency required by the Kotlin light-class APIs we use (resolves the IntelliJ Plugin Verifier compatibility problem).
0.1.3
  • Fix: actually suppress the "never used" warning on entrypoints. The Kotlin inspection checks the light element (PsiMethod/PsiClass), so we now unwrap to the Kotlin origin.
0.1.2
  • Fix: recognise expression-body entrypoints like fun Route.authRoutes() = katalystRouting { } — they are now correctly marked used and no longer flagged "calls no katalyst* DSL".
  • Gutter-icon detection moved off the fast path (no resolve in getLineMarkerInfo).
0.1.1
  • Declare support for K2 Kotlin mode (fixes "incompatible with the Kotlin plugin in K2 mode").
0.1.0
  • Initial release.
  • Marks Katalyst entrypoints (routes, middleware, websockets, exception handlers, services, components, repositories, tables, event handlers, schedulers, migrations, initializers, config loaders) as used — no more @Suppress("unused").

idea-plugin.name: TreasureBoat Coding Tools
idea-plugin.description:
TreasureBoat Coding Tools brings first-class IDE support to TreasureBoat — a modern Java framework for building database-driven web applications with a model-driven ORM (Enterprise Objects), rule-driven UI (Sangria), reusable components and Key-Value Coding.

The plugin understands your models, components and rules, so the IDE works with the framework, not around it: visual editors instead of hand-edited plists, generators instead of boilerplate, and deploy builds without leaving the IDE.

What's inside

  • EOModel editor — edit entities, attributes, relationships and fetch specs visually
  • Sangria rule editor — author and navigate the rules that drive your generated UI
  • Component editor — unified editing of HTML templates, bindings (WOD) and API, with KVC keypath awareness and navigation between HTML, WOD, API and Java
  • Migration editor — manage schema migrations and stored configuration as structured rules
  • Localization editor — edit per-locale strings side by side, and translate in place
  • Layout & Navigation editor — design the application's navigation and page layout
  • Code generation — REST controllers, Swagger annotations, EO classes and project templates
  • Model Data Creation (MDC) — build .eomodeld from annotated Java classes
  • One-click deploy builds — Legacy, Maven-embedded and Maven-deploy .woa bundles

Requires a free TreasureBoat ID to unlock the full framework and tooling — request a trial at treasureboat.org.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.2.22 — Still works on the next IDE

  • Creating a project on 2026.3 - StdModuleTypes is gone in the 2026.3 EAP, and the module builder named it directly, so the method that returns the module type would have thrown NoSuchClassError the moment anyone created a project there. The plugin declares no upper build bound - it is offered on every future IDE and has to keep working on them - so the Marketplace verifier reported 1.2.21 as binary incompatible. The type is now resolved through ModuleTypeManager and the platform's own id constant, which is what the platform's own helper does internally, so there is no class name left here for a future release to remove.

1.2.21 — A command line, and an editor that agrees with itself

  • Delete rules the editor set, and delete rules it removed - the model editor wrote cascade, deny and no action: the enum name, lowercased. TreasureBoat reads only the EODeleteRule… names and takes anything else as Nullify without a word, so a Cascade set here never cascaded. Reading was wrong in the other direction too, and that half was worse: EODeleteRuleCascade threw on the way in and was caught as Nullify, and Nullify is omitted when a model is written - so opening a correctly written model and saving it removed the rule from the file. Those rules had been working, and a delete rule only shows itself when something is deleted, so nothing looked wrong at the time. Both spellings are now read, in any case, and EODeleteRule… is written; open and save a model to rewrite its rules. A model saved by an earlier version may be missing rules it once had - they are in version control, as a deleteRule line removed with nothing put back.
  • A generated column keeps the attribute's name - the New Attribute dialog offered SAMPLE_SOMETHING for sample_something and had to be corrected by hand every time. It wrote SNAKE_CASE, uppercased unless the adaptor was MySQL or PostgreSQL - and uppercased when the adaptor was unknown, which is exactly the state that dialog is in before a database has been chosen. The uppercase helped nowhere: Oracle folds unquoted identifiers itself, and PostgreSQL quotes, so an uppercase name stays uppercase and case-sensitive for good. TreasureBoat's own TBBaseModel.eomodeld writes columnName and name identically and runs on all four databases, so a generated entity spelling its columns differently was the odd one out. The column is now the attribute name, whatever the adaptor.
  • Build and deploy without the IDE - the embedded build and the deploy existed only behind TreasureBoat → Deploy, so nothing outside the IDE could run them: not Jenkins, not a scripted test. The code moved into an IDE-free module and gained a command line: tb license, tb build meb, tb targets, tb deploy, tb docker up|down. The menu actions call the same classes, so the IDE behaves exactly as before, and the licence check is now one class both sides share rather than two that could drift.
  • A timeout that never fired - the Maven and ssh runners read the process output to end-of-file and only then started the timeout. The read finishes when the process exits, so the timeout was unreachable: a hung mvn hung the caller with it. In the IDE that was a progress bar somebody could cancel; on a build agent it is a job that never ends.
  • Components a deployed bundle cannot find - a project created before 1.2.12 keeps its components in src/main/resources/Components, which the build does not flatten, so the bundle carried Resources/Components/X.wo while a deployed application looks components up by bare name in Contents/Resources. Every page using one rendered empty, nothing was logged, and development never showed it because it reads the source tree. The build now stops and names the components.
  • Deploying the wrong tarball - clean empties target/deploy on every build, so "the newest matching tarball" was the wrong rule. A deploy now sends exactly the artifact it built or was given, and refuses a server whose build type does not match it.
  • A recreated container keeps its mounts - docker up removes and recreates the container, carrying over its ports, network, restart policy and environment. Mounts were not carried over, so a container that mounted its Properties came back without them and the application ran against an empty directory in silence. Bind mounts and named volumes are reconstructed; anything that cannot be rebuilt faithfully refuses the redeploy instead of being dropped.
  • The editor and the text tab are one file again - a change made in the Migration Editor did not appear under Text until you saved, and a change typed under Text was not there when you switched back. They were never two views of one file: the editor read and wrote the file on disk while the text tab edited the in-memory document, so each could be edited and one would silently overwrite the other. Both now go through the same document. Switching tabs needs no save because there is nothing left to synchronise, and the IDE's own handling starts working - the modified marker, save on focus loss, undo and Local History.
  • No Save button - Cmd+S already means save everywhere else in the IDE, and now it means it here too. Closing the editor no longer writes either: it used to save on close, which with the old arrangement would have written the editor's model over a text edit you had not saved yet.
  • Duplicate an entity - two entities in a migration are usually the same shape with one value changed, and building the second meant adding it and then retyping every attribute. The new toolbar button copies the selected entity with all its attributes and children, and places it directly after the original in the same operation, ready to edit.

1.2.20.1 — Sangria rules from the command line

  • idea tb-generate-rules writes an application's <Entity>.sangria files headlessly, as tb-generate-eos does for EO classes: tb-generate-rules [--disabled] [--rest] Model.eomodeld SangriaDir Entity.... Same generator as Create Entity Rules; the defaults are what an application's rule files hold in practice - enabled, every group but REST. It overwrites, since there is nobody to ask.

1.2.20 — A generated project runs, and a free user can download it

  • Anyone can now download TreasureBoat - a free or trial user could not get a jar at all. The framework repositories are private, a private repository cannot publish to public GitHub Packages, and GitHub Packages Maven needs a token to read even when public. The free set is now a static Maven repository on GitHub Pages, which is plain anonymous HTTPS, and a generated Simple application points at it and pins the published set. Verified the way a new user sees it, with an empty local repository and no credentials: everything resolves and the project builds.
  • A Simple application's front door is Main again - it answered with the login action, which is right for an Extended project and wrong for one that has no login screen: the first launch redirected to a page that does not exist and showed a 404. The two project types now generate different front doors, which is what they always needed.
  • The navigation bar is a face file, and every entry it lists exists - the generated bar named two entries and defined one, in a file the navigation manager only reads when no face file is present. The entry that worked was defined elsewhere, which is what made the arrangement look deliberate. A missing definition costs one line of INFO per render and the bar simply draws short, so it reads as unfinished rather than broken. The file is also named for the face now: with the old name and no face file beside it, the plugin's own navigation editor classified every generated application as a framework.
  • An Extended project starts in the look it is built for - Sangria is Keen-only, but a session starts in whichever look the framework defaults to, and nothing set one. The wrong look renders perfectly well, which is why this has been diagnosed three times in three applications. A generated project now pins Keen. A Simple one does not: it may still want Gumby.
  • A new project can sign in - CSRF checking is on by default and the login form is the first POST that matters, so a generated application refused its own sign-in. It is switched off in dev.properties only, which TreasureBoat loads exclusively in development, so a deployment keeps CSRF on.
  • No more favicon errors on every page - a project shipped two placeholder icons. TreasureBoat resolves icons twice, and the second mechanism probes for one of those exact files and then points all twenty-one icon tags at your bundle - where the other nineteen are not. Both mechanisms already fall back to tb-content-delivery, so the fix is to ship none. The generated README explains what to do if you want your own: all twenty-one, or none.
  • A README that says what to do first - create the database before the first run (TreasureBoat creates tables at startup but never the database, and the failure names a JDBC driver), the first login is wodka/wodka, the sample JWT and cipher keys are identical in every generated project and must be replaced, and the favicon rule above.
  • Every property file says which file it is - seven of them carried no load marker and app.properties carried one naming a file that does not exist. On the screen built for answering "did my setting get loaded?", a file that loaded and a file that was never read looked the same - and the unmarked ones were the connection string and your own overrides, the two you edit first.
  • Framework versions are one number again - the plugin pinned three different ones, none current, with the application's parent nine releases behind. All of them now read the current coordinated release.
  • Icons that were never going to render - twenty-one icons across the frameworks asked for a Font Awesome style the free package has no font for, and drew as empty boxes. They looked correct in the editor, which resolved them whether or not the Pro font was present, so they failed only at runtime on someone else's machine.

1.2.14 — The framework page knows what it is generating

  • Every SQL database is offered - all eleven tb-db-* adaptors are released, and the dropdown listed six. FrontBase, MaxDB, DB2, Derby and OpenBase were reachable only by ticking the adaptor on the Extended page, which does not write the connection properties that make it usable. A simple application is offered the four common ones and None; an Extended one gets all of them. Their driver, user and TreasureBoat plug-in now come from each adaptor module rather than a switch that repeated all four per database - which is how H2 came to be generated with no dbConnectPluginGLOBAL at all, though tb-db-h2 ships one.
  • An Extended project starts with what makes it Extended - ticking nothing produced tb-core-extensions, -foundation and -web: a simple application with extra folders, no Sangria, nothing to log in as. Sangria and the basemodel bridge are now the floor, bringing TBPerson, TBRole and the first user with them. A Reset button puts the selection back to it.
  • The wizard applies the project type - File > New > Project never told the framework panel which type it was generating, so none of the above appeared there and the Reset button did nothing, while the New TreasureBoat Project action had all of it. The two entry points must agree, and this is the sort of divergence that hides best: the page looked right, it was simply never told.
  • "Required" means it - the renderer greyed a locked checkbox and nothing else, so a framework marked (required) could be unticked and the Database group, decided on the previous page, was not read-only at all. A checkbox that looks disabled and still responds teaches that the label means nothing.

1.2.13 — An Extended project starts where it is supposed to

  • It asks for a login - the generated Main carried a bare @TBPageAccess, and requireLogin() defaults to false, so the application opened straight onto Main and never asked for anything. It now reads @TBPageAccess(navigationState = "Welcome", requireLogin = true), which is what AppGWare's Main reads. The user to log in with already existed: TBBM_FirstDataCreator creates one at first start and logs its name and password.
  • It can reach the Control Center - Navigationbar/shared.plist was an empty list of example comments, so nothing routed to TBKeenControlCenter. It now carries the Dashboard entry. Its fallback also returned an XML <plist><dict></dict> where the navigation manager reads an array — a fallback runs when the template could not be loaded, which is when nobody is looking.
  • No Login.plist is generated - it is a development quick-login file and its contents are credentials, which is why the real ones live outside the repository under ~/tb-content-private/Resources/ and why the pom excludes it from deploys. The generated one held requiresLogin = false: a key nothing reads, in a file that reads like the switch for whether login is required and is not one. That switch is the annotation above.
  • Sangria rules go in the Sangria folder - a generated project got d2w.d2wmodel at the resources root and an empty D2W/ beside it. Both are read, but neither AppGWare nor EdisonSystem has either, and the framework creates Sangria/ itself in development mode, so a project ended up with one of each. It is Sangria/_default.sangria now, the rule file for the default face. The entity-rules action follows suit.
  • The CMS property file uses the keys the framework reads - a project got two: tb-pro-cms.properties with wodka.cms.* keys, which nothing reads, and TBCMS.properties with the org.treasureboat.cms.* keys TBCMS actually reads but under a name TreasureBoat never looks for. Every CMS setting was inert. One file now, with the right keys.
  • The wizard shows a TreasureBoat icon - the New Project generator used the icon for a .wod file: a blue square with a W in it, for WebObjects.
  • The property files dialog can open its own files - it built paths from src/main/resources/Properties, the bundle file, rather than Property, the directory, so clicking any entry reported "Could not open file" for a file that was on disk all along.
  • The database is shown, not asked twice - page 2 listed every tb-db-* as tickable with only the chosen one locked, so a second adaptor could be ticked beside it and the page could show a database the project would not have. The group is read-only now, and tb-db-prototypes is ticked with the adaptor, which the pom always added and the page always showed unticked.

1.2.12 — What a new project looks like when you open it

  • One database in the pom, and not in a profile - the chosen adaptor sat in a profile marked activeByDefault, which does not mean "on unless overridden": Maven switches off every activeByDefault profile in a POM the moment any profile is activated with -P. A generated project also carries a snapshot profile, and -Psnapshot is the documented way to build against locally-built frameworks - so the ordinary development build silently left the project with no database adaptor at all. It is an ordinary dependency now, where no flag can remove it. All six databases used to get a profile each, and each carried a raw JDBC driver that nothing needs: every tb-db-* framework declares its own, and the hand-pinned versions here had already drifted - an Oracle project shipped ojdbc11:23.3.0.23.09 while tb-db-oracle depends on db-oracle, a dependency that does not resolve, waiting in a profile nobody had activated.
  • Components are generated where the build looks for them - Main.wo went to src/main/resources/Components, and tb-maven-plugin's resource-copy goal reads components from src/main/webapp, src/main/components and a top-level Components/. It was therefore never processed as a component: the plain resources mapping swept it up and landed it one level below where a real application has it. The conversion actions have always rewritten Components/ to src/main/webapp; only the creation path invented somewhere else.
  • The bundle Properties file is empty - it carried TBBundleExecutable and TBApplicationClass, which are Info.plist keys that nothing reads from there. Info.plist is generated by the Maven plugin at build time, so this was a second source of bundle identity beside the real one. TBWLoader needs the file to exist, not to say anything.
  • A new project opens without warnings in it - every generated serialVersionUID now carries @Serial, and the two component classes that lacked @Slf4j have it. Logging uses SLF4J placeholders rather than string concatenation: it is the first logging statement a developer sees in a project that is theirs, and it is the one they will copy into a loop.
  • No .gitkeep placeholders - git cannot store an empty directory, so committing one needs a file inside it, but none of these directories has to survive a clone. No real TreasureBoat project in the tree carries one.
  • The generated core delegate is spelled CoreDelegate - "Delegater" is not a word. Only the class the project owns is renamed; the framework keeps TBWCoreDelegaterBase and the coreDelegater() override point, and the template warns against "correcting" the override to match - one renamed to fit would compile and never be called.

1.2.11 — What a generated project declares, and what a build can run without you

  • A generated project's bundle Properties lands where TreasureBoat looks for it - the wizard wrote it to src/main/resources/Resources/Properties, and super-deploy-pom already maps src/main/resources to target/classes/Resources, so the file ended up one level too deep. The application then died at startup with Main bundle 'Properties' file can't be read, which describes packaging and not the path chosen when the project was generated. Invisible from the IDE - a development launch identifies the bundle from the build-tool classpath and never reads the file - so it surfaced only on a deployed .woa. The file is also generated empty now: it used to carry TBBundleExecutable and TBApplicationClass, which are Info.plist keys that nothing reads from there, making it a second source of bundle identity beside the real one.
  • Docker files a project can actually run - the generated Dockerfile assembled its own classpath from loose jars, which cannot start a TreasureBoat application at all: the framework identifies its main bundle from the deployment layout and does not recognise that shape. It now copies the Maven Embedded .woa, which carries every dependency and needs no Maven at runtime. The two generate actions also hardcoded port 8080 while the wizard assigns each project its own port, so the image published a port the application never bound - the container started, logged nothing unusual, and answered nothing. The port now comes from the project's own property files, read in the order the container merges them. The success dialogs gave instructions that did not work, and now name the embedded build, the real port, and the licence token a container cannot read from ~/tb-dev.license.
  • The wizard can add frameworks from the project's own directory - a new application in a mono-repo could only depend on published artifacts, so a framework sitting beside it had to be wired in by hand: a dependency, a <modules> entry and a relativePath, each easy to get subtly wrong. Sibling directories whose pom names super-tb-pom as its parent are now offered. Their coordinates are read from outside the <parent> block, because a framework that inherits its groupId would otherwise report the parent's - and the generated dependency would point at super-tb-pom, which resolves, builds, and produces an application missing the framework it asked for.
  • An Extended Application declares the skin it renders with - the generated project called Keen and declared no skin, reaching it only because tb-core-extensions happens to depend on it. A project that depends on a framework by inheritance fails, when it fails, with a component that cannot be found rather than a missing dependency. A simple application is left to pick its own.
  • MDC models can be generated without the IDE window - idea tb-generate-mdc <project> <package> generates the .eomodeld from annotated MDC_* classes, completing the chain MDC → .eomodeld → EO classes that tb-generate-eos started. It shares one implementation with the menu action, including where the files go. Generation also reports orphans now, from both the command and the menu item: it is additive, so deleting an MDC_* class leaves its plist, its index.eomodeld entry and its generated _Entity.java behind, all still compiling against a model that no longer describes them. A changed entity was loud; a dropped one was silent. They are named rather than deleted, and the command exits 3 when it finds any, so regenerate-and-diff can be a check rather than an inspection.
  • Fetch-specification bindings are found, or no typed method is generated - the parser looked for like as a whole word, which never matches inside caseInsensitiveLike, so that binding was not seen. The generated typed method then had no parameter for it and no binding of it: source that compiles, runs, and silently ignores the variable. caseInsensitiveLike is now recognised, as is a binding written before its operator - and more importantly, the typed method is only generated when every $binding in the qualifier was accounted for. An operator the parser does not know now costs a convenience method rather than producing a broken one; the dictionary-taking overload always works.
  • Every deploy build refuses development-only code - the check that keeps TBFDevelopment.skip(...) and DEV-ONLY markers out of a deployable only treats a build as deployable when it sees a legacy-build or wsr-build goal, or -Dorg.treasureboat.compile. The IDE's build actions pass none of those to Maven - the compile flag goes into the generated run script, as a runtime argument - so the check ran, found the markers, logged a warning and let the deployable through, on every build made from the IDE. All three build actions now make it strict.

1.2.10 — Receive License reaches production again

  • The scheme dropdown no longer sends a licence request to the wrong URL - 1.2.9 taught the Server, Path and Shared Secret fields to fall back to production when left empty, but not the http/https dropdown beside them. A dropdown always holds a value, so it could never be empty and never fell back: an http chosen once for a local server stayed selected while every other field showed production as placeholder text, and Receive License posted to http://www.treasureboat.org. The redirect to https turns a POST into a GET, so the server answered "Only POST requests are allowed" - a message that describes the symptom exactly and points nowhere near the setting that caused it. The scheme now follows the host: leave the host empty and you get production over https, name a host and the dropdown means what it says, so a local server over http still works.

1.2.9 — A new project builds, starts and runs

  • A generated project compiles - the wizard produced a Maven project whose dependencies could not resolve. tb-pro-keen was still offered after its Keen skin was extracted into tb-core-skin-keen; it stopped publishing at 21.0.3 while the rest of the pro group moved to 21.0.10, so selecting it asked Maven for a version that does not exist. tb-template-framework was in the same position - an 11.x artifact that the current super-pom no longer declares, which put an 11.x dependency into a 21.x project. Both are gone, tb-core-skin-keen takes Keen's place, and the ProY frameworks the super-pom does declare are now offered. The generated pom also tolerates a missing .git: the parent pom runs git-commit-id on every build and failed outright without a repository, so a project could not be compiled at all until you ran git init.
  • Source files you cannot compile are no longer written - PageConfigDelegate, NavigationQuery and QuartzDelegate import framework packages, and were written whether or not those frameworks were selected. The check that was supposed to prevent it named the wrong artifact: PageConfigDelegate imports org.treasureboat.basemodel.delegate, which ships in tb-pro-basemodel-bridge, not tb-features-basemodel as the package name suggests. Requirements are now read from each template's own imports and resolved against the contents of the published jars, so they cannot disagree with the code they describe.
  • Framework settings reach the frameworks - each framework's Property/ file was named for the framework's old name, TBJavaMail.properties rather than tb-core-mail.properties. TreasureBoat reads these by bundle name and nothing else, so the file was written, shipped in the bundle, and never read - setting an SMTP host in it had no effect and the framework still refused to start, reporting the property as missing. Files are now named after the bundle, are written for every framework the project actually carries rather than only the ones ticked in the wizard (tb-pro-cms brings in tb-core-mail, which will not start unconfigured), and each comes with a .<user> override beside it for machine-specific values.
  • The application starts - the generated EOModel carried its own connection dictionary, including an empty password. TreasureBoat pushes the dbConnect*GLOBAL properties into every model it loads, so the frameworks inherit their connection from the application; a model that also declares its own ended up one key larger than the framework models, and startup aborted comparing them. It is now empty, as a real application's is. Separately, the six TBApplication overrides the wizard generates were never registered, so all six were compiled and unused - and FirstDataCreator extended the empty base class rather than the BaseModel one that creates the system user, so nothing created it and the first EO migration to insert a row failed with NO SYSTEM USER IS SET and retried on every start. All six are registered, and each extends the class that suits the frameworks in the project.
  • A new project stops filling the log with its own defects - browsers ask for /favicon.ico and the apple-touch icons unprompted, and a project had nothing at the paths TreasureBoat rewrites those to, so every page load logged two failed resource reads. Placeholder icons now ship at those paths with a note on replacing them. Localizable.strings held a bare comment rather than a property list, which the localizer reported as a parse failure on every start; it is now a dictionary with one real entry showing the syntax.
  • A run configuration is created for you - every part of the TreasureBoat run configuration existed except anything that ever made one, so a new project had to have it built by hand before it could be started. One is now created when a project is opened, if it is a TreasureBoat application and has none. It never touches a configuration you have adjusted, and adding your own suppresses it for good.
  • EO classes can be generated without the IDE window - regenerating was reachable only by clicking a menu item, so every model change needed somebody at the keyboard, and a build could not do it at all. idea tb-generate-eos /path/to/Model.eomodeld now does the same work from a command line, sharing one implementation with the menu action so the two cannot disagree about what regenerating means. It also fixes a failure that was easy to miss from inside the IDE: the virtual file system refreshes a named directory but not its contents, so a .eomodeld it had cached from an earlier run kept its old set of plists and an entity added since was simply not seen - the run reported success and quietly generated the previous model. Measured at 19 files against the 29 actually on disk, the only difference being a warm caches directory. The command now refreshes the model recursively before reading it, and reports what it generated with an exit code a script can act on.
  • Model fetch specifications generate code that compiles - a fetch specification defined in the model produced a class that could not be compiled, so the feature was unusable: the point of it is that a named query lives in the model rather than in whichever Java method last assembled the qualifier. _Entity.vm has always asked a fetch specification for three properties it did not have, and Velocity does not fail on an unresolved reference - it writes the reference out as literal text, so the generated source carried ${fetchSpecification.capitalizedName} where a method name belonged. The three are now supplied, and a fetch specification generates a typed method alongside the dictionary-taking one. Worth knowing when trying this: the generator reads <Entity>.fsdefinition beside the plist while TreasureBoat reads the same dictionary inline in <Entity>.plist - define it in one and not the other and nothing happens, either no generated method or a fetchSpecificationNamed that returns null at runtime.

1.2.8 — A new install can fetch its licence

  • The licence server settings are applied, not just displayed - on a new installation Receive License could fail with the settings panel looking perfectly correct. Server and Path show the production values as placeholder text, which is indistinguishable from a filled-in field at a glance, so the panel read www.treasureboat.org and /TB/GWare while sending neither; and the Shared Secret had no default at all, so the request was signed with nothing. The defaults now apply whenever a field is left empty, on both the stored settings and the Receive License button, which reads the form directly. The fields themselves stay empty and keep showing the default as placeholder text, so a value you have set stays distinguishable from one you have not. Anyone already using the plugin is unaffected - a value you have set is never overridden - and an empty secret still means unsigned when you have pointed the plugin at your own development server, which is the one case where empty is a deliberate setting.

1.2.7 — Editors stop blaming themselves for your files

  • A new EOMigration file opens instead of reporting an IDE error - New → EOMigration File creates the file and opens it immediately, so the very first thing the editor sees is zero bytes. That went straight to the XML parser, which fails with premature end of file, and the failure was logged in the way that raises IntelliJ's Internal Error dialog - so creating a file produced a stack trace and an invitation to report a plugin bug, for doing nothing unusual at all. An empty file is not malformed, it is simply empty: it now opens as a blank Create migration ready to fill in. A whitespace-only file - what is left after clearing the editor - behaves the same, and genuinely broken XML is still reported as before.
  • A file that will not parse no longer looks like a plugin crash - the same handling was in six editors: the D2W rule and list-builder editors, both S2M editors, the Face Property editor and the Localizable Strings editor. Each reported a file it could not read as an IDE Internal Error, which blames the plugin for your data. Two of them recovered perfectly well - falling back to an empty model - and raised the dialog anyway, so an empty .d2wmodel behaved exactly like the migration file above; another stacked it on top of the error dialog it had already shown you. Every editor's own message is unchanged; only the spurious dialog is gone.
  • "TreasureBoat Project" removed from the Database tool window - the New popup in the Database panel draws from the same New group as File → New, so the action appeared there alongside the data source types, which is not a place a project can be created. It now shows only where there is somewhere in the project tree to create something - the same rule New Component… already followed, which is why that one never appeared there.

1.2.6 — Face property comments & faster first start after a Maven Simple deploy

  • The first row in the Face Property editor kept its comment - a comment typed against the topmost property was written to the file correctly but came back empty every time the editor reloaded, and only that one row was affected. In a property file a comment sits directly above the key it describes, so the first entry's comment lands at the very top of the file - where a file header would also be - and the reader claimed all of it as the header. A comment block is now read as the header only when a blank line separates it from the first key, which is also how the editor writes one; a block that runs straight into a key belongs to that key. Existing files are unaffected: a comment that was previously absorbed into the header now appears on its row, where you can edit it.
  • The deploy helper now resolves the Maven classpath at deploy time - a Maven Simple (MSB) build ships only a jar and a pom.xml, so run.sh works out the classpath on the first start and caches it in .classpath.txt. A freshly placed .woa has no such cache, so that first start paid for a full resolve - and right after a framework release it also had to download the new artifacts, which took about four minutes in one real case. TBMonitor saw no lifebeat for that whole window and counted the instance as dead. Worse with autostart on: while Maven resolves there is no JVM and no bound port, so the retry did not bounce off a port conflict - it started a second run.sh and a second Maven, both writing the same artifacts into the same local repository. The helper now does the resolve during the deploy, where nobody is watching a counter, and prints a PREWARM: line when it does. It is skipped for Legacy and Maven Embedded builds (they carry their own dependencies), skipped when a cache already exists, opt-out with --no-prewarm, and never fatal - if it fails the first start simply resolves as before.
  • The deploy helper reports its version - tb-deploy is pushed to servers by Install/Update Deploy Helper, so boxes can drift. It now carries a version, prints it with --version, and names it when installing and when checking a server, so you can tell what a given box is running.

1.2.5 — Sangria d2wType corrections & Monitor links

  • Monitor link for each deploy environment - deploy only places the .woa on the server; restarting the instance happens in TBMonitor, and with several servers it is easy to lose track of which Monitor belongs to which environment. Each target in the .treasureboat deploy editor now has a Monitor URL column, an Open Monitor button next to it, and the "Deploy → <environment>" notification offers Open Monitor once the deploy finishes. Entirely optional - environments without a URL are unchanged.
  • The enum d2wType is now spelled correctly - the EOModel editor's "Sangria UI" popup and the help reference both offered enums, but TreasureBoat only ever had enum (TBSangria_Display_enum and friends). Writing enum in a rule also failed to open its help page. Both now use enum.
  • Same fix for barcode - the popup offered barCode, which no framework recognizes; the real d2wType is barcode.
  • Sangria UI list synced with the frameworks - language (a live component) was hidden as legacy and is back; tagGID was missing and was added; plist gained the help page it never had. The attribute popup, the help reference and its index are now identical lists.
  • Relationship "Sangria UI" list cleaned - toManyAdvanced, toManyCheckboxes, toManyIsTrue, toOneAdvanced and toOneRadio came from the retired Eclipse model editor and exist in no TreasureBoat framework, so they are no longer offered. Values already saved in a model are still shown and left untouched.
  • d2wType code completion - in .d2wmodel rules, completion offered an invented list (money, email, richText, customType…) that had nothing to do with Sangria. It now offers the real d2wTypes.
  • Fixed a value-loss bug in the model editor - selecting an attribute or relationship whose d2wType was not in the popup left the previously selected property's value showing, and saved that wrong value over it. Unlisted and legacy values are now displayed as-is and round-trip unchanged.

1.2.4 — Navigation & binding improvements

  • Open a component from anywhere in its Java class - the gutter icon only sits on the class declaration, so large files meant scrolling to the top. Now Navigate → Related Symbol (Ctrl+Cmd+Up) lists the component's .wo folder and its .html/.wod/.api/.md, and a new Open TBComponent action (Navigate menu / right-click → Go To, assignable shortcut) opens it from any caret position.
  • Policy accessors no longer warned - $me.can.…, $me.cant.… and $me.raw.… bindings navigate a policy by a runtime key (like $localizer.…) and no longer show a "cannot resolve" warning.
  • Help documentation - clarified the two "migration" features (schema vs EO/data), added a Schema Migration page, and corrected WebObjects-era terminology in the component and API docs.

1.2.3 — Rename Component: Maven layout support

  • Rename Component now works on Maven/Gradle projects - "Rename TreasureBoat Component" previously only recognized the legacy Components/Sources layout and failed with "Could not find project root" on Maven modules. It now locates the .wo (under src/main/webapp) and .java (under src/main/java) in both layouts.

1.2.2 — Marketplace compatibility

  • Internal API removal - Replaced internal IntelliJ Platform APIs (module directory and plugin descriptor lookups) flagged by the Marketplace verifier with public equivalents. No functional changes.
  • Override-only API cleanup - Invoke actions via the platform's public helper instead of calling actionPerformed directly.
  • Future-proof version lookup - Read the plugin version from the bundled build info instead of the plugin-manager API (which recent IDEs mark internal).

1.2 — Session-less AJAX support

  • AJAX tag completion - for the new session-less tags: <tb:updateLink>, <tb:updateField>, <tb:updateSelect>, <tb:updateContainer>
  • Standalone API files - "Create Standalone API File" now works for dynamic elements

1.1 — First public release

  • Component Editor - Unified editing for WOD, HTML, API, and Java files
  • EOModel Editor - Visual editor for Entity-Relationship models with full CRUD support
  • Navigation Configuration Editor - Edit Navigationbar plist files with FaceID support
  • Sangria Rule Support - Sangria rule editing and validation
  • Project Templates - Create new TreasureBoat projects
  • Code Completion - Smart completion for bindings, key paths, and element types
  • Syntax Highlighting - Full support for WOD and plist file formats
  • Framework Support - Navigate and view framework NavigationMenu.plist files

idea-plugin.name: Jolta: Java Version Manager
idea-plugin.description:
The JDK your project asks for, selected for you — in the IDE, the terminal, and CI.

Pin a Java version once with a .java-version file and jolta keeps everything on it. This plugin makes IntelliJ IDEA one of the things that agrees.

  • Nothing to configure. Open a pinned project and the Project SDK, the Gradle JVM, and the Maven importer JDK are already right.
  • Set the version from the IDE. Pick a JDK from the status bar or Tools → Jolta and the pin is written for you — so your teammates, your terminal, and CI land on the same JDK. Don't have it? It downloads.
  • Live. Run jolta pin 25 in any terminal, or pull a teammate's commit, and the IDE follows within seconds. No restart, no re-import.
  • Run configurations too. JAVA_HOME and PATH point at the pinned JDK, so anything your tests shell out to agrees with the IDE.
  • SDK entries that don't rot. jolta upgrade moves a JDK and the SDK entry is repointed — never left dangling for you to clean up by hand.
  • It stays out of unpinned projects. No pin and no jolta default means the plugin leaves your SDK exactly as you set it.

Requires the jolta CLI: brew install OneAppPlatform/tap/jolta (or see the install guide). On macOS and Linux the plugin offers to install it for you.

Windows: the CLI needs a manual install for now — download jolta-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip from the releases page, unzip it, and run .\jolta.exe setup. Setup is first-class on Windows: it adds the shims to your user PATH in the registry and installs the JAVA_HOME hook for PowerShell. Sorry for the extra step — a winget package is submitted and awaiting review, which will make this a one-liner.

Support: free and open source (MIT). Questions, bugs and feature requests go to the issue tracker — that's the fastest way to reach us, and it means the answer helps the next person too.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.0

First release.

  • Opens a pinned project with the Project SDK, Gradle JVM and Maven importer JDK already set — nothing to configure.
  • Set the Java version from the IDE: pick a JDK from the status bar or Tools → Jolta and the .java-version pin is written for you. A version you don't have yet is downloaded.
  • Live: jolta pin 25 in any terminal, or a teammate's commit, and the IDE follows within seconds.
  • JAVA_HOME and PATH point at the pin for Java run configurations, so anything they shell out to agrees with the IDE.
  • SDK entries are repointed after jolta upgrade instead of being left dangling.
  • Offers to pin an unpinned project to the JDK it is already using, and leaves projects jolta doesn't govern completely alone.
  • Reports genuinely broken configuration — a JDK that has gone from disk, or a .java-version and .sdkmanrc that disagree — and stays quiet about differences that are deliberate, such as a Gradle toolchain.
  • Offers to install the jolta CLI if it isn't there.

idea-plugin.name: Async Self-Invocation Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning icon on a call to a Spring @Async method made from another method of the same declaring class -- Spring's own documentation states this bypasses the AOP proxy entirely: "a call to the async-marked method from within the target object is not intercepted... self-invocation... effectively bypasses the proxy and its interceptor chain." The call still compiles and runs -- just synchronously, on the caller's thread, with no error and no warning. JetBrains Ultimate's Spring plugin already has this exact inspection for @Transactional (SpringTransactionalMethodCallsInspection) but not for @Async -- confirmed by inspecting the Spring plugin's own bundled plugin.xml before building this.

100% static PSI analysis -- matches @Async by simple annotation name, not by resolving the real Spring classpath symbol, so it works whether the real Spring jar is on the classpath or not. Java and Kotlin.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only flags an unqualified or this.-qualified call within the exact same class -- a call through an injected self-reference (the @Lazy proxy workaround) is correctly never flagged, since it's qualified by a different expression.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Resilience Self-Invocation Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning icon on a call to a @Retryable (Spring Retry) or @CircuitBreaker/@Retry/ @RateLimiter/@Bulkhead/@TimeLimiter (Resilience4j) method made from another method of the same declaring class. All of these are AOP-proxy-based, the same mechanism as Spring's own @Transactional/ @Cacheable/@Async: self-invocation bypasses the proxy entirely, so the resilience behavior is silently never applied -- no retry, no circuit breaker, no rate limit -- with no error and no warning. Confirmed real: neither Spring Retry nor Resilience4j are covered by JetBrains Ultimate's own Spring plugin (verified by inspecting its bundled plugin.xml, which only registers this check for @Transactional/@Cacheable/ @Async).

100% static PSI analysis -- matches each annotation by simple name, not by resolving the real classpath symbol, so it works whether the real Spring Retry/Resilience4j jars are on the classpath or not. Java and Kotlin.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only flags an unqualified or this.-qualified call within the exact same class -- a call through an injected self-reference is correctly never flagged, since it's qualified by a different expression.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Odoo DevKit
idea-plugin.description:
Odoo-aware code intelligence for PyCharm

Odoo DevKit adds completion, navigation, type inference, and inspections across Python, XML views, QWeb/Owl templates, JavaScript, SQL, and manifest/data files. Every suggestion and navigation target is scoped to your addon's Odoo version and depends graph.

Website | Documentation | Issue tracker

Models, fields & modules

  • Model completion/navigation everywhere a model name appears (_name, _inherit, relational fields, env[...], XML model=/ref=), with an "add to depends" warning outside scope.
  • Field completion/navigation in decorators, domains, related=, _order, vals dicts, and XML, across _inherit and _inherits.
  • Module (addon) name completion in __manifest__.py and navigation to the addon directory.
  • Selection value completion, validation, and navigation, including selection_add across modules.
  • Gutter icons and per-locator navigation for Python _inherit and XML/Owl template inheritance.

Type inference & navigation

  • Recordset typing for self, env[...], relational chains, ORM chain calls, and test helpers (Form, tagged).
  • Go-to-declaration for fields, methods, magic fields, Selection values, and super-method calls, plus hover docs for field declarations.

QWeb & Owl templates

  • HTML5 completion plus the full context-aware t-* directive vocabulary.
  • Python injection with the correct evaluation context everywhere (eval=, context=, domain=, view modifiers, server actions, mail.template).
  • A dedicated Owl expression language for Owl t-* attributes, with completion/navigation into your JS components.
  • An XPath 1.0 evaluator powering view/template inheritance navigation.

JavaScript & Owl components

  • Completion/navigation for registry.category(...), useService(...), ES6 (@addon/path) and legacy odoo.define/require modules.
  • Owl component tag/prop completion and navigation, both-ways JS↔XML template navigation, and typed this.state/this.props/services.
  • Class-like support for Odoo patch(...) and patchWithCleanup(...): completion, navigation, and override gutters for prototype, static, and object patches, including reusable patch factories.
  • Works in both PyCharm editions, limited by PyCharm Community's own, more restricted JavaScript support.

SQL, inspections & file formats

  • PostgreSQL injection for cr.execute(...) and SQL constraints, with Odoo model/field-aware completion and navigation (PyCharm Professional).
  • Inspections for unresolved models/fields, invalid Selection values, and deprecated XML syntax, each aware of your project's Odoo version.
  • .po/.pot, .conf, and CSV data file support.

idea-plugin.name: SpEL Injection Sink Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Flags a Spring ExpressionParser.parseExpression(...) call whose argument is built from an HTTP endpoint parameter -- CWE-917 (Expression Language Injection), the exact mechanism CVE-2022-22963 (Spring Cloud Function) exploited: an attacker's raw input becomes SpEL SOURCE TEXT, re-parsed and evaluated as an expression. Also flags a hardcoded, compile-time-constant expression whose parsed AST references a dangerous T(...) type (Runtime, ProcessBuilder, System).

Built on a real, hand-written SpEL parser -- the second full custom grammar in this catalog (after the ReDoS Catastrophic-Backtracking Companion's own regex grammar), never depending on Spring itself being on the classpath.

Stated honestly: real competitors exist for the general category (CodeQL, batch/CI only, not inline IDE; Datadog Code Security, a JetBrains plugin but one rule among 500+ in an enterprise SAST requiring a Datadog account/subscription; Qodana taint analysis, requires a paid Ultimate Plus license, not Community Edition) -- none is a free, zero-account, Community-Edition-compatible, single-purpose plugin for this exact finding.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

idea-plugin.name: SixExit
idea-plugin.description:
SixExit (beta version) adds WebSquare 5 SP5 support to IntelliJ IDEA. This plugin is intended for developers who build WebSquare web applications primarily in code; it does not provide WYSIWYG design tools. The plugin's language is in Korean.

SixExit (베타 버전)은 IntelliJ IDEA에 웹스퀘어 5 SP5 개발을 지원하는 기능을 추가합니다. 이 플러그인은 주로 코딩으로 웹스퀘어 애플리케이션을 개발하는 분들을 돕기 위한 것이며, 화면을 비주얼하게 디자인하는 WYSIWYG 기능은 제공하지 않습니다.

기능:

화면 UI 코딩 지원

  • 문맥에 맞는 웹스퀘어 컴포넌트·표준 HTML 태그, 속성 이름과 값 제안
  • 태그·속성 빠른 문서 및 잘못된 태그·속성·속성 값과 계층 구조 검증
  • 이벤트와 callback 속성의 함수 제안·생성·빠른 문서·선언으로 이동
  • 웹스퀘어 프로젝트의 파일 경로 완성과 선언으로 이동

자바스크립트 코딩 지원

  • 웹스퀘어 객체의 멤버 완성, 매개변수 정보, 빠른 문서 및 XML 선언으로 이동
  • dataList·dataMap·gridView 등의 컬럼·키·열거형 매개변수 제안, 오류 검사 및 선언으로 이동
  • 웹스퀘어 컨벤션의 공통 스크립트 객체와 <projectCommon> 모듈의 완성, 문서, 선언/사용처 찾기
  • bind() 이벤트·콜백 함수 완성과 이벤트 핸들러 안의 this·매개변수 타입 인식
  • 설정한 공통 코드 CSV 기반의 코드명 인라인 힌트 및 코드/코드명 완성

IDE 기능 확장

  • 구조 도구 창에서 웹스퀘어 개요와 XML 트리를 제공하고, 캐럿 위치 찾기와 데이터 컬럼 사용처 찾기 제공
  • 내비게이션 바에 웹스퀘어 구조 경로 표시

각 기능에 대한 자세한 설명과 동영상 데모는 https://delight4.com/sixexit에서 보실 수 있습니다.

면책 조항. 웹스퀘어는 (주)인스웨이브의 제품입니다. SixExit은 인스웨이브의 공식 승인/제휴 제품이 아닙니다.

idea-plugin.name: z/OS Workbench for Zowe
idea-plugin.description:
Lightweight z/OS Explorer for IntelliJ IDEA powered by Zowe Client Java SDK

Connect seamlessly to IBM z/OS mainframes directly from IntelliJ IDEA to manage Data Sets, Unix System Services (USS) files, JES Jobs, TSO commands, and MVS consoles.

Note: This is an independent community contribution and is not officially affiliated with the Open Mainframe Project or IBM.

Key Features

  • Multi-Connection Profiles: Manage multiple z/OSMF connection profiles with secure credential storage via IntelliJ PasswordSafe.
  • Data Sets & PDS Members: Search data sets with persistent mask history. Browse, create, edit, rename, and delete PDS/PDSE members and Sequential (PS) files.
  • Unix System Services (USS): Full file tree browser with smart sorting (directories first), real-time live filtering (wildcards like *.sh), right-click file/directory CRUD actions, and lenient handling for ASCII control characters.
  • Remote Editor Integration: Edit remote Data Sets and USS text files directly in native IntelliJ editor tabs with automatic syntax highlighting and Ctrl+S writeback. Includes optimistic concurrency protection against remote mainframe changes.
  • JES Job Management: Monitor jobs, view spool outputs, submit JCL data sets, download spool files, with context-aware right-click actions (Cancel active jobs or Purge completed job output).
  • Symbols & Variables: Manage z/OS System Symbols and z/OSMF System Variables with scope filtering, real-time search, and full CRUD operations (Add, Edit, Delete, Rename).
  • Interactive Commands: Stateful TSO terminal session, MVS console commands, and remote USS SSH execution.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
v1.0.1

  • Change Tag (chtag): New USS right-click action to set file tags (ISO8859-1, UTF-8, IBM-1047, IBM-037, binary, remove, or custom code set) via UssChangeTag. Resolves ASCII files displaying as unreadable characters due to z/OSMF assuming untagged files are EBCDIC.
  • Open With Encoding: New USS right-click action to read and edit files using an explicit encoding without altering file tags on z/OS or requiring write permissions. Reopening under a different encoding replaces the stale editor tab cleanly.
  • Persistent USS Path History: Converted USS Path field into an editable dropdown combo box saving up to 20 recently listed directory paths across IDE restarts, complete with delete button and context menu history management.
  • Responsive UI & Component Wrapping: Added custom WrapLayout for toolbars across all tabs (Jobs, Data Sets, USS, Commands, Connection Manager) so control buttons and input fields automatically wrap to new rows when tool window panes or splitters are narrowed.
  • Detail View Line Wrapping & Tree Tooltips: Enabled word wrapping in all detail text areas and added hover tooltips for tree nodes in Jobs, Data Sets, and USS trees when item names are truncated.

v1.0.0 Initial Release

  • USS Enhancements: Live search/filtering, tree node sorting (directories first), right-click file/directory CRUD (Create, Rename, Delete), and lenient JSON parsing for control characters.
  • Data Set Operations: Search data sets with persistent mask history, view ISPF member metadata, and edit remote members with conflict protection.
  • Multi-Profile Manager: Connection profile manager with secure password storage and header profile selector.
  • Jobs & Commands: Real-time JES job monitoring, spool viewer, stateful TSO address space, MVS console, and USS SSH.

idea-plugin.name: JOL Java Object Layout
idea-plugin.description:
Java Object Layout (JOL) is a tool to analyze in memory object layout schemes in JVMs. It allows you to make an estimate how much memory the object takes. This allows to make the simplest but most efficient performance improvements. Just check your DTOs if they fit into 64 bytes of processor's cache line.

For example, in HotSpot VM on 64x processor an empty string "" takes 40 bytes i.e. 24 bytes for String object itself + 16 bytes for an internal empty char array.

idea-plugin.name: Spot Profiler for Java and Kotlin
idea-plugin.description:
Plugin for IntelliJ IDEA which simplifies measuring execution time for selected pieces of code.


Usage
Select target line(s) in a Java or Kotlin (Kotlin plugin version 1.4 or later is required) file, invoke 'Profile Code Fragment' from context menu, and run the code. If code is already executing in a debug session, an attempt to reload corresponding class will be performed automatically (can be disabled in settings).


Details
The plugin wraps the selected lines with the following code (Java example) 


      long start = System.nanoTime();
      ...
      long end = System.nanoTime();
      System.out.println("Location: " + (end - start));
Code isn't modified on disk, but just before passing it to the compiler. This will work only if project is built using IDEA's own build system (it won't work e.g. if the project is built using Gradle). The plugin then collects the printed output and displays it in editor.


Obviously, this approach is not suitable for micro-benchmarking, please use your own judgment on whether it is acceptable for your use case.

idea-plugin.name: Jeffrey Microscope
idea-plugin.description:
Jump from a JFR flame graph straight to your code.

Jeffrey Microscope is the companion IDE plugin for Jeffrey, a tool for analyzing Java Flight Recorder (JFR) recordings and heap dumps. While you explore a flame graph, a heap-dump view, or any other Microscope view, this plugin lets you click a stack frame or a class and land on the exact line of source in your already-open IntelliJ window.

The plugin stays out of your way — no toolbars, no tool windows, and two context-menu actions. It runs quietly in the background and enriches Jeffrey Microscope, letting Microscope discover your open IntelliJ projects and either navigate straight to the matching code or download the sources back into the application directly.

What it does

  • Frame-to-source navigation — resolves a fully-qualified class and method to a file, line, and column, opens it, and brings the IDE window to the front.
  • Inline source — serves source text back to Microscope so it can show code next to the profile, preferring attached sources over decompiled .class files.
  • Frame lookup without the jump — answers where a class and method live so an AI coding agent working through Microscope can ground its findings in real files and lines, without your editor moving while you work.
  • Send a recording for analysis — right-click a JFR recording, a heap dump, or a pprof/OpenTelemetry profile — compressed forms included — and open it straight in Microscope.
  • Recordings you can spot — every file that action accepts is drawn with the Jeffrey flame icon in the project tree and editor tabs, including the formats IntelliJ has no icon for at all.
  • A recording panel in the editor — open a recording and its tab tells you whether Microscope has analysed it, offers the button that does, and lays the views out as tiles: flame graph, allocations, GC, threads, traces and the rest, each with a line on what the page answers. A ready profile also shows its recording window, sample count, event types, sample loss and the auto-analysis findings, each titled by the rule that fired. Views the recording has no data for stay visible but dimmed, and so do a heap dump's views until its index is built. A heap dump whose index is not built yet offers to build it, right there, and shows the build's progress until the figures arrive. Rendered in the IDE's own browser, so it matches your theme and follows it when you switch.
  • Compare two recordings — a before and an after, measured against each other without leaving the IDE. Select two recordings and pick Compare in Microscope, select one while another's panel is open, or choose a baseline from the panel's own menu, which lists this project's recordings with each one's window and sample count. The panel names the baseline, prints its value under each figure, says whether the two are a like-for-like pair, and links out to the differential flame graph with the baseline already selected.
  • Hand it to a coding agent — one button starts Claude Code, Codex or Gemini in a terminal with the profile already identified, so the agent reads it through Microscope rather than trying to parse a JFR it cannot open. It runs whichever agent you used last, and its menu holds the rest — including the ones Jeffrey supports that this machine does not have, so the row stays one button wide however many it learns. With a baseline attached it hands over both profiles, so the agent compares them rather than reading one.
  • Checkout awareness — reports the branch and commit each window is on, so Microscope can warn when a profile describes different code than you have open.
  • Zero configuration — Microscope discovers the IDE automatically over IntelliJ's built-in server; there is nothing to pair or paste.

Private by design

  • Listens on localhost only — never reachable from the network.
  • Honors IntelliJ's trusted projects: untrusted projects are never navigated.
  • Toggle it off anytime under Settings → Tools → Jeffrey Plugin; a disabled IDE is completely invisible to Microscope.

Requires a running Jeffrey Microscope instance. Learn more at jeffrey-analyst.cafe.

idea-plugin.name: Database Navigator
idea-plugin.description:
Database Navigator

A Database Development and Management Tool

Database Navigator is a database development and management plugin for JetBrains IDEs. It brings database connections, object browsing, data editing, SQL and source-code editing, execution, debugging, transaction control, and AI-assisted workflows directly into your IDE.

Explore and edit - Browse schemas, tables, views, procedures, packages, dependencies, metadata, source, and DDL from the integrated Database Browser. Inspect, filter, sort, export, and edit data in rich table editors and result grids with transaction-aware commit and rollback support.

Code and run - Write, execute, compile, and debug SQL, PL/SQL, scripts, DDL files, stored programs, and database Java code from context-aware editors. Use execution history, output consoles, logging, reusable run configurations, session monitoring, and transaction monitoring.

Integrate and automate - Synchronize local DDL files, map project files to database connections, and apply environment-aware safeguards for sensitive targets. Use Database Assistant workflows, Oracle Select AI integration, vector embeddings, semantic search, RAG-assisted querying, and MCP Server Builder for SQL-backed tools.

This product is developed and maintained by Oracle.


Supported Databases
Oracle, MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL, and any JDBC-compliant database (experimental).
