idea-plugin.name: FactoryLine AI Proof
idea-plugin.description:
FactoryLine helps developers verify the evidence behind code changes before review. It challenges whether tests catch failures, checks changes against approved intent and scope, and surfaces stale proof and unresolved risks. Six audit lanes cover stateful workflows, authorization, recovery, API compatibility, migrations, and performance. Graph Ops connects findings to evidence and next steps. Junie support is tuned but optional; AppForge is an optional mobile-evidence module. FactoryLine is local-first, and people retain control of apply, merge, and release. a broken result. Then open Graph Ops to see the next local evidence step.

Tuned for Junie. Not dependent on Junie. FactoryLine gives Junie a progressive local taxonomy—intent, scope, evidence, challenge, and supervised handoff—so an agent can ask the right proof question at the right time. When Junie uses FactoryLine, its handoff can name the exact local proof tools it declared, hash the evidence it cited, and preserve its unknowns beside the diff. You do not need Junie, any AI assistant, or any external account to use FactoryLine: First Proof, Graph Ops, audit lanes, and local review work on their own.

Use your preferred coding agent and analyzer—FactoryLine independently checks the evidence behind a green result. It can prepare local, reviewable facts alongside Junie, Copilot, CodeRabbit, Devin, Qodana, or SonarQube. FactoryLine does not replace, control, contact, or imply endorsement by those products.

New in 0.9.8 — release alignment: the JetBrains adapter now matches the cross-platform FactoryLine bundle while preserving the read-only, human-owned proof boundary for Junie handoffs.

New in 0.9.6 — proof-coupled Junie handoffs and First Lap: start with First Proof, bind the work to sealed intent and forbidden outcomes, challenge the implementation independently, and inspect the exact diff, Oracle Firewall rules, six deep audit lanes, session trace, and hash-bound evidence in Graph Ops. The First Lap command creates plain-language mission, end-to-end journey, and verifier-only holdout files; release-critical verifiers must pass approved/defective/wrong-candidate calibration and one human-observed intake-to-handoff lap before supervised autonomy is considered. Incidents can be promoted into permanent regression gates, and only typed transient provider failures are retryable. Junie contribution cards carry the known tool, changed-file rationale, workspace-local hashes, unknowns, and visible credit line, all checked against the current taxonomy digest. Missing, stale, reordered, duplicated, altered, or wrong-contract evidence stays blocked. IDE and A2A agents receive the same supervised playbook; scope, policy, exceptions, apply, merge, publication, and deployment remain human-owned.

AppForge Mission Control: before an iOS team enters another App Review queue, it can inspect the exact candidate's local evidence story: user design input, storyboard, iPhone/iPad media, accessibility and full-stack checks, SaaS journey, and submission dossier. The tab makes missing proof visible while there is still time to fix it, which can avoid preventable rework and days-long repeat review cycles. It uses credential references rather than raw secrets and may prepare a supervised-agent packet; final TestFlight/App Review authority remains human-owned. It minimizes avoidable rejection risk; it cannot guarantee Apple approval.

SaaS Reality: inspect whether OAuth/OIDC identity, tenant authorization, checkout, webhook, entitlement, feature access, and revocation agree across Clerk, Auth0, Okta, Entra, Cognito, Supabase, Firebase, or another standards-compliant provider. The native status action and Graph Ops view read hash-verified local receipts; they never contact a provider, access credentials, change billing, grant access, deploy, or approve a release.

In 60 seconds: inspect an outcome, fuzzy PRD, or risky diff; challenge whether a test can actually reject the failure it claims to cover; then see the current proof gap before a human decides what may be applied.

Start now: open Tools | FactoryLine | Run First Proof, confirm the workspace, then inspect the local result. Generate an MVP when you need one; a starter is never called production-ready before relevant evidence exists.

Technical information

Runtime: local JVM plugin for the IntelliJ Platform (2025.2 / build 252 baseline), with no hosted service, source upload, API key, or background agent.

Integration: the plugin exposes supervised tool-window actions and read-only local MCP facts for First Proof, Oracle Firewall, Graph Ops, six audit lanes, session traces, and hash-bound receipts. It works with Junie, Codex, Copilot, CodeRabbit, Devin, Qodana, SonarQube, Cursor, and OpenCode, but does not require, control, or impersonate any of them.

Support and feedback: report reproducible issues at GitHub Issues; read the community forum for usage questions and release discussion. These links are the authoritative support channels for this plugin.

What this solves

  • Passing tests that prove nothing: expose missing or stale proof before it turns into a confident-looking review green light.
  • A clear PRD heading toward the wrong build: Intake Grill records a named, byte-bound intent, framework choice, acceptance evidence, and external-effects posture before a mission can require it.
  • AI retries that repeat a failed idea: Proof-Delta requires a changed candidate and fresh hash-bound evidence, or makes the no-gain halt visible instead of consuming another retry.
  • Agent trust that quietly ratchets upward: Earned Autonomy derives an expiry-bound local evidence tier and automatically demotes severe hollow-test or scope-escape findings; it never authenticates an agent or grants permission.
  • Unclear AI or teammate diffs: review the exact local scope, see the declared proof gap, and follow one fact-derived next action.
  • Several tasks in one working tree: review the full diff or focus only the active file, instead of mixing unrelated local changes.
  • AI repair scope can drift or tests can be weakened to get green: copy a sealed Proof Mission into Junie or another AI coding agent, return the actual Change List to independent Proof Review, validate only a candidate patch that stays inside scope, and keep final IDE apply under human control.
  • Large or remote workspaces feel opaque: measure local workspace shape and path-only WSL/remote context, then review generated/dependency directory signals without FactoryLine touching indexes, heap, caches, inspections, or remote settings.
  • The IDE slows down and guesses start replacing facts: record a short local window of aggregate heap, process CPU when available, indexing state, and EDT dispatch delay; compare a structural continuity baseline before deciding whether a project-model change deserves re-analysis.
  • Lost review context: save a hash-bound local JSON, Markdown, and Mermaid handoff packet that another developer can inspect.
  • Automation without control: every command needs confirmation; FactoryLine does not edit, commit, publish, deploy, upload source, or make a release decision.
  • Several plausible repairs: ProofSearch rejects failed proofs, surviving mutants, scope escapes, test weakening, and error suppression, then explains the smallest verified winner in the Graph Ops Counterfactual Arena.

Know what is safe to ship

  • Check changed code: see which proof is invalidated by your current diff.
  • Review the exact local scope: inspect the full current diff or just the active file in a dedicated Proof Review tab, with declared findings and one fact-derived next action.
  • Keep AI suggestions and proof distinct: use the optional GitHub Proof Review workflow beside CodeRabbit or another reviewer for one neutral, commit-bound evidence walkthrough. It does not need a vendor account, ingest AI comments, approve, or merge.
  • Keep an agent inside agreed scope: run the local factory plan verify CLI contract to compare a named human-approved plan with the exact diff and surface Proof Debt. It records obligations; it does not execute tests, approve, merge, or change IDE settings.
  • Make UI design reviewable: add the optional Prestige Design Review for a purpose-led brief and visible checks for hierarchy, responsive behavior, affordances, consistency, and declared design tokens. Its findings inform review; they do not certify accessibility, conversion, or production readiness.
  • Leave a durable local handoff: save the hash-bound review as JSON, Markdown, and Mermaid for a teammate or a later supervised repair attempt.
  • Use AI repair without losing team control: turn a selected Change List into a Scope Passport, bind a textual candidate patch to it, and make the separate verifier and human apply steps explicit.
  • Investigate workspace load safely: use Workspace Advisor for a bounded local measurement and manual review paths; it is not an IDE performance diagnosis and never mutates configuration.
  • Verify receipts: inspect local evidence before a release decision.
  • Measure real savings: compare paired time, token, and cost data without inferred values.
  • Run supervised workflows: assemble features, continue from safe boundaries, inspect durable mission graphs, and route secret-free BYOK policies.
  • Follow the exact evidence path: Unified Graph Ops visualizes local requirements, slices, missions, approvals, completions, proofs, verifier sessions, gates, traces, and artifacts without executing them.
  • Compare repairs without trusting another opinion: inspect every hash-bound candidate, exact rejection reason, mutation result, risk, changed scope, proof runtime, and measured-or-unavailable savings. Apply, merge, publish, and deploy remain locked.
  • Keep generation and grading separate: factory verifier binds independent worker and verifier evidence, immutable checks, and hard budgets. It validates receipts; an external supervised runner must enforce runtime isolation.
  • Clarify a PRD before the build compounds ambiguity: run factory prd grill PRD.md --root . for a capped, source-bound question sheet with answer stubs. It never rewrites the PRD or authorizes implementation.

Use FactoryLine when you want to

  • Turn an outcome into a buildable starting point: create a contained MVP from a plain-language goal, then extend it in your normal IDE workflow.
  • Review AI or teammate changes with evidence: connect requirements, tests, policies, and receipts before deciding what is ready to ship.
  • Recover the next safe step after a change: identify proof that can be reused, proof invalidated by a diff, and the fact-derived action to take next.
  • Make team automation inspectable: run supervised, local-first workflows and record paired time, token, and cost observations only when they are measured.

Local by design

The plugin asks before running a command. It does not upload project files or receipts, store API keys, sign artifacts, or decide whether a release is ready.

Works with IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, Rider, CLion, GoLand, RustRover, and DataGrip from the 2025.2 platform baseline.

Availability

FactoryLine's local proof core is free and open source. Optional paid features are not active in this Marketplace build: there is no checkout, entitlement, source upload, credential storage, signing authority, or automatic release authority.

Read the documentation, inspect the source, and review the license terms.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Make First Proof the front door: check whether an AI-generated test can actually fail before trusting a green result.
  • Connect approved intent, forbidden behavior, exact diff scope, Oracle Firewall rules, independent challenge evidence, session traces, and receipt digests in Graph Ops.
  • Expose six coordinated audit lanes for stateful behavior, tenant isolation, failure and recovery, API compatibility, migration integrity, and performance or resource regression.
  • Give IDE and A2A agents a supervised, fail-closed playbook; agents cannot silently weaken policy, widen scope, approve, merge, publish, or deploy.
  • Bring cumulative enterprise assurance, evidence memory, provider-neutral SaaS proof, and optional AppForge mobile delivery checks into the same local review surface.
  • Add SaaS Reality: one provider-neutral, hash-verified local status for OAuth/OIDC identity, tenant/role authorization, checkout, webhook, entitlement, access, and revocation. Unknowns block green; the plugin never contacts or mutates a provider.
  • Add declared Change Profiles to Engineering Judgment: selected Change Lists can expose a named new change kind, deterministic Senior Attention route, and review-due or successor drift. FactoryLine never infers source semantics or approves a change.
  • Add Guardian Core as the first tool-window tab: it summarizes a bounded, local, in-memory IDE-health sample window and exposes navigation-only review routes. Guardian does not diagnose a cause, rank plugins, change IDE settings, or apply a repair.
  • Add IDE Health Flight Recorder and Index Continuity Guard: bounded in-memory aggregate runtime samples plus explicit local structural baseline/compare evidence. Both are observation-only; neither changes IDE settings, caches, indexes, plugins, project files, or remote state, and neither claims a causal diagnosis or duration prediction.
  • Add Intent Ledger: make the selected native Change List's behavioral promise, non-goal, and negative case visible before code review; surface scope escape, stale proof, and coverage gaps using existing local evidence. Capture is named, exact-confirmed local metadata only; inspection never edits source, changes VCS state, runs a test, starts an agent, or declares production readiness.
  • Add Intake Grill, Proof-Delta, Gauntlet Survival Cards, and Earned Autonomy: bind intent before a mission, prevent evidence-free retry loops, make declared negative checks visible, and keep agent trust expiry-bound. These remain local supervision artifacts; they do not run an agent, authorize a repair, or certify production readiness.
  • Add refreshable local Assembly activity and a read-only Developer Memory Brief in the shared Studio and Graph Ops view: exact-diff next-proof actions, redacted Continuity facts, and observed local Git contribution context, without execution, repair, approval, identity, billing, or productivity authority.
  • Add Graph Forensics: sealed semantic lineage, first-divergence and causal-path analysis, deterministic stale-read/write, parallel-write, and duplicate-side-effect findings, plus a non-executing recovery preview.
  • Add ProofSearch and the Graph Ops Counterfactual Arena: compare 2 through 12 hash-bound repair candidates, reject hollow or unsafe candidates, show every loss reason, and select one deterministic verified winner without applying it.
  • Add full Graph Ops review controls for copying verification commands, exporting the displayed decision, validating winner guardrails, and visibly retaining apply, merge, publication, deployment, credential, and connector authority.
  • Add JetBrains Proof Review: review the full local diff or active file with structured, attention-first evidence, safe changed-file navigation, and an explicit local JSON/Markdown/Mermaid handoff packet.
  • Add Verified Repair Sandbox: select one native Change List, create a hash-bound Scope Passport, and reject textual candidate patches that cross its paths. Candidate generation, independent verification, and IDE patch application remain explicit supervised steps.
  • Add AI Agent Proof Mission: copy a sealed, vendor-neutral working contract into Junie or another coding agent, then route its returned Change List into local Proof Review. The plugin never starts or controls the agent, reads its chat, uploads source, or treats an agent completion claim as approval.
  • Add a dedicated Junie taxonomy and proof-coupled change acknowledgement: FactoryLine is tuned to work with Junie, but Junie is not required. Orient, bind intent and scope, review evidence, challenge risk, and only then hand over a sealed mission. A Junie handoff can now receive a visible, self-declared FactoryLine credit line that validates named tool vocabulary and hashes cited local evidence while retaining unknowns; it is not agent telemetry, a Junie score, proof of private tool calls, or approval. The project pack now exposes a copy-only manifest and an optional read-only factoryline-proof subagent with an explicit tool allowlist; installation remains conflict-safe and confirmation-gated. The optional enterprise, AppForge, SaaS, and delivery routes remain separate from ordinary code review.
  • Add Workspace Load Advisor + Remote/WSL Preflight: bounded local filesystem measurements, generated/dependency directory signals, path-only context, and optional local JSON/Markdown/Mermaid reports without IDE or remote mutation.
  • Add the Verifier Plane: hash-bound worker and independent-verifier receipts, deterministic no-progress review, and a visible Graph Ops verifier lane.
  • Add a concise use-case guide for MVP creation, evidence review, safe proof reuse, and supervised team automation.
  • Add Unified Graph Ops: a local, read-only visual map with one fact-derived next action.
  • Add PRD Grill: a deterministic, source-bound question frontier before PRD optimization, compilation, or scaffolding.
  • Add optional GitHub Proof Review delivery: a neutral, commit-bound local evidence walkthrough that can coexist with CodeRabbit or another AI reviewer without importing vendor credentials or comments as proof.
  • Add Plan-to-Proof Review: a strict, human-approved agent-plan envelope, exact diff alignment, named deep-review routing, and explicit Proof Debt through the local CLI and PR evidence surface.
  • Clarify the optional Prestige Design Review lane for UI-scoped work and its review-only boundary.
  • Add Run First Proof for a zero-configuration local setup check.
  • Clarify the Marketplace name, preview, getting-started flow, and privacy boundary.
  • Keep the stable plugin ID and verified compatibility across eight JetBrains IDEs.

idea-plugin.name: react-a11y
idea-plugin.description:
Inline WCAG 2.2 accessibility diagnostics and quick fixes for React and React Native, powered by react-a11y.

  • Live diagnostics as you type, with WCAG success criteria and severity on every issue
  • Quick fixes for mechanical problems (misspelled accessibility props, and more)
  • "Fix all" intention for everything auto-fixable in a file
  • Tools → react-a11y: Scan Project runs the project-wide checks (cross-file label resolution, Expo config) and lists results in a console with clickable locations
  • Auto-detects React Native/Expo projects and switches rule packs; respects react-a11y.config.json ignore globs and rule settings

The web rule pack covers what eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y does not (WCAG 2.2 criteria, structure, focus visibility, project-wide checks) — run both for full coverage. Requires Node.js 20+ on your machine. The version-pinned react-a11y CLI ships inside the plugin, and the plugin does not start external processes until the IDE marks the project as trusted.

idea-plugin.name: xslint for XSL/XSLT
idea-plugin.description:
xslint brings XSL/XSLT linting to your JetBrains IDE. As you edit any .xsl or .xslt file, it flags problems inline —
malformed XML, XPath expressions that don't compile, and stylistic, semantic, and logical mistakes — each pinpointed to
its exact line and column, with a quick-fix where the correction is unambiguous.

It's powered by xslint, a dedicated XSL linter running as a language server, so the diagnostics you see in the editor
are exactly the ones the xslint command line and the VS Code extension produce — one engine, everywhere.

idea-plugin.name: Test-Only Declaration Detector
idea-plugin.description:
Reports production Java declarations whose every caller lives in a test source root — production API kept alive only by the tests that assert on it. Such a declaration inflates the public surface, blocks refactoring, and still counts as covered in coverage reports.

Methods, fields and whole classes are reported. When a class turns out to exist only for the tests, it is reported once as a class rather than once per member, so the finding that matters — delete the file — is not buried under its own methods.

Each finding offers a quick fix that annotates the declaration as test-facing (@TestOnly, either @VisibleForTesting), which both silences this inspection and switches on the built-in Test-only usage in production code so production can no longer call it. Only annotations that resolve on the module's classpath are offered.

Why not just use Unused declaration?

IntelliJ can already compute this, via Unused declaration → Entry points → "When entry points are in test sources, mark callees as: unused". But that option works by stripping entry-point status from everything in a test source root, so your @Test methods are reported as unused too, with the identical "never used" message. The distinction is computed and then discarded. It is also a profile-wide setting shared with the on-the-fly unused-symbol inspection, so enabling it changes the daily editor experience.

This plugin reports the same finding as its own category, with its own severity and suppression id, leaving Unused declaration untouched.

What is excluded

  • Declarations with no callers at all — that is plain dead code, and Unused declaration's job.
  • Framework entry points, resolved through the platform's own registered entry points and your Settings | Editor | Inspections | Entry points configuration — so Spring @Bean, @KafkaListener, @Scheduled and @EventListener methods, JPA no-arg constructors and Jackson accessors are left alone.
  • Constructors, main, record accessors, and methods overriding library declarations.
  • Enum constants and record components, whose only source reference can legitimately be the test that names them while production reaches them through valueOf, a deserializer or a column mapping.
  • Nested, local and anonymous classes. Only top-level classes are reported, because a reference from the outer class is internal to the file but external to the nested one, and the plugin will not guess which reading you meant.
  • Declarations carrying an annotation from an editable list, seeded with @TestOnly, both @VisibleForTesting variants, and generated-code markers (@Generated, @AvroGenerated). Add your own team's conventions, or remove entries to report annotated declarations anyway.

Each finding is confirmed against the index before it is reported, so a reference from Spring XML, SpEL, a .properties file or javadoc suppresses it.

How to run it

  • Enable Declaration used only from test code in Settings | Editor | Inspections — it is off by default. Class and field reporting can be switched off there separately, leaving methods only.
  • Run Analyze | Inspect Code with test sources included in the scope. Without them, a test-only declaration is indistinguishable from a fully dead one, and the inspection refuses to guess.
  • This is a global inspection: it runs only via Inspect Code and will never highlight as you type.

Source, documentation and a worked example of every case: GitHub. MIT licensed.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.3.2
  • Renamed the plugin to Test-Only Declaration Detector, since it no longer reports only methods. The plugin id is unchanged, so this arrives as an ordinary update.
0.3.1
  • Reports fields and whole classes used only from test code, not just methods. A class that exists only for the tests is reported once, and its own methods and fields are not reported underneath it.
  • A class counts as used only when something outside it refers to it or to anything it declares — a static factory returning its own type no longer keeps it alive. Only top-level classes are considered.
  • New quick fix: annotate the declaration as test-facing. Offered only for annotations that resolve on the module's classpath and whose @Target permits that kind of declaration, so the fix can never leave the file uncompilable.
  • Class and field reporting can each be switched off in the inspection settings.
  • An annotation on any enclosing class now suppresses reporting, not only on the immediately containing one.
  • Renamed to Declaration used only from test code. The suppression id and profile key are unchanged, so existing settings carry over.
0.1.0
  • Initial release.
  • Reports production Java methods whose every caller lives in a test source root.
  • Excludes framework entry points, constructors, main, record accessors and methods overriding library declarations.
  • Confirms each finding against the index, so references from Spring XML, SpEL, properties files and javadoc suppress the report.
  • Editable list of annotations that suppress reporting, on the method or its class. Seeded with @TestOnly and both @VisibleForTesting variants, plus generated-code markers (@Generated, @AvroGenerated).

idea-plugin.name: Review Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Local, rule-based code review hints for Java and Kotlin — no account, no rate limit, no cloud call. Flags overly long functions, deeply nested conditionals, method-parameter dereferences with no preceding null check (Java; parameters declared @NotNull/@NonNull or of a primitive type are skipped), and TODO/FIXME comment density — every check configurable, every threshold adjustable, nothing ever requires signing in.

100% local: every rule runs against the code already open in the editor, on the platform's own background highlighting pass — never blocking, never phoning home.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no popups, no account required for any feature.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • A parameter declared non-null (@NotNull, @NonNull or @Nonnull, any package) was reported as dereferenced without a null check.
  • A reversed null check (if (null != customer)) was not recognized as a guard, so the dereference it protects was reported.

idea-plugin.name: SearchDeadCode
idea-plugin.description:
Finds dead Kotlin and Java code in Android projects and helps you delete it safely.

The plugin drives the searchdeadcode command-line analyzer. Run a scan from the Tools menu, review the findings in the editor (dead declarations are greyed out, with the detector id and a link to its documentation) and in the SearchDeadCode tool window, then act on each one:

  • Delete the declaration when the analyzer provides a safe whole-line fix
  • Ignore it in place with a mandatory reason (// deadcode:ignore(...))
  • Add it to the team baseline (.deadcode-baseline.json, the same file the CLI's CI profile picks up)

The analyzer binary is not bundled. The plugin looks for it on PATH (Homebrew, cargo, scoop and winget installs are found automatically) or offers to download the release matching the plugin version from GitHub, verified against its published SHA-256 checksum. Findings always come from the files on disk: the plugin saves your open documents before scanning and drops a file's findings the moment you edit it, so a stale line number can never delete the wrong code.
idea-plugin.change-notes: Tracks searchdeadcode 0.21.0 — one version across every channel. See the changelog for what changed in the analyzer.

idea-plugin.name: OpenUnderstand Metrics
idea-plugin.description:
Java source metrics (Cyclomatic, CountLine, MaxNesting, CountDeclMethod, PercentLackOfCohesion, CountClassCoupled) from OpenUnderstand, an open-source implementation of the SciTools Understand API.

Requires python3 3.9+ on the path. The analyser ships with the plugin and installs itself into a virtualenv of its own the first time you press Analyse Project; nothing to configure.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.5.0
  • References agree with Understand at 0.9 or better everywhere. On thirteen Java projects, every reference kind, every entity kind and every project scores precision, recall and F1 of at least 0.9 against SciTools Understand. Before, 19 reference kinds were below that, among them calls (0.80 on the JSON benchmark, now 0.997).
  • Calls on inherited methods and fields, on statically imported members, and on elements of generic JDK containers (queue.peek().next()) now resolve, so the References view and the coupling and fan metrics see them.
  • Overloaded methods keep their own parameters and locals, so the Symbol Table lists one entry per declaration, as Understand does.
  • Metric macro F1 on the JSON benchmark 0.984 to 0.986, no metric below 0.9.
  • Ships analyser 0.6.0. The bundled virtualenv is keyed on the analyser version, so the first Analyse Project after updating builds a fresh one.
0.4.0
  • Java 9 to 25. Records, sealed types and permits, pattern matching for instanceof and switch, record patterns, switch expressions and yield, var, text blocks, local enums and interfaces, and module-info.java are parsed and analysed the way Understand analyses them. Before, a file using any of them failed to parse and showed no metrics at all.
  • On a Java 25 project (jenetics' incubator module) metric macro F1 against Understand went from 0.859 to 0.934, and no metric scores lower than before.
  • On Java 8 code nothing got worse and several metrics improved: on the JSON benchmark CountLineCode 0.964 to 0.994, CountDeclMethodPublic 0.955 to 0.982, and PercentLackOfCohesion 0.912 to 0.980.
  • Symbol Table and References buttons. The first lists every declared entity with its kind, type, parent and location; the second lists every reference to or from the selected entity, so selecting a row and pressing it again walks the graph.
  • Not supported: Java 25 compact source files (a method with no class around it).
  • Ships analyser 0.5.0. The bundled virtualenv is keyed on the analyser version, so the first Analyse Project after updating builds a fresh one.
0.3.0
  • Every metric in the tool window now agrees with SciTools Understand at F1 0.90 or better, measured over all 67 names on the JSON benchmark. The lowest was 0.500. Macro F1 is 0.970 and no metric fails to answer.
  • Largest movements: CountDeclClass 0.500 to 1.000, CountClassCoupled 0.585 to 0.906, CountOutput 0.655 to 0.916, CountInput 0.794 to 0.935, and CountClassBase and CountClassDerived to 1.000.
  • Anonymous classes and lambdas are entities of their own now, so they appear in the table with their own metrics instead of folding their contents into the enclosing method.
  • Ships analyser 0.4.0. The bundled virtualenv is keyed on the analyser version, so the first Analyse Project after updating builds a fresh one.
0.1.2
  • Fixed: the plugin icon was not well-formed XML. A double hyphen inside an XML comment ends the document for a strict parser, so the icon shipped in 0.1.1 failed to load.
  • Ships a newer build of the analyser.
0.1.1
  • Compatibility. Requires 2025.1 or later. 0.1.0 declared 2024.2+ but was built against 2025.1, and was binary incompatible with 2024.2 and 2024.3 -- it called a FileSaverDescriptor constructor that is a varargs one on those builds. Verified against 2025.1 through 2026.2.
  • Fixed: the analysis could fail with 'openunderstand' is not a package. The dumper was written to the shared temp directory, and Python puts a script's own directory first on its path, so a file left there by an earlier run shadowed the analyser. It is unpacked into a private directory now.
  • No interpreter to configure. The Python... button and the search of the machine are gone. The plugin builds a virtualenv of its own with python3 and installs the analyser it ships with, once, on the first Analyse Project.
  • Fixed: numeric columns sorted as text -- 10 came before 2 -- because the table reported every column as untyped. Double-clicking a row now only navigates, instead of also opening the cell for editing.
  • Metrics: CountDeclMethodProtected and CountDeclMethodDefault counted methods by matching the class name against the method's own name, so most classes reported 0. Both now agree with Understand (F1 1.000 and 0.949 on the JSON benchmark).

idea-plugin.name: CrateScope
idea-plugin.description:
CrateScope answers the questions a Rust workspace raises and the command line answers slowly: why a crate resolved to two versions, what cargo update would change before you run it, which dependency set your minimum Rust version, and which of your crates carries a published security advisory. It reads cargo metadata — the same resolution cargo itself uses — so nothing it shows can drift from what actually builds, and it works in RustRover, CLion and IntelliJ IDEA alike, Community included.

What cargo update would do, before you run it. Nobody runs it confidently; it can move forty crates and nothing says which until afterwards. CrateScope reads cargo's own index cache — no network request, nothing about your project sent anywhere — and reports what moves, what crosses a compatibility boundary, whether your Rust floor rises, which duplicates appear or heal, and which releases exist that no requirement in your workspace allows. That last one is how projects end up years behind without anyone noticing.

The Rust version you actually need. An MSRV rises when a routine update pulls in something newer, and the usual way to find out is a CI job failing on a toolchain that worked yesterday. CrateScope names your floor and every crate that sets it.

Security advisories, from the database you already have. If you have ever run cargo audit, CrateScope reads the advisory database it keeps and matches it against your resolved graph, separating real vulnerabilities from unmaintained and unsound notices. It downloads nothing.

Dependencies nothing references. Declared crates with no reference anywhere in a member's sources, reported as a question rather than a verdict — without a Rust parser a crate used only through a derive macro looks identical to one that is dead, so it never offers to delete anything.

Underneath all of it are two live views of the same resolution: a tree that opens instantly on large workspaces and a layered graph you can pan, zoom and click through, sharing one selection and one inspector. Select a crate to see every path from a workspace member down to it, shortest first — the cargo tree -i answer without leaving the editor — while its dependents, its subtree and its duplicate siblings light up and everything else dims. The feature inspector shows which dependent enabled each Cargo feature, usually the real reason a crate forked in the first place.

The Insights tab adds the reports that are awkward to get from a terminal: dependency cost, showing how many crates each line in your Cargo.toml uniquely accounts for; default features that pull in crates nothing needs, with the count that would actually leave your graph; crates several workspace members declare identically, which belong once at the root; a licence audit with copyleft and undeclared licences flagged; attribution export for everything you ship; the longest dependency chain that bounds how far your build can parallelise; and per-crate compile times from cargo build --timings, which can be overlaid on the graph as heat.

Everything here is free. CrateScope needs only cargo on your PATH, ships with zero third-party libraries, exports to SVG and Graphviz DOT, refreshes whenever Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock changes, and is available in English, 日本語, 한국어 and 简体中文. Your dependency data never leaves your machine.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Everything in this release is free, with no limits. Nothing in CrateScope is metered today, and installing 2026.2.0 changes nothing about what you can do.

What does change is the listing: CrateScope is now registered as freemium, so the IDE shows a Paid tag and a purchase option. This is the release that tells you what will eventually sit behind it, because finding out afterwards is the part that would be unfair. Planned to become metered — the focus filter, the full cargo update breakdown, policy checks, bulk deduplication and the notices export. Nothing switches on quietly: CrateScope will tell you inside the IDE before any of it starts counting, and the Features section of Settings > Tools > CrateScope always lists every feature's current terms.

Two things will not change. Everything released in 2026.1.1 stays free permanently, and diagnosis is always free — seeing which crate forked, what your Rust floor is, which advisories apply, or what an update would do will never cost anything. Only the automatic edits and the deeper reports are candidates.

Added

  • Security advisories — RustSec advisories affecting the crates you resolve, vulnerabilities separated from unmaintained and unsound notices. Reads the database cargo audit keeps locally; downloads nothing.
  • Rust version — the MSRV your workspace actually needs, and which crates set it. Crates declaring none are counted rather than assumed harmless.
  • Available updates — what cargo update would do before you run it: what moves, what crosses a compatibility boundary, whether your Rust floor rises, which duplicates appear or heal, and which releases no requirement here allows. Read from cargo's own index cache, so no network request is made.
  • Duplicate advisor — why a crate resolved twice, which declaration holds the old copy, and a one-click fix when it is a manifest you own.
  • Default-feature trim — dependencies whose defaults pull in crates nothing needs, listed only where turning them off would genuinely remove something.
  • Workspace hoist — crates several members declare identically, moved to [workspace.dependencies] in a single undo across every file.
  • Possibly unreferenced — declared dependencies with no reference found in a member's sources. Reported as a question, never as a verdict, and never wired to a delete.
  • Policy check — a committed cratescope-policy.json of MSRV, licence, duplicate and crate-count rules, with every violation naming the crates responsible.
  • Third-party notices — attribution for every crate you ship, as Markdown.
  • Release notes — opened once, the first time the IDE starts after an upgrade.

Changed

  • The focused tree now shows every crate the focused graph shows. An ancestor whose route to a workspace member was cut by the depth limit used to be drawn in one view and missing from the other.
  • Settings gained a Features section listing every feature and its terms, and a Network section with one switch for the configuration check and one for release announcements. The check is the plugin's only request of its own, made at most once an hour and only while the tool window is open; your dependency data is never part of it.

Fixed

  • cargo update previews no longer offer pre-release versions. A 1.0.0-alpha is not a release cargo would resolve to, and reporting it as one sent people chasing an alpha.
  • Occasional announcements — a new release, or what a licence includes — shown once each, with their own off switch.

idea-plugin.name: Airflow DAG Lint
idea-plugin.description:
Catches Apache Airflow DAG mistakes in the editor, instead of letting them surface in the scheduler.

What it finds

  • Airflow 3 migration breakage — imports that were moved or removed, such as airflow.operators.python_operator, airflow.operators.dummy_operator, airflow.contrib.*, airflow.utils.dates and SubDagOperator, each reported with its replacement.
  • Removed arguments — schedule_interval, provide_context, full_filepath.
  • Duplicate task_id — Airflow refuses to load a DAG whose tasks share an id.
  • Invalid schedules — malformed cron expressions, out-of-range fields, bad step values, and presets that do not exist.

Only files that actually look like DAGs are analysed, so it stays quiet in the rest of your project. Everything runs locally and nothing is uploaded.

idea-plugin.name: Secret Guard
idea-plugin.description:
Catches hardcoded API keys, tokens and private keys while you type, before they ever reach a commit.

Detects credentials from AWS, GitHub, Google, Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, Slack, SendGrid and npm, plus private key blocks, JSON Web Tokens, database URLs with inline passwords, and generic hardcoded secrets identified by entropy analysis.

Works on every file type — Java, Kotlin, Python, YAML, JSON, Terraform, shell scripts and more — so it covers all JetBrains IDEs.

Built to keep quiet: placeholders such as your_api_key, ${ENV_VAR} and redacted values are ignored, and low-entropy strings are filtered out. Nothing is uploaded anywhere; all analysis runs locally.

idea-plugin.name: Secrets Leak Detector
idea-plugin.description:
Secrets Leak Detector scans your files and flags hardcoded secrets — API keys, tokens, and private keys — directly in the editor, before they end up in a commit.

What it detects

  • AWS access and secret keys
  • GitHub personal access tokens
  • Slack tokens
  • Google Cloud API keys and service account private keys
  • Stripe live secret/restricted keys
  • JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
  • Database connection strings with a plaintext password (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis)
  • RSA/EC/OpenSSH private keys
  • Generic API keys and access tokens, using keyword matching and entropy analysis

The inspection runs on all text files, not just source code — so secrets hiding in .env, .yml, .properties, and other config files are caught too.

One-click fix

Each detected secret comes with a quick fix (Alt+Enter) to instantly redact it with a placeholder value.

Low noise

Placeholder values, repeated-character strings, and low-entropy matches are filtered out, and files under node_modules, build, .git, and other VCS-ignored paths are skipped.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Initial secret detection inspection (SecretLeakInspection), applied to all text files
  • Detection for AWS access/secret keys, GitHub tokens, Slack tokens, RSA/EC/OpenSSH private keys, and generic API keys/access tokens
  • Detection for Google Cloud API keys, Google service account private keys, Stripe live secret keys, JWTs, and database connection strings with plaintext passwords
  • "Replace with placeholder" quick fix to redact a detected secret in one click
  • False-positive reduction: placeholder value filtering, repeated-character detection, and Shannon entropy analysis on generic API key matches
  • Path-based exclusions (node_modules, build, .gradle, .git, .idea, dist, out) and VCS-ignored file exclusion
  • Plugin icon (light and dark theme variants)
  • Unit test suite covering detection, quick fix, and false-positive filtering

Removed

  • Template scaffold sample code (tool window, startup activity, sample project service)

idea-plugin.name: Nuxty - Nuxt.js Support
idea-plugin.description:
Enhanced Nuxt.js support for IntelliJ-based IDEs.

Features:

  • Route auto-completion and navigation
  • Project creation wizard
  • Nuxt 3 file-based routing, dynamic segments included
  • Route inspection and quick fixes
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • The plugin has its own icon in the plugin manager and on the Marketplace. The previous build showed the generic SDK logo.

idea-plugin.name: Secret & Card Leak Guard
idea-plugin.description:
Secret & Card Leak Guard — catch real PII before it hits a commit

A background inspection that scans every file — code, fixtures, .env, JSON, logs — for values that look like a real card number, IBAN, or US Social Security Number, and tells them apart from safe test data the same way a payment gateway or the SSA itself does.

  • Card numbers — Luhn-valid, but the BIN is not one of the well-known payment-gateway test ranges (the same ranges Kassi Test Data generates from).
  • IBAN — passes the ISO 7064 mod-97 check, but isn't one of Kassi's own reserved test IBANs.
  • US SSN — structurally issuable (area/group/serial outside the SSA's never-issued ranges), so it could plausibly be assigned to a real person.
  • Secrets — an AWS access key ID (AKIA…), a JWT, or a PEM private-key block — high-precision patterns that shouldn't sit in a repo.

Financial/PII findings offer a one-click replace with a synthetic, checksum-valid equivalent from a reserved test range (so re-scanning never re-flags the fix); secrets offer a redact fix.

CI mode: a headless runner scans your files outside the IDE and writes a SARIF 2.1.0 report with a line-independent baseline (only new findings fail), so the same check can gate a commit or pull request. The matched secret is never written to the report.

100% offline and algorithmic. Zero network calls, zero data collection, nothing ever leaves your IDE.

More Kassi tools for QA & fintech: Kassi Test Data — generate valid IBANs, cards, BIC/SWIFT, VAT and national IDs; and Checksum & Regex Playground.

Source, issues & docs: github.com/VadimToptunov/kassi-plugins
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0

  • More detectors: AWS access key ID, JWT, and PEM private-key blocks — high-precision secret patterns, each with a one-click redact fix.

1.0.0

  • Initial release: whole-file inspection for real-looking card numbers, IBANs and US SSNs, with a one-click "replace with synthetic test data" quick-fix.
  • All detection/classification logic reuses the shared, tested :engine module.

idea-plugin.name: Go Language Helper
idea-plugin.description:
Go support for JetBrains IDEs that do not ship it, such as PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA Community, WebStorm, PhpStorm and RubyMine.

Installation

  1. Install this plugin and restart the IDE.
  2. Open a Go file. If gopls is missing, a banner offers to install it. Click Install gopls and wait for it to finish.

That is all. A local Go toolchain is required, from go.dev/dl, because gopls is installed and run with the go command.

Editing

  • Recognises .go, go.mod and go.work files, each with its own syntax highlighting, colour scheme page, comment toggling, brace matching and quote handling.

Code intelligence

Provided by the official gopls language server:

  • Completion, including symbols from packages you have not imported yet
  • Diagnostics as you type, with quick fixes
  • Hover documentation and inlay hints for inferred types and parameter names
  • Go to definition, find usages, call hierarchy and type hierarchy
  • Rename, formatting, folding, signature help and the structure view

Running Go

  • Run configurations for go run, go build, go test and go vet
  • Gutter icons next to func main() and next to each test, benchmark, fuzz target and example

Toolchain

  • Finds go and gopls the way a terminal would, including the common install locations that are missing from an IDE started from a shortcut
  • Offers to install gopls for you when it is not there

Scope

This is a basic Go helper. It is not intended to duplicate GoLand, and it does not try to. Everything here is syntax highlighting plus whatever gopls can answer over the Language Server Protocol, so features that need a full Go compiler front end inside the IDE are simply absent: refactorings beyond rename, debugging, profiling, coverage, framework support, and the deeper inspections and code generation that GoLand provides.

If you write Go seriously, or want any of the above, consider buying GoLand from JetBrains. This plugin exists for the times you are already living in another IDE and want to read and edit some Go without switching.

Compatibility

Works in any JetBrains IDE from build 251 (2025.1) onwards: PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA Community, WebStorm, PhpStorm, RubyMine, CLion, Rider, DataGrip and Android Studio.

Not for GoLand, which ships JetBrains' own Go support, and not for any IDE where the official Go plugin is installed, such as IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate with that plugin added. Both claim .go files, so the IDE refuses to enable them together. Where the official plugin is available, it is the better tool and you should use it.

Details

  • This plugin needs LSP4IJ, which carries the Language Server Protocol client. Installing from the Marketplace pulls it in automatically, so there is nothing to do. Installing from disk does not, so install LSP4IJ first in that case.
  • Settings live under Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Go. Discovery covers the usual setups, so in most cases there is nothing to change. The panel is there for an unusual install location, extra gopls flags, staticcheck and gofumpt, inlay hints, and a raw JSON box for any gopls option without a checkbox.
  • Server errors are written to View | Tool Windows | LSP Consoles rather than raised as notifications, because gopls reports an error for any file it has no package metadata for, and the standard library's builtin.go is permanently one of those.

idea-plugin.name: Pacmon
idea-plugin.description:
Your dependency manifest says what you depend on. Pacmon adds why.

Every dependency gets a short note: why it is here, what must not change, what to check before an upgrade. The note shows in package.json, Cargo.toml, Maven pom.xml, a Gradle build file, mix.exs, gleam.toml, build.zig.zon, pyproject.toml, a pip requirements file, a .NET project file, Gemfile, a gemspec, Directory.Packages.props, or go.mod as quick documentation, and you write it from there.

Notes are plain Markdown under .pacmon/, separated by ecosystem. No database, no service, no account: files that you read, diff and commit like any other. AI coding agents read the same files before they touch a package.

  • Five ways into a note from a dependency manifest, each one you turn on or off: a mark at the dependency declaration — filled when it has a note, hollow when it does not — Ctrl+click on the name itself, a clickable line above the dependency, the words at the end of the line, and a lightbulb on the caret line. The first line of the note shows at the end of the line; the whole note shows as quick documentation.
  • Write a note from the manifest in the Pacmon tool window or in a popup over the line, with a layer for people and a layer for agents.
  • Documentation Coverage lists which dependencies have a note and which do not.
  • Problems in the notes file are underlined as you write, and Format DEPENDENCY-NOTES.md rewrites the file into canonical form.
  • Set Up AI Instructions writes the rules for AI coding agents to .pacmon/AGENT-RULES.md and points AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and similar files to it.

Pacmon reads and writes files in your project and makes no network requests; it does not call any AI service. The VS Code extension reads the same files, and the format is documented at pacmon.dev/format.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Pacmon supports Ruby projects in VS Code and JetBrains/RubyMine. Literal gems in Gemfile, gems.rb and *.gemspec get markers, hover, note editing and shared coverage backed by .pacmon/ruby/DEPENDENCY-NOTES.md. Groups, platforms, runtime dependencies and development dependencies retain their scopes. Parsing is static: Pacmon never runs Ruby, Bundler or RubyGems, and ignores dynamic declarations, eval_gemfile, Gemfile.lock and transitive gems.

  • Pacmon supports PHP/Composer projects in VS Code. Package and platform requirements in the root require and require-dev objects of composer.json get markers, hover, note editing and coverage backed by .pacmon/composer/DEPENDENCY-NOTES.md. Parsing is static: Pacmon never runs PHP or Composer, and ignores other package-link fields, composer.lock and transitive packages.

  • Pacmon supports C/C++ projects that use vcpkg or Conan in VS Code. Dependencies in the root dependencies array and the features.<name>.dependencies arrays of vcpkg.json, in the requires, tool_requires, test_requires and build_requires sections of conanfile.txt, and in the literal requirement fields and self.* calls of conanfile.py get markers, hover, note editing and coverage backed by .pacmon/vcpkg/DEPENDENCY-NOTES.md and .pacmon/conan/DEPENDENCY-NOTES.md. vcpkg host dependencies keep a scope of their own. Parsing is static: Pacmon never runs vcpkg, Conan or the recipe's Python code, and ignores overrides, baselines, dynamic expressions, lockfiles and transitive packages.

  • The VS Code and Open VSX pages describe dependency review and allowlisting. Like the Visual Studio Marketplace page, they say that a notes file can be the allowlist of the packages a project has reviewed and accepted, with their risk, runtime, exposure and advisory log, and that a dependency without a note is shown, not blocked. The README also says which editors add the pointer to agent instruction files.

  • The JetBrains Marketplace page links to https://pacmon.dev, as the VS Code, Open VSX and Visual Studio Marketplace pages already do.

  • JetBrains IDEs write the same agent pointer as VS Code. The three lines Set Up AI Instructions adds to AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and the other instruction files now name the Ruby, .NET/NuGet, vcpkg, Conan and PHP/Composer notes files too.

The formatter runs in a process of its own, on the IDE's runtime, so the project SDK can be any version. A project that applies the dev.openjavaformat.java-format Gradle plugin takes the formatter version from the build; every other project uses the version bundled with this plugin.

idea-plugin.name: Duke Engine
idea-plugin.description:
Editor support for the files that hold a Duke Engine game's content: its .duke data files — its world, its maps, units, projectiles, effects, sounds. Duke Engine is a deterministic Java game engine; what a block may hold is read from the game's own records, so the plugin knows no particular game.

.duke files

  • Highlighting for block words, End, keys, values, numbers, strings, [a, b] lists and ; comments; brace matching and line comments
  • Every line of a block names a field of its class: Geometry = Cylinder with its fields under it, Modules = [ a block for each ], Armor for a map
  • Ctrl+Click from a key to the record component it fills, and from a class — a block's word or the class after = — to the Java class it is read as: Monster to its record, MoveUpdate to the module class, Cylinder to the shape
  • Keys and maps completed from the record the block is; after =, the classes the field may be, enum constants, Yes/No and asset paths; inside a list of records, the records it holds
  • Links between blocks, as the records mark them: Animations = Humanoid completed from the blocks there are, opened by Ctrl+Click and checked; clip names completed from the model and animation files a unit is drawn from, read out of the files themselves
  • Checked as the engine reads them: an unknown block or key, a value its type cannot read, a list where one value goes, a key written twice, a block with no End — each said in the engine's own words
  • A header written Monster Brute is fixed to Monster with Name = Brute inside
  • Asset and data paths, each written whole from the resource root, completed, checked with exact letter case, and opened by Ctrl+Click
  • Renaming a module class, a record component or an enum constant renames it in the data files
  • Folding for every block and every list over several lines, and a structure view of the blocks

A new game

  • File → New → Project → Duke Game writes a game that already runs: two units, a light and a camera as .duke blocks, a couple of the kit's effects with a unit wearing one, a Main that opens the 3D client, and a test that loads the whole thing headless

Duke Inspector

  • The block under the caret as a form, drawn from its record: every field with its default, grouped as the record groups them, each edited the way its type is — a number, Yes or No, a choice, a file, a link to another block, an animation clip, a colour, a nested record, a list of modules as cards — and its Javadoc as help
  • Every change is a line in the file: a default set is a line written, a reset is the line taken out, and Ctrl+Z takes back either
  • New from a template: a file with the record's own fields, listed in the game's file list
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • The model and HUD previews opened on nothing and logged NoClassDefFoundError: com/intellij/ui/jcef/JBCefApp on 2026.1 and newer, where JCEF is a plugin of its own rather than part of the platform. The plugin never said it needed one, so JBCefApp.isSupported() — the check written to answer "is there a browser" — threw before it could be asked.
  • A link to a block that ships inside a library read as a link to nothing. Effect = EmberEyes, and every other reference to the kit, was marked unknown for any game that takes the engine from a repository rather than from a checkout beside it: the kit's effects are .duke files inside uz.duke-engine:kit, and only the project was searched. Libraries are searched too now.

Changed

  • A new plugin icon.

idea-plugin.name: Fluxora Modulith
idea-plugin.description:
Spring Modulith architecture analysis for IntelliJ IDEA.

Fluxora Modulith helps Java and Spring developers understand, visualize, and enforce modular application boundaries directly inside IntelliJ IDEA.

Designed for projects using Spring Modulith concepts, Fluxora Modulith analyzes your project's package structure, module dependencies, @ApplicationModule configuration, allowedDependencies, named interfaces, and architectural boundaries.

Features

  • Spring Modulith module detection — Discover application modules from the current project structure.
  • Module dependency analysis — Detect dependencies between recognized application modules.
  • Architecture inspections — Identify unwanted cross-module dependencies directly in the editor.
  • @ApplicationModule support — Understand explicit module configuration and dependency rules.
  • allowedDependencies support — Validate dependencies against configured module boundaries.
  • Named interfaces — Define and validate module APIs and exposed interfaces.
  • Dependency cycle detection — Identify cycles between application modules.
  • Module Graph — Visualize relationships between application modules.
  • Module Structure — Explore packages and module boundaries from the IDE.
  • Quick fixes — Resolve supported architecture issues directly through IntelliJ intentions.
  • Module navigation — Navigate between modules, packages, and dependencies.
  • Architecture verification — Verify module boundaries and dependency rules from a dedicated verification view.
  • Architecture export — Export architecture information for documentation and analysis.

Built for real Java projects

Fluxora Modulith works from the current IntelliJ project structure and Java PSI rather than relying on application-specific package names or business logic. It is designed to work with different Java and Spring projects following Spring Modulith-style modular architecture.

Getting started

  1. Install Fluxora Modulith from JetBrains Marketplace.
  2. Open a Java/Spring project.
  3. Open the Fluxora Modulith tool window.
  4. Explore your modules and dependencies.
  5. Use inspections and architecture verification to identify boundary issues.

GitHub

idea-plugin.name: jscpd
idea-plugin.description:
Copy/paste detection while you type. The plugin runs jscpd as a language server, so every clone, dead symbol or over-complex function shows up as a highlight in the file you are editing, with a gutter icon colored by kind, an intention that jumps to the other copy, and a tool window with the clones of the whole project.
  • Exact copies, renamed copies, near-miss copies, functions with the same syntax-tree shape, and semantic clones.
  • Dead code (unused files, exports, symbols, imports, members) and complexity, when turned on.
  • A migration view for jscpd --compare: pick the folder you port from and the folder you port to, and jscpd pairs their functions.
The plugin looks for jscpd 5.4.0 or newer in PATH and offers to download the release build when it is missing.

idea-plugin.name: AST Lens
idea-plugin.description:
Explore Java and Kotlin code through interactive UAST visualizations.

AST Lens helps developers inspect source structure and understand relationships across a file or an entire project directly inside IntelliJ IDEA.

  • Visualize UAST structure, method calls, and class or package dependencies.
  • Compare the PSI and UAST representations of the same source file.
  • Navigate bidirectionally between graph nodes and source code.
  • Find callers, callees, dependants, implemented interfaces, and inheritors.
  • Detect large classes, complex methods, and circular dependencies.
  • Filter syntax noise and export graphs as JSON, Mermaid, or Graphviz.

Privacy: all analysis runs locally. AST Lens does not collect telemetry and does not transmit source code or analysis results to external services.

  • Added bidirectional navigation between graphs and source code.

idea-plugin.name: SQL Migration Risk Guard
idea-plugin.description:
AFK MESH SQL Migration Risk Guard

Review PostgreSQL database migrations before they reach production.

SQL Migration Risk Guard analyzes Flyway SQL migration files and supported Liquibase changelogs inside IntelliJ IDEA. It highlights potentially destructive DDL, UPDATE and DELETE statements without a WHERE condition, risky column type or nullability changes, and index operations that may block writes. It checks Flyway filenames and duplicate versions across your project.

Built for careful review

  • Line-level editor warnings with Critical, High, Medium, and Low severity.
  • Structural SQL parsing instead of keyword-only security claims.
  • Liquibase XML, YAML, and JSON changelogs for documented change types and embedded SQL.
  • A project tool window with reviewable findings and navigation to the source.
  • HTML, JSON, and SARIF 2.1.0 reports for code review and CI workflows.
  • Conservative recommendations for staged changes, backfills, validation, and lock-aware index creation.
  • Works in IntelliJ IDEA Community; it does not require Database Tools or a database connection.

Local by default

The analyzer reads project migration files on your computer. It does not connect to a database, execute migrations, or send source code to AFK MESH. JetBrains Marketplace provides plugin license and trial handling.

No static analyzer can know the contents or size of your production database. Findings describe potential risks; parser gaps are shown as incomplete analysis.
idea-plugin.change-notes: • Initial release: local PostgreSQL migration analysis, editor highlights, Flyway sequence checks, Liquibase changelog checks, and HTML, JSON, and SARIF report export.

IDE support for Tera template files (.tera) — a Rust template engine with Jinja2-style syntax.

  • Missing loop variable or in keyword in for tags

  • Dangling or doubled dot operators (e.g. item., loop..index)

Supported Keywords

for · if · elif · else · block · macro · raw · filter · set · set_global · extends · include · import · from · break · continue

为 Tera 模板文件（.tera）提供 IDE 支持。 Tera 是一个使用 Jinja2 风格语法的 Rust 模板引擎。

语法高亮

  • 变量块  {{ }}
  • 标签块  {% %}
  • 注释  {# #}
  • 空白裁剪语法  {{- -}}  {%- -%}
  • 细粒度 token 着色：关键字、标识符、字符串、数字、运算符

错误检测

  • 未闭合的定界符（{{、{%、{#）

  • else / elif 出现在 if 块外
  • 不接受参数的关键字后附带多余内容（如 {% endif something %}）
  • for 标签缺少循环变量或 in 关键字
  • 非法标签名（如 {% in ... %}）
  • 悬空或重复的点号运算符（如 item.、loop..index）

支持的关键字

for · if · elif · else · block · macro · raw · filter · set · set_global · extends · include · import · from · break · continue

idea-plugin.name: Inno Setup
idea-plugin.description:
Created with AI

Brings first-class language support for Inno Setup installer scripts to the whole JetBrains IDE family. Inno Setup scripts (.iss) describe a complete Windows installer — files, registry keys, shortcuts, tasks, components and optional Pascal scripting. This plugin turns the IDE into a full-featured editor for them, so you no longer have to switch to the Inno Setup Compiler to write, navigate and validate your scripts.

Editing & understanding scripts

  • Syntax highlighting — sections, directive keys, parameters, constants ({app}, {autopf}, …) and embedded Pascal [Code] blocks are coloured distinctly. Colours are fully customisable in Settings → Editor → Color Scheme.
  • Context-aware code completion — section names, directive keys, parameter keys, known flag values and constants are suggested as you type, with automatic pop-ups after typing [ or {.
  • Inline documentation — hover over any section, directive, parameter or preprocessor directive to read its description without leaving the editor.
  • Error checking & validation — unknown sections, invalid directives/parameters and unrecognised constants are flagged directly in the editor, including constants embedded inside quoted strings.
  • Structure view & navigation bar — get a bird’s-eye overview of every section and its entries and jump straight to them.
  • Code folding — collapse whole sections and long parameter entries independently.
  • Brace & quote matching — auto-closes and highlights matching {}, [], () and ".
  • Line commenting — comment and uncomment lines with the usual shortcut.
  • Move statements — move parameter entries up and down with the standard shortcut.
  • Inlay hints — language flag icons are shown inline next to Languages: values and in [Languages] / [LangOptions] entries.

References & refactoring

  • Reference resolution & go-to — navigate between Name: declarations and their usages in Tasks:, Components: and Types: parameters, between [CustomMessages] entries and their {cm:…} usages, and between [Languages] names and their language-specific message keys.
  • Find usages — list every reference to a name, custom message or preprocessor define.
  • Rename refactoring — safely rename a declaration and all of its references in one step, including {#Name} usages of preprocessor defines.

Preprocessor (ISPP)

  • Preprocessor directives (#define, #include, #if, …) are parsed, highlighted, completed and documented just like script code.
  • #define constants resolve, can be renamed and have their usages found across the script.
  • Include handling — inline an #include directly into the script, or extract a selection into a new include file, via intention actions. View the fully #include-resolved effective script in a read-only tab from the context menu.

Building & running

  • Compile from the IDE — build a single .iss script via ISCC from the context menu, or have scripts compiled automatically when the project is built. Compiler output is shown in the console with foldable detail lines.
  • Run installers — a dedicated run configuration and a gutter icon next to the [Setup] section let you launch a compiled installer directly.
  • Settings — configure the Inno Setup installation location IDE-wide and build options per project under Build, Execution, Deployment → Inno Setup.

Additional file types

  • Language files (.isl) — Inno Setup translation files are recognised, highlighted and validated alongside your scripts, with their own new-file template.
  • Template files (.ist) — free-text fragments for use as alternative #include targets, with brace matching and section completion.

Works in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, CLion, Rider, WebStorm, GoLand, RubyMine, DataGrip and every other IntelliJ-platform IDE.

Full documentation — including a complete reference for every Inno Setup section and parameter — is available at https://kleinerhacker.github.io/intellij-plugin.inno-setup/.

Disclaimer: this is an unofficial, community-developed plugin. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Jordan Russell, Martijn Laan or jrsoftware.org. “Inno Setup” and the Inno Setup logo are the property of their respective owners and are used here only to identify the software this plugin supports. Inno Setup itself is not bundled with this plugin and has to be installed separately. The bundled section, parameter, constant and preprocessor descriptions are derived from the official Inno Setup documentation, Copyright © 1997-2026 Jordan Russell, portions Copyright © 2000-2026 Martijn Laan.

idea-plugin.name: Java Code Guard
idea-plugin.description:
Java Code Guard - Static analysis plugin for detecting unsafe patterns in Java code.

Java Code Guard — 面向团队的 Java 代码规范检查与一键修复插件，规则集对齐《阿里巴巴 Java 开发手册》核心强制条款并补充通用最佳实践。

核心特性
  • 32 条检查规则，覆盖编程规约 / 异常日志 / OOP / 并发 / 集合 / 控制语句 / 通用质量七大类
  • 全部支持 Alt+Enter 一键修复，编码阶段即时统一风格、规避隐患
  • 规则在 Settings → Editor → Inspections 中按 Java | 阿里巴巴开发手册 分组展示，可单独开关
  • 内置可选 Pro 激活机制，激活后解锁全部快速修复能力，适合团队 & CI 强制执行
规则概览
  • 编程规约：控制语句大括号、布尔字段 is 前缀、Executors 建池、包装类比较、Long 字面量后缀、循环内 DB 调用（N+1）、循环内字符串拼接、正则预编译、集合初始化容量、资源未关闭、字符串 == 比较、常量命名、数组声明、foreach 修改集合、switch 缺 default、方法参数过多
  • 异常日志：空 catch 块、日志 + 拼接、宽泛异常捕获、finally 块 return、printStackTrace 替代日志
  • OOP 规约：POJO 强制包装类型、构造器调用可重写方法、equals 用 getClass 判断、实例访问静态成员、finalize 重写
  • 并发规约：static SimpleDateFormat（线程不安全）
  • 集合处理：isEmpty 替代 size()、entrySet 遍历 Map
  • 控制语句：if 嵌套超过 3 层
  • 通用质量：魔法数字检测

开源地址：https://github.com/zwtao17512/java-code-guard　|　问题反馈：549230214@qq.com

idea-plugin.name: SQL DAL Maker
idea-plugin.description:
SQL DAL Maker generates the data access layer: DTO, Model, and DAO classes for PHP, Java, C++, Python, and Go.

It works like this:

  1. XML manifest. The manifest describes what to generate: the DTO and model classes, the DAO methods, and the SQL behind them.
  2. Translate. The manifest is translated into complete source code — free of any direct call to PDO, JDBC, or QtSql. Those stay behind a DataStore interface that you own.

Reverse engineering serves both. It can write a first draft of the manifest, so you rarely start from an empty file — but the manifest is an ordinary text file and can just as well be written by hand. And it runs again during translation: the generator reads live metadata over JDBC — tables, views, and the result sets of your own SQL — to resolve everything the manifest leaves open. That is why the database must be up and reachable whenever you generate.

The manifest persists, so regeneration is repeatable: when the schema changes, you re-run the generator and your corrections are still there.

Documentation and demo projects: sqldalmaker.sourceforge.net

idea-plugin.name: Extra Icons
idea-plugin.description:
Make your IDE more pleasant to use:
  • Adds 500+ icons for files like Travis YML, GitLab YML, Angular files, etc. Many icons have variants, so if you are not happy with the default icon, you can choose another.
  • Shows an icon for Git submodule folders.
  • Highly configurable: see File > Settings > Appearance & Behavior > Extra Icons to select extra icons to (de)activate. This is configurable at the IDE and project level.

  • You can override almost all IDE icons, including toolbars, menus, etc.
  • You can import and export icons from external files. This also means you can easily share icon themes with friends. You can also download online icon packs (example: restore the old file icons when using the new UI).
  • For more information, please see the online documentation.
  • JetBrains Gateway is no longer supported (it actually has never been fully supported).
License types
— Extra Icons offers monthly and yearly licenses.
— Extra Icons Lifetime (new!) offers lifetime licenses: pay once, use it and get updates forever.

There are two different plugins because JetBrains does not allow plugin developers to offer all the license types (monthly/yearly and lifetime) for the same plugin. Both plugins offer the exact same features. The only difference is the license.

Documentation | Issues and Feature Requests

idea-plugin.name: New Relic CodeStream
idea-plugin.description:
Shift left by making code performance part of the earliest stages of the development process.

  • See how the services built from your code are performing, with information about golden metrics, errors, transaction anomalies, SLOs, and more.
  • View any of your New Relic dashboards in the IDE, with easy access to your favorites.
  • Investigate errors more quickly by stepping through the stack trace and collaborating with teammates.
  • Search logs from your IDE to investigate issues without context switching.
  • Run NRQL queries, and save and share queries with your teammates via .nrql files.

Requirements

  • Requires a New Relic account. Don't have one? Create a free account and get 100 GB/month of free data ingestion.
  • Requires version 2023.2.1 or later of any JetBrains IDE, and is also available for VS Code or Visual Studio.
  • Your repository must be managed by Git, or a Git hosting service like GitHub.
  • For Windows users, CodeStream now requires a 64-bit version of the OS.

Log Search

Dashboards are at the very core of your New Relic experience, and any dashboard can be viewed right from your IDE.


Log Search

No need to slow down your investigation by context switching between your IDE and your browser to search logs. You can even search for output from specific log lines in your code.


Error Investigation

See performance data, at the method level, right in your editor. Always-on view ensures that performance issues are factored into the work at hand. You can even see metrics for your lower environments, and head off performance issues before they hit production.


Anomaly Detection

CodeStream allows you to catch problems before they escalate by identifying transactions with performance issues. An error rate heading in the wrong direction since your last release? View the performance over time, and jump straight into to relevant errors to get to the root of the problem.



Discover anomalies in the Transaction Performance section of the CodeStream pane, or right inline in your editor!


Performance Monitoring

Get an in-IDE view of how the services built from your code are performing, in any environment. Golden metrics, service-level objectives and related services give you the big picture at a glance.


Help & Feedback

Check out the user guide for more information on getting started with New Relic CodeStream. Please follow @newrelic for product updates and to share feedback and questions. You can also contact support.

idea-plugin.name: Sourcery
idea-plugin.description:
Sourcery is an AI-powered code reviewer and coding assistant that helps you write better code faster.

  • Get code reviews in your IDE whenever you want.
  • Immediately improve your code quality with suggestions and fixes.
  • Tackle repetitive tasks in seconds.

Sourcery Overview:

Sourcery reviews your code on demand and gives you feedback like you'd expect from a peer review.

Open up the Sourcery sidebar, choose the context of the code you want to review, and Sourcery will start giving you feedback.

Sourcery for Open Source

Sourcery is available for free, without needing an account, for Open Source projects.

If you are working on non Open Source projects you'll need to sign up for a paid Sourcery account, but you can try it out for free with our 14 day trial. A Sourcery account gives you access to code reviews in your IDE, through our CLI, or in GitHub.

Frequently Asked Questions:

Which platforms are supported?

Sourcery for JetBrains runs on Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon Macs. Intel Macs are not supported - if you're on an Intel Mac you can use the Sourcery extension for VS Code instead.

Can I use Sourcery at work?

Sourcery is fully free to use for Open Source projects, but requires a paid license for non Open Source work. You can try out Sourcery with a 14 day free trial (no credit card required) to see it in action in your IDE, through our CLI, or in GitHub.

idea-plugin.name: Packmind
idea-plugin.description:
Packmind Tech Coach brings the collective knowledge and expertise of your senior engineers, combined with industry best practices, directly into each developer's IDE. Through contextualized reviews and intelligent suggestions, Packmind Tech Coach accelerates developer learning while ensuring consistent, high-quality code.

With Packmind Tech Coach, capturing and sharing good or bad coding patterns is effortless. Instantly highlight code for discussion in practice reviews, and once a new practice is validated by the team, Packmind automatically deploys it across every developer's IDE.

This approach fosters a culture of continuous skill growth and shared knowledge. Packmind provides context, explains the rationale behind suggestions, and offers autofix recommendations, turning every coding session into a learning experience.

Features :
  • Get suggestions of code improvement based on your team best practices and industry standards (clean code, performance and security good practices, etc...)
  • Create a new coding practices directly from your IDE to share with your team.
  • Update an existing coding practice with new positive or negative examples.
  • Detect violations of your coding practices and suggest Autofix
  • Search and browse your team's practices and standards.
  • Track ongoing discussions around practices being reviewed by the team.

Extension Settings
This extension contributes the following settings:
  • Api Key: Your api key generated from your Packmind profile
