idea-plugin.name: Dependency Scout
idea-plugin.description:
Dependency Scout helps you keep your Maven and Gradle dependencies up to date.

Features:

  • Automatic detection of outdated dependencies in build.gradle, libs.versions.toml, gradle.properties and Maven pom.xml files
  • Floating hints showing available version updates
  • An inspection that flags outdated dependencies, configurable through the inspection profile
  • Alt+Enter quick-fix intentions to update dependencies
  • Code completion of available versions inside a version literal
  • A batch review dialog to pick and apply many updates at once, in a single undoable step
  • Support for Gradle version catalogs (libs.versions.toml)
  • Support for Maven projects (pom.xml dependencies and plugins, including ${property} versions)
  • Gradle wrapper updates, including refreshing the distribution SHA-256 checksum
  • BOM-aware: versions managed by an imported BOM are not reported as outdated
  • Configurable version policies, plus project-level rules in a checked-in .dependencyscout.json
  • Support for Maven Central and private Nexus repository
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Review all your updates in one place. A new Review Dependency Updates dialog lists every available upgrade in a single table, lets you pick a target version per row, offers select all / patch only / patch + minor shortcuts, and applies everything as one change you can undo with a single Ctrl+Z. Dependencies sharing a version catalog entry or a version property are updated once, not repeatedly. Open it from the Tools menu or the tool window's Update All button.
  • Version completion where you type the version. Invoke code completion inside a version string and Dependency Scout offers the available versions for that dependency, each marked with how big a jump it is and when it was released. Works in Gradle Kotlin DSL, version catalogs, gradle.properties and Maven pom.xml. (Inside a Groovy dependencies { } block the bundled Gradle plugin claims completion for those strings, so its own list appears there instead.)
  • See how old a version is before you take it. Versions published to Maven Central now show their release date in the completion popup, the tool window and the review dialog, so you can tell a fresh release from one that has been out for two years.
  • Keep your Gradle wrapper current. The wrapper is now checked like any other dependency, and updating it re-fetches the distribution checksum so it cannot go stale. A new Alt+Enter fix adds or repairs a missing distributionSha256Sum.
  • Team-wide update rules. Check a .dependencyscout.json into your repository to cap how far the whole project may be upgraded, or pin individual libraries to a version line with glob patterns. The file gets completion and validation as you edit it. Rules limit what is suggested — you can still choose any version yourself from the picker or completion.
  • BOM-managed versions are left alone. A dependency whose version comes from an imported platform or BOM is no longer flagged as outdated, because upgrading it on its own only diverges from the platform you opted into. Supports Gradle platform/enforcedPlatform/mavenBom and Maven import-scope and <parent>.
  • One-click upgrades from the tool window. Click the Update badge on a row to upgrade just that dependency, after a confirmation telling you both versions and how old the new one is.
  • Open on Maven Repository from the tool window's toolbar or right-click menu.

Changed

  • The dependency list appears immediately. The tool window now shows every dependency your project declares — name, current version and module — as soon as it has read your build files, instead of staying blank until every repository has answered. Each row's latest version fills in as it arrives, so you can find and read the dependency you came for while the rest is still loading, and rows you have selected stay selected.
  • Scans no longer get in your way. Opening the tool window, saving a build file and typing in one no longer make the IDE pause. Editing a build file now refreshes just that file rather than rescanning the whole project, and scanning makes far fewer network requests than before, so results come back quicker — especially on large multi-module projects.
  • Pending upgrades no longer look like problems. Outdated dependencies are reported as weak warnings in their own style, so a build file with a dozen available upgrades no longer reports a dozen warnings. The highlight is a subtle underline you can restyle under Settings | Editor | Color Scheme | Dependency Scout, and it is switched on or off through the inspection settings (Dependency Scout → Outdated dependency) rather than the inlay hint setting.
  • Upgrades look the same everywhere. The tool window, review dialog and completion popup share one visual language: green for a patch bump, blue for minor, amber for major, with an icon showing whether a row is a library, a Gradle plugin or a quality tool. Long lists are easier to scan because the group is greyed and the artifact name stands out.
  • Fewer repeated lookups after a restart. Known versions are remembered between IDE sessions, so a fresh session no longer begins by re-fetching everything it already knew.
  • More version formats understood. Calendar versions, a leading v, release trains such as Hoxton.SR12, and versions with any number of segments are now ranked correctly.
  • Installing no longer needs an IDE restart. Dependency Scout can be installed, enabled and disabled while the IDE keeps running.

Fixed

  • Dependencies declared against a configuration your build defines itself — including the "myConfig"("group:artifact:version") form used in Kotlin DSL — were not detected at all. They now appear everywhere other dependencies do.
  • // hold and // pin comments were honoured in the editor but ignored by the tool window and the review dialog, which offered upgrades the comment had explicitly ruled out. Every surface now respects them.
  • A dependency whose versions could not be fetched showed its error tooltip on unrelated rows below it, claiming a lookup had failed for dependencies that were perfectly fine.
  • The tool window could show a stale list after a build file was renamed, moved or deleted.

idea-plugin.name: MilkJ Markdown
idea-plugin.description:
MilkJ Markdown is a WYSIWYG Markdown editor for JetBrains IDEs. Edit .md files as rich text in a native editor tab, then switch to Markdown source whenever you need it.

Powered by Milkdown, MilkJ works alongside the built-in Markdown editor and keeps both editing surfaces synchronized. Use it for README files, documentation, project notes, and AI-generated plans without leaving your IDE.

Features
  • WYSIWYG rich-text editing with two-way Markdown source synchronization.
  • Tables, task lists, headings, links, images, blockquotes, and highlighted code blocks.
  • Paste or drop images: they are saved next to the Markdown file and linked by relative path.
  • Mermaid diagram previews and LaTeX math rendering.
  • Harper spelling and grammar checking, a custom dictionary, and importable Weirpacks.
  • Cmd/Ctrl-click navigation from Markdown links and project paths to files and line ranges, and from web links to the browser.
  • Configurable themes, fonts, zoom, and the option to open Markdown files in MilkJ by default.
Open a Markdown file and select the MilkJ editor tab to get started.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.1.24
  • Rich-text edits are no longer reverted in documents whose Markdown is written differently from MilkJ's own style (setext headings, __bold__, * or + bullets, unpadded tables, YAML frontmatter).
  • Everything outside the block you edit now stays byte-for-byte as you wrote it, including list spacing, emphasis markers, escapes and table padding.
  • Fixed long freezes (up to half a minute on 1 MB files) when an edit to a large document could not be matched to its Markdown.

0.1.23
  • Heading links such as [Usage](#usage) now jump to that heading when clicked, resolved the way GitHub does (duplicate headings included).
  • Choose the text, heading, and code fonts under Settings | Tools | MilkJ with the IDE's own font picker. Leave a font on <None> to keep the editor theme's font.

0.1.22
  • Updated Harper proofreading to 2.10.0 for improved grammar corrections and dictionary coverage.

0.1.21
  • Find now scrolls the active match into view when moving to the next or previous result, while keeping focus in the search field.

0.1.20
  • Pasted and dropped images are now saved as files next to the Markdown document (in a configurable folder, images/ by default) and referenced by relative path, instead of ending up as temporary blob: URLs that broke on reload.
  • "Follow IDE" theme now switches live when the IDE look and feel changes, without reopening the file.
  • Each MilkJ tab remembers its caret and scroll position across reopening and IDE restarts.
  • Zoom the editor with Cmd/Ctrl and +, - or 0, or from Settings | Tools | MilkJ; the level applies to every MilkJ tab.
  • Also opens .mdown, .mkd and .mkdn files.
  • The settings page was rebuilt; the bundled third-party license list is now complete and shipped inside the plugin.

0.1.19
  • Web links are now clickable: clicking an http, https, or mailto link opens it in your system's default browser instead of doing nothing.

0.1.18
  • Added a document outline: select the new button in the editor's top-left corner or press Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O to open a heading rail beside the text. Select a heading to jump to it, and the current section highlights as you scroll.

0.1.17
  • Harper proofreading now defaults to British English instead of following your system language (which fell back to American English on most systems). You can still pick another dialect under Settings | Tools | MilkJ.

0.1.16
  • Raw HTML in Markdown now renders as a sanitized preview, including centered headings, details blocks, tables, and local or remote images, while preserving the original HTML source.
  • Click a rendered Markdown image to edit its complete Markdown source directly, for both project-local and remote images.
  • Unsafe HTML such as scripts, event handlers, inline styles, embedded frames, and dangerous URLs is removed from the preview.

0.1.15
  • Rich-text edits now merge by aligning parsed Markdown blocks against the editor's content, not just by diffing text: an edit inside one block (a table, a list item, a blockquote) keeps every other block byte-exact, even when an unrelated IDE change landed while the edit was in flight.
  • List edits keep their bullet style and untouched items intact more often, including inside nested lists and blockquotes.
  • Fixed the caret jumping after IntelliJ's save normalization (e.g. trimming a trailing space) echoed a change back to the editor.

0.1.14
  • Structural edits inside heavily formatted regions (e.g. deleting a table row) no longer fail to sync and get reverted: the edited region adopts the editor's formatting while everything else keeps its original bytes.

0.1.13
  • Edits in long documents below wide tables (or other heavily normalized Markdown) no longer fail to sync and get reverted.
  • The caret is now always visible in every theme; it could previously disappear entirely when the embedded browser lost focus state.

0.1.12
  • Stability fixes for rich-text editing: no more caret jumps or reverted edits while typing.

0.1.11
  • Rich-text edits now preserve the original Markdown source around each change, including frontmatter, raw HTML, custom extensions, and existing formatting.
  • Edits that cannot be mapped back safely are reverted with a warning instead of rewriting unsupported syntax.
  • Renamed the Marketplace listing to MilkJ Markdown so its purpose is clearer when browsing and searching for Markdown tools.
  • Refreshed the Marketplace description and project documentation with clearer features, installation steps, and use cases.

0.1.10
  • Added Cmd/Ctrl-click navigation from Markdown links and bare project paths to files and line ranges in the JetBrains editor.
  • Relative targets resolve safely from the Markdown file or project root, with clear warnings for invalid or out-of-project targets.
  • Added support for running the plugin against the unified IntelliJ IDEA distribution used from 2025.3 onward.

0.1.9
  • Added Harper spell checking for rendered Markdown.
  • Added a persistent custom dictionary, with quick-add actions in the correction popup and full management in MilkJ settings.
  • Added import and management of Harper Weirpacks for custom grammar and style rules.
  • Dictionary changes automatically update every open MilkJ editor.

0.1.7
  • No more spurious "File Cache Conflict" dialogs: MilkJ no longer writes into the document unless you actually edited in the MilkJ tab.
  • External edits update the editor in place instead of rebuilding it (cursor and scroll are kept).
  • Edits sync as minimal text ranges — finer undo steps and no caret jumps in the native tab.
  • Read-only files are now read-only in MilkJ too, and a notification appears if a conflicting external change discards an unsynced edit.
  • Works even when the bundled Markdown plugin is disabled.
  • New "Shortcuts" reference tab next to the MilkJ editor (can be hidden in Settings | Tools | MilkJ).
  • Mermaid diagrams render through the code-block preview panel.
  • Compatible with 2026.2 EAP, where JCEF moved into the separate "Web Browser (JCEF)" plugin.

idea-plugin.name: Spring Properties Navigator
idea-plugin.description:
Spring Properties Navigator makes Spring configuration files easier to explore and maintain.

It adds bidirectional editor navigation between configuration keys and the Java code that defines or consumes them, in both .properties and YAML (application.yml) files, covering structured @ConfigurationProperties models and direct @Value("${...}") usages.

  • Navigate from a property key to the matching configuration class, field, accessor, or value injection point.
  • Works in both .properties and YAML configuration files, including nested mappings and sequences.
  • Jump the other way: gutter icons on @ConfigurationProperties members and @Value injections navigate to the configuration entries that set them.
  • Understand Spring relaxed names such as kebab-case, camelCase, and snake_case.
  • Follow nested properties through indexed collections, maps, arrays, and optional values.
  • Reduce false unresolved-property warnings when a key is resolved by the plugin.
  • Configurable under Settings | Tools | Spring Properties Navigator.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 1.0.0 - Initial release.
  • Navigation from .properties and YAML keys to @ConfigurationProperties classes, bindable members, and @Value("${...}") injection points.
  • Reverse navigation: gutter icons on @ConfigurationProperties members and @Value("${...}") injections jump to the configuration entries that set them.
  • Spring relaxed names, indexed collections, maps, arrays, and optional values.
  • Reduced false unresolved-property warnings for keys the plugin resolves, in both .properties and YAML.
  • Settings page under Settings | Tools | Spring Properties Navigator.

idea-plugin.name: Architecture Analysis
idea-plugin.description:
Architecture Analysis

Architecture Analysis is an advanced architecture governance and software intelligence platform for IntelliJ IDEA.

It continuously analyzes your codebase to identify:

  • Architectural violations
  • Circular dependencies
  • Forbidden relationships
  • Excessive coupling
  • Architecture drift
  • Technical debt indicators

Designed for Hexagonal Architecture, Clean Architecture, Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Modular Monoliths and Microservices.

Key capabilities:

  • Dependency mapping
  • Dependency graph visualization
  • Boundary validation
  • Coupling analysis
  • Architecture risk detection
  • Governance dashboards

Free forever: core hexagonal/layer/coupling analyzers, HTML report and local history. A Commercial license adds scenario, persistence, DTO/mapper and custom-rule analyzers, PDF/Mermaid export, unlimited history and CI/CD trend statistics.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2026.2.0

  • Re-published under a new release number after the Marketplace channel rejected a re-upload of 2026.1.0. No functional changes to the analyzers; confirms the Marketplace product descriptor code and hardens the release packaging pipeline.

2026.1.0

  • Architecture Analysis is now a JetBrains Marketplace Freemium plugin: the core analysis remains free and a Marketplace license or trial unlocks Commercial features.
  • The architectureCheck Gradle task now posts (and keeps updated) a Markdown comment on the GitHub pull request being built, with the score, grade, violation counts and trend - commercial edition, requires GITHUB_TOKEN in the workflow step.
  • Added a baseline diff: the CI/CD step summary and the new PR comment now show exactly which violations a change introduced or fixed against the committed .architecture-analysis/baseline.json, instead of only the total violation count.

0.1.5

  • Introduced Free and Commercial editions. Free stays fully functional with the core hexagonal/layer/coupling analyzers, HTML report, basic metrics JSON and up to 10 local history entries per project.
  • Commercial unlocks the scenario, persistence, DTO/mapper and custom-rule analyzers, PDF and Mermaid dependency graph export, unlimited local history and CI/CD trend statistics.
  • Added a license key field in Settings and an ARCHGUARD_LICENSE_KEY environment variable / --license-key CLI option to activate the Commercial edition in CI/CD.
  • The architectureCheck Gradle task now publishes a job summary to GitHub Actions and tracks score/violations trend across runs on the Commercial edition.

idea-plugin.name: HTTP Client Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Edit and run .http requests in a Postman-like UI. Browse requests in a tree and configure them visually instead of editing raw text.

HTTP Client Companion adds a visual layer on top of the JetBrains HTTP Client. Your requests still live in plain .http files — the plugin opens them in a form-based editor where the method, URL, query parameters, headers, body, and auth are laid out as fields and tables, and shows the response right beside the request. A dedicated tool window turns the .http files in your project into a navigable request tree.

Visual request editor

  • Method selector and URL field, with one-click Send and Save.
  • Params: edit query parameters and path variables in a key/value table that stays in sync with the URL.
  • Headers: manage request headers in a table, toggling each one on or off.
  • Body: Plain text, JSON, HTML, and XML with syntax highlighting and reformatting, plus multipart form-data, URL-encoded forms, and binary file upload.
  • Auth: Basic and Bearer Token authentication.
  • Scripts: pre-request and post-response JavaScript.

Response viewer

  • Status code, time, and size at a glance, shown side by side with the request.
  • Pretty, Raw, and Headers views, with formatting for JSON, XML, and HTML.

Request tree tool window

  • .http files as folders and ### request blocks as nodes.
  • A Drafts root backed by a scratch file for quick, throwaway requests.
  • Create, rename, duplicate, and delete files and requests; run a single request or every request in a file or directory; jump from a node to its source line.
  • Live sync with the file system — external edits, renames, and deletions appear immediately, and requests with unsaved changes are shown in bold.

Variables & environments

  • {{variable}} references in the URL, params, headers, body, and auth fields.
  • Pick an environment from the toolbar; hover a variable to see its resolved value and jump to where it is defined.

Requirements

  • Requires the JetBrains HTTP Client that ships with IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate and other commercial JetBrains IDEs.
  • Uses the native .http file format, so your requests stay portable and editable as plain text.


HTTP Client Companion is a commercial plugin with a free 14-day trial.

  • Authentication — Basic and Bearer Token.
  • Scripts — pre-request and post-response JavaScript editors.
  • Response viewer beside the request — status code, time, and size, with Pretty, Raw, and Headers views.
  • Request tree tool window mirroring the project's .http files, with each file's ### request blocks expanded as children.
  • Drafts root backed by a drafts.http scratch file; "New HTTP Draft" appends a request and opens it in the form.
  • Tree actions — New .http file, New draft, New request, Rename, Duplicate, Delete, Run, Run all in file/directory, and Jump to source.
  • Variables and environments — {{variable}} references across the URL, params, headers, body, and auth, with an environment selector, resolved-value tooltips, and go-to-declaration.
  • Live sync — the tree reflects files as they are created, renamed, deleted, or edited, and bolds requests with unsaved changes.

idea-plugin.name: Profiles
idea-plugin.description:
Group your projects into named sets — Work, Home, a client, a side project — or whatever you want to name them, and switch between them from one dropdown in the main toolbar. Pick a profile, and it opens that profile's projects, each in its own window, and closes the ones that aren't in it, so your open windows always match whatever you're working on.

It's a profile switcher in the plain sense: many projects per profile, and you switch to them by switching profiles. These are your real, separate projects — never merged into one window — so run configurations, indexes, branches and open files are all kept exactly as you left them.

Where you use it

  • In the editor — the Profiles dropdown sits in the main toolbar, next to the project and branch widgets.
  • On the Welcome screen — a "New Profile Workspace" button builds a profile and opens its projects before you've opened anything.

Features

  • Group any number of projects into a profile.
  • One click switches the whole set: opens the profile's projects, closes the rest.
  • Give each profile an icon (a built-in icon or your own emoji), shown in the toolbar.
  • Create a profile from the projects you already have open, or by picking folders.
  • Bulk import — point at a folder of repos and create a profile per subfolder, with checkboxes to pick exactly what to include.
  • Keyboard — bind shortcuts for "Switch Profile" (a searchable picker) and next/previous profile.
  • Re-capture your open windows into the active profile in one click; see each profile's project count in the dropdown.
  • Manage profiles — reorder, duplicate, rename, add/remove projects, clean up missing folders, and export/import as JSON — under Settings > Tools > Profiles.
  • Light on memory: only the active profile stays open.

Open source under GPL-3.0 — github.com/ArcaneArts/Intelij-Profiles.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• New: create profiles in bulk from a folder of repos — one profile per subfolder, with checkboxes to choose what to include.
  • New: keybindable "Switch Profile" picker plus next/previous-profile actions.
  • New: project counts in the dropdown; re-capture open windows into the active profile.
  • Settings: reorder, duplicate, remove missing folders, and export/import profiles as JSON.

idea-plugin.name: copy-code-ref

idea-plugin.name: Builder Builder
idea-plugin.description:
Generates a nested Builder class for a Java class's fields. Available from the Code > Generate menu (Alt+Insert), right below toString().

Features:

  • Choose exactly which fields the builder should expose, via a field chooser dialog.
  • If the class already has a constructor matching the selected fields, the builder calls it instead of assigning fields directly. Works with immutable classes and private constructors.

idea-plugin.name: Shard
idea-plugin.description:
Shard

Keyboard-driven control over editor splitters and tabs.

Shard adds actions to manage the editor layout without the mouse:

  • Focus a neighbouring splitter in any direction.
  • Split the editor in any direction, optionally moving the active tab into the new splitter.
  • Move splitters by swapping them with a neighbour.
  • Move tabs within a splitter or into a neighbouring one.

When multiple splitters neighbour the active one, Shard can pick the target by either recency or distance.

Shard also takes over closing tabs, so pinned tabs stay open until they are unpinned.

Everything is configurable in Settings | Tools | Shard. Most actions come without a default shortcut — bind them using the Configure Keybinds... button found there.

A {{variable}} that isn't defined in any of those sources is flagged with a red "unresolved variable" underline

idea-plugin.change-notes:
🚀 Features

  • Initial release: .bru file type, syntax highlighting (blocks, keys, values, {{template}} variables, ~-disabled entries), brace matching, block folding, and a color settings page.
  • Code completion: top-level block names (inserting the { } body, hiding blocks already in the file), keys of structured blocks (meta, HTTP methods, auth:*, settings) with : inserted, and enumerated values (body types, auth types, meta type, API-key placement).
  • Template variables: {{ auto-closes with }}; variable names are completed from the closest environments directory (both vars entries and vars:secret names), in values and inside raw bodies/scripts; Go to Declaration on {{variable}} navigates to its definition in the environment files (one target per file defining it). {{process.env.NAME}} references complete from and navigate to the NAME=... assignment in the closest .env file.
  • Unresolved-variable inspection: a {{variable}} not found in any variable source is underlined in red. To avoid noise, a reference is only flagged when its source exists — plain names only when an environments directory is present, {{process.env.NAME}} only when a .env file is.
  • The go-to-declaration chooser for a variable defined in several environments now labels each entry with its file name (e.g. dev.bru, prod.bru) instead of the shared directory path.

idea-plugin.name: Typing & Time Counter - Fun Break Reminder
idea-plugin.description:
Typing & Time Counter is a fun IntelliJ plugin that counts your keystrokes, tracks active coding time, reminds you to take humorous breaks with punchy typing effects, and keeps you motivated with meme-filled status messages. All data stays 100% local.

还在用「我感觉今天码了不少」自我安慰？装上它，你的摸鱼和爆肝都将被无情计量。🐷

一个蹲在 IDE 里陪你肝代码的小工具，专治「不知道自己到底敲了多少」的现代病：

  • 📊 码字计数：今日 / 累计码了多少字、肝了多久、手速（CPM）几何。别再说「我写了好多」，让数据打脸。

  • 🤫 全程不枯燥：状态栏和提醒文案全是梗，陪你笑着重构人生（和代码）。

数据全存在你本地 IDE 配置里，绝不上传，社恐友好。打开右侧「码字计时器」工具窗，随时围观自己的辉煌战绩。

装上它，今晚周报「工作时长」一栏，终于有底气了。💪

👋 作者的话：这是我作为新人开发者的第一个小作品（v0.5，2026-07-17），难免有不完善的地方。如果它能给你的敲码日常带来一点点乐趣，就是我最大的动力！欢迎大家放心试用，也非常期待你的反馈——后续我会持续打磨、优化、加新功能，请多多支持，一起把它养大～ 🌱

Typing & Time Counter · Fun Break Reminder

Still comforting yourself with "I feel like I coded a lot today"? Install this, and both your slacking and your grinding will be mercilessly measured. 🐷

A tiny sidekick that sits in your IDE and cures the modern disease of "no idea how much I actually typed":

  • 📊 Typing counter: today's / total characters, active time, and speed (CPM). Let the data do the talking.
  • ⏰ Funny break reminder: after you grind for a set time, a cheeky bubble nudges you to stand up and save your neck and back. Tap "Done resting", or "Snooze" for a few more minutes.

  • 🤫 Never boring: the status bar and reminders are full of jokes, so you can refactor your life (and your code) with a smile.

All data stays in your local IDE config and is never uploaded. Open the "Typing Timer" tool window on the right to watch your own glorious stats.

If it brings a bit of fun to your coding day, that's my greatest motivation! Feel free to give it a try, and I'd love your feedback — I'll keep polishing, improving and adding features. Thanks for your support, let's grow it together～ 🌱

idea-plugin.name: Ansible Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Encrypt and decrypt Ansible Vault (1.1/AES256 format) directly in the editor, without leaving the IDE and without depending on ansible-vault being installed (reimplemented with javax.crypto, verified against the official Ansible test suite).

Select plain text -> Encrypt Selection as Ansible Vault, or a $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256 block -> Decrypt Ansible Vault Selection. Both available from the editor's context menu. The password is never saved or cached.

FQCN-aware completion for ansible.builtin.*, community.general.*, and ansible.posix.* modules (649 total), Jinja2 ({{ }}/{% %}/{# #}) syntax highlighting inside Ansible YAML, Ctrl+Click navigation from a role reference to its tasks/main.yml, and static secret/permission hygiene checks (missing no_log on password-shaped arguments or vault-shaped include_vars, hardcoded validate_certs: false, files created without an explicit mode, unquoted decimal modes like mode: 755, shell pipelines without pipefail, state: latest on package managers, git checkouts of HEAD, and a dict or list as copy's content) -- evaluated statically, no ansible-lint/ansible-core binary required -- are also available (Ansible Companion Pro).

Free: a migration check for ansible-core 2.20 -- facts used as top-level variables (ansible_os_family, ansible_distribution, ...) get a quick fix to ansible_facts.os_family before ansible-core 2.24 stops injecting them.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Migration check for ansible-core 2.20 (free). Gathered facts used as top-level variables (ansible_os_family, ansible_distribution, ansible_default_ipv4, ...) get a weak warning and a quick fix that rewrites them to ansible_facts.os_family (also as Fix all in file). ansible-core 2.20 deprecates injecting facts as variables and 2.24 stops (INJECT_FACTS_AS_VARS becomes False). Checked inside {{ }}/{% %} and in when/failed_when/changed_when/until/that; connection settings and magic variables (ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_python_interpreter, ...) are never reported, nor is text inside a quoted string or a variable reached through another object. It is a normal inspection, so it can be turned off or re-leveled.
  • The rest of ansible-lint's safety profile (Ansible Companion Pro), still with no binary required:
    • A package manager task with state: latest (package-latest) — fine with update_only: true (dnf/yum) or only_upgrade: true (apt); a state given by a Jinja expression is never flagged; the old key=value style is read for these tasks.
    • git with version: HEAD, or hg with revision: tip (latest) — only an explicit reference is reported, not an omitted version.
    • A dict or list as copy's content (avoid-implicit[copy-content]).

Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Run In Terminal
idea-plugin.description:
Run scripts or an editor selection in a real terminal / console / shell, open a folder in your favorite console with one click, or just open a file with its own (or a custom) application.

Works with Command Prompt (cmd), Windows PowerShell, PowerShell 7 (pwsh), Git Bash, WSL Bash, and any custom shell or console application you configure — from the project tree, an editor selection, or the toolbar.

Ready to run out of the box: .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .sh, .py, .vbs, .js (Node.js), .rb and .php scripts — add any other extension in Settings.

Right-click any file or directory in the Project view, or a selection in the editor, to open a terminal or console right there — at the exact file or directory location you're working in.

Four ways in: two context-menu actions for your project tree, one for any text selection in the editor, and pinned toolbar icons for instant access to your favorite consoles (or other tools):

>_ Run in Terminal

  • Script files: .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .sh, .py, .vbs, .js (Node.js), .rb, .php by default — configurable per extension, comma-separated lists supported.
  • Embedded Terminal tab, or a standalone external window — your choice per extension.
  • cmd.exe, Windows PowerShell, PowerShell 7, Git Bash, WSL bash, or any custom interpreter command.
  • Embedded tabs start the selected shell directly; external mode opens a separate OS window.
  • "Keep Open" per row (on by default): keeps the console open after the script finishes.
  • Run in Terminal with Arguments... (new) — type or paste extra command-line arguments before running, with autocomplete from previously used ones. Can be hidden in Settings.

Remote Development (Windows Client + WSL Host)

  • Choose Host to use the embedded IDE Terminal with native Linux paths and Host tools, or Client to open a separate Windows window.
  • WSL paths are translated automatically for Windows applications. Explicit Git Bash means Git for Windows; WSL Bash and Auto + .sh use the WSL environment where appropriate.
  • Open Now and Client-selected Standalone Application rows launch on Windows Client.
  • Settings live locally on your Windows machine (the Client side) — nothing needs to be configured or kept in sync on the remote Host. When updating the plugin under a Remote Development session, update it on both sides (Client and Host) to the same version — mixing versions between them can make the plugin behave as if settings were lost, even though they weren't.

>_ Run Selection (new)

  • Right-click any text selection in the editor — no file needed — and choose Run Selection In Terminal (or press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+O). Runs in any of your enabled consoles.
  • One console enabled → runs directly. Several enabled → a submenu to pick which one, each with its own small icon.
  • Its own "Consoles" settings table — the five built-in consoles are always there as fixed rows; freely add as many extra rows as you like, each picking any console kind (including a second row of a built-in kind with its own settings), a Custom Interpreter, or a Standalone Application.
  • A configurable max selection length, and a live Test Area (a real, syntax-highlighted mini-editor) to try it right there in Settings.
  • Own default shortcut Ctrl+Alt+Shift+O, separate from the file shortcut below.
  • Run Selection with Arguments... (new) — the same argument prompt for a selection.
  • Optional: run a selection from the source file's own folder, so %~dp0/$PSScriptRoot and sibling files work.

>_ Open Folder Here (new)

  • Pin your favorite consoles as individual icons on the main toolbar — one click opens that console at whatever directory is currently relevant (open file's folder, selected project-tree folder, or project root), nothing to run.
  • Its own "Pinned Toolbar" settings table, same shape as Consoles above, with two independent per-row checkboxes — "Toolbar" and "Menu" — for the toolbar icon, a project-tree right-click "Open Folder Here" submenu, both, or neither.
  • Custom rows can point at literally any application. A Standalone Application command stays literal unless it explicitly contains a template variable; no directory is silently appended.
  • Built-in Explorer/Finder/Files row: opens the current folder directly in the OS's own native file manager — no cmd.exe wrapper. Explorer on Windows (thoroughly tested); Finder on macOS and the default file manager on Linux via open -R/xdg-open (best-effort — verified by code review, not yet confirmed on an actual Mac/Linux machine). Selecting exactly one file in the project tree opens it highlighted instead of just its folder (Windows and macOS; Linux has no single command that works reliably across desktop environments, so it opens the folder instead). Works for WSL-mounted paths too, translated to the real \\wsl.localhost\... form Explorer understands.

⇗ Open Now

  • Non-console files — media, documents, web pages, and more.
  • System default application, or a custom one of your choice.
  • Opens immediately — no picker dialog, no console involved.

Also included:

  • Custom Command templates: {path}, {file}, {dir}, {name}, {stem}, {project}, {relativePath}, {wslPath}, {windowsPath}, and {args} (the text typed into Run with Arguments). Type { (or press Ctrl+Space) in a command field to choose one. Run Selection variables point to its generated temp script; raw selected text is never inserted into a command.
  • Smarter Auto reads PowerShell/Bash/Python shebangs, prefers PowerShell 7 when available, invokes Python explicitly, and prioritizes native WSL tooling for WSL projects. A setting chooses the fallback shell for ordinary Windows files.
  • A per-row "Test" button and icon picker on all tables — for a Custom Interpreter/Standalone Application row, use the icon straight from its own program automatically, pick any image or executable's icon yourself, or revert to the built-in default.
  • Default shortcuts Ctrl+Shift+O (files) and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+O (selection), each with automatic conflict detection.
  • Export/Import Settings — save every table plus the other settings as one JSON blob (copy/paste or a file), and load it back later or on another machine. Forward/backward compatible by design.
  • "Select All / Deselect All" for every checkbox column, on all four tables.
  • Optional self-diagnostics report, covering every table's settings.
  • Diagnostics show frontend and backend versions/build timestamps; an optional in-memory debug trace helps diagnose Remote Development routing.
  • One Reset All to Defaults button, with role-aware defaults for Local and Remote Development.

How to use: right-click a file in the project tree or a text selection in the editor, then pick Run in Terminal, Run Selection In Terminal, or Open Now; or click a pinned console icon on the main toolbar for Open Folder Here. Configure consoles/apps at Settings/Preferences → Other Settings → Run in Terminal.

Found a bug? Report it at github.com/alvolturbo/run-in-terminal-issues.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.2.7
  • New "Run with Arguments": right-click a script file and choose "Run in Terminal with Arguments...", or right-click an editor selection and choose "Run Selection with Arguments...", to type or paste extra command-line arguments before running.
  • Previously used arguments are suggested as you type, with a "Clear History" button right in the dialog.
  • Works with every console type: arguments go after the script for Command Prompt, PowerShell, PowerShell 7, Git Bash, WSL Bash and Python (Auto); Custom Interpreter and Standalone Application rows place them wherever the new {args} template variable is written.
  • On by default - it only adds the second menu item; hide it with the new checkbox in Settings.
  • New option "Run Selection from the source file's folder" (on by default, can be turned off in Settings): the temporary script is created next to the file the selection came from, so scripts that call sibling files via %~dp0, $PSScriptRoot or relative paths work. The temporary file is removed automatically (PowerShell right away, other consoles after about 10 minutes).
1.2.6
  • The built-in Explorer row now picks the right command for whichever OS actually runs the backend - Explorer on Windows, Finder on macOS, the default file manager on Linux. macOS/Linux behavior is best-effort.
1.2.5
  • Embedded Terminal tabs now open through the public Reworked Terminal API instead of an internal one - same behavior, just no longer relying on an unstable internal API for something this central.
  • New "Reuse an existing embedded Terminal tab" option (off by default) - when on, a request for the same console/directory/command reuses an already-open tab instead of always creating a new one.
  • Settings page interface improvements: clearer Select All/Deselect All labels, a more accurate "Pinned Toolbar / Menu" table name, and a reordered section layout.
1.2.4
  • New default rows: .js (Node.js), .rb (Ruby), .php - same "wrong or missing default file association" fix already applied to .vbs.
  • The Console dropdown (Script Types, Consoles, and Pinned Toolbar tables) now lists every installed WSL distribution as its own "WSL Bash (<name>)" entry, alongside the existing generic "WSL Bash" (Windows' own default distro) - pick the exact distro a row should use right there, no extra column.
  • New example Pinned Toolbar row: PuTTY, as a Standalone Application - shown dimmed/"(not found)" until PuTTY is actually installed; off both the toolbar and the right-click menu by default.
  • New built-in Pinned Toolbar row: Explorer - opens the current folder directly in Windows Explorer, no cmd.exe wrapper. Selecting exactly one file in the project tree opens it highlighted instead of just its folder. On the right-click menu by default; off the toolbar by default.
  • Settings table columns can now be freely resized, and double-clicking a column border auto-fits it to its content (like Excel) - widths are remembered across Settings reopens/restarts.
1.2.3
  • Added Custom Command variables: {path}, {file}, {dir}, {name}, {stem}, {project}, {relativePath}, {wslPath}, and {windowsPath}, with completion after typing { or pressing Ctrl+Space.
  • Run Selection exposes its generated temp script through file variables; raw selected text is never inserted into a command.
  • Auto now recognizes PowerShell, Bash, and Python from extensions or shebangs, prefers PowerShell 7 when available, and prioritizes WSL/native Bash for WSL projects.
  • Added a configurable fallback shell for ordinary Windows files.
1.2.2
  • Minor bug fix.
1.2.1
  • Fixed: "Open Folder Here" (toolbar icon, no specific file/folder in focus) could resolve to the wrong directory under Remote Development, opening an internal Client-side cache path instead of the real project root - now falls back correctly to the actual Host project directory.
  • "Run Selection In Terminal"'s max-length limit now always reflects the value actually set in Settings, even under Remote Development (previously the limit could silently be read from a stale, separate copy).
  • Actions (Run in Terminal, Run Selection, Open Folder Here, Open Now, Settings page Test buttons) no longer block the UI thread waiting on Remote Development round-trips - smoother, no more risk of a brief freeze right after clicking.
1.2.0
  • Remote Development support: choose Host for the embedded IDE Terminal or Client for a separate Windows window, with automatic WSL path translation.
  • Embedded tabs start the selected shell directly: Command Prompt, Windows PowerShell, PowerShell 7, Git Bash, or WSL Bash.
  • Open Now and Client-selected Standalone Applications launch on Windows Client; Auto prefers WSL for .sh in Remote WSL projects.
  • Clear Host/Client labels, role-aware defaults, Reset All to Defaults, and diagnostics showing frontend/backend build timestamps.
  • Official JetBrains Split Mode architecture; minimum IDE version is 2026.1.
1.1.2
  • New: an "Open Folder Here" submenu when right-clicking a folder in the project tree, listing every row pinned to it - same targets as the toolbar icons, but for a specific folder. Each Pinned Toolbar row now has two independent checkboxes, "Toolbar" and "Menu" - on toolbar, in the menu, both, or neither.
  • New: Export/Import Settings - a collapsible section on the settings page saves every table (plus max selection length, notifications) as one JSON blob, and loads it back later or on another machine.
  • New: "Select All / Deselect All" for every checkbox column across all four tables, not just Run Selection.
1.1.1
  • Minor fixes and internal improvements.
1.1.0

New in the interface:

  • "Run Selection" - select any text in the editor, right-click, and choose "Run Selection In Terminal" to run it in a console. No file needed. More than one console enabled? A small menu lets you pick which one.
  • "Open Folder Here" - pin your favorite consoles to the main toolbar as icons. One click opens that console right in the folder you're currently working in - nothing runs, it just opens. Besides consoles, you can also pin any other application to a toolbar icon and launch it with one click.

New in Settings:

  • New Test Area - a real mini code editor to try Run Selection right there, without leaving Settings.

New capabilities:

  • New console option, "Standalone Application" - launches a regular app directly (not through a console), so no extra terminal window pops up.

  • New default row for .vbs (via Custom Interpreter/cscript.exe).

idea-plugin.name: Project Switcher
idea-plugin.description:
Switch between open and recent projects from a compact keyboard-driven popup.

Press Alt+F2 to open Project Switcher, and again to close it. Type to filter projects by name or location. Search tolerates common typos and supports keyboard-layout correction. Open projects are listed from the most recently used, and the previous project is selected, so Alt+F2 then Enter switches back to it.

Shortcuts
  • Up / Down — select the previous or next row
  • Page Up / Page Down, Home / End — navigate longer lists
  • Enter or a click — open the selection according to the IDE's Open project in setting
  • Shift+Enter or Shift+click — open a recent project in the current window
  • Ctrl+Enter or Ctrl+click — open a recent project in a new window
  • Cmd+W on macOS, Ctrl+W elsewhere — close an open project or remove a recent one
  • Esc — clear the query; with no query, dismiss the popup
An open project always receives focus in its existing window. The current-window and new-window modifiers affect only recent projects.

In Settings | Tools | Project Switcher, you can replace speed search with a search field above the list or display the selected project's location and available shortcuts below it. You can also choose Delete and Backspace in place of Cmd+W for closing projects.

Assign your own shortcut in Settings | Keymap | Switch Project or run the action from Tools | Switch Project.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Installation works on 2026.3 EAP after a compatibility issue with reopening recent projects previously prevented it.
  • Even when typing outpaces list updates, Enter opens the project that matches the full query entered so far.
  • Settings | Tools | Project Switcher offers a search field above the list as an alternative to speed search.
  • The popup sorts open projects by last use, newest first, and preselects the previous project so that Alt+F2, then Enter, takes you back to it.
  • Closing the current project with Cmd+W on macOS or Ctrl+W on other systems works with other projects open and returns focus to the previously used project.
  • Long lists have a scrollbar and support Page Up, Page Down, Home and End, while selection changes scroll only far enough to keep the selected row visible.
  • After a project is closed or removed from the popup, the list keeps its icons and scroll position without briefly showing a loading message.
  • Search ignores the home-directory portion of paths, gives project-name matches priority over location matches, and displays the location when it is the sole match.
  • Separate options in Settings | Tools | Project Switcher show the selected project's location and available shortcuts below the list.
  • Choosing Delete and Backspace in Settings | Tools | Project Switcher replaces Cmd+W and Ctrl+W for closing or removing projects, with one project closed per press, an empty query required, and a selection change required after erasing a query.
  • Recent projects open in the current window with Shift+click or in a new window with Ctrl+click, matching Shift+Enter and Ctrl+Enter respectively.
  • Any keymap shortcut assigned to Switch Project toggles the popup closed on a second press, including shortcuts other than Alt+F2.
  • From its first frame, the popup displays the cached project list with sharp icons, then updates both in the background.
  • All project icons load concurrently rather than in groups of four, and Power Save Mode skips the wait for icons the IDE does not generate.
  • A dimmed recent-project entry indicates that its directory is missing.
  • To open a recent project on WSL or another non-local file system, the plugin uses the IDE's reopen action so the environment is prepared first.
  • Open projects remain available in the popup if the IDE fails to assemble the recent-project list, rather than being replaced by an error.
  • Remote development hosts no longer load the plugin because they cannot display its popup, and JetBrains Client no longer shows its action.

idea-plugin.name: Bracket Colorizer
idea-plugin.description:
Colorizes matching brackets by nesting depth ("rainbow brackets"): every pair of (), [], {} (and optionally <>) gets the color of its nesting level, so brackets that sit inside each other are easy to tell apart.

Uses each language's syntax highlighter to avoid recognized comments, strings, regular expression literals, and markup text. Files without a working syntax highlighter are left unchanged.

Plain text and Markdown files are skipped, so that ordinary link syntax such as [text](url) stays calm. Code fenced inside a Markdown file is still colorized.

The colors are fully configurable, either in the Bracket Colorizer tool window on the right hand side of the IDE (applied live) or under Settings | Editor | Bracket Colorizer: pick a color per nesting level, add or remove levels, and optionally mark unmatched brackets.

Instead of hand picked colors you can also pick a ready made palette under From template: the bracket colors of VS Code Dark+, VS Code Light+, VS Code High Contrast Dark, One Dark Pro, Dracula, Nord, or the Viasfora rainbow. Your own colors can be saved as a named template as well. A template also carries the bracket types, the repeat, bold and unmatched switches, which it ticks in the form when it is selected and which stay editable afterwards. Change template edits the one that is selected, and Customize templates manages the list: remove entries, clear it completely, or put the built in templates back without losing the ones you saved.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.2.0

Nesting colors no longer have to be picked one at a time. Next to the hand picked colors there is now a second way to dress up your brackets: templates. Seven of them ship with the plugin, each holding the bracket colors of a color scheme you probably know already, namely VS Code Dark+, VS Code Light+, VS Code High Contrast Dark, One Dark Pro, Dracula, Nord, and the Viasfora rainbow. Pick one from the dropdown and the whole form follows along: the level colors, the color for unmatched brackets, which bracket types are colorized, and the repeat, bold and unmatched switches. Nothing is locked afterwards, so a template is a starting point rather than a cage.

Your own palettes belong in that list just as much. Save as template turns the colors you picked by hand into a named entry of your own. Change template opens any template, including the ones that ship with the plugin, so its name, its colors, its number of levels and its switches can be reworked, then kept with Save or thrown away with Discard. Customize templates keeps the list itself in order: change or remove single entries, clear the whole list, or put the built in templates back the way they shipped. Restoring them never touches the templates you saved yourself.

Your hand picked colors stay exactly where they are while a template is in use, so switching back to them is always a single click.

1.0.0

Initial public release with configurable nesting colors, live tool window settings, unmatched bracket highlighting, and optional angle bracket support.

idea-plugin.name: Classic Toolbars Toggle

idea-plugin.name: Git Hygiene Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Lightweight inline git blame — author and date at the end of each line — designed from the ground up to never block the editor. Every git operation runs off the EDT via a real git subprocess, with an aggressive, two-key cache (repo HEAD commit + the file's own modification time) so switching between files never triggers a recompute. A commit, checkout or pull moves HEAD and is picked up on the next repaint, recomputed in the background; while a file has unsaved edits its annotations are hidden until it is saved, so a line is never labeled with another line's author.

No git4idea dependency — shells out to the real git binary for everything, keeping the entire git interaction surface inside one well-understood, already-proven-safe pattern.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no popups.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • After a commit, the lines it committed kept showing "Not Committed Yet": HEAD was resolved once per repository and never again. The cached HEAD is now tied to a cheap stamp of the files that change whenever HEAD moves (commit, checkout, reset, pull), so the blame is recomputed for the new commit. Right after a commit those files are updated in sequence, so the background task waits for them to settle before trusting the HEAD it read.
  • A new file that wasn't committed yet never got its blame in that session, not even after committing it: the failed git blame left the file marked as "in progress" forever. It now gets an empty result for that HEAD, and is blamed again once it is committed.
  • With unsaved edits, every annotation below an inserted or deleted line was shifted by one line (each line showed the author of the line above it). While a file has unsaved changes the annotations are now hidden; they come back, recomputed, as soon as the file is saved.
  • The listing said the blame appears at the end of the current line; it appears at the end of each line.

idea-plugin.name: Tool Finder
idea-plugin.description:
Find and open IDE tool windows from a keyboard-driven popup.

Press Ctrl+Alt+F2 (Cmd+Opt+F2 on macOS) to open Tool Finder, and again to close it. Type to filter tool windows by name or ID. The list separates active, recent and new tool windows, and each row shows the tool window's own IDE shortcut when it has one.

Shortcuts
  • Up / Down - move the selection
  • Enter - activate the selected tool window, or hide it when it is the focused one
  • Delete / Backspace - hide the selected active tool window while the search field is empty
  • Esc - clear the search, then close the popup
Unavailable tool windows can be included under Settings | Tools | Tool Finder. They are shown dimmed and cannot be activated in the current context. The same page toggles the tool window shortcuts.

The shortcut can be changed under Settings | Keymap by searching for Tool Finder. The action is also available from Tools | Tool Finder.
idea-plugin.change-notes: • The popup responds to the keyboard and the mouse again on 2026.2.3, where typing, Up, Down and Enter had stopped working.

idea-plugin.description: QuickBox is an ultra-fast, visually stunning snippet and link manager built directly into your IntelliJ IDE using JetBrains Compose. Stop losing track of important commands, API keys, and reference documentation links. Automatically sync your most important code snippets to GitHub Gists.

idea-plugin.name: CodingTime
idea-plugin.description:
CodingTime keeps track of how much time you actually spend coding — locally, with no account and no network traffic.

  • Counts only active editing time: a configurable idle timeout ends a session when you stop working.
  • Live status bar widget with today's total.
  • Dashboard tool window with a daily activity chart plus breakdowns by language and project.
  • All statistics stay on this machine, in the IDE configuration directory.

idea-plugin.name: CrudGenerator
idea-plugin.description:
CrudGenerator

Generate a complete, production-ready Spring Boot CRUD from a single JPA entity — DTOs, MapStruct mappers, Spring Data repositories, application services, REST controllers, domain events and their tests, written through the IntelliJ PSI tree in seconds.

Right-click any @Entity class, pick an action, get a clean-architecture module (domain, application, infrastructure packages per bounded context) ready to run against Spring Boot 3 or Spring Boot 4.

What it generates

From one entity class, the plugin writes the full CRUD layer that would otherwise have to be built by hand:

  • DTOs (Request / Response) with Bean Validation and OpenAPI annotations
  • Support builder classes for readable test fixtures
  • Custom exceptions shared across the bounded context
  • MapStruct mappers between entities, DTOs and embedded types
  • Spring Data repositories wired to the entity's package
  • Application services orchestrating persistence and domain events
  • Domain events and listeners (event-driven create / update flow)
  • REST controllers with the standard CRUD endpoints
  • Unit and integration tests for every generated artifact

How it fits your project

  • Designed for Spring Boot 3 and Spring Boot 4 (Java 17+ target; the plugin itself is built on Java 25).
  • Compatible with Maven and Gradle (Groovy and Kotlin DSL). Missing dependencies (Lombok, MapStruct, the annotation-processor configuration) are added to your build file automatically when the plugin detects they are absent.
  • Honors a clean-architecture layout. DDD (default) or Layered package structure — pick the one you prefer in Settings → Tools → CrudGenerator. Switching structure mid-project keeps the previous layout's files in place; the next entity generation lands in the new layout.
  • Type names follow an Italian (default) or English naming profile. Methods and local variables stay readable regardless of the chosen profile.

Optional integrations

  • Spring Security — when the target project declares spring-boot-starter-security, the plugin generates a complete auth bounded context (User / Role entities, repository, CustomUserDetailsService, SecurityConfig with HTTP Basic, a default admin seeder) plus a shared OpenApiConfig.
  • Spring HATEOAS — enable the hypermedia API option in Settings to get an <Entity>Assembler and HATEOAS-aware list endpoints returning EntityModel / PagedModel.
  • IntelliJ MCP Server — when the MCP Server plugin is installed, the complete CRUD pipeline is exposed as the generate_crud tool, so AI assistants can drive generation.
  • Extension points — four plugin-owned extension points let third parties plug in custom generation steps, field-type mappers or build-tool adapters without touching the core.

Getting started

  1. Right-click any @Entity class in the Project view.
  2. Open the CRUD Generator submenu.
  3. Pick Generate CRUD for the whole pipeline, or any of the eight granular actions for a single layer.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1 or later.
  • The Lombok IntelliJ plugin must be installed.
  • The target project must use Spring Boot 3 or 4 with Lombok, MapStruct, Jakarta EE and Spring Data on the classpath.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

Changed

Fixed

  • `List`/`Set` fields whose element type is `@Embeddable` are no longer copied verbatim into generated DTOs. Every generated `Crea*Request`/`Aggiorna*Request`/`*Response` now wraps such a collection in `List<DTO>` / `Set<DTO>`, the same dedicated-DTO convention already applied to a scalar `@Embeddable` field, instead of leaking the domain-internal value object directly into the REST contract. (#21)
  • A primitive `boolean` entity field is now generated as `Boolean` on every `Crea*Request`/`Aggiorna*Request`, instead of the primitive type. Jackson could not leave the primitive field unset, so any partial request body that omitted it — most notably a partial `Aggiorna*Request` update — failed to deserialize with `HttpMessageNotReadableException`; the response and the entity keep the primitive field, since a value is always present there. (#21)
  • The generated `Aggiorna*ServiceTest` now detects an update that applies no setter. The entity returned by the mocked `findById` starts empty, `save` returns the entity it receives, and the test asserts the post-update entity state against the request for every property the update service actually assigns (matching setter and type, or the string-to-enum conversion). Previously the only assertions compared the request with a response fabricated by the mocked mapper, so the test passed even when the update logic mutated nothing. (#21)
  • Generated domain events are now actually published. `Crea*Service` and `Aggiorna*Service` now publish `CreaAggiorna*Event` (with `TipoEvento.CREAZIONE`/`AGGIORNAMENTO`) and `Cancella*Service` now publishes `Cancella*Event`, through the corresponding `*EventPublisher` injected as a constructor dependency; previously the whole event/listener/publisher family generated by "Generate Events" was dead code, never constructed or invoked by any service. (#21)
  • A request property that the entity cannot receive no longer disappears in silence from the generated update service. When the source getter has no matching setter on the target, the generated code now carries a `//TODO non espone set(...)` line naming the property that is not propagated, the same convention already used where the assignment cannot be written. Previously such a field was skipped with no comment and no log, so an update simply had no effect on it with nothing in the generated code to show why. (#21)
  • Generated classes with injected dependencies no longer rely on Lombok to declare their constructor. `Common*Service`, `Cerca*Service`, `RicercaAvanzata*Service`, the REST controller (Standard, HAL and JSON:API, in both class and record shape), the two `*EventPublisher` classes and the JPA `Jpa*Specification` now carry an explicit constructor assigning each `final` field, replacing `@AllArgsConstructor`/`@RequiredArgsConstructor`. The generated signatures are unchanged, so nothing on the Spring side moves; the output is now consistent with `Crea*Service`/`Aggiorna*Service`/`Cancella*Service` and compiles for teams whose convention forbids Lombok-generated constructors. (#21)

Removed

idea-plugin.name: Edge Reader
idea-plugin.description:
A private, local-first electronic book reader integrated into JetBrains IDEs.

Edge Reader provides a collapsible reading shelf with secure EPUB, large-file TXT, bounded PDF, Markdown, and local HTML reading, navigation, search, bookmarks, and progress restoration.

idea-plugin.name: Java Nullity Syntax
idea-plugin.description:
Java Nullity Syntax makes Java nullability annotations easier to read and write.

Nullability annotations recognized by IntelliJ IDEA are displayed as concise type suffixes:

  • ! for non-null types
  • ? for nullable types
  • no suffix for types without a nullability annotation

For example:

Map<@NotNull String, @Nullable List<@NotNull Item>> values;

is displayed as:

Map<String!, List<Item!>?> values;

This changes only how the code looks in the editor. When you copy, paste, compile, or commit the code, it contains ordinary Java annotations.

Write annotations using suffixes

Type ? or ! immediately after a Java type to add the corresponding project-default nullability annotation. Typing the opposite suffix replaces an existing nullability annotation. Deleting a ? or ! suffix removes the corresponding annotation.

Configuration

Java Nullity Syntax is enabled by default. You can disable its editor presentation entirely or configure the ! and ? suffixes independently under Settings | Tools | Java Nullity Syntax.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0 — Initial release

  • Displays recognized Java nullability annotations as ! and ? suffixes.
  • Adds or replaces nullability annotations by typing a suffix after a Java type.
  • Removes the corresponding annotation when its suffix is deleted.
  • Provides independent controls for non-null and nullable syntax.

idea-plugin.name: chao-garden
idea-plugin.description:
Add a few chao to your JetBrains IDE with this plugin!

Adds a small chao garden tool window to your JetBrains IDE. Spawn one or more chao, name them, and watch them wander, fly, sit, and occasionally peek at your code.

Chao types include neutral, hero, and dark. Their size can be configured in the plugin settings.

Changes

You can see the changes between the different versions in the CHANGELOG.md file.

Installation

You can install this plugin throught the plugin menu in your Settings or through the JetBrains Marketplace.

Configuration

Open the settings using Ctrl + Alt + S on Windows/Linux or Cmd + , on macOS and navigate to Tools > Chao Garden.

In the settings, you can choose the size of the chao. Choose between small, medium and large.

Usage

A "Chao Garden" tool window will appear on the right side of your IDE. You can add a specific type of chao or add a random chao, and name them!

They will explore their new home immediately. Have you tried hovering over them with your mouse?

To see everything a chao can do, have a look at CHAO.md.

References

This project is a port of the Visual Studio Code equivalent, which was originally inspired by and based on vscode-pokemon by Jakob Hoeg Mørk and vscode-pets by Anthony Shaw.

All Chao Sprites belong to Sega/Sonic Team. Sprites found on Spriters Resource:

  • Neutral Chao Sprite by Sonikku
  • Dark Chao Sprite by Mikel "Melonhead" Crawford
  • Hero Chao Sprite by Mikel "Melonhead" Crawford

Gifs created using Gimp. Icons created using Inkscape.

idea-plugin.name: GitHub Toolbar Button
idea-plugin.description:
Adds a button to the main toolbar that opens the current project's GitHub repository page in your default browser.

The button is present in every project. When the project has no Git repository, no remote, or a remote that is not on a recognized GitHub host, the button is disabled and its tooltip explains why.

A submenu under Git in the main menu, in the VCS Operations popup, and in the Project View context menu also opens the repository's pull requests, issues, Actions runs, and releases. Each is a separate command, so any of them can be bound to a keyboard shortcut.

Self-hosted GitHub Enterprise hosts can be added under Settings | Tools | GitHub Toolbar Button. Hosts are matched exactly, so adding one recognizes that host and not lookalikes of it.

idea-plugin.name: VaultLink
idea-plugin.description: Detects a HashiCorp Vault mount/secret encoded in the project name, authenticates via OIDC, LDAP, Token, or Userpass, and exposes the secret's keys as environment variables for running and debugging the project.
idea-plugin.change-notes:

Added

  • Tool Window: each variable row can now be disabled (excluded from injection, reversibly — the row stays visible, greyed and struck through) or edited (overrides the value that gets injected, marked with an "edited" chip and revertible to Vault's value). Changes apply immediately to whichever destination is active (live Run Config injection and/or .env), without a refetch. The secret itself is never modified in Vault, and edited values live only in memory — lost when the IDE closes.

A new Both strategy applies the secret to both the live Run Config injection and the .env file, matching what the README already described.

idea-plugin.name: Bracket Pair Guides
idea-plugin.description:
VS Code-style bracket pair guides for JetBrains IDEs.

Bracket Pair Guides colors each matching opening and closing bracket pair by nesting depth and draws a focused guide for the innermost pair containing the caret. Single-line pairs use a horizontal guide; multiline pairs are connected by opening and closing arms joined by a vertical segment.

  • Six repeating, customizable nesting colors
  • Separate controls for horizontal and vertical guides, width, and opacity
  • Optional border or background emphasis on active endpoints
  • Language-aware matching through installed JetBrains language plugins
  • Optional suppression of IntelliJ's built-in matched-brace highlighting

Bracket colors and guides are added without recoloring variables, tags, or surrounding code. Exact bracket support depends on the brace matcher provided by each installed language plugin. Supported language families can be enabled or disabled individually.

Configure the plugin under Settings | Editor | Bracket Pair Guides. Requires IntelliJ Platform 2024.1 or newer.

The plugin does not collect telemetry, transmit source code, or make network requests.

Documentation · Report an issue

Independent and not affiliated with Microsoft.

idea-plugin.name: Repo Lens
idea-plugin.description:
A code review navigator. Repo Lens collects review candidates into one tool window, jumps from any finding straight to the code, and copies findings as structured Markdown you can paste into any AI chat or review thread.

Checks: large files, types and functions; too many parameters; deep nesting; package dependency cycles; unused public API candidates; oversized diffs; long-lived TODO / FIXME markers; hotspots (change frequency combined with structural findings, with a fully explainable score).

Scopes: Project, Current File, Selected Files, Module, Local Changes, and Branch Diff (merge-base against your base branch, uncommitted and untracked work included).

Languages: universal checks run on any text file; structure analysis covers Java, Kotlin, Go, and JavaScript / TypeScript / JSX / TSX through optional providers that load only when the matching language plugin is present. Git-based evidence (change frequency, author counts, marker age) appears when the Git plugin is available.

Noise control: filters, per-finding ignore, pattern-based suppress rules, and exclusion globs. Findings are evidence with measured values and thresholds, never verdicts.

Repo Lens calls no AI API, stores no keys, requires no server, sends nothing anywhere, and writes the clipboard only on an explicit Copy action.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.0 — Initial public release.

  • Ten checks: large files / types / functions, too many parameters, deep nesting, package dependency cycles, unused public API candidates, oversized diffs, long-lived TODO / FIXME markers, and explainable hotspots.
  • Six scopes: Project, Current File, Selected Files, Module, Local Changes, and Branch Diff (merge-base semantics, uncommitted and untracked work included).
  • Structure analysis for Java, Kotlin, Go, and JavaScript / TypeScript through optional providers; Git-based evidence when the Git plugin is present.
  • Noise control: filters, per-finding ignore, suppress rules, exclusion globs.
  • Copy, Copy with Code, and Copy for AI export selected findings as structured Markdown — locally, with no AI provider involved.
  • English and Japanese UI.

idea-plugin.name: Spaceflow
idea-plugin.description:
Virtual desktops, but for the inside of the IDE

Boost your productivity | Protect your flow | Get back into the zone

Save and restore the editor layout of each task you work on, with its splitters, tabs and tool windows, and switch between them by shortcut.

Highlight the focused editor, tool window and caret row in colors you choose, so you can see where the focus is.

Five keyboard driven tools in one install, for people who work across many files in a large codebase or a monorepo.

Why

Do you remember how Firefox changed everything with the novice invention of something as simple as tabs in 2003?

Real work is done in dozens of files, split and arranged the way we want. Then a bug arrives, you tear it all down, and rebuilding it afterwards is a task of its own. If you move between different areas of a large codebase every day, you already know the cost.

Watch the 8 minute walkthrough

Twelve chapters, shown in a real project.

Visit spaceflow.io.momomo.com for more information.

Spaces

Instant workspace snapshots

A Space keeps a whole working context and hands it back exactly as you left it. It saves automatically and switches by shortcut. It remembers:

  • Splitters, their layout, the editors and their order
  • Tool windows, with the Project tree state and scroll position
  • Which splitter and tool window had focus
  • Run and Debug configurations
  • Breakpoints, watches and bookmarks

Keep one for backend, one for frontend, one for scripts and one for the bug that just arrived.

Slide

Fly across the IDE

Four arrow keys and a modifier move focus by direction, through every splitter and straight into the tool window on that side. There is no shortcut per tool window to remember.

Splitters

Create layouts at speed

  • Send a tab in any direction, and a splitter is created where there is none
  • Swap two whole splitters
  • Resize splitters and tool windows from the keyboard

Tabs

A pin that holds

The close key stops closing the tabs you pinned on purpose. Closing skips a pinned tab and moves to the next one, and one pinned tab per splitter keeps the layout standing.

Illuminate

See clearly what is focused

Paints the focused editor, tool window and caret row in colors you choose, so a keystroke never lands in the pane you were not looking at. Scheme colors are read first and put back afterwards.

Why it matters

It pays the first time you are interrupted, and on a large codebase it pays every hour. More so now that working with AI tools means holding several tasks open at once.

Works in every IDE

Spaceflow works on the editor itself, not on a language, so it runs in every IntelliJ based IDE from 2025.3 onwards.

Try it

There is a 30 day free trial. Nearly every shortcut can be bound right on the plugin settings page, so setting up takes minutes.

Questions, feedback, ideas and feature requests are welcome. If you cannot afford the plugin, write to us at hello@momomo.com.
