idea-plugin.name: Orgbench: Salesforce Compare & Deploy
idea-plugin.description:
Orgbench — compare two Salesforce orgs and deploy only the difference, without leaving your IDE.

Pick a source and a target — a Salesforce org or a local git repository on either side — choose the metadata you care about, and Orgbench shows what's added and what changed, component by component, with a side-by-side diff on any row. Tick what you want moved. Everything runs on your machine through the Salesforce CLI you're already authenticated with: no cloud service, no vendor account, no managed package in your org, and your metadata never leaves your laptop.

A native core, not a web app. Orgbench is a single native binary (written in Rust) driving your local Salesforce CLI — no bundled Node runtime, nothing installed in your org. It runs outside the IDE's process, so a large comparison — hundreds of components across dozens of metadata types — neither bloats the IDE's memory nor takes it down.

What you can do with it

  • Find and pick exactly what to deploy. Filter by label or API name across objects, fields, Apex, LWC/Aura, Visualforce, layouts, flows — 223 items in fifteen groups, Revenue Cloud records included; selections across types accumulate into one session you can export to a file and import back later.
  • Move the field and its permissions in one go. Field-level security, object CRUD, Apex class and Visualforce page access, tab visibility and record type visibility travel with the components you checked — additively (never revokes) or as a full sync — into exactly the Permission Sets and Profiles you select. Managed-package and standard components get rows too, as permission subjects — their permissions travel while their metadata never deploys. The part change sets and the CLI leave to you.
  • Choose how much risk you want. Validate only dry-runs the whole package against the target. All or nothing sends it as one deployment that rolls back completely on any failure. Best-effort sends the same package but keeps every component Salesforce accepted and reports the ones it rejected — so a big package lands in one pass, and your next run only deals with what failed. Quick Deploy promotes an already-validated package without uploading or re-running tests.
  • Fix it in the diff, ship the fix. The source side of the diff view is editable for any component whose row is a single document — Apex, Visualforce pages, objects, fields, flows, layouts and more — and the deployment sends your edited version. The source org is never modified, the edit is marked on the row and can be reverted, and it lives only inside that comparison session. Bundles and multi-component container files stay read-only.
  • Deploy one field on a page layout. Switch page layouts to "Select fields and related lists" and move a single field or related list into the higher org without touching anything else on that layout.
  • Use git as either end. Org → org, org → git, git → org, git → git. A git target ends in one local commit containing only what you selected — Orgbench never pushes and never switches your branches.
  • Let dependencies pick themselves. Checking a field pulls in its missing object; checking a list view pulls in the fields it references — visibly, as rows you can uncheck.

What it never does

Never deletes metadata in the target — a component that exists only in the target produces no row and is never touched. The one deletion is a Revenue Cloud record you mark with Fix on the Target health check screen. Never deploys managed-package or standard-object metadata — such rows exist to carry permissions, and a managed or standard field deploys at most its two history-tracking toggles, spliced into the target's own document, never the source definition. Never creates an object you didn't tick: auto-selected dependencies are visible rows you can uncheck before deploying. Never touches your tokens — authentication stays in the Salesforce CLI, and diagnostics are sanitized before you see them. Partial deployment happens only in the mode built for it: Best-effort keeps what succeeds because you chose that trade-off — and by default it is not offered against a recognized production org, unless Allow Best Effort against production was on when Compare was pressed — while All or nothing rolls back the whole package on any failure. A package carrying Apex or Flows always passes through the test-selection screen before it goes to any org.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2024.2 or newer.
  • Salesforce CLI installed, with at least one authenticated org — or use the built-in "+" button to log in through the CLI's own browser flow.
  • macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel), Windows x64, or Linux x64. Linux arm64 is not supported.

Privacy and licensing

  • No telemetry. Nothing about you or your orgs is collected or transmitted — see the Privacy Policy and the EULA.
  • Orgbench is free during early access. A paid tier for advanced features is planned; nothing is gated today. License validation is fully offline — the key is checked locally and is never transmitted.

Salesforce is a trademark of Salesforce, Inc. Orgbench is an independent product and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Salesforce.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.1.4

Released 2026-09-25 for IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code. This release covers everything that changed since 0.1.1, the previous public release.

Orgbench 0.1.4 brings Revenue Cloud into the compare-and-deploy workflow: pricing metadata with its dependencies selected for you, and Product Bundles and Constraint Models transferred between two orgs as records. Permission Sets, Permission Set Groups and Profiles are now their own comparison types, Best Effort recovers from more of the rejections Salesforce answers with, and Linux x64 is now supported. As before, everything runs locally over your own Salesforce CLI.

Highlights

  • Revenue Cloud pricing metadata. Context Definitions, Decision Tables, pricing procedure versions, Pricing Recipes and eight more pricing types can be compared and deployed. Check the top of a chain, such as a Pricing Recipe, and the components it needs are checked for you. Every one of those checks is visible and can be removed.
  • Product Bundles and Constraint Models between two orgs. Both are compared as documents built from the org's records and deployed in Best Effort. Prepare Orgs sets up the external keys used to match records between the orgs. The Target health check screen shows what in the target would block the transfer before anything is sent.
  • Permission Sets, Permission Set Groups and Profiles as their own types. They are compared and deployed as whole documents. In Best Effort a Permission Set Group document is trimmed to what the target knows; a Permission Set or Profile document is trimmed the same way when both source and target are orgs. The row's message names what was left out.
  • Best Effort that recovers more often. It makes a limited number of retries for known rejections. A new setting lets you use Best Effort against a production org if you choose to (see Allow Best Effort against production below).
  • Linux x64. It is the fourth supported platform in both editors.
  • Less clicking. Orgbench remembers the source and target aliases you used last. A folder can be made into a git target with one button. In IntelliJ, pressing a deploy button starts the deployment right away.

Revenue Cloud pricing metadata

Turn on the Revenue Cloud category in the settings to use it. It is off by default. In IntelliJ it is under Settings | Tools | Orgbench | Metadata categories. In VS Code, add RevenueCloud to orgbench.metadataCategories.

  • Twelve pricing metadata types. Context Definition, Decision Table, Decision Table Dataset Link, Decision Matrix Definition and its versions, Expression Set Definitions, Expression Set Message Token, Expression Set Object Alias, Pricing Action Parameters, Pricing Recipe, Procedure Plan Definition and Product Attribute Set.

  • Pricing procedures travel as versions. The Expression Set Definitions entry lists pricing procedure versions. If the target doesn't have the procedure's definition yet, checking a version also checks that definition. The definition is then sent without its other versions, so an org target gets only the versions you checked, and the row's message says so.

  • Dependencies are checked for you without the Tooling API. Orgbench reads each source document to find what it references:

    • a Pricing Recipe checks its pricing procedure and decision tables;
    • a pricing procedure checks the decision tables its lookup steps name and its context definition;
    • a Context Definition checks the custom fields and objects it reads data from, and the other context definitions it maps to;
    • a Decision Table checks its fields and source object;
    • a Dataset Link checks its table and source object.

    With an org as the source, the comparison also fetches those referenced components. With a git source, the dependencies are checked only among rows already in the table.

  • Context Definitions fit the target. With an org on both sides, entries that read fields the target doesn't have are left out when a Context Definition is deployed, and the row's message lists them. When the source org runs a newer Salesforce release than the target, the document's release version is changed to the target's. Deploying a context always creates a new version and never deletes or deactivates an existing one.

  • Pricing procedure activation (Best Effort, against a target that accepts records). A version can be active in the source while the target runs a different version as active. In that case the version is sent as inactive. Once it deploys, Orgbench deactivates the target's old version and activates the new one, and the row's message says what happened. In Validate and Deploy (all or nothing), nothing is rewritten or activated. The target must be confirmed non-production, or production with Allow Best Effort against production on when Compare was pressed.

  • Older target releases. Below Metadata API 68.0, a usageSubtype or pricingUsageSubType value of RevenueCloud is removed from the document before it is sent, and the row's message names what was removed.

Product Bundles and Constraint Models

The Revenue Cloud category also lists Product Bundle and Constraint Model. Their rows are records, not metadata files. They are compared between two orgs only, never with a git repository, and need Metadata API 67.0 or newer.

  • What you compare. Orgbench builds a document for each bundle from its catalog records. The document includes classifications, component groups, related components, child products, selling model options and price book entries. A model's document includes its definition, its versions, the CML text of each version and its tags. Open the diff to see the document.

  • Dependencies. Checking a bundle adds the constraint models that tag it to the comparison. Those models are checked if they have an active version in the source. A bundle also checks any child product that is itself a bundle.

  • Deploying. When a record row is checked, only Best Effort is offered, because records have no dry run and cannot be rolled back. Bundle records are sent through the REST API before the metadata package, layer by layer. Records in the target are matched by external key first and then by natural identity (a name, a code or the parent chain). The model is deployed as its definition, followed by its tags, its CML and the activation of its source-active version. The Metadata API package itself never switches the target's active version: every version is sent inactive, and the version the target currently runs as active is left out of the package. After the tags and CML, Orgbench activates the version that is active in the source, deactivating the target's current one first, and the row's message says what happened.

  • Prepare Orgs. The Revenue Cloud category also lists 33 configuration objects. Prepare Orgs writes a shared external key on their records in both orgs, so records can be matched between the orgs. It is shown on the selection screen when an enabled category contains records, and it asks you to confirm, naming both orgs, before it runs. It writes only the key values, and when it creates a new key field, it gives your own profile access to that field. It deletes nothing, and running it again changes nothing. It is the only operation in Orgbench that writes to the source org. Once both orgs already have their keys, the button shrinks to a refresh icon.

  • Target health check. Before a Product Bundle deploys, Orgbench reads the target and makes the same decisions the transfer will make. If it finds nothing, the screen does not appear. Otherwise it lists three kinds of findings, before anything is sent:

    • target records that the target will refuse to save;
    • duplicate records the transfer can't choose between;
    • missing relationship types, selling models or price books.

    Each finding says what to do. A Record Id column links to each record in the target org. The buttons are Fix, Deploy without fixing, Re-check and Cancel.

  • What Fix deletes. Fix deletes only the findings you left checked. They can only be records of three leaf objects: product related components, product selling model options and price book entries. Orgbench deletes them by the record IDs it read during the check. Deleting is immediate and cannot be undone: the records are created anew only by the deployment that follows, so if you stop before it runs, they stay deleted. Constraint model tags that address a deleted record are deleted by Salesforce with it; they come back only for the models deployed in the same run, and each finding says how many such tags it carries. Orgbench then checks the target again, and you press Deploy yourself. Apart from Fix, transferring records never deletes anything in the target: not a record, a tag or a version.

  • Production. By default, records are never sent to an org Orgbench recognizes as production, and never to a target whose type it could not confirm.

Permission Sets, Permission Set Groups and Profiles

These types are in the Security & Sharing category.

  • Permission Set. The whole document is sent, and it replaces the permission set in the target.
  • Permission Set Group. Before it is sent, the group is trimmed to the permission sets the target has or that this deployment creates, and the row's message names what was left out. Checking a group also checks the permission sets it needs that the target doesn't have yet. A set the target already has is never redeployed this way.
  • Profile. The document is merged into the target profile rather than replacing it. You can create a custom profile. A standard profile can't be added and its row says why.
  • Trimmed to the target in Best Effort, org to org. With an org on both sides, a Permission Set or Profile document drops the user permissions, and the references to fields, objects, classes, pages, tabs and other components, that the target doesn't know. Anything sent in the same deployment is never cut. The row's message lists what was left out.
  • The permission transfer. A container that is deployed by its own comparison row is unavailable on the Select Permission Containers screen, and so is a new permission set whose license the target lacks. The reason is shown on the row. A permission set that the transfer creates now carries the source's description and license. The container screen appears only when a checked row actually carries permissions to transfer.

Best Effort

  • Limited retries of the affected rows. Best Effort against an org now retries after specific rejections, resending only the rejected rows:
    • a Permission Set Group, once;
    • a Context Definition, up to three times;
    • a Permission Set, up to three times;
    • a Profile, up to five times;
    • rows that fail with only Salesforce's generic "An unexpected error occurred", once, together.
  • Retry rows alone. The new setting Retry rows alone after a Salesforce unexpected error (Best Effort) is off by default. Turn it on to deploy each row still failing with the generic error once more on its own. With it off, the row's message names the setting.
  • Allow Best Effort against production. This new setting — Allow Best Effort against production (Revenue Cloud) in IntelliJ, orgbench.allowBestEffortOnProduction in VS Code — is off by default. It makes Best Effort, and the record transfer, available against an org Orgbench recognizes as production. It also lets Orgbench switch the active version of a deployed pricing procedure or Constraint Model in that org. Orgbench reads it when you press Compare. Partial deployments can leave data incomplete, so use it with care.
  • Object children fail together. Salesforce deploys an object's fields and children as one component. When it rejects one of them, the others are now reported as failed as well, with the reason, instead of as succeeded.

Everyday workflow

  • Remembered aliases. The source and target aliases you picked last are selected again the next time Orgbench opens. Only aliases are remembered, and only on this machine. A git repository is not remembered.
  • Initialize a git repository. If the folder you chose as a git target is not a repository yet, an Initialize a Git repository here button appears. Orgbench asks you to confirm, naming the full path, and then runs only git init: no commit, no branch and no push.
  • Pasted repository paths. The path field now accepts surrounding quotes, a leading ~ and invisible characters copied along with the path. If git itself can't run on the machine, the message says so and explains how to fix it.
  • Reload Orgs also reloads the component list of the type on screen.
  • Metadata API version. A comparison and its deployment now use the lower of the two orgs' Metadata API versions, so a type that only a newer release offers can be fetched.
  • Editing large documents. In the diff view you can edit a metadata document of up to 16 MiB. Code bodies are still limited to 1,000,000 characters.
  • Dependency cascades for more metadata. A custom field checks its global value set. A lookup field checks the object it points to and the fields its filter names. A roll-up summary field checks the fields it summarizes and filters on. A custom metadata record checks its type and fields.

Changes in behavior since 0.1.1

  • The default permission transfer mode is now Additive permissions in both editors. It was Do not transfer permissions. If you want to keep Do not transfer permissions, check the setting after upgrading: a mode you never changed from the old default follows the new default.
  • 27 metadata types were removed from the type list. They either cannot be transferred between orgs or are meaningless to transfer:
    • Auth Providers, External Auth Identity Providers, External Data Sources and SAML SSO Configs;
    • Inbound Network Connections and Outbound Network Connections;
    • Person Account Owner Power Users, My Domain Discoverable Logins, Profile Password Policies and Profile Session Settings;
    • Apex Email Notifications and Feature Parameter Booleans, Dates and Integers;
    • Lightning Bolts, Networks and Digital Experience Configs;
    • Call Ctr Agent Fav Trfr Dests, Service AI Setup Definitions, Service AI Setup Fields, Conversation Vendor Infos and Conversation Channel Definitions;
    • UI Preview Message Tab Defs, Wave Analytic Asset Collections, Analytic Snapshots, Translations and Custom Indexes.
  • Analytics dashboards, visualizations and workspaces, and External Data Connectors, moved to Marketing & Data Cloud. This category now appears in the settings and is off by default. If you used those types, turn it on.
  • Industries is now part of Revenue Cloud. A saved Industries category is read as Revenue Cloud.
  • IntelliJ: the Confirm Deployment dialog is gone. Pressing Validate, Deploy or Best Effort starts the deployment right away, without a confirmation dialog. VS Code already worked this way.
  • The Select Permission Containers screen opens only when it has something to do. A transfer mode must be on, and at least one checked row must carry permissions. Otherwise the screen before it is the last step.

Fixes

  • Transferring permissions from a git repository source into an org target no longer stops with an internal error.
  • When loading the component list fails, the error now shows Salesforce's reason instead of a CLI "update available" notice.
  • Unnamed fields and children of an object whose sibling Salesforce rejected are no longer reported as succeeded (see Best Effort).

Requirements

  • IntelliJ: IntelliJ IDEA 2024.2 or newer, or another IDE built on the IntelliJ platform.
  • VS Code: VS Code 1.85 or newer. Install the VSIX for your platform: orgbench-darwin-arm64.vsix, orgbench-darwin-x64.vsix, orgbench-win32-x64.vsix or orgbench-linux-x64.vsix.
  • Platforms: macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel), Windows x64 or Linux x64. Linux on ARM is not supported.
  • Salesforce CLI (sf), installed and signed in to at least one org under an alias.
  • Product Bundles and Constraint Models need two orgs on Metadata API 67.0 or newer.
  • Licensing: Orgbench is free during early access, and nothing is gated today. License checks are fully offline.

0.1.1 — early access

First public release.

  • Compare Salesforce metadata between two orgs, an org and a git branch, or two branches, in any combination.
  • Up to 172 metadata types across 14 groups, with row-level diffs and automatic dependency selection.
  • Three deploy modes: best-effort, validate-only (with Quick Deploy), and all-or-nothing, with an Apex test-selection screen.
  • Transfer six kinds of permissions — fields, objects, Apex classes, Visualforce pages, tabs, and record types — including managed and standard components, with a container preview screen.
  • Edit any single-document component in the diff window before deploying.
  • Export and import a session as a JSON file to resume or share a comparison.
  • A VS Code extension sharing the same native core.
  • No telemetry and no vendor cloud: everything runs on your machine through your local Salesforce CLI, and license validation is fully offline.

idea-plugin.name: Flexible for Spryker
idea-plugin.description:
Spryker Commerce OS development for IntelliJ IDEA and PhpStorm. Edit Transfer XML, OMS state machines, and Propel schemas with completion, documentation, validation, and rename. Preview state machines as graphs, control the Docker SDK, debug with Xdebug, profile, and browse modules. For Spryker B2B, B2C, and Marketplace shops.

Unofficial third-party plugin - not affiliated with or endorsed by Spryker.

We are a young project and your feedback shapes the plugin. Feature requests, bug reports, or just your opinion - leave a review, open an issue on GitHub, or email us at info@ilscipio.com.

Language Support

  • Transfer XML (.transfer.xml) - syntax highlighting, completion, validation, structure view
  • OMS State Machine XML - state machine definition support with cross-referencing
  • Propel Schema XML (.schema.xml) - database schema support with validation

Framework Integration

  • Auto-detection of Spryker projects via composer.json
  • Spryker SDK management with Docker SDK support
  • Module marketplace for browsing and installing Spryker packages
  • Spryker-aware PHP completion and navigation (PhpStorm)

Developer Tools

  • Xdebug remote debugging with Docker path mapping
  • Xdebug profiler integration with cachegrind parsing
  • Guided setup wizard for new users
  • Notification system for project events

Code Intelligence

  • YAML-based documentation on hover
  • Code inspections for common Spryker issues
  • Live templates for rapid development
  • Find Usages and Rename refactoring

idea-plugin.name: Scratchpad Notes
idea-plugin.description:
A notepad that lives in your IDE, with the conversions you would otherwise open a browser tab, an online formatter or Notepad for. Paste a payload, read it, transform it, compare it - without leaving the window you are already working in.

Notes are plain files in a folder you choose, so they survive restarts, can be backed up, searched and version controlled like anything else on disk. Open the panel with Alt+Shift+N; every action also lives in a searchable command palette (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+A), so nothing has to be memorised.

Notes

  • Multi-tab scratchpad with syntax highlighting for JSON, XML, SQL, YAML, HTML, Markdown and JavaScript, plus folding and structure breadcrumbs
  • Language detection on paste; a tab you set by hand stays as you set it
  • Drag and drop files into the panel, save any tab back out, or open a note as a normal editor tab
  • Send the current editor selection straight to the scratchpad

Conversions

  • JSON and XML: format, minify, validate, escape and unescape - one shortcut formats whichever of the two the tab actually holds
  • Base64 for text and for files, URL encode/decode, JWT header and payload inspection with readable expiry times
  • Case conversion (including Turkish-locale upper/lower), sort, de-duplicate, trim, number and join lines, text statistics
  • MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512 digests and UUID generation

Compare

  • The IDE's own diff viewer: compare two tabs, or the current tab against the clipboard, with side-by-side or unified layout

e-Documents (UBL-TR)

For teams working with Turkish e-Invoice, e-Archive and e-Despatch documents:

  • Convert a UBL-TR document to JSON shaped like the UBLDocument model - and back to XML. Invoice, CreditNote, DespatchAdvice and ReceiptAdvice are supported
  • Replace embedded base64 blobs (presentation XSLT, attached PDFs, logos) with short placeholders so the document becomes readable, or extract each blob to a file named after its mime type
  • Validate against Schematron: both hand written .sch schemas and the rule sets that ship already compiled to XSLT. The report lists every violation with its line, and the caret jumps to the first one

Everything runs locally. Nothing is uploaded, and no document ever leaves your machine. This is a reading and validation aid, not an official validator.

Bundles Saxon-HE (Mozilla Public License 2.0), which is what runs compiled Schematron rule sets.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.3

  • Preview on the toolbar shows a UBL-TR document rendered with the presentation stylesheet it carries - or a page of HTML as it stands - inside the IDE, in the IDE's own browser engine, with a button to open it in the system browser. And Export as PDF... writes that same rendering to a file. Turkish letters are covered by system fonts, so the words that identify a document are not broken.
  • The toolbar is shorter: the tab commands moved into one menu, as did the view toggles and folding, and entries that were variants of a neighbouring one (single hashes besides SHA-256 and "All Digests", URL-safe base64, random hex, reverse/join/number lines) are gone.
  • An eye appears next to the syntax box when the note is something that can be shown as a page - which is also how you see, without opening anything, whether an XML carries its own layout.
  • Fixed the threading error logged when a tab was clicked on 2025.3 and newer builds, and the toolbar no longer decides what to enable on the UI thread - which is what the IDE was reporting as seconds of EDT time while it started up.

1.0.2

  • The tab strip no longer reaches into the platform's internal API, which is what the Marketplace verifier objected to. It is built through the public interface instead; the only visible difference is that "New Tab" now lives on the toolbar rather than as a "+" at the end of the strip.

1.0.1

  • Fixed the panel failing to open on 2025.3 and newer builds, the errors logged when a command was picked from the toolbar menu or a file dropped onto the panel, and the blank tab that could follow a drop.
  • Only the four most recently used tabs keep an editor; language detection no longer copies the whole note after every pause in typing.
  • UBL-TR: the document root is read from the payload instead of always writing an Invoice, and you are asked where the payload leaves a real choice. Despatch advice shipments and the fields only the older backend model carries are converted in both directions.

idea-plugin.name: Spring Service Navigator
idea-plugin.description:
See your microservice call graph — works in Community Edition. Spring Service Navigator maps every inter-service HTTP call across all modules in your workspace and lets you navigate between callers and endpoints in one click. No running servers, no instrumentation, no configuration required.

Service Map — workspace-level dependency graph

The headline feature: a dedicated tool window that builds a complete picture of your microservice architecture from source code alone.

  • Service Map — hierarchical call graph grouped by source service and target service; double-click any call to navigate to the caller
  • Endpoints — complete list of all REST endpoints across every service, with live search: type a URL fragment, HTTP verb, or service name to filter instantly
  • Statistics — KPI cards (services, endpoints, calls), breakdown by HTTP client type and HTTP verb, sortable per-service inbound/outbound call table
  • Dependency Matrix — colour-coded service-to-service call count grid; instantly see which services are tightly coupled
  • Unresolved Callers — calls that could not be matched to any known endpoint are surfaced here with a warning icon, so broken or stale URLs never hide in plain sight
  • Dependency Graph — a visual topology diagram of your microservices, with edge thickness scaling to call volume; click any node or edge to filter the Service Map

Endpoint search (Search Everywhere + Ctrl+Alt+E)

Press Shift Shift and open the Endpoints tab, or press Ctrl+Alt+E directly. Type any combination of HTTP verb, URL fragment, service name, or controller method name (e.g. post order, users/{id}, get payment) and jump straight to the controller method. Path variables are treated as wildcards on both sides, so users/{userId} finds /api/users/{id}.

Instant cross-service navigation

Every RestTemplate, WebClient, RestClient, @FeignClient, and @HttpExchange call site gets a gutter icon. One click jumps directly to the controller method in the target service — even if it lives in a different module on the other side of the workspace. URL path variables, String.format patterns, UriComponentsBuilder chains, and lambda URI builders are all resolved automatically.

Know who calls your endpoints

Every @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and other endpoint methods get a reverse-navigation gutter icon. Click it to see every caller across every service in the workspace — with service name, class, and line number. Essential when you need to understand the blast radius of a contract change before you make it.

Ctrl+Click from URL strings

URL string literals and OpenAPI YAML path entries are treated as navigable references. Ctrl+Click on "/api/orders/{id}" in any Java file or OpenAPI spec jumps directly to the matching controller method — the same way you navigate between classes.

Full HTTP client coverage

  • RestTemplate — getForObject, postForEntity, exchange, and all other methods
  • WebClient (Project Reactor) — fluent .uri().retrieve().bodyToMono() chains
  • RestClient (Spring 6.1 / Spring Boot 3.2+) — fluent .uri().retrieve().body() chains
  • @FeignClient — declarative interface methods with all Spring MVC mapping annotations
  • @HttpExchange / @GetExchange / @PostExchange (Spring 6.1+) — declarative HTTP interfaces with type-level URL prefix support

Works across separate repos, not just one workspace

Microservices kept in separate git repos are covered too. Attach a sibling repo as an additional content root of the IntelliJ window you already have open (plain IntelliJ project structure, zero plugin configuration) — or, if each service is opened in its own separate IntelliJ window, list sibling repos under Settings → Tools → Spring Service Navigator → External Repo Paths. Point at an individual repo, or at a base directory containing several — nested services are discovered automatically. Gutter icons, reverse navigation, and the Service Map all include them.

Works on the source tree — no runtime required

Analysis is powered by JavaParser and runs entirely on .java source files. The plugin never compiles, instruments, or runs any of your code. Background scanning keeps the IDE fully responsive — results appear within seconds of opening a project, and all scans show a cancellable progress bar.

Supports

  • Spring Boot 2.x and 3.x
  • Multi-module Gradle and Maven workspaces, and microservices split across separate git repos
  • OpenAPI 3 YAML specifications
  • IntelliJ IDEA Community and Ultimate 2024.3 and later

Try it

Want to see it in action before pointing it at your own codebase? Clone the example workspaces — three ready-made multi-service Spring Boot projects covering all four HTTP client types and both layered and hexagonal architectures.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0 — Cross-repo scanning, smarter URL resolution, faster scans

  • Cross-repo scanning — works whether your services live in one workspace or several separate repos. Attach a sibling repo as an additional content root of the current IntelliJ window (zero configuration), or, for services each opened in their own window, list them under Settings → Tools → Spring Service Navigator → External Repo Paths — point at an individual repo or a base directory containing several; nested services are discovered automatically
  • Reverse-navigation caller tooltip now groups callers by service and client type with a rich, color-coded layout, and the Service Map tool window gained a sixth tab: Dependency Graph
  • Ternary URL resolution (cond ? "/a" : "/b") — when both branches point at the same endpoint, one gutter icon navigates straight there; when they point at two genuinely different endpoints, clicking the icon opens a picker to choose which one, and both relationships now show up correctly in the CLI/JSON report, the Service Map tool window, and each endpoint's own inbound-caller popup
  • @ConfigurationProperties and hand-written getter methods are now resolved as base-URL sources, the same way @Value fields already were
  • Config-sourced base URLs are resolved against every application-{profile}.* file present, not just the default application.*, and a nested ${ENV_VAR:default} placeholder's default value is now used
  • A variable reassigned partway through a method (url = "..."; ...; url = "...";) now resolves each call against the value actually in effect at that point, instead of one value for the whole method
  • restTemplate.exchange(url, method, ...)'s HTTP method is now resolved from the runtime argument in the gutter icon too, matching the CLI/core scanner — previously it was hardcoded to GET, which could point the icon at the wrong endpoint when a path mapped both GET and POST
  • Fixed inconsistent/duplicate gutter icons on some ternary expressions
  • RestClient call sites are no longer misclassified as WebClient calls, undercounting RestClient entries in the tool window and reverse-navigation index
  • Gutter icons refresh automatically on content-root/module changes — no IDE restart required
  • Large-workspace scans are significantly faster — a shared parse pass now feeds all detectors instead of each independently re-parsing the same files, with no change in results

1.0.0 — Initial release

  • Gutter icons on every RestTemplate, WebClient, RestClient, @FeignClient, and @HttpExchange/@GetExchange/… call site — one click navigates to the target @RestController endpoint across any module in the workspace
  • Reverse-navigation gutter icons on @RestController endpoint methods — click to see every caller across all services, with service name, class, and line number
  • Service Map tool window with five tabs: Service Map, Endpoints, Statistics, Dependency Matrix, and Unresolved Callers
  • Endpoint search — press Ctrl+Alt+E or use the Search Everywhere Endpoints tab to search by HTTP verb, URL fragment, service name, or method name; path variables are treated as wildcards
  • Live search field in the Endpoints tab of the tool window for instant filtering
  • Ctrl+Click navigation from URL string literals in Java source files and from path entries in OpenAPI 3 YAML specifications
  • URL resolution handles path variables, String.format patterns, UriComponentsBuilder chains, and lambda URI builders
  • Cancellable progress bar for all background scans — safe to cancel at any time without IDE freeze

  • Scan error notifications via the balloon notification system; unparseable files reported in the statistics panel

  • Supports Spring Boot 2.x and 3.x, multi-module Gradle and Maven workspaces, IntelliJ IDEA Community and Ultimate 2024.3 and later

idea-plugin.name: Coharyn Impact
idea-plugin.description:
Know what your code change will affect before you ship it.

You changed one Java method. Which controllers, services, entities, config keys and tests does that touch? Coharyn Impact reconstructs the evidence around your uncommitted changes and shows the blast radius — with a transparent risk score — before the code reaches review or production.

Assess Current Changes

Coharyn maps your Git diff to semantic symbol changes (a signature change is not a body edit; a rename is not silence), then rebuilds the relationships around them:

  • direct and transitive callers and references,
  • interface implementations and overrides,
  • Spring components in the chain — detected from real annotations, never naming conventions,
  • JPA persistence-model impact,
  • configuration keys and their @Value / @ConfigurationProperties consumers,
  • related tests — and affected paths where no related test was discovered.

Assess Selected Symbol — free forever

Place the caret on any method, class or field → Coharyn → Assess Impact. Direct relationships, evidence view and source navigation, permanently free.

Evidence, not guesses

Every relationship carries its source location and discovery mechanism, labelled CONFIRMED (resolved by the IDE's semantic index), STRONG (structural) or HEURISTIC (convention — always visibly flagged). Analysis is deterministic — no LLM, no cloud. Where evidence is missing, Coharyn says exactly that: "Not established from available evidence."

A risk score you can audit

Change Impact Risk is a 0–100 score from a documented, deterministic model. Expand Why this score? to see every contributing factor.

Change Pack (Pro)

Export the whole assessment as Markdown — changed symbols, dependency evidence, potential breaking changes, relevant tests, recommended validation, risk breakdown — and paste it into your pull request, Jira ticket or change record.

Privacy: your source code never leaves your IDE

All analysis runs locally. No network calls, no telemetry, no AI services, no code upload. The plugin ships zero third-party dependencies and no network code. Licensing is handled entirely by your JetBrains account.

Supported environment

IntelliJ IDEA 2025.3 – 2026.2 (Community and Ultimate) · Java · Spring / Spring Boot · JPA/Hibernate · JUnit · .properties / .yml / .yaml · any VCS your IDE supports. Kotlin files are detected and listed; semantic Kotlin analysis is on the roadmap (Beta).

Free vs Pro

Free: selected-symbol assessment, direct relationships, evidence, navigation.
Pro (7-day free trial): Assess Current Changes, full impact depth, Change Pack export.

Website · Documentation · Support · Privacy
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.0

  • Initial release: Assess Current Changes (Pro) and Assess Selected Symbol (Free).
  • Java, Spring, JPA, configuration and test impact analysis with evidence-backed relationships.
  • Deterministic, transparent risk scoring with full breakdown.
  • Change Pack Markdown export for pull requests and change records.
  • 100% local analysis — your source code never leaves your IDE.

idea-plugin.name: Run Configuration Doctor
idea-plugin.description:
Preflight diagnostics for JetBrains Run Configurations.

Run Configuration Doctor checks local configuration prerequisites before execution and reports concise, actionable results.

Freemium: all existing FREE diagnostics and workflow features remain free. An optional JetBrains Marketplace PRO license or trial unlocks the advanced checks below; no separate plugin is needed.

FREE

  • Validates working directories, executables, environment variables, files, macros, before-launch tasks, ports, and optional Docker/Kubernetes connectivity, including WSL-backed IntelliJ Docker servers.
  • FREE environment templates reuse required variable names from explicitly selected .env.example files without loading sample values. Local dependency checks verify that declared TCP ports accept loopback connections.
  • Creates and immediately opens .run-doctor.yml, or safely adds a commented starter section when the selected configuration is missing.
  • Provides theme-aware severity colors, sortable results, project-local reversible finding ignores, and standalone HTML report export.
  • Has no telemetry or uploads and uses only fixed, bounded local CLI probes when Docker or Kubernetes checks are configured.

PRO — optional license or trial

  • Diagnose all project Run Configurations in one cancellable pass, with a health overview, per-configuration details, and a standalone HTML export.
  • Docker Compose file/service validation, running-container health, and required environment-variable names in actual service containers.
  • Kubernetes required-resource existence/readiness and workload environment names, including ConfigMap and Secret key names without reading their values.

Use More Actions… → Manage PRO License… in Run Doctor to open JetBrains license management. Without a confirmed entitlement, PRO checks are skipped and FREE features keep working. License activation and related server communication are handled by the IDE; Run Doctor verifies the IDE's signed confirmation locally.

Optional project configuration

Add .run-doctor.yml to the project root when requirements cannot be discovered automatically. The configuration name must exactly match IntelliJ IDEA.

version: 1
runConfigurations:
  "Backend":
    requiredFiles:
      - .env
    ports:
      - 8080
    docker:
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Changes since 26.36.23

This update adds FREE environment templates and local dependency checks, plus a PRO overview for all configurations.

  • FREE: selected diagnoses now show OUT OF DATE after the IDE observes edits to .run-doctor.yml, attached environment files, or selected environment templates. Old findings are cleared and active diagnosis is cancelled. Save unsaved inputs, then choose Run Diagnosis; checks never restart automatically. Outdated reports cannot be exported or ignored.
  • PRO batch HTML reports now color health and severity in light and dark themes; the overview table remains usable in narrow windows.
  • Cancelling diagnosis now stops the running Docker/kubectl probe and prevents follow-up probes within that check. Existing application and service processes are left running.
  • Environment checks now preserve uncertainty through variable references and ordered attached files. Required variables affected by scripts or unreadable sources are shown as unconfirmed instead of a false READY or a definite missing-value error.
  • PRO: diagnose all project Run Configurations from More Actions… or Tools. Review each configuration’s health and findings, cancel with clearly marked partial results, and export the overview and details as one HTML report. The IDE selection stays unchanged.
  • A missing environment variable is now reported as unconfirmed when an attached script could supply it, including blank Run Configuration values. Diagnosis never executes environment scripts.
  • FREE: reuse .env.example-style files through environmentTemplates to find missing required variables without copying names into YAML. Sample values are never loaded or shown.
  • FREE: check that databases, caches, and other explicitly declared requiredLocalPorts accept local TCP connections. The bounded check sends no application data and does not claim application health.
  • Introduces an optional JetBrains Marketplace PRO license or trial for advanced Docker Compose/container and Kubernetes resource/environment checks. All existing FREE diagnostics, templates, finding ignores, and HTML exports remain free.
  • Adds Manage PRO License… under More Actions… and Tools → Run Configuration Doctor. Without a confirmed entitlement, only PRO checks are skipped; choose Run Diagnosis after activation to refresh the edition and results.
  • Limits Docker/kubectl output during capture and reports oversized responses as unconfirmed instead of trusting partial data. Other confirmed errors and warnings remain visible.
  • Clears stale results when you edit or rename the selected Run Configuration, updates its displayed name immediately, and stops cancelled diagnoses before they start later checks.
  • Fixes Windows environment-variable checks when names use different capitalization, including attached files, inherited values, blank overrides, and variable references.
  • Adds a purple unknown-result counter to the tool window and HTML export. An unconfirmed check now produces overall UNKNOWN health instead of a misleading READY result.
  • Adds color-coded overall READY, WARNING, NOT READY, or UNKNOWN health to standalone HTML reports.
  • Honors each Run Configuration's own PATH and Windows PATHEXT during executable lookup, including disabled parent-environment inheritance. Relative PATH entries now use the configuration's working directory.
  • Limits reversible ignores to actionable failed or unknown findings; stored ignores remain dormant while a check is healthy or inapplicable.
  • Avoids false duplicate-path warnings when one file intentionally has different roles, while still detecting repeated declarations within the same source.
  • Preserves every source and occurrence for missing path references, and lists every affected configuration field when the same unresolved macro is reused.
  • Keeps the remaining diagnosis running when one check cannot determine whether it applies, reporting that check as UNKNOWN without exposing its internal error.

idea-plugin.name: Next Key
idea-plugin.description:
Hold a modifier key and see what you can press next.

Hold Ctrl for half a second and a panel lists every shortcut that starts with Ctrl. Keep holding and add Alt — the list becomes the Ctrl+Alt shortcuts. Let go and it disappears. Shortcuts that take two presses work the same way: press the first, and every key that can follow appears.

The list is read from your own keymap, so it matches the bindings you actually have, including the ones other plugins add. Entries are grouped by what they do, and keys are labelled the way they are on your keyboard.

The panel starts out listing the shortcuts most people use. In Settings | Tools | Next Key you can show or hide any shortcut, rename one, move it to another category, change how long a modifier has to be held, and adjust transparency.

Available in English and Simplified Chinese. Source and issue tracker on GitHub.

idea-plugin.name: Python Environments
idea-plugin.description:
Manage Python versions, virtual environments and dependencies without leaving your IDE. Python Environments brings installed interpreters, project environments and packages into one tool window, connected to PyCharm's native interpreter settings and code insight.

  • Packages first: browse installed packages, install or update a package, and run your project's native dependency workflow.
  • Know your environment: see SDK names, Python versions, paths and disk usage. Inspect matching project, module and Run/Debug references.
  • Choose your Python: browse available versions, install an interpreter and create an environment at your chosen location.
  • Keep your tools: use uv, pyenv, mise, asdf, Homebrew, Python Install Manager, Conda, Mamba or Micromamba where supported by the host.
  • Use native dependency managers: pip, uv, Poetry, Pipenv, PDM, Hatch, Pixi and pip-tools workflows keep their own environment and manifest rules.
  • Protect installations in use: removal checks known IDE and environment references and verifies the owning manager.

Python and dependency managers are selected independently. Automatic detection explains ambiguous evidence; executable paths and manager setup live in Settings. Missing uv and Unix pyenv can be installed from the plugin; other managers retain their official installer.

Open View > Tool Windows > Python Environments in a Python-enabled IDE. Select an existing environment or create one, then use Packages, Environments and Python versions.

Commands run on the project host. Docker, WSL and SSH interpreter adapters are not included. Removal checks cover known references, not every closed project or running process.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.0

  • Manage Python versions, virtual environments and packages in one IDE tool window.
  • Switch the native project interpreter and keep package metadata and code insight in sync.
  • Inspect environment SDK names, Python versions, disk usage and matching project or Run/Debug references.
  • Install Python from supported managers, browse version catalogues and create environments at a chosen path.

idea-plugin.name: FieldColorizer
idea-plugin.description:
FieldColorizer helps you visually distinguish application layers by highlighting class/field names based on custom suffixes.

Right-click any field, define a suffix (e.g. Dao, Repository, Validator), pick a color — and every field matching that suffix gets colorized in the editor.

Features

  • Custom, user-defined suffix rules
  • Per-suffix color persisted between IDE restarts
  • Works on both field name and field type

How to use

  1. Place the caret directly on a field name in your Java code, for example the userDao part of private UserDao userDao;
  2. Right-click to open the editor context menu
  3. Scroll to the bottom of the menu and click Field Colorizer (it appears as a regular menu item, not a submenu)
  4. A dialog appears:
    • If this suffix (e.g. Dao) is new, you'll first be asked to confirm or edit it
    • Then a color picker opens — choose a color and press OK
  5. All fields whose name or type ends with that suffix are immediately highlighted with the chosen color
  6. Repeat steps 1–4 for other suffixes (Repository, Validator, etc.) to color-code your architecture layers

Clicking on an already-colored field again reopens the color picker, pre-filled with the current color, so you can change it at any time.

idea-plugin.name: Environment Switcher
idea-plugin.description:
Switch the environment your run configurations target from a dropdown in the toolbar, the way Postman switches environments. Define dev, test, staging, prod once; every run configuration you launch receives the selected environment's variables.

Features

  • Environment dropdown next to the run widget, with a colour per environment.
  • Run | Edit Environments… dialog: variables per environment, common variables, per-module overrides, copy environment, import from a folder of .env files.
  • Secrets stay in the IDE password safe (your OS keychain); the shared project file lists only their names. Optionally keep everything in the project file for private repos.
  • Works with Application, JAR Application and Spring Boot run configurations out of the box; enable any Java-based type in settings.
  • Optional confirmation before running against an environment such as production.
  • Missing-secret policy (warn or block), ${NAME} expansion, auto-marking of sensitive variable names.
  • Team-friendly: commit .idea/environmentSwitcher.xml; each developer keeps their own selection and secrets.

Variables set explicitly on a run configuration always win over the environment.

Source, issues and documentation on GitHub.
