idea-plugin.name: Tasklane
idea-plugin.description:
Tasklane keeps a to-do list inside your project, one per repository, next to the code it talks about. No account, no server, no network call: tasks live in a local database under .idea/tasklane/, which the plugin keeps out of version control for you, while the workflow you configure — states and priorities — can be committed and shared with your team.

It is built for the notes you take while you code — the ones that never survive the trip to an external tracker — and it stays fast with a million of them.

The tool window

  • States are tabs in a row above the search field, each with a live count (ToDo 5). The count comes from the same pass that fills the list, so it always agrees with the search and the view filter. Every tab keeps its own selection and folded groups, and the tab you left open comes back when you reopen the project.
  • A toolbar with New Task — a split button: the body creates in the current tab, the arrow lets you pick another target state —, Edit, Delete, Group By, Search All Repositories, Open Board, Export and Settings.
  • A repository selector and a view filter in the window header. The filter shows All tasks, Open, Overdue or Bookmarked, stacks with the search instead of replacing it, and is remembered.
  • Group by date, priority or tag — or not at all — chosen per state. By date: Today, then one section per day that has tasks, each with its date (Sep 14, Sep 10, 2025), and No date last, against the date the state anchors on: created, updated or completed. By priority: highest first, only priorities with tasks. By tag: a task with two tags appears under both, untagged tasks in a group at the end.
  • Every header folds with a click on its chevron or with ←/→, and shows how many tasks it holds. Today is shown even when empty — No tasks today · You're all caught up! — because that is exactly what you came to check.
  • An empty repository shows where to start: links to create a task, quick-add from anywhere, anchor a task to the code at the editor's caret, import the project's TODO comments and, with the IDE's MCP Server plugin, connect an AI agent — each with its shortcut from the Keymap. The first code anchor and the first screenshot get a Got It that explains them, right where they appear.
  • Archive what is done: hide tasks completed more than N days ago, if you want to. Only in the list of a done state — search still finds them — and never silently: the list says how many are hidden, with a link to show them.
  • Manual order, per state: Group By ▸ Manual Order, then drag a card by the grip that appears on its right, below the bookmark and menu, or press ⌘⇧↑/↓. The list does not jump when you switch: it starts from the order you were seeing.
  • Checklists: - [ ] item lines are drawn as checkboxes on the card — in the title too — and a click ticks them, writing the x into the body. A ☑ 2/5 badge counts them.
  • Ungrouped order: bookmarked tasks first, then by priority, then the most recent.
  • Built for huge lists. The list loads a page at a time and says how many are left (4,213 more) — scrolling to it loads the next page —, groups with more than 500 tasks start folded, and all the heavy work runs off the UI thread. With 100,000 tasks a project opens its list in about 9 ms.

The board

  • Every state side by side, in an editor tab: Open Board in the tool window toolbar or in Tools. The editor has the width the tool window lacks, so this is where you plan; the tool window stays for everyday work.
  • The same cards, with the same menu, shortcuts and ⌘Z. Each column keeps its grouping and order, and its header has a + to create right there.
  • Drag a card to another column by its grip to change its state — a whole selection, if the card is part of one. In a manually ordered column it lands between the two cards you drop it on. Move To and ⇧⌥←/→ work too, and the selection follows the cards to their new column.
  • One search, filter and repository for the whole board — the same ones as the tool window.

The card

  • A card per task: a priority stripe down its left edge, a checkbox that completes it, the title over up to three lines, one line of the body, and a row of badges — priority, code anchors, due date, tags, a link and image counter, and the date. Searching across repositories adds the repository name.
  • Markdown in place: bold, italics, code and strikethrough show their style, not their marks. Underscores are left alone, because a_name_like_this is an identifier far more often than it is italics. Fenced code blocks are drawn as code, in the editor font, with nothing inside them interpreted. Completed tasks are struck through.
  • Links open with a single click, in the title or anywhere in the body — even in its greyed-out lines. Plain URLs, www. addresses and Markdown links are recognised, shown shortened (youtrack.jetbrains.com/…/ABC-123) and opened in full, with the full URL in the tooltip. The link counter opens a list of all of them. Only http and https are clickable, links inside code spans are examples rather than destinations, and trailing punctuation is not part of a link.
  • Change the priority from the card: click the priority badge for the list of priorities with their colours.
  • Filter by a tag from the card: click #api to add it to the search, click it again to drop it. Tags with a colour show in it.
  • Jump to the code from the Auth.kt:42 badge, with the full path and the code that is there today in its tooltip. On a narrow card the priority and anchor badges shrink to their icon instead of disappearing — guaranteed down to the narrowest the window can be — and the icon still works.
  • Expand a card with the chevron on its right to read the whole task without leaving the list: the full title, every line of the body and the images, each one after the line that names it, and the code of any anchored block. Click an image to see it full size. The chevron only appears when the card is hiding something.
  • Select card text with the mouse and copy it with ⌘C / Ctrl+C; Escape clears the selection.
  • Bookmark a task from the icon on its row to pin it to the top of its group, whatever its priority. The bookmark stays visible on bookmarked tasks; the ⋮ menu appears on hover.
  • Double-click or Enter opens the task.

Working with tasks

  • A context menu with New Task, Edit, Toggle Completed, Bookmark, Move To ▸, Priority ▸, Due ▸, Tags ▸, Hand Off to Agent, Export and Delete — the same one as the row's ⋮ menu.
  • Move tasks between states with Move To ▸, or one tab at a time with ⇧⌥←/→, without opening a dialog. ⌥←/→ just switches the tab you are looking at.
  • Set the due date or the tags without a dialog: Due ▸ has the dialog's presets, Pick Date… and Clear; Tags ▸ Add… adds tags to every selected task, keeping the ones they have, and Remove ▸ takes one of the selection's tags off them all.
  • Everything works on a multiple selection: complete, bookmark, move, change priority, due date or tags, delete. Many tasks at once are one operation and one repaint; above ten it runs in the background with a progress bar, and cancelling undoes it.
  • Undo anything: ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z in the list undoes the last thing you did — complete, move, reprioritise, reorder, tick a checkbox, edit, create or delete —, on one task or a whole selection at once, and ⌘⇧Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes it. The status bar says what was undone. Each repository keeps its own history, and what an AI agent does through MCP is not in it. A deletion also offers a 3 tasks deleted — Undo notification that brings them back exactly as they were — same dates, same place, same images.
  • Paste or drop into the list: ⌘V creates tasks from the clipboard in the state you are looking at — one per line of text, without its bullets, numbers or checkboxes; a screenshot becomes a task with it —, and dropping images, files or text from your file manager, the Project view, a browser or the editor does the same. No dialog, and one ⌘Z takes it all back.
  • The checkbox — or Toggle Completed — moves a task to the done state and back to the default one. Entering a done state stamps the completion date, which is what grouping Done by date uses.

The task dialog

  • One dialog to create and edit, so a task jotted down in a hurry is not born different from one written calmly.
  • Write in Markdown with a formatting toolbar: bold, italics, code, link, image, bulleted list, numbered list and checklist.
  • Images you can paste, drop or pick: a screenshot from the clipboard, an image file copied or dragged in, or one chosen from disk. It lands under the line your caret was on and shows right there as a preview; the text only shows [image]. ⌘Z undoes it like any other edit, clicking the preview opens it full size, and deleting [image] removes it. A missing image shows a marker instead of disappearing.
  • State and priority as dropdowns, seeded from the tab you were on.
  • A due date from presets — today, tomorrow, end of week, next week — or from a calendar. It falls due at the end of the day, so a task set for today is not born overdue; once past, the card shows it in red and the Overdue filter finds it. A reminder tells you what in the active repository is overdue or due today, once per task per day.
  • Counts in the status bar: ToDo 3 · Doing 1 · 2 overdue for the active repository, with what is overdue in red. You choose which states it counts and whether it counts overdue tasks; click a count to open that tab, or the overdue tasks. Hide it from the status bar's own menu.
  • Tags as chips, typed separated by comma or space, removed with their cross or with Backspace. In the search field they are #api. The field suggests the repository's tags as you type, with how many tasks each has, so #api and #apis do not grow side by side.
  • Code anchors as chips, each one removable: captured from the editor, or typed as path:line with the path completed as you type. A GitHub #L42 link or a stack trace's (42) works too.
  • Priority triggers: typing !!! Fix the login creates Fix the login at High. The prefix moves the priority dropdown as you type and is never saved. The longest match wins, a trailing space is required, deleting the prefix gives the old priority back, and picking one by hand beats it. Only when creating.
  • Escape closes the dialog even with the caret inside the body.

For AI agents (MCP)

  • Your tasks become tools of the IDE's MCP server. With Settings ▸ Tools ▸ MCP Server enabled, Claude Code, Junie, AI Assistant or any MCP client can list tasks, read one with its code anchors at the line where the code is now and the files of its screenshots, create tasks for the work it leaves pending instead of writing // TODO — with screenshots or diagrams attached —, tick checklist items as it goes and complete the task when it is done.
  • No delete tool, on purpose: deleting stays with you and its Undo. Nothing is loaded unless the MCP Server plugin is enabled, and Tasklane opens no port of its own.
  • Hand Off to Agent in the card menu opens a tab of the IDE's terminal in the task's repository, with your agent working on that task — claude out of the box. The task stays where it is while the agent works, and the agent completes it when it is done. Add as many agents as you like in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ AI agent, each with its name and command (codex {prompt}, gemini -i {prompt}…): with more than one, Hand Off to Agent becomes a submenu to pick one. The prompt is yours too, and the request is quoted for your shell, so a task title never runs as a command. Copy Agent Prompt copies the same request for an agent's chat, and Copy Agent Instructions a paragraph for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. The Terminal plugin is optional.

Search

  • It reads the whole body, not just the title, and ignores case and accents in both directions: autenticacion finds autenticación. Results are ranked by relevance, with matches in the title weighing more, and the list shows the 200 best.
  • A folded card shows the body line that matched, not the first one, with every term highlighted — accents ignored, like the search. In a narrow tool window the line is cut at the front so the match stays in sight.
  • Operators: state:doing, p:high, repo:backend, is:open / is:done / is:overdue / is:bookmarked, has:due, has:checklist, has:tag, has:link, has:image, has:code, has:broken-anchor, file:AuthService (part of an anchored path) and #tag. Values are prefixes, quoted when they have spaces (state:"In Review"); several values of one operator mean or, different operators add up, and free text asks for every term. A half-typed operator is ignored instead of emptying the list.
  • Dates: due:, closed:, created: and updated: with today, week, month, a day (>2026-09-01) or a distance from today (<7d). A leading - excludes: -#wip, -is:done.
  • Autocompletion: the field suggests states, priorities, tags and every operator's values as you type; Ctrl+Space lists the operators.
  • ⌘K / Ctrl+K focuses the field from the list, Enter keeps the query in the field's history and returns to the list, and Escape clears it.
  • Search All Repositories — shown when the window has more than one — searches every repository and labels each row with its own.
  • Search Everywhere (⇧⇧) finds tasks too, with the same syntax, in its own Tasklane tab. Enter opens the tool window on the task.

In the editor

  • Tasks that point at the code. New Tasklane Task from Here, in the editor's context menu and the Tools menu — or ⌘⌥⇧R / Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R —, opens the dialog with the file, the line and the exact character already attached; a selection within a line comes in as the body. With a file selected in the Project view instead, the task points at the file.
  • Anchor a block, not just a line. Select several lines and the task is anchored from the first to the last: its badge reads Login.kt:42-58, the editor tints the whole block in the task's priority colour, and the expanded card shows its code as it is today. Type src/Login.kt:42-58 in the dialog, or paste a GitHub #L42-L58 link, to the same effect.
  • Anchors that survive edits. The line is stored with its text, not just its number, and found again by that text: an extra import, a re-indent or a moved function break nothing. If the line is gone the file still opens where it was, and if the file is gone you are told.
  • Anchors that survive renames. Rename or move a file — or its whole folder — in the IDE, by hand or with a refactoring, and the anchors follow it. A file that disappears any other way shows its badge struck through with a warning icon, and has:broken-anchor finds every task left pointing nowhere.
  • The code points back. A line with an open task is marked in the colour of the task's priority. Hover the mark to see the title, state, priority, due date and tags; click it to open the tool window with that task selected, switching repository if needed.
  • Two kinds of mark, and you pick: a gutter icon, which never moves your code; or an inline chip on the exact character, carrying the task's state in capitals (TODO, DOING) and showing the task's screenshots in its tooltip. Or no mark at all.
  • TODO comments become tasks. Alt+Enter on a TODO offers Move TODO to Tasklane: the task is anchored to that line and tagged with the keyword, and the comment leaves the code — ⌘Z in the editor puts it back. Import TODO Comments… turns every TODO in the project into a task in one go, without touching the code, and never imports one twice. Both use the IDE's own TODO patterns.
  • Only open tasks are marked, and a mark goes the moment its task is done. Several tasks on one line share a mark coloured by the highest priority, and the tooltip lists them. Marks work in any file, .txt included.

Repositories

  • One task list per repository. Git repositories registered in the project — submodules included — each keep their own tasks, and a repository added while the IDE is open shows up without a restart. Without Git, the project root works as a single repository. With only one, the selector hides and its name goes to the window title.
  • Nothing is ever hidden. A repository deeper than the detection depth that already has tasks appears under Other, and one whose folder is gone stays in the list as (missing) with its tasks. Moving the whole project breaks nothing.
  • Everything that deletes acts on the active repository only.

Export, import and maintenance

The Export menu only exports; Import and Maintenance are menus of their own.

  • Copy to the clipboard as Markdown or plain text: this whole tab, the date group the selection is in, or just the selected rows. With a search active you copy the search result. A date group comes out as the log of its day — ## 2026-09-11 and a numbered list — ready for a journal or a weekly report. Past 10,000 tasks you are offered a file instead.
  • Save to a file from Export ▸ Save to File: a state, a date group, the selection or the whole repository. The extension you type picks the format: CSV — one row per task with title, description, state, priority, tags, due date, bookmark, code anchors, links, dates and id, readable by Excel with accents intact —, Markdown or plain text.
  • Repository Archive: the whole repository as one .zip — tasks.xml, the pasted images and a manifest.
  • Import an archive from Import ▸ Archive, picking the .zip from disk. You see how many tasks are new, updated or already there before anything is written. It adds and never replaces: the most recent version of a task wins, and a copy of the database is made first.
  • Repository to XML, the tasks.xml interchange format any version of the plugin can read. Characters XML cannot hold — pasted terminal output — are replaced and counted instead of failing the export.
  • Repair Database in Maintenance checks the task database on demand and, if it is damaged, reopens the project and recovers it without deleting anything.
  • Delete all the tasks of a repository with Maintenance ▸ Delete All Tasks in …, after a confirmation that says how many. The repository stays, empty.
  • Export and Remove a repository whose folder is gone: every task is exported and counted before anything is deleted.
  • Exports run in the background, can be cancelled, capture the list as it was when you clicked even if you keep editing, and write files in full or not at all.

Images

  • Stored at their original size, next to the tasks of their repository: a pasted screenshot as a lossless PNG, a dropped or copied file byte for byte. Each file is named after the SHA-256 of its content, so the same image in two tasks is stored once.
  • The list paints thumbnails and never decodes a large original; the full image opens on click, loaded in the background.
  • Pin an image over the editor: the enlarged view has a pin that keeps it on top while you code — the bug to reproduce, the design to copy. The 1 img counter on a card opens it too, and previews it on hover.
  • Unused images are cleaned up on their own, a day after the last task stopped pointing at them.
  • Settings shows how much the active repository's images weigh, with Delete Unused Images to clean up right away and Delete All Images… to empty them after a confirmation (tasks are left untouched).
  • A warning when a repository's images pass a threshold — 5 GB by default, configurable or off. It never deletes anything.

Settings → Tools → Tasklane

  • States, as a table: name, default state for new tasks, whether it means done, how it groups its tasks and which date it groups by. The order is the order of the tabs: drag a row by its handle or use the arrows. Deleting a state asks where its tasks should go, and making a state terminal offers to fill in completion dates from the last modification. Three more checkboxes per state are yours alone, not shared with the project: whether it has a tab in the tool window, a column on the board, and a count in the status bar. Out of the box every state shows in the tool window and on the board.
  • Priorities, highest first as in the tool window: name, default, trigger, and a colour for light and dark themes picked with the platform colour picker. Drag rows to change the priority order; deleting one asks where its tasks should go.
  • Tags of the active repository, most used first, with how many tasks each has: rename one in its cell — to an existing name to merge the two —, delete it from its tasks or give them another tag instead, and give it an optional colour for light and dark themes. Renaming does not touch the tasks' modification date.
  • Nothing is written until Apply — Cancel leaves the project as it was —, and mistakes are flagged first: blank names, two priorities with the same trigger, a trigger with a space. There is always at least one state and one priority.
  • Priority triggers can be turned off altogether.
  • Repository depth: how deep to look for repositories under the project root — a view filter, never a delete.
  • Code anchor marks: gutter icon, inline chip or none. This one is yours alone and is not shared with the project.
  • Due dates: turn the overdue / due-today reminder on or off. Yours alone, like the anchor marks.
  • Status bar: whether the widget counts overdue tasks — which states it counts is a column of the states table. Yours alone too.
  • Completed tasks: hide tasks completed more than N days ago from the list of a done state, or show them all (the default). Yours alone.
  • Images: their weight for the active repository, the two clean-up buttons and the warning threshold.
  • AI agent: your agents — a name and a command each — and the prompt of Hand Off to Agent, and the button that copies the instructions for CLAUDE.md. Yours alone, for every project.
  • Save as template for new projects, so configuring per project does not mean configuring every project, and a direct link to the Keymap.

From anywhere in the IDE

  • Quick Add with ⌘⌥R / Ctrl+Alt+R opens the full task dialog without going through the tool window; the task lands in the active repository. It is also in the Tools menu.
  • Every action is in Search Everywhere and in Settings → Keymap under Plugins → Tasklane, so anything you use daily can get its own key.
  • Fully usable from the keyboard: Tab walks the state row (Space or Enter opens a tab), the search field and the list — and, inside the selected card, its links, checkboxes, anchors, priority, tags and images, which Enter or Space activates. In the list, ⌘N creates a task, Space completes, the IDE's bookmark key bookmarks, 1…9 set the priority, ⌘↵ expands the card and ⌘C copies it; Delete removes the selected tasks and ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z brings them back; ⌘⇧↑/↓ moves a task in a manually ordered state. Reassigning any of them in the Keymap applies at once. The list, the search field and the dialog fields have names for screen readers.
  • Search Everywhere (⇧⇧) finds tasks without opening the tool window.

Where your tasks live, and how they are kept safe

  • Tasks live in .idea/tasklane/tasklane.db, a local SQLite database the plugin keeps out of your diffs with its own .gitignore. States and priorities live in .idea/tasklane.xml, which is meant to be committed: that is how a team shares a workflow.
  • A daily backup, tasklane.db.backup, made in the background only when something changed.
  • A check after an unclean shutdown: if the database is damaged, nothing more is written into it and reopening the project repairs it.
  • A damaged database repairs itself: the damaged file is set aside and never deleted, everything that can still be read is rescued, and only what cannot comes from the daily backup. Most damage is to an index, and then nothing is lost; a notice always says which case it was.
  • Tested by killing the process in the middle of an edit, the migration, the image cleanup, the backup and the repair itself: what was committed survives, what was halfway leaves nothing behind, and the next start finishes the job.
  • Changing the configuration never loses tasks: tasks whose state or priority disappears move to the default one, you are told how many with a Show them link, and they go back on their own if it reappears.
  • Projects from before 2.0 move their tasks.xml into the database automatically, in the background, resuming if the IDE closes halfway. The original is kept as tasks.xml.migrated. A file written by a newer version of the plugin opens read-only instead of being downgraded.
  • Tasklane: Diagnostics reports how many tasks and images there are, what they take up on disk, the state of the backup and the recent latencies, ready to copy into a bug report.

Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1.5 or newer, or any IDE built on the IntelliJ Platform. Git is optional.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2.28.2 — fixes

  • The plugin version for the repository archive no longer comes from an internal platform API. No format changes.

2.28.1 — fixes

  • Removed the use of an internal platform API and a deprecated file-dialog constructor. No format changes.

2.28.0 — export, import and repair

  • Import a .zip archive from disk (Import ▸ Archive). You see how many tasks are new, updated or already there before anything is written; it adds, never replaces, and the most recent version of a task wins. A copy of the database is made first.
  • Repository Archive: tasks, images and a manifest in one .zip.
  • Save to File a state, a date group, the selection or the whole repository; the extension (.md, .csv, .txt) picks the format.
  • The Export menu only exports now: Import and Maintenance are menus of their own.
  • Repair Database checks the database on demand, and any connection that sees damage now says so. A database whose schema is unreadable (malformed database schema) is recovered by reading its pages directly, without losing what was written after the last backup.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.27.0 — more than one agent

  • As many AI agents as you like in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ AI agent: a table with a name and a command for each one — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, the same agent with another model… — to add, remove and reorder.
  • With more than one, Hand Off to Agent becomes a submenu to pick the agent, in the order of the table. From its Keymap shortcut, it asks which one. The terminal tab carries the agent's name.
  • The prompt stays one for all of them. Your current command becomes the only agent, unnamed, until you change it.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.26.2 — no internal APIs

  • The digit shown next to each entry of Priority no longer goes through an internal platform API. Nothing changes on screen.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.26.1 — ready for the Marketplace

  • The plugin description is up to date: Hand Off to Agent no longer moves the task to Doing, code anchors can be typed, and it now covers undo and redo, pasting and dropping into the list, TODO comments, the matching line in search, pinned images and the first steps.
  • Two deprecated platform APIs replaced. Importing TODO comments still waits for indexing, and now yields to the IDE's writes instead of holding them back.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.26.0 — first steps

  • An empty repository shows where to start: links to create a task (⌘N), quick-add from anywhere (⌘⌥R), anchor a task to the code at the editor's caret (⌘⌥⇧R), import the project's TODO comments and, with the IDE's MCP Server plugin, connect an AI agent.
  • A Got It the first time you anchor a task, right under the line: what the mark does, and that the anchor follows the code.
  • A Got It the first time a task gets a screenshot, under its thumbnail in the list: click to enlarge, pin it over the editor, and it stays in .idea/tasklane, out of version control.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.25.1 — handing off doesn't move the task

  • Hand Off to Agent leaves the task where it is: no more Doing while the agent works. When it's done, the agent closes it with tasklane_complete_task, straight to Done, and the default prompt now asks for exactly that.
  • The Move the task to Doing checkbox is gone from the AI agent settings.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.25.0 — the whole window from the keyboard

  • In the list: ⌘N creates a task, Space completes the selection, the IDE's bookmark key bookmarks it, 1…9 set its priority, ⌘↵ expands the card and ⌘C copies its text.
  • Tab walks the selected card: links, checkboxes, code anchors, priority, tags and images, with a focus ring; Enter or Space does what a click would.
  • ⌘⌥⇧R / Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R for New Tasklane Task from Here.
  • New Keymap actions: every grouping, manual order, the four view filters, Next Repository, Expand Card and Copy Task Text. Reassigning a list shortcut now applies at once.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.24.0 — due dates and tags from the menu

  • Due ▸ in the card menu: Today, Tomorrow, End of Week, Next Week, Pick Date… and Clear — for one task or the whole selection, no dialog.
  • Tags ▸ Add… adds tags to every selected task, keeping the ones they have, with the repository's tags suggested as you type; Remove ▸ lists the selection's tags and takes one off them all. Case-insensitive, like the rest of the tags.
  • One undo step for the whole selection, and Due Today, Clear Due Date or Add Tags… can have a shortcut in the Keymap.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.23.0 — tags, for real

  • The tags field suggests the repository's tags as you type, with how many tasks each has, most used first — so #api and #apis stop growing side by side.
  • Click #api on a card to filter by it: it goes into the tool window's search, which the board shares. Click it again to drop it.
  • A tags table in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane for the active repository: rename a tag in its cell, rename it to an existing one to merge the two, or delete it — from its tasks, or giving them another tag instead. Renaming does not touch the tasks' modification date.
  • Optional colour per tag, light and dark like the priorities', on cards, in the dialog and in the suggestions.

Compatibility: no database change; tasklane.xml gains a <tags> list only when a tag has a colour.

2.22.0 — hand a task off to an AI agent

  • Hand Off to Agent in the card menu opens a tab of the IDE's terminal in the task's repository, with your agent working on that task — claude out of the box — and moves it to Doing. One undo step.
  • Copy Agent Prompt copies the same request, for an agent's chat; Copy Agent Instructions, a paragraph for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md: pending work goes to Tasklane, not to TODO comments.
  • The command is yours in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ AI agent, and so is the prompt: codex {prompt}, gemini -i {prompt}… The request is quoted for your shell, so a task title never runs as a command.
  • The Terminal plugin is optional: without it, copying the prompt still works.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.21.0 — the full query language

  • is:overdue and is:bookmarked in the search box, plus has:due, has:checklist and has:tag.
  • Dates: due:, closed:, created: and updated: with today, yesterday, tomorrow, week, month, a day (2026-09-01, or >2026-09-01 as a bound) or a distance from today (<7d, >2w). due:<7d includes what is already overdue.
  • Exclude with -: -#wip, -p:low, -is:done, -draft.
  • Autocompletion in the search box: values after state:, p:, is:, has: or a date operator, the repository's tags after #, and every operator with ⌃Space.
  • Search Everywhere and the MCP tools get it too; and an agent asking for state:Done in the query no longer gets zero results.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.20.0 — search shows why a task matched

  • While searching, a folded card shows the body line that matched, not the first one: if token is on line twelve, you see line twelve, with the term highlighted. With several terms, the line that matches the most.
  • The match stays in sight in a narrow tool window: if it would fall past the cut, the line is cut at the front instead — …caduca el token de.
  • Highlighting ignores accents, like the search: autenticacion already found autenticación, and now highlights it too. It also reaches the body, code blocks and links, and each term is highlighted on its own, in any order.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.19.0 — paste and drop into the list

  • ⌘V on the list creates tasks from the clipboard, in the state you are looking at — on the board, in that column. Text becomes one task per line, without its bullets, numbers or checkboxes: copy the list from a meeting or a chat and it is there. A URL is one more line, and the task gets its link. A screenshot becomes a task with it.
  • Drop onto the list from Finder, the Project view, the browser or the editor: an image gives a task with the screenshot, a code or text file a task anchored to it, and text one task per line.
  • No dialog and no question unless there are more than ten: what was created is selected — press Enter to write its title — and one ⌘Z removes it all. Past ten lines you can also make it a single task with the whole text.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.18.0 — screenshots for AI agents

  • Agents see the screenshots: tasklane_get_task now gives the path of each image file of the task, which Claude Code, Junie and other MCP clients can open. tasklane_list_tasks says how many images a task has, and its query takes has:image.
  • Agents attach screenshots: tasklane_create_task and tasklane_update_task take images, file paths added at the end of the body. An image the task already has is not added twice.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.17.1 — choose where each state shows

  • Three more checkboxes per state in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ States: Tool window, Board and Status bar. Out of the box every state has a tab in the tool window and a column on the board, new states too.
  • The states the status bar counts are now picked in that column, instead of a separate row of checkboxes; overdue tasks stay in their own group.
  • ⌥←/→ and ⇧⌥←/→ skip the states you do not show.
  • The three are yours alone, not shared with the project.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.17.0 — the board

  • Every state side by side, in an editor tab: Open Board in the tool window toolbar or in Tools. The tool window stays for everyday work; the board has the editor's width, for planning.
  • Each column is the tool window's list: the same cards, menu, shortcuts and ⌘Z, with its own grouping and order. Its header shows the count, with + to create right there and Group By.
  • Drag a card to another column by its grip to change its state — the whole selection, if the card is part of one. In a manually ordered column it lands between the two cards you drop it on. The board and the column scroll by themselves near their edges.
  • The selection follows the cards to their new column, also with Move To and ⇧⌥←/→; ⌥←/→ moves between columns. One undo step puts the cards back in their column and their place.
  • The board shares the search, the repository and the view filter with the tool window.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.16.0 — undo everything, not just deleting

  • ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z in the list undoes what you just did: completing, moving to another state, changing the priority, bookmarking, reordering, ticking a checklist item, editing, creating or deleting — one task or a whole selection. ⌘⇧Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes it. Up to 100 steps.
  • Each repository has its own history. ⌘Z undoes the last thing done in the repository you are looking at, never something you cannot see.
  • It says what it undid in the status bar — Undone: move 3 tasks to Done —, because the tasks may come back to another tab.
  • Undo puts back what you changed and nothing else. If an AI agent edited the task since, its edit stays. Undo brings back the original dates too, so a task returns to its date group.
  • What an agent does through the MCP tools is not on your undo stack.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.15.0 — anchor a block of code

  • Anchor a whole block, not just a line. Select several lines and use New Tasklane Task from Here: the task is anchored from the first line to the last, and its badge reads Login.kt:42-58. Type ranges the same way in the task dialog or through the MCP tools; GitHub links with a #L42-L58 range keep their end now.
  • The editor tints the block with a hint of the priority colour while the task is open, under the usual gutter icon or inline chip.
  • The expanded card shows the code of the block as it is in the file today, and follows your edits. The badge's tooltip shows it too, for single-line anchors as well.
  • Creating a task from a multi-line selection no longer copies the code into the task: the block is anchored and shown by the card, and the body is left for your note.

Compatibility: a new column is added to the task database the first time the project opens; the schema version does not change. Earlier versions keep reading and editing your tasks, but a task they save keeps only the first line of its block.

2.14.0 — counts in the status bar

  • Your list in the status bar. ToDo 3 · Doing 1 · 2 overdue for the active repository, counted like its tabs, with what is overdue in red. It updates as you work and the moment something falls due.
  • You choose what it counts in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ Status bar: any of your states, and overdue tasks or not. Out of the box, the states that are not done, plus overdue tasks.
  • Every count is a link. A state opens its tab; the overdue count takes you to those tasks; anywhere else opens Tasklane. Hide or show it by right-clicking the status bar.

Compatibility: no format change. A new partial index on open tasks with a due date is created the first time the project opens; earlier versions ignore it.

2.13.0 — anchors that survive renames

  • Anchors follow their file. Rename or move a file in the IDE — by hand, with a refactoring, or by renaming the class it is named after — and the tasks anchored to it point at the new path. Moving a folder takes everything inside with it. The tasks keep their dates: moving a file is not editing them.
  • Broken anchors show. When a file disappears any other way (a mv or rm in the terminal, a git checkout), its badge is struck through with a warning icon, in the task dialog too, and it heals on its own if the file comes back.
  • has:broken-anchor finds every task left pointing nowhere, in the search box, in Search Everywhere and through the MCP tools.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.12.0 — Tasklane for AI agents

  • Your tasks are now tools of the IDE's MCP server. Turn it on in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ MCP Server and an agent such as Claude Code, Junie or AI Assistant can list your tasks, read one with its code anchors at the line where the code is now, write down the work it leaves pending instead of adding // TODO comments, tick checklist items as it goes and complete the task when it is done. Seven tools, all prefixed tasklane_.
  • Safe by design: there is no delete tool, completing twice never reopens a task, unknown state or priority names fail listing the valid ones, and a database that is being repaired refuses to write.
  • Nothing changes unless the MCP Server plugin is enabled; Tasklane opens no port of its own.

Compatibility: no format change.

2.11.2 — the reorder grip, better placed

The grip of a manually ordered card now sits halfway down the space below the bookmark and menu, slightly in from the right edge, so it reads as part of the card rather than of the badge row. No format change.

2.11.1 — a grip to reorder, and bigger checkboxes

  • Drag cards by a grip. In a manually ordered state, a grip appears in the bottom-right corner of the card under the mouse — the space below the bookmark and menu that was always empty. It replaces dragging by the colour stripe, which was eight pixels wide and gave no hint it could be dragged.
  • Bigger checklist boxes. The boxes are now drawn instead of taken from the font, so they are the size of a letter, and ticked ones are filled in blue like the IDE's own checkboxes.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.11.0 and 2.11.1 open each other’s projects.

2.11.0 — manual order and checklists

  • Order a state by hand. Group By ▸ Manual Order, then drag a card by its colour stripe, or press ⌘⇧↑/↓ (Move Up / Move Down in the context menu). Switching does not move anything: the manual order starts as the one you were seeing. Bookmarked tasks stay on top, new tasks come in at the top, and grouping still works — you order within each group.
  • Checklists are back. - [ ] item lines are drawn as checkboxes on the card — in the title too, which is why they were removed in 1.0.0 — and one click ticks them, writing the x into the body. Ticked items are struck through, and a ☑ 2/5 badge counts them. The task dialog has a Checklist button.

Compatibility: no format change. Opening an existing project builds one new index once. 2.10.0 opens 2.11.0 projects and simply ignores the manual order.

2.10.0 — tasks in Search Everywhere, and archiving what is done

  • Search Everywhere finds your tasks. Press ⇧⇧ and type: tasks show up in the All tab and in their own Tasklane tab, with the same syntax and scope as the tool window search. Enter opens the tool window on the task, even if it was closed.
  • Archive what is done. In Settings → Tools → Tasklane, hide tasks completed more than N days ago. Only in the list of a done state — the tab counts what it shows, and search still finds everything — and never silently: the list says how many are hidden, with a link to show them. Off by default.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.9.0 and 2.10.0 open each other’s projects.

2.9.0 — undo deletions and due-date reminders

  • Deleting can be undone. Deleting tasks still asks nothing, but it now shows a N tasks deleted — Undo notification, and ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z in the task list brings the last deletion back. Tasks return exactly as they were: same dates, same place, same images. Also for deleting a whole group, up to 10,000 tasks.
  • Due-date reminders. A notification says how many tasks of the active repository are overdue or due today — when the project opens, when you switch repository and every half hour, only for tasks not mentioned yet today. Show takes you to them. Turn it off from the notification or in Settings → Tools → Tasklane.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.8.0 and 2.9.0 open each other’s projects.

2.8.0 — typed anchors, TODO comments and code blocks

  • Anchor a task by typing where it points. In the task dialog, write plans/deploy.md:28 — a path relative to the project and a line — in the Code row and press Enter. You get the same anchor as creating the task from the editor: the gutter mark, the tooltip and the click back to the line, which is found again if the file changes.
  • Also accepts path:line:column, a bare path, path#L28 as copied from GitHub, and path(28). A path that does not exist, a folder or a line past the end of the file stops the dialog and says why.
  • Files written by another program a moment ago are found too, and the field autocompletes project paths as you type.
  • Fenced code blocks. Text between ``` lines is drawn on the card as a code block, in the editor font and taken literally. The code button of the dialog fences a multi-line selection.
  • Alt+Enter on a TODO comment → Move TODO to Tasklane. The TODO becomes an anchored task and the comment is removed from the code (undo brings it back). Comments that say more than the TODO are kept.
  • Import TODO Comments… turns every TODO of the project into an anchored task in one go, without touching the code and without duplicating the ones already imported.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.6.3 and 2.8.0 open each other’s projects.

2.6.3 — scrolling and rendering fixes in the task list

A bug fix release: scrolling the task list could jump, and cards could be drawn at the wrong height.

  • The list no longer jumps while you scroll. Loading more tasks, expanding a group or a screenshot finishing loading could shift every card and move the list out from under you. The task you are reading now stays where it is.
  • Cards are drawn at their correct height. After the tool window changed width — including when the scrollbar appears on its own — cards were briefly laid out for the previous width, so a wrapped title could lose its last line and push the priority, due date and tag row out of the card.
  • The end of the list is reachable again. The list could report itself shorter than it is, leaving the last card clipped against the bottom edge with no way to scroll further.
  • Scrolling through a large group no longer collapses the groups below it. Loading a second page of tasks could silently fold away the rest of the list.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.6.2 and 2.6.3 open each other’s projects.

2.6.2 — copying tells you the truth

  • “N task(s) copied” now means the text really is on the clipboard. When the clipboard was busy — a history manager, a menu closing — the copy could fail silently and the notification claimed a copy that never happened, so pasting returned the previous content. Tasklane now verifies the clipboard, retries, and reports an error if the text cannot be written.
  • “Export and Remove” no longer deletes tasks after a copy it could not verify. If the clipboard rejects the export, the repository is left untouched.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.6.1 and 2.6.2 open each other’s projects.

2.6.1 — pin an image while you code

  • An enlarged screenshot can be pinned. The pin in its header keeps the window above the editor and stops it from closing when you click elsewhere, so you can write code with the image in front of you. Unpinned it still closes on the first click outside.
  • The image counter on a row is now a button: click it to enlarge the task’s screenshots without expanding the card, and hover it to see the screenshot itself instead of a sentence.
  • The preview of an expanded card no longer disappears now and then when the scroll bar comes and goes: it shrinks those few pixels instead of dropping out of the row.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.5.2 and 2.6.1 open each other’s projects.

2.5.2 — task workflow fixes

  • Copy task text with one click, without card metadata or Markdown markers.
  • Delete complete grouped views from the context menu.
  • Search stays stable while typing across state panels.
  • Task editor text remains readable on dark IDE themes.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.5.1 and 2.5.2 open each other’s projects.

2.5.1 — new screenshots

  • New listing screenshots: the tool window, an expanded card, the task dialogs, the context and export menus, the editor mark and the settings, retaken on the current UI.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.5.0 and 2.5.1 open each other’s projects.

2.5.0 — IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1.5 or newer

  • Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1.5 or newer (build 261.27258.48), or any IDE of the platform from that build on. 2025.2, 2025.3 and 2026.1.0–2026.1.4 are no longer supported: they keep 2.4.0, which works as before.
  • No deprecated or scheduled-for-removal API: the Plugin Verifier findings of 2.4.0 are gone — ReadAction.compute, the DynamicBundle(String) constructor and SimpleListCellRenderer.create.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.4.0 and 2.5.0 open each other’s projects.

2.4.0 — hardening

What the previous releases took for granted is now tested by force: crashes, damaged databases and long sessions.

  • A damaged task database repairs itself. The damaged file is set aside and never deleted, everything that can still be read is rescued, and only what cannot comes from the daily backup. A broken index — the most common kind of damage — is repaired with nothing lost. Tasks are read-only while it runs, a notice says what happened, and an interrupted repair finishes on the next start.
  • Damage found while the project is open stops all writes, so nothing more is lost inside a broken file, and offers to reopen the project to repair it.
  • SQLite is now bundled instead of using the one inside the IDE, which is internal API. Same database file, same schema: nothing to migrate.
  • Crash tests kill the process in the middle of an edit, the migration, the image cleanup, the backup and the repair itself; a nightly build runs the scale benchmark on a million tasks with the IDE’s default 2 GB heap and fails if any latency or memory budget is exceeded.

Compatibility: no format change; 2.3.0 and 2.4.0 open each other’s projects.

2.3.0 — a day per section, and a repository you can empty

  • Date sections are days. Today, then one section per day that has tasks, each with its date — no more Yesterday, This week or whole months of earlier years.
  • Save a repository to a file as CSV, Markdown or plain text, from Export › Save Repository As. CSV is one row per task, ready for a spreadsheet.
  • Delete all tasks in a repository, separately and after a confirmation that says how many. The repository stays, empty.
  • Links in a card's body open with a click, not only from the link counter.
  • The code anchor badge never falls off a narrow card: when Auth.kt:42 does not fit, its icon stays and still jumps to the code. The priority badge does the same with its colour dot.
  • Settings: priorities are listed highest first, as in the tool window; rows of both tables can be dragged by their handle; and clicking a colour swatch opens the colour picker and actually changes the colour.
  • The expand, bookmark and menu icons of a card sit closer together.

Fixed: clicking a code anchor badge threw a read-access error on recent IDEs instead of opening the file; picking a priority colour in Settings did nothing; and the Plugin Verifier findings are gone — no internal API, no KeymapUtil.INSTANCE reference that broke 2026.1, and no calls to deprecated ToolWindowFactory or checkbox renderer methods.

Images are stored at their original size. The 400 px cap is gone: a screenshot of code at 400 px cannot be read.

  • A pasted screenshot is saved as a lossless PNG; a dropped, chosen or copied file is saved byte for byte. Measured on a 2880 px screenshot: pasting takes 129 ms of background CPU instead of 8 and 1.25 MB instead of 46 KB; dropping a file went from 47 ms to 1 ms.
  • Settings always shows how much the active repository’s images weigh, with two buttons for that repository only: Delete Unused Images removes right away every image no task points at, and Delete All Images…, after a confirmation, removes all of them — tasks are left untouched and show the missing image.
  • The image size warning is per repository and names it.
  • The task dialog paints its previews from a bounded copy and opening an image full size loads it in the background, so large originals never decode on the UI thread.

Compatibility: no database format change; the schema stays at version 1. Images keep their place and name, and the old imageMaxSize setting is simply ignored.

2.2.0 — the big operations

Exporting a million tasks is still reading a million tasks. What changes is everything around it: it no longer holds what it reads, no longer runs on the UI thread, no longer blocks anything else, and can be cancelled.

  • Exports stream. With 100,000 tasks, copying a 33,000-row state used to hold 280 MB; it now peaks at 2.2 MB. Exporting the repository to tasks.xml held 1.5 GB; now 15 MB. What comes out is the tab as it was when you clicked, even if you keep editing.
  • Past 10,000 tasks, export to a file instead of flooding the clipboard. The file is written in full or not at all.
  • Acting on many tasks at once — move, complete, bookmark, change priority, delete — is one operation and one repaint, not one per row. Above ten rows it runs in the background with a progress bar, and cancelling undoes it. Bookmarking 2,000 tasks went from 1.9 s to 0.74 s.
  • “Export and Remove” works at any size. The repository goes read-only, every task is exported and counted before anything is deleted, and removal runs in batches: with 100,000 tasks, the longest any other action waits went from 12.3 s to 263 ms.
  • A daily backup of the task database, tasklane.db.backup, made in the background only when something changed. After an unclean IDE shutdown the database is checked, and if it is damaged you are told, with the date of that backup.

Fixed: a repository renamed or deleted from disk vanished from the selector with its tasks inside (since 2.0.0); exporting a new repository to XML ended in a “corrupt file” warning; exporting to XML during an unfinished migration overwrote the original; the migration notice showed {1} instead of a path.

Compatibility: no format change. The database schema stays at version 1, and 2.1.0 opens a project used by 2.2.0 as if nothing happened.

2.1.0 — pasted images stop weighing

Screenshots used to live in one flat folder that had to be listed whole every time the project opened, and the list decoded the full-size original to paint a thumbnail-sized preview. Neither happens any more.

  • The list never decodes a large screenshot again. Ones saved at 1600 px get a 256 px thumbnail, made in the background the first time they are shown. A card with ten of them took 134 MB of memory and 176 ms to open; it is now 36 MB and 8.7 ms. Clicking a preview still opens the full original.
  • New screenshots are scaled to 400 px instead of 1600. Measured on PNGs calibrated against a real screen capture: 407 KB per shot at 1600, 33 KB at 400. Images you already saved are left exactly as they are — a blob is named after its own checksum, so rescaling one would mean rewriting every task that points at it.
  • Images are stored in subfolders (attachments/ab/cd/<sha>.png). With ten million files, a single folder is not slow — it is unusable. Whatever you have is moved in the background, in batches, and nothing stops being visible while it happens.
  • Finding which images are unused stops looking at the disk. The database keeps count: with 100,000 images saved, that went from a 329 ms folder scan on every open to a 0.49 ms query — and unlike the scan, it does not grow with how much you have saved.
  • A warning when images pass 5 GB, with the size and what to do about it. Nothing is ever deleted because of it, and the threshold can be raised or switched off in the settings.
  • A weekly background reconciliation adopts images that appear in the folder without the plugin knowing, and marks as missing the ones deleted from outside it.
  • Tasklane: Diagnostics now counts images from the database: the figure is exact instead of stopping at 200,000, and it says how many are stored above today’s scaling cap.

Compatibility: an older version of the plugin will not find images that have already been moved and will paint them as missing. Nothing is lost — the files are there, in their subfolders, and they come back as soon as you open the project with 2.1 again — and tasks keep reading and editing normally.

2.0.0 — your tasks move into a database

Tasks no longer live in a tasks.xml that was read whole on open and rewritten whole on save. They live in a local SQLite database — the one the IDE already ships. Nothing about the window changes: same order, same groups, same counts. Everything about the cost does.

  • Opening a project stops reading your tasks. With 100,000 tasks, opening the tool window and painting it went from 3,027 ms to 9.2 ms. The window asks for the page you can see, not for the list.
  • Memory stops growing with the project. Measured: 2.5 MB with 100,000 tasks, against the 1.3 GB it took to keep the model alive in memory. It is the same figure with ten thousand as with a million.
  • Saving is a transaction, not a dump. Editing one task used to rewrite the whole file — 1,168 ms on 100,000 tasks — behind a half-second delay. It is now 0.44 ms and there is no delay, so an IDE crash no longer takes the last thing you typed.
  • Search uses a full-text index instead of walking every task. On 100,000, the worst possible query — a word present in almost all of them — went from 115 ms to 40 ms.
  • Deleting a state with tasks in it is instant, however many it has: one instruction to the database instead of a pass over all of them.
  • Your old file is kept. The migration runs once, in the background, with a progress bar, and can be cancelled and resumed. The old tasks.xml is left beside the database as tasks.xml.migrated — renaming it back is how you go back. And Copy → Export Repository to XML writes your tasks out to that format whenever you want, so nothing is locked in.
  • Fixed: an unreadable tasks.xml used to leave the repository blank until the backup was read. What could be read now gets in anyway, and only the rest is looked for in the backup.

1.6.0 — the list stops weighing what the project weighs

  • Repainting the list no longer depends on how big the project is. On 100,000 tasks, opening the tool window went from 1,179 ms to 4.1 ms, and repainting after completing a task from 1,194 ms to 0.31 ms. On a million, from 10.2 s to 0.61 ms. The tree is no longer rebuilt on every change: it is brought up to date row by row, and the rows that did not change keep the height they were already measured at.
  • The list loads a page at a time. At the end of a group there is a row telling you how many tasks are left; scrolling to it, clicking it or pressing Enter brings the next ones. Same gesture as Find in Files.
  • Big groups start collapsed, with their count in the header — and so do the ones below, once the ones above already fill the screen. Opening one loads its first page right then. What you open or close always wins.
  • Revealing a task from an editor mark no longer has to load everything above it: the list opens at its height and says how much is left above.
  • Fixed: every repaint walked the whole project on the UI thread just to forget expanded cards that no longer existed. On big lists that cleanup cost more than the repaint itself — and it was never needed, since task ids are not reused.
  • Fixed: copying a state or a group to the clipboard copied whatever happened to be painted. It now asks for the full list again, which is what “copy this state” means even when the list loads in chunks.

1.5.0 — big lists stop weighing

  • A command costs eight times less. On a list of 100,000 tasks, a command went from 4.14 ms to 0.51 ms. The model now reports what it changed instead of the service working it out by walking everything after every keystroke.
  • Saving the edit dialog sends one change, not six. Body, state, priority, tags, due date and anchors used to go as six separate commands, each producing a new state — six copies of the list and up to six tree repaints for one click on Save. Editing a task on a list of 100,000 went from 26 ms to 6 ms.
  • New action: Tasklane: Diagnostics. How many tasks you have, what they weigh on disk, how many images and how much deduplication saves you, and the last hour of latencies per operation. One button copies the whole report, because where it belongs is an issue. It says so plainly when repainting goes over its budget, since that one happens on the UI thread.
  • Fixed: the image caches are bounded by memory, not by number of entries. A 1600px screenshot decoded takes 10.2 MB and sixteen were kept — up to 164 MB of heap with twenty tasks on screen. The caps are now 64 MB and 16 MB, actually counted.
  • Fixed: deleting a task that was already gone still rebuilt the list, with a repaint and a disk write behind it. And accepting the edit dialog without changing anything still moved the task's modified date.

1.4.1 — the mark reads, and what you copy carries its date

  • The inline chip's tooltip shows the task's screenshots. Half a task is a pasted image — the error you saw, the design to copy — and the tooltip used to give you the title and the state in exactly the case where looking at the picture was the answer. Up to two per tooltip, scaled, highest priority first.
  • A date group is copied as the log of its day. In Markdown the heading is the date in ISO form and the tasks are a numbered list, ready to paste into a journal or a weekly report. “Done · Today” stopped being true the next day, and the - [x] box is noise once the whole group means “this got done that day”. Only for groups that are one actual day: this week, a month and undated keep the tab heading and their boxes rather than invent a date. Plain text is unchanged.
  • Fixed: the inline chip sat flush against the code on both sides, so websi·TODO·te read as a single word. It keeps a little air now — the space belongs to the mark, not to your file.

1.4.0 — the whole card, where you can reach it

  • Every card shows its priority badge now, the default priority included. It used to stay quiet — it would be the same word on every row — but since the badge became the button that changes the priority, staying quiet hid the control on exactly the cards nobody has touched yet. The colour dot is part of the button too.
  • The Priority submenu has an icon: it was the only entry in the context menu without one.
  • Fixed: with a narrow tool window, a card with a few tags asked for more width than there was, and the platform popped the rest of the row outside the panel on hover — with the buttons on its right inside. Reaching for them closed it.
  • Fixed: cards could lose their bottom line — priority, date and tags gone, with no hint why. The tree kept a width of its own and stopped following the panel, so a card was measured at one width and painted at another. It follows the panel now, and the window will not go below 300px wide.
  • Fixed: a word with no spaces in it — a long identifier, an unshortened URL — used to stretch the whole row, and the buttons on the right stopped landing where they are drawn: clicking the bookmark folded the card. Those lines are cut with an ellipsis now.

1.3.0 — cards you can read and act on

  • Card text is selectable. Drag across a card to select its text and press Cmd/Ctrl+C to copy it. Escape clears the selection.
  • Expand a card with the new chevron on its right to read the whole task in place — the title without the three-line cap and every line of the body, not just the first one. Click it again to fold it back. It only shows up when the card is actually hiding something.
  • Images show up in an expanded card, scaled, with the same border and the same loading marker as in the dialog, each one right after the line that references it. Click one to see it full size. A folded card still shows the 1 img counter instead.
  • Change the priority without opening the dialog. Click the priority badge on a card for a list of priorities with their colours, or use the new Priority submenu in the context menu to change every selected task at once.

1.2.1

  • Fixed: the inline mark's popup vanished after a fraction of a second, with the mouse still on it. It now stays for as long as you hover it.

1.2.0 — and the code points back

  • Anchored lines are marked in the editor, in the colour of the task's priority. Hover the mark to read the task, click it to open it in the tool window.
  • Only tasks that are still open get a mark: a task in a done state is history, not a note about the code.
  • Choose the mark in Settings → Tools → Tasklane: a gutter icon, or an inline chip on the exact character the task was about. The choice is yours alone — it is not shared with the project.
  • An anchor now remembers the column too, so it takes you back to the character and not just to the line.

1.1.0 — tasks that point at the code

  • New Tasklane Task from Here in the editor's context menu creates a task anchored to the file and line you are looking at, with the selected text as its body. The card shows a Auth.kt:42 badge that jumps straight back there.
  • An anchor survives edits above it: the line is found again by its text, not by its number.
  • New search operators: file: and has:code.
  • Move To sends the selected tasks to another state without opening the dialog, with Shift+Alt+Left/Right to move them one tab at a time. Alt+Left/Right switches state tabs again.
  • Fixed: group headers would not fold. The platform silently refuses to collapse a top-level node in a tree without root handles.

idea-plugin.name: OpenVox Language
idea-plugin.description:
Language tools for OpenVox and Puppet manifests (.pp), with completion, navigation, refactoring, and EPP template editing (.epp). Supports OpenVox 8 and OpenVox 9 prereleases (checked against 9.0.0-rc1).

  • Editing - syntax highlighting with a configurable colour scheme, brace matching, folding, live templates and a structure view.
  • Formatting - aligns the => of every attribute in a resource body, hash and selector, as the style guide requires, with its own code style page.
  • Navigation - go to the declaration of a class, defined type, function, type alias, parameter or variable; find usages; rename; Go to Class and Go to Symbol; jump from epp(), template() and source => to the file they name.
  • Completion - resource attributes and their allowed values, data types and type aliases, resource types, fact keys inside $facts[...], built-in and project functions, and variables in scope.
  • Quick documentation for built-in functions, resource types, attributes and data types, with compatibility notes for OpenVox 8 and 9.
  • Inspections - unknown function, unknown attribute, unresolved variable, unused parameter, and legacy top-scope facts with a quick fix that rewrites them as $facts[...].
  • External validation - optional puppet parser validate and puppet-lint integration.
  • Modern language constructs throughout: parameterised data types such as Optional[Variant[String[1], Enum['a','b']]], Sensitive, Init, type aliases, Puppet-language functions, lambdas, heredocs and EPP tags.

This plugin is community-maintained and is not affiliated with Perforce or Vox Pupuli.

idea-plugin.name: Ocean Theme
idea-plugin.description:
Inspired by the deep sea and the quiet glow of life far below the surface, this theme layers dark teal and blue-green shadows with bioluminescent cyan, coral pink, and sea glass accents to create a calm and immersive coding environment. Deep, cool backgrounds keep the editor restful, while bright cyans, soft pinks, and warm sandbar tones add clarity and focus to key syntax elements.

Features
  • Complete IDE theming across the editor, tool windows, menus, dialogs, popups and the new UI, styled as one coherent surface
  • Carefully tuned syntax highlighting with semantic, language-aware coloring for readable code
  • Purposeful, distinct colors for keywords, strings, numbers, variables, parameters and comments
  • Calm, nature-inspired palette designed for long, comfortable coding sessions
  • Consistent look across every JetBrains IDE, from IntelliJ IDEA and PyCharm to WebStorm, CLion, GoLand and Rider
  • Full support for the new UI and Islands
  • Actively maintained and regularly refined


Enjoying our themes? Giving us a 5-star rating on the JetBrains Marketplace helps us grow and create more themes!

Have feedback or found an issue? Please report it on our Issue Tracker.
