idea-plugin.name: Lattice
idea-plugin.description:
Lattice — In-App Database Manager for IntelliJ IDEA

A database client for IntelliJ IDEA. Connect to, explore, query, create, and modify your databases without leaving your editor.

Key Features:

  • Supported Databases: MySQL and HSQLDB with a compatible JDBC driver. Tested server releases include MySQL 5.5, 5.6, 5.7 and 8.4, and HSQLDB 2.2.9 through 2.7.4 (Embedded File, In-Memory, and Server modes).
  • Database Explorer: Tree view of Catalogs/Databases, Schemas, Tables, Views, Columns (with data types, primary key, and auto-increment indicators).
  • Interactive Data Grid: Inline cell editing with early type checking, auto-generated key protection, periodic auto-refresh, add/delete rows, batch commit, revert, filter (WHERE clause), and pagination.
  • SQL Query Console: Execute queries with syntax support, Ctrl+Enter execution, result tables, affected row counts, elapsed time, and query history.
  • Visual DDL Wizards: Create databases, design tables, alter tables (add, rename, modify definition, and drop columns), truncate tables, and rename tables.
  • Export: Export data directly to CSV, JSON, and SQL INSERTs, and export/view CREATE TABLE DDL.
idea-plugin.change-notes: IntelliJ IDEA 2025+ / Java 21 compatibility, selectable JDBC versions, verified downloads, local JAR selection, server-version detection, and older MySQL/HSQLDB compatibility fixes.

idea-plugin.name: Version Checker
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Dynamic plugin support, with packaged-plugin unload/reload tests covering service disposal, cancelled checks and timers, open previews, and class-loader release.
  • Refresh Dependency Versions in supported build files' editor context menu, plus clearer Refresh Current File and Refresh Whole Project menu actions.
  • Cancellable status-bar progress for manual refreshes and automatic inspection checks, with whole-project refresh progress advancing by build file.
  • Optional periodic repository checks in project settings, with a configurable 1–1440 minute interval (30 minutes by default). Checks refresh highlighting while the project is open and skip offline providers, unsaved build files, indexing and active checks.

Changed

  • Maven dependency goals receive exact inclusion filters from supported declarations, reducing inherited lookups whose results cannot be reported for the selected POM.
  • Compatible npm checks share lazy Node/npm runtime resolution while active, including version-manager shims. Runtime probes are cancellable, refreshes resolve again, and completed scans retain no runtime session.
  • Build and release validation run authenticated native Maven, npm and Gradle integration tests, with a pinned Node/npm fixture runtime.
  • npm retrieves stable versions and their deprecation notices together, selecting candidates locally and retaining the older query path for incompatible responses.
  • Maven discovery and bulk-preview validation capture shared imported-POM/settings fingerprints once per read pass, reusing ancestor configuration stamps while revalidating all inputs before applying edits. Unsaved settings and .mvn configuration changes now reject stale previews too.
  • npm discovery and manifest hashes stay warm across unrelated source edits; manifest content and structure changes still invalidate workspace ownership and prepared edits. Hashes track saved bytes and unsaved text separately.
  • npm workspace manifests share successful raw metadata and in-flight requests with bounded memory, configuration isolation and refresh generations; report expiry retains the original metadata freshness deadline.
  • Maven goals and retrieval fallbacks reuse one captured set of coordinates, config properties, explicit profiles and effective repository data per scan.
  • Optional performance debug traces and authenticated request-count benchmarks cover Maven filtering and the combined npm query.
  • Bulk-update previews use non-modal windows owned by the plugin service. Unloading closes them and cancels pending responses before any edits can be applied.
  • Maven goals share one fresh server embedder per POM and skip dependency, plugin or parent categories with no supported declarations.
  • Independent npm packages are queried concurrently with a limit of four, sharing metadata and deprecation queries for aliases of the same package.
  • Gradle checks cache build-file discovery and content hashes, traverse nested linked modules once, and share a root fingerprint during discovery and bulk validation. Edits, file moves and linked settings still invalidate stale results and previews.
  • Completed checks combine nearby highlighting updates and restart inspections only for affected build files, reducing repeated project-wide analysis across Maven, npm and Gradle.

Fixed

  • Maven property quick fixes and bulk edits select the unique active profile owner, including overrides of root dependency properties. Ambiguous active owners require review; shared edits cannot target a shadowed default property.
  • Scheduled npm checks skip workspaces with unsaved applicable registry or runtime configuration, including ancestor inputs, and resume after save without saving documents from the timer.
  • Gradle stable qualifiers are compared without case differences, JRE/Android variants remain isolated, and service-pack releases advance numerically even with mixed-case qualifiers. Equivalent versions and reverse service-pack updates are not offered.
  • Gradle settings fingerprints use the supported installation-path API on IntelliJ 2026.1 while retaining compatibility with 2025.3.
  • npm and Gradle document listeners use their cache service as the disposable parent, so listeners are removed on plugin unload as well as project close.
  • Refreshes pick up newly published releases despite Maven's daily metadata cache or npm's cached registry metadata. Maven refreshes only the selected artifacts' effective repository metadata timestamps, retaining downloaded artifacts and local-install metadata.
  • Refresh progress now covers the actual repository checks and resulting inspection updates, instead of finishing after background checks were merely queued.

idea-plugin.name: Not My TODO
idea-plugin.description:
A TODO list attached to your code, with items you can hand to an AI agent to fix.

  • Capture: select code, press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Z (or right-click, Add TODO), and type. !p1..!p3 sets the priority and #word adds a tag. With nothing selected it saves a plain note.
  • List: the Not My TODO tool window at the bottom. Search with words, an id like T-12, #tag and !p1. Double-click an item to jump to its code.
  • Anchors: items follow their code as you edit, switch branches, or let an agent change files. If the code can no longer be found the item shows "Anchor lost", and you can re-attach it to a selection. An item can be attached to several places, and to a whole file as well as to lines.
  • Fix with Claude: sends an item, with its code and the lines around it, to Claude Code in a terminal tab or to the clipboard.
  • MCP tools: with the IDE's MCP server enabled, agents can use todo_list, todo_get, todo_create, todo_update, todo_comment, todo_batch and todo_decided to read items, add their own, comment on them, record what was decided, and mark them fixed.

Items are stored in .todos/items.json in the project root, so an agent without MCP can read the file directly.

Requires a JetBrains IDE version 2026.2 or newer.

Open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Source code and issue tracker: github.com/konove/not-my-todo.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.2.0

  • Items can be attached to several places, and to a whole file as well as to lines.
  • Items have a comment log, so an agent can add a finding without rewriting the details.
  • Items can be blocked by another item, marked as a duplicate, or made part of a parent item. A blocked item shows a padlock.
  • Items can carry an effort estimate of s, m or l; search for it with !s, !m and !l.
  • Items record where they came from, the commit that fixed them and a note on what was done.
  • An agent that needs a decision asks in a comment, and a balloon shows the question. The item keeps what was asked and what was answered.
  • New MCP tools: todo_comment, todo_batch and todo_decided. todo_list filters by several tags, excluded tags, several statuses, a directory, text, effort, lost anchors, blocked items and parent, and has a compact mode. Its tag parameter is now tags.
  • The detail pane puts the code beside the text, and the list, the detail pane and the gutter popup show an item as the same chips. The filter bar wraps when the list is narrow.
  • .todos/items.json is now written as version 2, which keeps fields added by newer versions of the plugin. Files written by 0.1.0 are still read; 0.1.0 cannot read a file written by this version.

0.1.0

  • First release: capture TODO items from the editor, a tool window to search and manage them, anchors that follow the code, Fix with Claude, and MCP tools for agents.

idea-plugin.name: ProdWarden
idea-plugin.description:
Stop destructive SQL on the connections that matter, without slowing down the rest.

Mark a connection as sensitive (production, a customer database...) and ProdWarden will not let a dangerous statement run there until you type the connection name to confirm. Everywhere else you work exactly as before.

Between "no protection" and a read-only connection there was nothing: DataGrip's built-in unsafe-query warning is global and goes away with one click. ProdWarden adds real friction only where a mistake is expensive.

What it blocks on sensitive connections

  • DELETE and UPDATE without a WHERE clause
  • DROP TABLE, DROP DATABASE / DROP SCHEMA
  • TRUNCATE
  • Your own keywords, e.g. ALTER TABLE (Settings | Tools | ProdWarden)

Comments, string literals, quoted identifiers and dollar-quoted blocks are ignored, so SELECT 'DROP TABLE' or a commented-out WHERE do not fool it. Subqueries and CTEs are understood.

Where it applies

  • Query consoles and .sql files: Execute and its alternative variants
  • Run configurations that execute an SQL script
  • Truncate and Drop from the Database tool window (context menu and the Delete key)

After you confirm in ProdWarden, DataGrip's own unsafe-query warning is skipped for that execution, so you do not have to confirm twice.

How to use it

  1. Right-click a connection in the Database tool window and check ProdWarden: Sensitive connection.
  2. Run a dangerous statement there: ProdWarden shows what it found and asks you to type the connection name.

Free beta

ProdWarden is free while in beta, with everything unlocked: as many sensitive connections as you need and your own blocked keywords. A paid Pro edition is planned for later. When it arrives, the protection you have already set up stays: connections already marked and keywords already saved will keep protecting you.

Feedback is very welcome: it decides what comes next.

Good to know

  • Everything runs locally. ProdWarden does not send queries, results or connection details anywhere.
  • Detection is text-based and understands PostgreSQL and MySQL/MariaDB syntax: their comments and escapes, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, DO blocks and DELETE/UPDATE inside a WITH. It was checked against real PostgreSQL 18 and MariaDB 10.4 servers.
  • A condition that is always true, such as WHERE 1=1, is accepted. A DELETE or UPDATE with a JOIN or LIMIT but no WHERE asks for confirmation even if it only touches some rows.
  • Not covered: editing rows in the data editor, Import from SQL and running stored routines.
  • Interface in English and Spanish (Settings | Tools | ProdWarden | Language).
  • Requires the Database Tools and SQL plugin (DataGrip, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate and other IDEs that bundle it).

En español

Marca una conexión como sensible y ProdWarden no dejará ejecutar en ella un DELETE/UPDATE sin WHERE, DROP, TRUNCATE o tus palabras clave hasta que escribas el nombre de la conexión. En el resto de conexiones no cambia nada. Beta gratuita con todo desbloqueado: conexiones sensibles ilimitadas y palabras clave propias. Más adelante habrá una versión Pro de pago; lo que ya tengas configurado seguirá protegiéndote. Interfaz en inglés y español.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
First public release (free beta).

Added

  • Mark connections as sensitive from the Database tool window (persists across restarts and renames).
  • On sensitive connections, block DELETE/UPDATE without WHERE, DROP TABLE, DROP DATABASE/DROP SCHEMA, TRUNCATE and custom keywords until the connection name is typed.
  • Covers query consoles, .sql files, SQL script run configurations and Truncate/Drop from the Database tool window.
  • Skips DataGrip's built-in unsafe-query warning after confirming in ProdWarden.
  • English and Spanish interface.
  • Free beta with everything unlocked: unlimited sensitive connections and custom keywords. A paid Pro edition is planned for later; protection you have already set up will keep working.

idea-plugin.name: OpenText Core Application Security

The OpenText Core Application Security plugin for IntelliJ enables you to package and submit your projects for static application security testing (SAST) scans to OpenText Core Application Security directly from the IDE. The main features are:
1) packaging and uploading to OpenText Core Application Security for analysis
2) viewing and remediating identified security issues
3) AI-powered remediation guidance to fix vulnerabilities

The plugin automatically gathers the source code and dependencies from the project that are needed for the OpenText Core Application Security scan. The plugin provides an interface to view the scan results with code navigation, explanations of the vulnerabilities, and recommendations on how to fix them. The plugin also provides the ability to audit the issues and add comments, which directly sync with the OpenText Core Application Security portal. The plugin introduces AI-powered remediation guidance that delivers intelligent fix suggestions for identified vulnerabilities which can be automatically applied to the affected code.

Application security must be seamless throughout the software development lifecycle. OpenText Core Application Security is built into your DevOps process to foster an environment of "DevSecOps". By integrating into the tools you use to test your applications, you find issues early and often and fix them as part of the development testing cycles. However, checking the box just doesn't cut it anymore. Quality results and fixing issues efficiently matter just as much as a fast scan to truly deliver secure software in a DevOps world. Go beyond “check the box” application security with OpenText Core Application Security - because great code demands great security.

  • Boost developer’s productivity
Features | Case Studies | References

CodeMR visualizes code metrics and high level quality attributes (coupling, complexity, cohesion and size) in different views, such as Package Structure, TreeMap, Sunburst, Dependency and Graph Views.

idea-plugin.name: PT Application Inspector
idea-plugin.description:
Overview

The PT Application Inspector plugin finds vulnerabilities and undocumented features in application source code. In addition to code analysis, built-in modules detect errors in configuration files and vulnerabilities in third-party components and libraries used in application development. The plugin supports the following languages: C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, PHP, Python, Ruby, Scala, SQL, Solidity, TypeScript, C/C++, Objective-C, and Swift.

The plugin also partially supports 1C and Dart. You cannot start scans for 1C or Dart projects with the plugin, but you can use the plugin to create PT AI Enterprise Server projects in these languages or load scan results for 1C or Dart projects from PT AI Enterprise Server (the plugin will then display vulnerabilities detected in these projects). The "Hardcoded secrets" and "Vulnerable components and their use" modules are also partially supported. You can use the plugin to create PT AI Enterprise Server projects with these modules, or to load scan results for projects with these modules from PT AI Enterprise Server (the plugin will then display vulnerabilities detected by these modules).

Note. The scanning of projects in C/C++ and Objective-C is not supported in macOS.

How it works

Enabling and disabling the plugin

You can enable or disable the plugin in an open project by clicking the icon in the bottom right toolbar. If it is not the first time you are opening the project, the plugin is enabled automatically (scan and action history is saved). You can also set up the plugin to be automatically enabled when a new project is opened.

When the plugin is enabled, the .ai folder is created in the project. This folder contains a database, log files, and a configuration file. For Git to ignore the .ai folder, create an empty file .gitignore in the project folder.

Installing the code analyzer

For the plugin to operate correctly, the PT Application Inspector code analyzer is required. You can install it automatically by clicking Download Analyzer in the pop-up notification in the IntelliJ IDEA interface or manually by downloading it from the link in the instructions below.

To manually install the code analyzer:

  1. Download the archive with the analyzer using one of the links:

    • For Windows: download

    • For Linux: download

    • For macOS: download

  2. In macOS, run the following command to remove the com.apple.quarantine attribute:

    xattr -d com.apple.quarantine <analyzer_file_path.pkg>

    Then run the installation file and follow the instructions.

  3. In Windows and Linux, unpack the archive to one of the following locations:

    • In Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Application Inspector Analyzer

    • In Linux: ~/application-inspector-analyzer

Stopping a scan

To stop a project scan, click Stop scan in the PT Application Inspector panel or close the progress bar in the bottom toolbar.

Some vulnerabilities have additional exploitation conditions displayed in the Additional Conditions tab.

When you scroll through the sections of the diagram, the vulnerability information is automatically pinned until you move on to another vulnerability. If you want to view the information about a certain vulnerability while working on the code, you can pin this vulnerability manually.

Several vulnerabilities can have the same exit point. If these vulnerabilities belong to the same type, they are grouped together and displayed as one problem with different exploitation options. You can view detailed information about such vulnerabilities in the [PT AI] Vulnerability Details panel.

Note. If you confirm one vulnerability from the group, the whole problem will be confirmed automatically. To discard an entire problem, you must discard all the vulnerabilities in the group.

Managing detected vulnerabilities

The PT Application Inspector plugin contains a set of tools for managing detected vulnerabilities. With these tools, you can do the following:

  • Filter vulnerabilities by severity, status, and suppression from scan results by clicking the eye button.
  • Confirm and discard vulnerabilities by clicking Confirm or Discard on the [PT AI] Vulnerability Details panel.
  • Confirm, discard, and suppress vulnerabilities in their context menu in the code editor. There you can also perform group actions on all vulnerabilities in the file. For example, click Confirm vulnerability → Fix all code vulnerabilities in the file.
  • Manage the statuses of several vulnerabilities by selecting them in the Detected Vulnerabilities tab and changing the status using the corresponding button.

You can start the assistant from the pop-up notification that appears when the scan is completed or by clicking the Assistant button. You can choose to go through the whole scenario or only certain steps.

How to get a recommendation:

  1. Select a vulnerability on the Detected Vulnerabilities tab or by clicking Suggest fix in the code editor context menu.

  2. Select the How to Fix tab.

  3. Click Create.

You can apply the suggested fix or generate an alternative option.

Integration with PT AI Enterprise Edition

The PT Application Inspector plugin can be integrated with PT AI Enterprise Edition. The integration allows all team members to work with the source code from different environments, which makes the development process more secure.

To configure the integration:

  1. In the IntelliJ IDEA main menu, click Tools → PT Application Inspector → Connect to PT AI Server.

  2. Enter the PT AI Enterprise Server address and click Connect.

    • Send a local project for scanning to PT AI Enterprise Server with or without saving the results on the server.

For more information about the integration, see the PT AI Enterprise Edition User Guide.

Managing branches

If a project is a Git repository, the plugin uses a current branch as the local working branch. Local scan results, vulnerability statuses, and data on synchronization from PT AI Enterprise Server are associated with that branch.

When you set up synchronization between a local project and a PT AI Enterprise Server project, you must select the branch on the server that matches a current local branch. You can map a different branch later by selecting Tools → PT Application Inspector → Change PT AI Server Project Branch or by clicking a branch name in the scan results panel.

Branch mapping is needed for the following operations:

  • Uploading source code to PT AI Enterprise Server

  • Sending a local project to PT AI Enterprise Server for scanning

  • Synchronization of vulnerability statuses and scan results
idea-plugin.change-notes: • Added support for PT AI Enterprise Edition API version 6.1.0: the plugin now displays vulnerabilities detected in Dart projects. These vulnerabilities become available after you load the scan results from PT AI Enterprise Server.

idea-plugin.name: Cortex Cloud
idea-plugin.description:
Cortex Cloud Plugin for JetBrains

The Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin seamlessly is able to integrate with Cortex Cloud or Prisma Cloud's security checks into your JetBrains environment. This plugin provides real-time feedback on potential security issues as you write code, ensuring that security is prioritized throughout the development process.

With the Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin, developers can conveniently access features such as vulnerability scanning, code remediation, and policy enforcement directly within their coding workflow. Additionally, the plugin detects Infrastructure as Code (IaC) misconfigurations in templates like Kubernetes and Terraform, scans for Software Composition Analysis (SCA) vulnerabilities, identifies secrets vulnerabilities, and ensures compliance with software licensing requirements.

Policies and enforcement rules can be centrally managed within the platform, providing a streamlined approach to security management across your organization's development projects.

Features

  • IaC Misconfigurations: Detect misconfigurations in IaC templates (e.g., Kubernetes, Terraform).
  • SCA Vulnerabilities: Identify security issues in open-source dependencies.
  • Secrets Detection: Uncover vulnerabilities related to stored secrets.
  • License Compliance: Ensure adherence to software licensing requirements.

Installation

To install the Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin, follow these steps:

  1. Open your JetBrains product.
  2. Navigate to the Plugins configuration menu by opening the IDE settings and selecting the Plugins section.
  3. Search for Cortex Cloud in the Marketplace tab.
  4. Click on the Cortex Cloud plugin in the search results.
  5. Click the Install button

Configuration

To adjust the Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin settings, follow these steps:

  1. Open Visual Studio Code.
  2. Navigate to the extension settings by opening the IDE settings and navigating to Tools/Cortex Cloud.
  3. Update the following fields:
    • API Key ID: The Cortex Cloud or Prisma Cloud access key ID
    • API Key: The Cortex Cloud or Prisma Cloud API key (secret).
    • Platform URL: Your Platform URL e.g. https://api-<customer>.xdr.<region>.paloaltonetworks.com/ or https://api.prismacloud.io.
    • CLI version: Leave blank to use the latest scanner version, or specify a version of Cortex CLI or Checkov
    • CLI Path: Specifies the path to the CLI scanner. Leave empty to let the extension manage the scanner installation (recommended)
    • Certificate: Add the CA certificate as a .pem file format
    • Use Enforcement Rules: Relevant to Prisma platform only. Enforce soft-fail thresholds for Prisma Cloud scans set by Enforcement apply for JetBrains scans Hard-fail and comment bot are not supported by the IDE. For more information on Enforcement, refer to the Enforcement documentation
    • External checks dir: Provide the path to the folder containing custom security checks
    • Specific Frameworks: Scan specific frameworks such as arm json secrets serverless. You can add multiple frameworks using spaces between the values in the command. Refer to Cortex CLI or Checkov CLI for more information.
    • Environment Variables: Environment variables passed to the scanner during scans. Use for variables like ‘CKV_SKIP_CHECK | CKV_TF_1', etc.

Usage

Once configured, you can start using the Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin to enhance your development workflow:

  1. Write your code as usual.
  2. The plugin will provide real-time feedback and security suggestions as you work.
  3. Use the provided actions and commands to address security issues and ensure compliance with best practices.

Additional Resources

  • Cortex Cloud Documentation: Additional information and documentation on using the Cortex Cloud JetBrains Plugin.

CodeStats is an open source plugin for JetBrains IDE's that provides insightful statistics and a timeline view about your project. It not only helps you understand your codebase better with detailed metrics but also visualizes your coding journey over time.

  • Line counts
  • File sizes
  • Blank Lines
  • Comment Lines
  • Documentation Lines

With CodeStats, you can easily measure your project's size, source code line count, and view a timeline of your code-related activities.

Features

Getting Started

Contributing

idea-plugin.name: TornadoInsight
idea-plugin.description:
TornadoInsight is an open source IntelliJ plugin that aims to enhance the experience of developers when working with TornadoVM.
  • TornadoInsight provides a built-in on-the-fly static checker, empowering developers to identify unsupported Java features in TornadoVM and understand the reasons behind these limitations.
  • TornadoInsight introduces a dynamic testing framework that enables developers to easily test individual TornadoVM tasks. It automatically wraps TornadoVM tasks, invoking the native TornadoVM runtime on the developers' machines for seamless debugging and testing.

What's New in 1.6.0

TornadoInsight 1.6.0 adds compatibility with TornadoVM 6.0.0. The plugin reads the JDK requirement that TornadoVM 6.0.0 records in $TORNADOVM_HOME/etc/tornado.jdk and accepts any project JDK at or above that minimum. A GraalVM project JDK is now flagged with a clear error, because TornadoVM 6.0.0 and newer bundle their own Graal compiler and JVMCI and must run on a standard OpenJDK build.

What's New in 1.4.2

Important: Starting with version 1.4.2, the required environment variable has been renamed from TORNADO_SDK to TORNADOVM_HOME to align with TornadoVM's updated naming conventions. Please update your environment configuration before upgrading.

TornadoInsight 1.4.2 is compatible with TornadoVM 2.2.0 (onwards) and features automatic SDK detection. The plugin can now detect your installed TornadoVM SDK automatically without requiring a custom build from source. This streamlined setup makes it easier than ever to get started with TornadoVM development.

Getting started

TornadoInsight is available for versions 2023.1.7 and higher of compatible JetBrains IDEs. It invokes Java and TornadoVM at runtime on the computer where the plugin is installed, and therefore, developers must have installed Java and TornadoVM prior to using the plugin:
  • TornadoVM >= v2.2.0 (for TornadoInsight 1.4.2+); TornadoVM 6.0.0 is supported from TornadoInsight 1.6.0
  • JDK 21 or newer, matching the requirement of your TornadoVM SDK (a standard OpenJDK build, not a GraalVM one)

Install TornadoVM SDK

You can use SDKMAN! to install TornadoVM. The default version is OpenCL, but you can install any supported backend for your platform: 
sdk install tornadovm

Environment Variable Configuration (v1.4.2+)

Since version v1.4.2, TornadoInsight requires the TORNADOVM_HOME environment variable to be defined and visible to the IntelliJ IDEA process.

On modern operating systems, GUI applications (such as IntelliJ started from JetBrains Toolbox, the Dock, or an application launcher) do not always inherit shell variables defined in files like ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc. For this reason, TORNADOVM_HOME must be configured using OS-appropriate mechanisms, as described below. To find the path for your TornadoVM SDK, run: 

which tornado
Required Variable: 
TORNADOVM_HOME=/absolute/path/to/tornado-sdk
macOS:
  • Run in terminal: launchctl setenv TORNADOVM_HOME /absolute/path/to/tornado-sdk
  • Fully quit IntelliJ IDEA (Cmd + Q) and relaunch it
Linux (systemd):
  • Create directory: mkdir -p ~/.config/environment.d
  • Create file: ~/.config/environment.d/tornado.conf
  • Add line: TORNADOVM_HOME=/absolute/path/to/tornado-sdk
  • Log out and log back in, then start IntelliJ IDEA
Windows:
  • Open System Properties → Environment Variables
  • Add User variable: TORNADOVM_HOME=C:\path\to\tornado-sdk
  • Restart IntelliJ IDEA

Plugin Configuration

The dynamic inspection feature of TornadoInsight is configured after the installation of the plugin, as follows:
  • Navigate to "Settings" and select "TornadoInsight" from the menu.
  • With TornadoInsight 1.4.2+, the plugin automatically detects your installed TornadoVM SDK and uses the Java SDK from your Project Settings. You only need to indicate a tentative "array size" that can be used by TornadoInsight to set the size of the input and output arrays of a TornadoVM task.
For more information, please follow our documentation.
Enjoy and share your feedback!
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Version 1.6.0

  • TornadoVM 6.0.0 compatibility: The JDK compatibility check now reads the etc/tornado.jdk contract that TornadoVM 6.0.0 ships (minimum JDK plus preview flag) instead of the removed tornado --version JDK marker, and accepts any project JDK at or above that minimum.
  • GraalVM JDK guard: A GraalVM project JDK is detected and reported with a clear error instead of a JVM crash, since TornadoVM 6.0.0+ bundles its own Graal compiler and JVMCI.
  • The info console reports the resolved TornadoVM JDK requirement and the project JDK in use.

Version 1.4.2

  • Environment Variable Update: The required environment variable has been renamed from TORNADO_SDK to TORNADOVM_HOME to align with TornadoVM's updated naming conventions. Please update your environment configuration accordingly.

Version 1.4.0

  • TornadoVM 2.0+ Support: Full compatibility with TornadoVM 2.0 and later versions
  • Automatic SDK Detection: The plugin now automatically detects your installed TornadoVM SDK without requiring manual configuration of the TornadoVM root directory
  • Streamlined Setup: No longer requires building TornadoVM from source - works directly with installed TornadoVM SDK packages
  • Improved Configuration: Simplified settings panel without explicit declaration of the Java SDK path. Instead, the plugin reuses the user-defined Java SDK from Project Settings

idea-plugin.name: Cloud (IaC) Security
idea-plugin.description:
Docker and Kubernetes Security Scanner for JetBrains IDEs (e.g., IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, and more).

What is inside?

The plugin provides two main features:

  • Docker Security Scanner: it covers Trivy and Hadolint rules and also provides rules to match Docker Best Practices.
  • Kubernetes Security Scanner: it covers pod security standards.

Why this plugin?

  • Seamless integration into the IDE without installing external tools.
  • Verifies your files on the fly and highlight problems earlier, and that make shift left happens.
  • Quick-fixes for problems are available for some inspections that could help fix problems faster.
  • Supports complicated verifications, such as tracking variables and arguments as sources of issues.
  • Pure Kotlin implementation, leveraging the power of IDEs.

What does the plugin offer?

  • Dockerfile Analysis: Scanner for security vulnerabilities and Docker image optimization with over 40 checks.
  • Docker Compose: Scanner for security vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
  • Kubernetes: Scanner for security issues to align with the Pod Security Standards.
  • Quick Fixes: Resolve issues faster using built-in quick fixes.

What problems can the plugin detect?

You can find more information about detected problems:

  • Detailed documentation on the bundled Cloud Security inspection
  • In-IDE pop-up messages describing each issue, each of which links to a dedicated article in the documentation

Planned features

  • Kubernetes: Implementing more rules to align with the NSA and CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide.

References

  • Trivy checks – entry point for Docker rules.
  • Hadolint – source of additional Docker rules.
  • Pod Security Standards – entry point for Kubernetes rules.
  • Kubescape Rego library – source of Kubernetes rules.

Thanks

  • My mother, who supported me every step of the way and who is no longer with us.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

idea-plugin.name: Security Analysis by Qodana
idea-plugin.description:
Security Analysis by Qodana

This plugin leverages IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate’s built-in interprocedural data flow analysis engine to deliver robust security (taint) analysis for your code.

About Taint Analysis

Taint analysis is a method used in security testing to trace the flow of potentially harmful (“tainted”) data through a program. It identifies paths where an untrusted input (source) might reach sensitive operations (sinks) without proper validation or sanitization, helping to prevent security vulnerabilities like SQL injection, XSS, and more.

Supported Vulnerability Types

Using preconfigured settings, this plugin detects the following types of vulnerabilities:
  • Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
  • Command Injection
  • SQL Injection
  • Path Traversal

Supported Languages

Currently supports Java and Kotlin.

Upcoming Features

Soon, users will have the flexibility to define custom configurations, including custom sinks, sources, sanitizers, and more.

Third-Party Software list

Third-party software components are used as part of settings of the plugin. List of those components and their corresponding licenses could be found in the plugin contents.

idea-plugin.name: named-elements
idea-plugin.description:
This is a powerful plugin designed to streamline the process of understanding and navigating your codebase. It scans a selected directory and generates a comprehensive, sortable table of all named code elements, tailored to the specific programming languages found within your project.

Key Features:

  • The plugin extracts and lists all significant named elements. This includes:
    • Classes and Interfaces
    • Functions and Methods
    • Variables and Constants
    • Enums and Structs
    • Namespaces and Modules
  • Interactive and Sortable Table: The generated output is a clean, interactive table. You can easily sort the table columns by element name, type, or count to quickly find what you're looking for.
  • Quick Navigation: Each entry in the table is an actionable link. Clicking on an element will instantly take you to its exact location in the source code, making it effortless to jump between definitions and implementations.

How It Works:

  1. Select a Directory or the whole Projekt and start the action "Analyze Named Elements...".
  2. Scan and Analyze: The plugin will recursively scan the selected directory and analyze the files to extract all named elements.
  3. Generate Table: A new panel or window will appear, displaying the interactive table with all the extracted information.

Benefits:

  • Improved Code Comprehension: Quickly get a high-level overview of a new or unfamiliar codebase.
  • Enhanced Productivity: Spend less time searching for code and more time writing it.
  • Simplified Refactoring: Easily identify all related functions, variables, or classes before making changes.

Whether you're a new developer joining a team or a senior engineer tasked with refactoring a legacy system, the Named Elements Analyzer is an indispensable tool for mastering your codebase.

idea-plugin.vendor: Brad Chamberlain (fork of Hu Dong's work)
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Changed

  • Minimum supported version is now CLion 2026.2 (build 262)
  • Build against CLion 2026.2.2 with JDK 25, Kotlin 2.4.20, IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.18.1 and Gradle 9.7.1
  • Build layout aligned with the IntelliJ Platform Plugin Template (repositories and plugin versions in settings.gradle.kts, no version catalog)
  • Plugin verification runs against CLion 2026.2 and the latest CLion 2026.3 EAP
  • Plugin description and name are now defined in plugin.xml; change notes are generated from this changelog
  • Gradle wrapper JAR is now committed to the repository
  • cpplint now runs in the background as an external annotator, outside the editor's read action, with a 30 second timeout and proper cancellation
  • Quick fixes no longer save the file to disk, and support the intention preview
  • Python can be given as a command on PATH (for example python3)
  • Configuration errors are shown once per project instead of every minute, and no longer raise IDE internal errors

Added

  • Unit tests for output parsing, line mapping and every quick fix transformation
  • Quick fixes for "At least two spaces is best between code and comments" and "Extra space before last semicolon"
  • .cu and .cuh files are linted, matching cpplint's defaults

Fixed

  • Linting could hang when cpplint produced a lot of output (stdout and stderr were read one after the other)
  • Highlights landed on the wrong lines while the file had unsaved changes; results are now mapped onto the editor text
  • Quick fixes could edit the wrong line after other edits; each fix now checks its line is unchanged first
  • Header guard fix could overwrite unrelated #ifndef/#define lines, missed guards behind block comments, and ignored most of cpplint's suggested guard names
  • #endif comment fix never applied to the case cpplint reports (#endif FOO_H_)
  • Comma, comment and semicolon fixes could change string literals, URLs and unrelated lines
  • NOLINT suppression broke macro line continuations and could not add a second category
  • Tab replacement ignored tab stops and broke alignment
  • Settings "Test Configuration" and "Auto-Detect Paths" could freeze the dialog; they now run in the background with a timeout, and skip the Microsoft Store Python alias
  • Options containing leading spaces or quoted values were passed to cpplint incorrectly
  • Inspection description was not shown in Settings

Removed

  • Qodana and Kover build integrations
  • Unused Cygwin/MinGW helpers and file picker code

idea-plugin.name: VulnSpeed - GPU-Accelerated SAST

VulnSpeed — GPU-Accelerated SAST for Real-Time Vulnerability Detection

Security scanning at the speed of thought. VulnSpeed detects OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25 vulnerabilities as you type across 7 languages, with one-click auto-fixes and optional GPU acceleration for instant results on large codebases.

Real-Time Detection

  • As-You-Type Scanning — Vulnerabilities highlighted inline in the editor with severity levels

Secrets Detection

  • Near-Zero False Positives — Vendor-specific token formats, not noisy entropy heuristics

Remediation & Workflow

  • One-Click Auto-Fix — Alt+Enter to apply automated remediation suggestions instantly
  • Inline Suppression — // vulnspeed-ignore or // vulnspeed-ignore: RULE_ID comments to accept findings where you decide they are fine

  • Security Dashboard — Tool window with vulnerability list, statistics, and quick access to fixes

Advanced Analysis

  • GPU Acceleration — Metal/CUDA/Vulkan accelerated engine, 50-100x faster than CPU scanning
  • Taint Analysis — Advanced data flow tracking across function boundaries
  • AI False Positive Filtering — ML-based filtering to reduce noise
  • Custom Security Rules — Define organization-specific vulnerability patterns
  • Compliance Reports — Generate SOC 2, HIPAA, and PCI DSS reports
  • CI/CD Integration — Run VulnSpeed in your pipeline for gated security checks

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2025.1+ (or any JetBrains IDE)
  • JDK 17+
  • 2 GB free RAM
  • GPU optional (Metal, CUDA, or Vulkan for Pro acceleration)

Support

  • Documentation
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2026.6.6 — Internal API removal (clean re-release)

  • Plugin-version lookup no longer calls the internal PluginManager.findEnabledPlugin(PluginId) method — replaced with the public PluginManagerCore.getPlugin(PluginId) API (6 call sites)
  • Re-verified build: 0 internal-API usages against IntelliJ 2025.1 – 2026.1

2026.6.1 — Platform API cleanup

  • Plugin-version lookup migrated to the public PluginManager API; removed internal-API imports from the editor annotator

2026.6.0 — Secrets, Suppression & Reports

  • Secrets Detection — 12 new high-signal rules for AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Google, SendGrid, Twilio, npm tokens, private key blocks, JWTs, and credentials in URLs (CWE-798)
  • Inline Suppression — // vulnspeed-ignore and // vulnspeed-ignore: RULE_ID comments suppress findings on a line; vulnspeed-ignore-file opts out a whole file
  • HTML Report Export — Self-contained HTML security report with severity summary cards and per-finding detail, ready to share
  • Kotlin inline highlighting — As-you-type annotations now also run in Kotlin files (was advertised but never registered)
  • Fixed: Findings in the first 10 columns of a line crashed snippet extraction and were silently dropped
  • Fixed: Editor annotations were created asynchronously after the highlighting pass ended, so inline highlights never appeared reliably
  • New tool window icon and dark-theme plugin icon

2026.4.1 — Archive Fix

  • Fixed archive extraction — Rebuilt plugin distribution to fix "archive cannot be extracted" error on JetBrains Marketplace

What's New

  • Multi-Language Support - Full scanning for Java, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C/C++, and Swift
  • One-Click Auto-Fix - Automated remediation suggestions applied instantly via Alt+Enter

  • Security Dashboard - Bottom panel displaying vulnerability list, statistics, severity breakdown, and quick access to fixes
  • GPU-Accelerated Scanning - Metal, CUDA, and Vulkan accelerated engine for 50-100x faster analysis on large codebases
  • Advanced Taint Analysis - Data flow and taint tracking to trace vulnerability propagation paths
  • AI False Positive Filtering - Machine learning based filtering to reduce noise and surface real vulnerabilities
  • Compliance Reports - Generate SOC 2, HIPAA, and PCI DSS compliance reports from scan results

idea-plugin.name: Xygeni Security
idea-plugin.description:
Xygeni Security Plugin

Secure your codebase with Secrets, SAST, SCA, IaC & Supply Chain scanning directly within your VS Code environment.

Xygeni Security Scanner is a powerful extension that brings comprehensive security scanning to your fingertips. It integrates seamlessly with your development workflow, allowing you to identify and remediate security vulnerabilities early in the process.

Key features:

  • Comprehensive Scanning: Detects a wide range of security issues:
    • Secrets: Find hardcoded credentials, API keys, and other sensitive data.
    • SAST (Static Application Security Testing): Analyze your source code for common vulnerabilities.
    • SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Identify vulnerabilities in your open-source dependencies.
    • IaC (Infrastructure as Code): Scan your IaC files (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation) for misconfigurations.
    • Misconfigurations: Detect security misconfigurations in your application and services.
  • Seamless Integration: The extension adds a dedicated Xygeni view to your activity bar for easy access.
  • Guided Setup: A simple configuration process to connect to the Xygeni service.
  • In-Editor Issue Highlighting: View security findings directly in your code, making it easy to pinpoint and fix issues.
  • Detailed Vulnerability Information: Get rich details for each identified issue, including severity, description, and remediation guidance.
  • Code Flow Visualization: For SAST issues, visualize the complete vulnerability path through both interactive Graph and Path views, identifying sources, sinks, and intermediate frames.
  • Scan on Save: Automatically scan your project on file save to identify issues as they are introduced (configurable in settings).

Getting started:

  1. Install the plugin from JetBrains marketplace. Once installed, the plugin automatically downloads and sets up the Xygeni Scanner.
  2. Open the Xygeni View and the Xygeni console: After installation, click the Xygeni icon in the activity bar to open the view and console.
  3. Configure the plugin:
    • You will be prompted to configure the connection to the Xygeni service.
    • Obtain an API token from your Xygeni Dashboard. If you don’t have an account, you can sign up for a free trial.
    • Enter the Xygeni API URL and your API token in the configuration view.
  4. Run a scan.
    • Ensure the Xygeni Scanner is fully installed (check the tool window for status). The Run scan button will be active once the installation is complete.
    • Click on the Run scan button to initiate a scan of your workspace.
  5. View and Refresh results:
    • Scan results are displayed in the Xygeni view, categorized by type (SAST, SCA, Secrets, etc.).
    • Use the Reload icon in any report header to refresh the findings manually.
    • Click an issue to view the file where the issue is found.
    • Click twice on an issue to view detailed information and explore the Code Flow tab for SAST vulnerabilities.
  6. Fix issues:
    • On the detailed information, select the FIX tab to remediate the vulnerability.

idea-plugin.name: Jinja2 Enhanced Support
idea-plugin.description:
Jinja2 Enhanced — Professional Template Support for JetBrains IDEs

Complete Jinja2/Jinja template language support with a custom hand-written parser, intelligent code analysis, smart completion, reference resolution, and a rich extension API.

🎯 Core Language Features

  • Custom Hand-Written Parser — Modular recursive-descent parser with specialized parsers for expressions, statements, and blocks ensuring accurate AST generation
  • Full Jinja2 Syntax Coverage — All statements (for, if, macro, block, call, filter, set, with, autoescape, raw), template directives (extends, include, import, from…import), all extensions (do, break/continue, trans, debug), and line statements/comments with configurable prefixes
  • Advanced Syntax Highlighting — Lexical analysis with context-aware token classification and full whitespace control modifier support ({{-, -%}, -}}, {%-)
  • Rainbow Highlighting — Color-coded block and bracket matching with three independent annotators (blocks, brackets, expressions) for improved code readability
  • Semantic Highlighting — Context-aware coloring for variables, macros, macro parameters, block names, and import aliases
  • Code Folding — Smart folding for all block structures: for, if, macro, block, call, filter, with, autoescape, raw, comments
  • Brace Matching — Intelligent delimiter matching for all Jinja2 bracket types

🧠 Smart Code Completion

  • Context-Aware Completion — Completions vary by cursor position: inside tags, inside expressions, after | (filters), after is (tests), or at tag start
  • Built-in Filters — All Jinja2 filters with signatures and descriptions (abs, capitalize, default, escape, join, sort, tojson, and more)
  • Built-in Tests — All Jinja2 tests (defined, even, odd, iterable, mapping, none, divisibleby, and more)
  • Built-in Functions — range, namespace, cycler, joiner, lipsum, dict
  • Scope-Aware Variables — Variables from set, for loop variables, loop.* inside loops, macro parameters, caller inside call blocks, self.blockname() references
  • Macro Attributes — Completion and documentation for macro object properties (name, arguments, catch_kwargs, etc.)
  • Type-Based Member Completion — Define type schemas for context variables and get field completions for user.profile.name style access chains

🔍 Code Quality & Inspections

  • Undefined Variable Detection — Identifies variables and macros used before declaration with scope-aware analysis
  • Undefined Attribute Detection — Warns about attribute access not described in the type schema
  • Duplicate Macro Detection — Warns about duplicate macro definitions within the same template
  • Invalid Inheritance Checks — Validates proper usage of extends, block, and super()
  • Invalid Tag Context Detection — Ensures tags are used correctly (elif/else inside if, endfor paired with for, etc.)
  • Logical Error Inspections — Detects always-true/false conditions and meaningless checks
  • Unused Construct Detection — Highlights declared but never-used variables and macros
  • Extension Usage Checks — Warns about {% do %} without the extension enabled
  • Quick Fix: Add # noqa — Suppress any inspection inline

🔗 Navigation & Reference Resolution

  • Go to Definition — Navigate to macro definitions (including imported ones), block definitions in parent templates, variable declarations, and template files
  • Template File Navigation — Ctrl+Click on paths in extends, include, and import to open the target template
  • Import Resolution — Fully resolves macros from {% from "..." import macro %} and module aliases from {% import "..." as module %}
  • Block Reference Navigation — Navigate between block definitions across the template inheritance chain
  • Find Usages — Find all usages of macros, blocks, variables, and module aliases across templates

📖 Documentation (Ctrl+Q)

  • Inline documentation for all built-in filters, tests, functions, and tags
  • Signatures and usage examples shown in the documentation popup
  • Built-in Documentation Viewer — Side panel and editor tabs for quick reference

🎨 Code Formatting

  • Configurable Code Style — Customizable indentation, spacing, and blank line settings (Settings → Editor → Code Style → Jinja2)
  • Intelligent Spacing Rules — Operators, argument lists, and delimiters ({{ expr }}, {% tag %}) formatted correctly
  • Format on Ctrl+Alt+L — Full reformatting support

⚙️ Editor Helpers

  • Auto-Close Delimiters — Typing {% → inserts %}, {{ → }}, {# → #}
  • Intention Actions — Quick add/remove whitespace trim modifiers on Jinja2 delimiters
  • Line & Block Commenting — Ctrl+/ wraps selection in {# ... #}
  • Breadcrumbs — Navigation bar showing path through nested blocks, macros, and tags
  • Spellcheck Integration — Checks string literals, comments, and template text; Jinja2 syntax is excluded
  • Live Templates — Snippets for for, if, block, macro, set, extends, and more

💉 Language Injection

  • Inject Jinja2 into string literals in Python, YAML, HTML, and other languages
  • Automatic detection notification for files containing Jinja2 syntax
  • Configurable injection rules via extension point

🔌 Extension API (15 Extension Points)

Other plugins can extend Jinja2 Enhanced support for their frameworks:

  • Custom Filters, Tests, Functions — Register with documentation and signatures
  • Context Variables & Type Schemas — Describe framework-provided variables with full type information for member completion
  • Custom Tags — Register tag behaviors and custom assignment tags (like Django's {% with %} variants)
  • Template Roots — Point to framework-specific template directories
  • Jinja API Config Override — Custom delimiters, whitespace control, extensions, undefined behavior
  • Macro Modules — Provide pre-defined macro modules for framework-specific helpers

⚙️ Configuration

  • Plugin Settings: Settings → Languages & Frameworks → Jinja2
  • Jinja API Settings: Custom delimiters, enabled extensions, whitespace control, autoescape mode
  • Code Style: Settings → Editor → Code Style → Jinja2
  • Color Scheme: Settings → Editor → Color Scheme → Jinja2
  • Inspections: Settings → Editor → Inspections → Jinja2Enhanced

🧪 Quality Assurance

  • 100+ lexer tests covering all token types and edge cases
  • 100+ parser test files validating all Jinja2 constructs, nested structures, and error conditions
  • Tests for highlighting, formatting, inspections, completion, and reference resolution

Supports IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, and all JetBrains IDEs (2023.1+)

⭐ If you find this plugin helpful, please leave a review on the Marketplace!
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Version 2026.3.1

Framework-aware template assistance, richer type information, and more extension points for Jinja2 integrations.

Smarter Template Assistance

  • Completion, inspections, navigation, and Quick Documentation now understand types supplied by frameworks, including nested attributes, mappings, collections, unions, and callable values.
  • Variables contributed by a framework now participate in completion, type inference, navigation, and shadowing just like template-local variables.
  • Dynamic object members can provide completion, validation, documentation, and navigation. Members without a physical declaration can still open a virtual declaration in the IDE.
  • Improved diagnostics for unknown attributes and method calls when type information is available from an integration.
  • Added validation support for attributes of Jinja's loop object.

Framework & Extension API

  • New APIs let framework integrations contribute variables, functions, macros, indexed symbols, reference resolution, completion items, dynamic types, type schemas, inspection rules, and quick fixes.
  • Contributed functions and macros now offer signatures, documentation, completion, navigation, and Find Usages support.
  • Added file-aware Jinja environment configuration, allowing integrations to customize delimiters and syntax settings for individual template files.
  • Language injection rules can now target precise ranges inside a host element.
  • Live templates can be limited to the appropriate native or framework-provided Jinja template contexts.
  • Examples and API documentation are available for the new extension points, making it easier to build and test framework integrations.

Fixes & Reliability

  • Improved reliability of IDE analysis for templates and injected fragments, including safer handling of background processing.
  • Improved cache invalidation so changes from framework integrations are reflected more consistently in editor assistance.
  • Improved compatibility with code shrinking in packaged plugin builds.

Version 2026.3.0

Major parser reliability improvements, new language features, and enhanced code completion.

New Features

  • Added support for line statements and line comments — configurable prefixes for single-line Jinja2 syntax (e.g., # for, ## comment).
  • Added block set with filter support — capture block content and apply filters ({% set x | upper %}...{% endset %}).
  • Added macro attributes — completion, navigation, and documentation for macro object properties (name, arguments, catch_kwargs, etc.).
  • Added self.blockname() support — completions, navigation, and documentation for self-referencing block output.
  • Added % string formatting operator support in expressions.
  • Added intention action to add whitespace trim modifiers ({%-, -%}) to Jinja2 delimiters.

Code Completion Enhancements

  • Added missing built-in tests: true, false, escaped, filter, test.
  • Added comparison test aliases: eq, ne, gt, ge, lt, le, in.
  • Added d and e filter aliases (shortcuts for default and escape).

Parser & Error Handling

  • Significantly improved parser reliability across all statement types (for, if, set, macro, trans, raw, and custom blocks).
  • Better error recovery for malformed expressions, unclosed tags, and invalid syntax — fewer false-positive errors in complex templates.
  • Improved handling of unterminated comment blocks with clearer error messages.
  • Fixed operator precedence: power operator (**) now correctly left-associative per Jinja2 spec.
  • Added brace matching for trimmed comment delimiters ({#-, -#}).

Formatting

  • Improved whitespace normalization in block bodies for more consistent formatting results.

Other

  • Added JetBrains Marketplace error reporter for automatic crash reporting.

Version 2026.2.0

Improved in-IDE documentation experience and compatibility with the latest IntelliJ-based IDEs.

In-IDE Documentation

  • Plugin documentation now opens in an editor tab, making it easier to read and keep alongside your code.
  • Documentation pages use the IDE's embedded browser for richer and more reliable rendering.

IDE Compatibility

  • Updated compatibility for current and upcoming IntelliJ-based IDE releases.

Improvements

  • Reduced unnecessary Jinja2 detection notifications for files that are already recognized as Jinja2 templates.

idea-plugin.name: KotlinPoet Assistant
idea-plugin.description:
Brings first-class IDE support for CodeBlock format strings directly into IntelliJ IDEA. If you use KotlinPoet to generate Kotlin code, this plugin helps you write format strings confidently — with real-time validation, smart navigation, inline documentation, and a live preview of what your builder chain will produce.

Results are approximations. This plugin is a development aid, not a code generator. Some previews may differ from the actual KotlinPoet runtime output (e.g., import resolution, indent context, variables). When in doubt, trust your tests.

Features at a Glance

  • 🔴 Inspections — Missing arguments, extra arguments, type mismatches, invalid named keys, and format syntax errors, all reported inline with quick fixes.
  • 🎨 Syntax Highlighting — Placeholders (%L, %S, %T, …) and control symbols («, », ⇥, ⇤, …) are highlighted in a distinct color so they stand out from surrounding string content.
  • 🔗 Navigate to Argument — Ctrl+Click (or Cmd+Click) on a placeholder jumps straight to the argument it is bound to.
  • 📖 Inline Documentation — Hover over any placeholder or control symbol for a quick-doc popup with a description and a link to the official KotlinPoet docs.
  • ✅ Completion — Typing % inside a CodeBlock format string pops up a completion list for all supported placeholders (%L, %S, %T, %N, %M, %P, %%).
  • 🔍 Find Usages — Find all format-string positions that reference a particular argument, alongside the argument declaration itself.
  • 🪟 Chain Preview Tool Window — A bottom tool window that shows the approximated output of the entire CodeBlock builder chain at the current caret, complete with per-call metadata, state-machine violations, and an indented text preview.
  • 💡 Inlay Hints — Optional per-call end-of-line hints showing the approximate emission of each builder call, plus a collapsible block preview above the terminal build() call.

This plugin is not affiliated with or endorsed by Square or KotlinPoet.

Made with ❤️ by Rey A. with help from Claude · Report an issue · KotlinPoet Official docs
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Missing argument (KotlinPoetMissingArgument) — reports a placeholder with no corresponding argument; causes IllegalArgumentException at runtime. Level: Error.
  • Extra argument (KotlinPoetExtraArgument) — reports a surplus argument with no matching placeholder. Level: Error for relative/positional, Information for named maps (shared maps are a valid pattern). Quick fix: Remove extra argument.
  • Argument type mismatch (KotlinPoetTypeMismatch) — reports an argument whose resolved type is incompatible with the placeholder kind it is bound to (%T expects TypeName/KClass, %M expects MemberName, etc.). Level: Warning / Information depending on kind.
  • Named argument case (KotlinPoetNamedCase) — reports a named-argument key that does not match KotlinPoet's required pattern [a-z]+[\w_]*. Level: Warning. Quick fix: Rename 'X' to 'x' (renames key in both the format string and the map literal simultaneously).
  • Format syntax (KotlinPoetFormatSyntax) — reports parser-level issues in format strings:
    • Dangling % — quick fixes: Escape as %%, Remove invalid format token.
    • Unknown placeholder type (e.g., %Z) — quick fix: Remove invalid format token.
    • Invalid positional index (e.g., %0L) — quick fix: Fix index to %1L.
    • Mixed argument styles (relative + positional + named in the same string) — quick fixes: Convert to named style, Convert to relative style, Convert to positional style (the latter two use a live template for interactive renaming).

Technical

  • Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2025.2+ (build 252+) with K2 Kotlin plugin mode. K1 is not supported.
  • Domain layer is PSI-free and IntelliJ-free; fully unit-testable without the platform.
  • Analysis results are cached per KtCallExpression via CachedValuesManager to avoid redundant K2 sessions on every annotator/inspection pass.
  • Format string parsed from PSI (FormatText/FormatTextSegment) preserving absolute file offsets for precise range highlighting and navigation — no raw string reparsing.
  • StringFormatParserImpl never throws for malformed input; all issues are accumulated as errors/warnings in FormatStringModel.
  • Chain analysis uses an immutable state machine (EmissionState + EmissionStateDelta) safe to cache per call and compose across the chain.

idea-plugin.name: HDL and Vivado + MCP Support
idea-plugin.description:
Let an AI assistant drive Vivado while you watch — and work alongside it.

FPGA work means living in two windows: your editor for the RTL, and Vivado for everything else. This plugin closes that gap, and then goes further — it can hand your live Vivado session to an AI assistant, so building a block design or chasing a timing failure becomes a conversation instead of an afternoon of clicking.

The part that makes it usable: the Vivado GUI stays open and you keep using it. You watch the assistant wire up the block design in the canvas as it happens, and you can click, inspect and type your own Tcl in the same session while it works. Human in the loop, not a black box that hands you a result.

Everything it does, at a glance

  • AI assistant (MCP), with you in the loop — let Claude Code, Junie or Codex drive your live Vivado session while the GUI stays open in front of you. Watch each block design get wired and each run kick off as it happens, and keep clicking and typing in the same session while the assistant works. Off by default.
  • Vivado Console — a live Tcl terminal on a running session; the Vivado GUI stays usable while you type.
  • Verilog & SystemVerilog — highlighting, completion, commenting, and module/endmodule-aware brace matching.
  • Tcl & XDC — highlighting, folding, ${var} handling, and Vivado command completion.
  • Cross-module linting — Icarus Verilog or Verilator inline, analysing your whole design so cross-file instantiations resolve.
  • One-click Vivado — build a project from a folder, open an .xpr, run Tcl/XDC scripts, package IP.
  • Vitis & Vitis HLS — open a workspace or create an HLS kernel from a folder.

——— In detail ———

AI assistants can drive your Vivado session

Connect Claude Code, Junie, Codex, or any client that speaks the Model Context Protocol, and it gets 27 curated, parameter-checked Vivado commands — the same ones you have. It can create and open projects, add sources, set the top module, build and wire block designs, apply board presets, run connection automation, assign addresses, generate HDL wrappers, run synthesis and implementation, produce a bitstream, and program a device.

Ask for what you want:

  • "Create a Zynq project for my KV260, add the PS, and wire up an AXI GPIO."
  • "Synthesis failed — read the log and tell me what broke."
  • "Add these RTL files, set top to design_1_wrapper, and build a bitstream."

This is not a headless robot — you are sitting next to it

The assistant drives the same Vivado session you are looking at. The GUI is open the whole time, so you see the block design get wired up, the IP get configured and the runs start — live, in the canvas, not as a summary afterwards.

And you are not locked out while it works. You can keep using Vivado alongside the assistant: click around the block design, open a report, or type your own Tcl into the Vivado Console. Every command — yours and the assistant's — goes through one queue, so the two of you share the session without colliding. If you do not like where it is heading, you can act on it immediately rather than waiting for it to finish.

You stay in charge the whole time:

  • You start it, every time. The server never starts on its own, and a safety agreement explains what you are enabling before it opens.
  • Arbitrary Tcl is opt-in. The unrestricted-Tcl tools are hidden from the assistant and refused unless you enable them for that one session.
  • Locked down. Loopback only, no CORS headers, browser origins and rebound host names refused, and a fresh bearer token minted for every session.
  • Nothing happens silently. Every command is printed to the Vivado Console before it executes, so you watch the work as it happens — and you can type into the same session while the assistant works.
  • Vivado must be running. No live session means every tool is refused.

Vivado Console — the terminal underneath it

The same channel the assistant uses is yours to type into: a bidirectional Tcl terminal attached to a live Vivado session. Because it talks over a socket rather than stdin, the Vivado GUI stays fully usable while you work. 27 parameterised commands are available from a toolbar palette, with command history on the up/down arrows.

Language support

  • Verilog and SystemVerilog (.v .vh .sv .svh) — syntax highlighting, context-aware completion, commenting, and brace matching that pairs module/endmodule, begin/end, case/endcase and the rest.
  • Tcl and XDC (.tcl .xdc) — highlighting, code folding for proc bodies and braced blocks, ${var} handling, and completion for common Vivado commands.

Linting that understands your whole design

  • Real-time errors and warnings from Icarus Verilog or Verilator, inline in the editor.
  • Mark a folder as the Top Folder and the linter analyses your modules together — cross-file instantiations resolve instead of showing up as phantom errors.
  • A debugger panel with the raw tool output when you need to see exactly what ran.

Vivado and Vitis

  • Build a project from a folder of HDL, or open an existing .xpr.
  • Run a Tcl or XDC script from the project view (Ctrl+Alt+R).
  • Package IP through IP Composer, and open Vitis workspaces or create Vitis HLS kernels.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2025.1 or newer.
  • Xilinx Vivado (2023.2 or newer recommended) for the Vivado features — set the path in Settings → Tools → HDL Settings.
  • Icarus Verilog or Verilator for linting. Everything else works without them.

Source, issue tracker and documentation on GitHub.

Parts of this plugin were developed with AI assistance. Every release is reviewed and covered by an automated test suite; please report anything that looks wrong.
Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by AMD/Xilinx or JetBrains. Vivado, Vitis and Xilinx are trademarks of Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. IntelliJ IDEA is a trademark of JetBrains s.r.o.

idea-plugin.name: Simplified Annotations
idea-plugin.description:
Three annotation families for Java with companion IDE tooling: @ResourcePath (static resource-path validation), @XContract (superset of JetBrains @Contract), and @ClassBuilder (Lombok-@Builder superset with annotation-processor code generation).

@ClassBuilder

  • Annotation processor generates a sibling <TypeName>Builder.java for every class, record, or interface annotated with @ClassBuilder. Interfaces also get a matching <Name>Impl concrete class.
  • Full Lombok @Builder parity: configurable method names (builderMethodName, buildMethodName, fromMethodName, toBuilderMethodName), method prefix, access level, custom factory method, exclusions.
  • Setter-shape extras that Lombok doesn't cover: dual Optional<T> setters, zero-arg + typed boolean pairs with @Negate, @PrintFormat string overloads via @Formattable, @Collector varargs / iterable bulk overloads with opt-in single-element add/put, clear, and lazy put-if-absent for collections and maps, defensive-copy from(T), and a mutate() instance shorthand.
  • Per-field rules as standalone annotations: retainInit - on by default, and overridable per field with @BuilderDefault - copies the field's declared initializer into the builder so unset fields start at the intended value (UUID.randomUUID(), sensible strings, pre-populated collections) instead of the JVM default; @BuilderIgnore excludes a single field; @ObtainVia redirects from(T) to a non-standard accessor - an instance method, a static helper, or a different field - when the target type doesn't expose a matching getter.
  • @BuildFlag validation enforces nonNull / notEmpty / group mutual-requirement / regex pattern / length limit in the generated build(). The checks are emitted into the builder, so a constraint costs nothing on the runtime classpath.
  • @XContract annotations are emitted on every generated method so IntelliJ data-flow analysis understands fresh-object and this-return shapes.
  • IDE inspections: Bootstrap-methods missing (ERROR-level) with a quick-fix that inserts builder() / from(T) / mutate() all at once; @ClassBuilder field annotations catches mistakes like @Formattable on a non-String field.

@ResourcePath

  • Resource Path inspection - verifies that every annotated field, parameter, or method return resolves to a file that exists in the project's content source roots (or in user-configured additional roots). Supports an optional base attribute that prefixes the validated path.
  • Resource Path Base-Prefix Usage inspection - catches the common runtime mistake of passing a @ResourcePath(base="X") parameter raw into a resource-loading call (Class.getResourceAsStream, new File(...), etc.) without prepending X/. Offers a quick-fix. Also flags base mismatches across method boundaries.
  • Value resolution follows literals, concatenation, final/static/enum fields, local variables, method-call return values (recursively), and enum-constructor bindings, with bounded recursion and result size.
  • Settings: custom resource-root paths, glob-based file exclusions, separate severity for invalid-base errors.

@XContract

  • Superset of JetBrains @Contract with a richer grammar: relational comparisons, && / || with grouping, named-parameter references, instanceof conditions, typed throws returns, chained comparisons (0 <= index < size()), and full pure / mutates support.
  • A built-in InferredAnnotationProvider synthesises an equivalent @Contract for every @XContract method, so IntelliJ's data-flow analysis works from a single annotation.
  • XContract inspection validates contract syntax, parameter references, type references, mutates tokens, and flags overrides that weaken a super method's contract.
  • XContract Violation at Call Site inspection warns when a call's literal arguments deterministically trigger a fail or throws clause.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • A chain subclass no longer builds a slot for its parent's lazy storage.
  • The expanded sources a javadoc run reads no longer keep a deleted type.
  • Two compilation units sharing a file name no longer overwrite each other's copy in the javadoc source expansion.
  • The editor's entry points beside a declared builder are the ones the build emits.
  • The editor no longer re-declares the abstract self() and build() in a chained abstract's builder.
  • A merged slot is compared against the type the builder holds it in.
  • A chain whose ancestor declares a builder the extends clause cannot name is refused rather than emitted.
  • A link whose ancestor's builder is out of its reach is refused on the link.
  • A link overrides a public self() publicly.
  • A final self() on a root built without the processor is refused on the link.
  • A generated setter clashing with an inherited method of its erasure is refused on the builder.
  • A link outside its root builder's intersection bound is refused on its own annotation.
  • A link in another package naming its root fully qualified builds.
  • The chain's copy constructor is offered in the editor.
  • A hand-written copy constructor naming the builder through its target is kept alone.
  • A final field a hand-written constructor leaves alone keeps its initializer.
  • A builder's slot fields resolve in the editor.
  • The entry points a merged builder has no constructor for are skipped with a note.
  • builderConstructorAccess = NONE is one error on the annotation.
  • access = NONE is one error on the annotation.
  • @BuilderArgsConstructor(access = NONE) is one error.
  • A written @BuilderArgsConstructor(access) sets the all-args constructor's access in the editor.
  • @Lazy(access = NONE) is an error in the editor too.
  • An interface target's entry points are offered in the editor.
  • The editor offers no nested Builder on an interface target.
  • An interface target's entry points carry @XContract.
  • An interface target with from = NONE builds, and mutate() copies every slot.
  • A naming attribute written as a constant is read as its value in the editor.
  • A written INHERIT takes the style's name.
  • A slot's own @SetterNames pattern needs no placeholder in the editor.
  • An accessor or lazy name written as a constant is read as its value in the editor.
  • The editor no longer invents a chain builder's constructor.
  • A package-private generated member is closed to another package in the editor too.
  • A second processor run over one compilation adds nothing.
  • An initializer calling a generated accessor is computed on the instance.
  • The javadoc source expansion no longer documents a chain builder's setters and self() with another member's sentence.
  • The editor's generated members follow an edit to what they are built from.
  • Every refusal of a constructor or static factory target is reported in the editor.
  • The editor offers no builder(..) beside an author's own on a constructor or factory target.
  • A link extending a generic root without its type arguments is refused on its annotation.
  • A static factory with a self-bounded type parameter gets a builder() the editor accepts.
  • A write to a lifted final field outside a constructor stays red in the editor.
  • A final field with an initializer keeps it under @ClassBuilder(factoryMethod) with no constructor written.
  • A constructor an args annotation generates beside the builder's keeps a lifted field's initializer value.
  • A refused @NoArgsConstructor contributes no constructor in the editor.
  • A primitive @Lazy field compiles under @ClassBuilder.
  • An instance default reading a @Lazy field builds.
  • from(T) and mutate() read a @Lazy field through the getter its scheme names.
  • from(T) and mutate() no longer read a field through a method of another type.
  • The merge's note lists only a constructor written on the declared builder, and a skipped entry point's note on a constructor or factory target sits on the annotated member.
  • A setter that cannot override a method of Object is reported on its slot.

Changed

  • BREAKING: mergeDeclaredBuilder is removed, and a declared builder is always merged into.
  • BREAKING: a declared builder that writes no constructor takes builderConstructorAccess.
  • BREAKING: constructorAccess = NONE and builderConstructorAccess = NONE are errors on every target.
  • BREAKING: a Lombok constructor annotation beside a written constructor keeps a final field's initializer.
  • BREAKING: a final field written only under a named constant condition keeps its initializer.
  • The Marketplace change notes list each entry's bold lead alone when the release is too long for them.
  • The README documents the dependency scope the artifact is actually built for.

Added

  • A SuperBuilder chain merges into a builder it declares.
  • A constructor or static factory target merges into the builder its enclosing type declares.
  • An inspection for a declared builder the merge cannot append to.
  • A warning where builderConstructorAccess cannot reach the declared builder.
  • A warning where builderConstructorAccess is written on a chain role or an interface.
  • A weak warning where the entry points are skipped beside a declared builder.
