idea-plugin.name: UTEM Code Security
idea-plugin.description:
UTEM Code Security brings the UTEM (Unified Threat Exposure Management) platform's code-scanning engine into your JetBrains IDE.

The plugin wraps the utem-cli binary and surfaces findings without leaving the editor:

  • Scan-on-save — every file save triggers an incremental scan (debounced, off the EDT) so issues land in the IDE within seconds of you saving.
  • Inline highlights — findings render as native IntelliJ annotations with severity mapped to HighlightSeverity (CRITICAL / HIGH → ERROR, MEDIUM → WARNING, LOW → WEAK_WARNING).
  • One-click remediation — an IntentionAction ("Apply UTEM fix") applies any remediation.diff suggested by the CLI.
  • Findings tool window — "UTEM" panel at the bottom lists every finding across the project, grouped by severity, with double-click to open the offending range.
  • Hourly policy refresh — a background com.intellij.util.Alarm tick re-fetches the active policy from the configured UTEM backend, so org-wide policy changes propagate automatically.
  • Settings — configure the CLI binary path, backend URL, API token, optional policy id, scan-on-save toggle, and CLI timeout under Settings → Tools → UTEM.

Requirements: a utem-cli binary on PATH (or an absolute path configured in settings) and a reachable UTEM backend. The plugin never embeds scan logic itself — it delegates entirely to the CLI, so engine upgrades land transparently.

Companion plugin to the UTEM VS Code extension.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.1.4 — Deprecation cleanup

  • Construct CredentialAttributes via the named-arg primary constructor form so 2025+ IDE builds no longer flag the positional overload as deprecated. Read the password via PasswordSafe.get(attrs)?.getPasswordAsString(), which is the recommended pattern in the current SDK docs.

0.1.3 — Security hardening

  • API token now stored in PasswordSafe (the OS keychain on macOS/Windows, an encrypted file otherwise) instead of plain text in utem.xml. Existing tokens are migrated automatically on first read after upgrade and the legacy XML slot is cleared.
  • Backend URL must be https:// — the Settings dialog now refuses to save plaintext http:// URLs (with a localhost dev-backend exemption) so the API token never transits in the clear.
  • Token + backend URL plumbed to utem-cli via environment variables (UTEM_API_TOKEN, UTEM_BACKEND_URL) instead of argv, so they never leak via ps listings.
  • Subprocess stderr is now truncated and redacted before landing in idea.log; bearer-token and high-entropy substrings are masked, so users sharing logs with bug reports don't accidentally leak credentials.
  • File paths in subprocess error logs reduced to basename only to avoid leaking project structure.
  • Stopped bundling kotlin-stdlib / org.jetbrains:annotations; the IntelliJ platform already provides both. Removes a known classpath-conflict source and shrinks the distribution from ~2.3 MB to ~700 KB.

0.1.2 — Marketplace configuration fix

  • Set since-build to the full IDE build number (242.20224.300) so the JetBrains Marketplace descriptor validator accepts the upload — bare branch numbers like 242 are rejected as invalid configuration. No behavioural change; the plugin still targets IntelliJ 2024.2 and later builds.

0.1.1 — Compatibility fix

  • Drop deprecated AnnotationBuilder.needsUpdateOnTyping(false) call — ExternalAnnotator already provides the same default, and the API is scheduled for removal in a future IntelliJ release. No behavioural change.

0.1.0 — Initial release

  • Scan-on-save with 500ms debounce (per-document coalescing).
  • Inline finding highlights via ExternalAnnotator, severity mapped to native IntelliJ severities.
  • IntentionAction quick-fix applies CLI-provided remediation diffs.
  • Hourly background policy refresh via pooled-thread Alarm — never blocks the EDT.
  • "UTEM" tool window listing findings across files with double-click to open.
  • Application-level settings page under Settings → Tools → UTEM (binary path, backend URL, API token, policy id, scan-on-save toggle, CLI timeout).
  • Built on the IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.x with JDK 17 toolchain.
  • Compatible with IntelliJ-based IDEs build 242+ (IntelliJ IDEA 2024.2 and later, including PyCharm, GoLand, WebStorm, RubyMine, Rider, etc.).

idea-plugin.name: Cyclopt
idea-plugin.description:
Enterprise-Grade Code Quality Analysis for JetBrains IDEs

Cyclopt brings comprehensive code analysis directly into your IDE. Catch bugs, security vulnerabilities, code duplication, and quality issues before they reach production with detection for vibe coded files and intelligent pre-commit hooks.

⚡ Core Features:

  • Multi-Analyzer Support: Metrics, Violations, SAST, and Code Duplication in parallel
  • AI Detection: Auto-analyze when AI tools (Copilot, AI Assistant) modify or create files
  • Pre-Commit Protection: Block commits with critical issues (IDE handler + Git bash hook)
  • Quick Fixes: ALT+ENTER for instant actions, 12+ live templates for security fixes
  • Professional Reports: Export as HTML (styled), JSON, or CSV with auto-open
  • Real-Time Highlighting: Inline annotations with severity-based color coding
  • Modern UI: Tree-based results, statistics header, toolbar actions, dark mode support

🚀 Getting Started:

  1. Setup Wizard appears on first use
  2. Enter your API token from cyclopt.com
  3. Test connection and select analyzers
  4. Press Ctrl+Alt+Y to analyze your current file
  5. View results in the Cyclopt tool window

⌨️ Quick Actions:

  • Analyze File: Ctrl+Alt+Y (Win/Linux) or Cmd+Alt+Y (Mac)
  • Quick Fix: ALT+ENTER on highlighted issues
  • Security Templates: Type "cyfix-" + TAB
  • Suppress Issues: Type "cysuppress" + TAB

🔧 Supported:

Languages: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, PHP, Dart

Dependencies: package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, build.gradle, composer.json, pubspec.yaml, and more

Vulnerability Scanning: Standalone command to scan dependency files for known CVEs. Also accepts npm audit JSON output. Access via Tools → Cyclopt → Scan Vulnerabilities.

💡 Key Capabilities:

  • Auto-analysis on save or AI modifications with configurable delays
  • Severity filtering (Critical, Error, Warning, Info, Hint)
  • Send findings to AI Assistant for guided fixes
  • Status bar widget with real-time issue counts

Spring Buddy is a correctness companion that models Spring consequences in real-time. It identifies "Legal Java" that results in "Illegal Spring," catching proxy bypasses, transaction pitfalls, and persistence risks before they reach your CI pipeline.

Key Capabilities

  • Transaction Visualization & Pitfalls: Inline hints show propagation (Join, Start, Suspend, Nested). Detects proxy bypasses like self-invocation, private/final methods, and @Transactional on @PostConstruct.

  • Test Ecosystem Intelligence: Deep support for AssertJ migration and Mockito style alignment. Recognizes ArchUnit, MockMvc, and WebTestClient patterns as valid assertions.
  • Spring Java Format: Automates compliance for variable naming, import/method ordering, visibility rules, and utility constructors.
  • Refactor Safety Net: Bundled inspection runner to validate Spring semantics after large-scale AI or manual refactors.

Stop debugging framework behavior and start seeing it directly in your editor.

idea-plugin.name: CIMNotebook
idea-plugin.description:
Real-time SPARQL and SHACL validation against CIM/CGMES schema profiles, powered by the CIMLangServer language server. Write a SPARQL query or a SHACL shape and get immediate feedback as you type: unknown classes and properties are underlined, syntax errors are highlighted, and semantic issues such as domain/range mismatches are flagged — all resolved against your actual RDFS profile files.

📖 Full documentation: opencgmes.soptim.de/cimnotebook/intellij — including the opencgmes.jsonc configuration reference, the validation check catalogue, and troubleshooting.

Features

  • Syntax highlighting for SPARQL (.rq, .sparql) and SHACL / Turtle (.ttl, .shacl).
  • Real-time diagnostics — unknown classes and properties, typos in the standard vocabularies (rdf/rdfs/owl/sh), domain/range mismatches, datatype conflicts, invalid enumeration values, and contradictory SHACL constraints. Full catalogue: validation checks.
  • Hover documentation — the full IRI, rdfs:label / rdfs:comment, domain/range, and source profile for any CIM term (e.g. cim:ACLineSegment).
  • Auto-completion — type : after a prefix such as cim: for class and property suggestions; enumeration members are suggested in object position, and standard-vocabulary prefixes (rdf:, rdfs:, owl:, sh:) complete too.
  • Go to definition — Ctrl+Click / Cmd+Click a CIM term to jump to its declaration in the profile file.
  • Workspace symbol search — press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+N (Go to Symbol) and type a term name to find any schema term.
  • Explain Query — right-click a SPARQL query for its Jena-style static algebra plan (original and optimized), computed without executing anything.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ 2024.2 or later. The plugin runs the language server on the IDE's bundled Java runtime, which is Java 21+ from 2024.2 onward.
  • The LSP4IJ plugin. When you install CIMNotebook from the Marketplace it is pulled in automatically; if you install CIMNotebook from a downloaded .zip, install LSP4IJ manually first (Settings → Plugins → Marketplace → search "LSP4IJ").
  • A Java 21+ runtime. By default the plugin uses the IDE's own runtime; you can point it at a different one in settings.

Getting started

  1. Install LSP4IJ if prompted — it is a required dependency and provides the LSP client.
  2. Open a .rq, .sparql, .ttl or .shacl file. Point CIMNotebook at your CGMES profiles via an opencgmes.jsonc (see below) or a # [endpoint=...] directive in the query; without either, CIMNotebook checks syntax only. The server starts, loads the schema in the background, and begins validating.
  3. (Optional) Customise via Tools → CIMNotebook: Create Config File, which scaffolds an opencgmes.jsonc. All settings live under a "cimvocabcheck" section; the nearest file (walking up from each query) wins. To use your own RDFS profiles: 
    {
  "cimvocabcheck": {
    "schemasDirectory": "schemas/cgmes-3.0"
  }
}
    The file is watched and the schema reloads automatically whenever it changes.

Settings

Under Settings / Preferences → Tools → CIMNotebook:

  • Server JAR — leave empty to use the JAR bundled with the plugin, or point to your own cimvocabcheck-lsp.jar.
  • Java executable — leave empty to use the IDE's runtime, or set a path to a Java 21+ executable.
  • JVM arguments — extra arguments passed before -jar, e.g. -Xmx512m.

Validation configuration

opencgmes.jsonc (the "cimvocabcheck" section) also supports strictness (permissive / default / strict / pedantic), namedGraphs (map graph IRIs to profile versions), prefixes (default PREFIX declarations injected into queries) and standardVocabulary. See the full reference at opencgmes.soptim.de/cimvocabcheck/configuration.

Troubleshooting

  • No syntax highlighting / file not recognised — confirm the file extension is one of .rq, .sparql, .ttl, .shacl. If a previously installed plugin already claimed .ttl, add the association under Settings → Editor → File Types → SHACL.
  • No diagnostics appearing — with no schema configured CIMNotebook reports only syntax errors; for full validation add an opencgmes.jsonc with schemas or a # [endpoint=...] directive. If even syntax errors are missing, the server likely did not start — make sure LSP4IJ is enabled and open the Language Servers tool window (from LSP4IJ) to see CIMLangServer's status and logs.
  • Server fails to start — usually a Java version problem. Set Settings → Tools → CIMNotebook → Java executable to a Java 21+ path.

More symptoms and fixes: opencgmes.soptim.de/cimnotebook/troubleshooting.

idea-plugin.name: Audit Builder
idea-plugin.description:
Write structured code audits without leaving the IDE.

Capture findings straight from the editor, or let the bundled detectors propose drafts, triage them in the Audit tool window, then export a numbered report as plain text, Markdown or HTML.

Findings live in .audit/findings.xml at the project root so the audit can be reviewed and committed alongside the code.

The detectors look for patterns that static analysis usually misses: a bare return that escapes a lambda instead of skipping an element, an emptiness guard that abandons the enclosing method, an empty catch block that silently skips the rest of its try, a read path that answers a failure with an empty result the next write puts back, a String.split result indexed without a length check, a static collection shared across threads, a Map.get auto-unboxed into a primitive, an assert used as a runtime guard, and Fabric packet handlers mutating game state on the netty event loop.

A hit is raised to P0 only when the scan can follow the calls to a real write: an empty catch over code that reaches Files.writeString, a blank fallback that a caller stores and something else writes back, a build input excluded from the repository. The path it followed is printed in the finding, and a claim it cannot establish stays where it was.

idea-plugin.name: Fortify Code Security
idea-plugin.description:
Fortify Code Security for JetBrains IDE Tools

Fortify Code Security

Fortify Code Security helps developers find and fix security issues where they code by bringing the full power of OpenText Fortify Application Security Testing directly into their JetBrains IDE.

Perform SAST and SCA with Fortify on Demand, submit remote scans via Fortify ScanCentral SAST, or run local SAST scans with Fortify SAST (Static Code Analyzer) — all powered by the Fortify CLI (fcli). Developers can view, audit, and collaborate on vulnerabilities directly in the IDE, including direct navigation to affected line of code and access to Fortify Remediation Aviator for contextual explanations, guidance, and suggested code fixes.

The plugin also installs Fortify Skills, which teach AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and more) how to run scans, query findings, and autonomously remediate vulnerabilities on your behalf — with an optional local fcli MCP server for deeper, programmatic AI agent integration.

With Fortify Code Security, you can produce secure code at scale, keeping your focus on building features — not chasing vulnerabilities.

Features

Application Security Testing

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

Scan your source code for security vulnerabilities using Fortify's industry-leading SAST engine — whichever deployment model fits your environment:

  • Fortify on Demand — Submit SAST scan requests to OpenText's cloud-based security testing platform. Ideal for teams that want a fully managed scanning service with no on-premise infrastructure.
  • Fortify ScanCentral SAST — For on-premise or private cloud customers, submit scan packages to your organization's ScanCentral SAST infrastructure for enterprise-scale, centralized analysis.
  • Local scans with Fortify SAST — Run translation and analysis directly on your local machine, keeping code entirely within your environment or handling complex translation scenarios.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Identify vulnerabilities in your open source dependencies with Fortify SCA via Fortify on Demand. Run SCA as a standalone scan to get a full picture of your open source risk, or combine it with a SAST scan to cover both first-party and third-party vulnerabilities in a single workflow.

Results Review & Vulnerability Triage

Connect to Fortify on Demand (FoD) or Fortify Application Security Center (SSC) to review scan results and perform vulnerability auditing — all without leaving IntelliJ.

  • Browse and filter vulnerabilities by severity, category, status, and more
  • View detailed finding information including data flow traces and analysis notes
  • Audit findings by setting analysis tags (e.g., Exploitable, Not an Issue, Reliability Issue)
  • Add comments and suppression notes to findings
  • Navigate directly from a finding to the vulnerable line of code in your editor
  • Synchronize audit decisions back to SSC or FoD in real time

AI-Powered Remediation with Fortify Remediation Aviator

Accelerate vulnerability remediation with Fortify Remediation Aviator, OpenText's AI-powered security guidance engine.

  • Receive detailed, context-aware remediation advice for each identified vulnerability
  • Understand the root cause and attack vectors associated with a finding
  • Get step-by-step fix recommendations tailored to your specific code and language
  • Apply AI-suggested code fixes automatically directly within the editor
  • Reduce mean time to remediation (MTTR) with intelligent, actionable guidance

AI Agent Integration

Fortify Code Security extends AppSec capabilities to the AI-native developer workflow, letting AI coding assistants interact with Fortify directly on your behalf — running scans, querying results, auditing findings, and generating fixes — without you having to leave the conversation.

Fortify Skills for AI Coding Assistants

The plugin installs the OpenText Fortify Skills — a set of domain-specific AI agent skills that teach your AI coding assistant how to use Fortify effectively via command line. These skills activate automatically when you ask security-related questions or issue Fortify-related commands in your AI assistant of choice.

The following skills are included:

Skill What it enables
fortify-fod Manage Fortify on Demand applications, releases, and scans; triage issues; run OSS analysis; generate portfolio reports
fortify-ssc Manage SSC application versions, artifacts, and scan jobs; perform issue triage and audit workflows
fortify-remediate Fix vulnerabilities detected by Fortify SAST, SC SAST, and SCA; leverage Fortify Aviator AI remediation guidance
fortify-cicd-integration Add Fortify scanning to CI/CD pipelines across GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, and Jenkins
fortify-create-app Create and manage Fortify applications and releases in FoD or SSC
fcli-common Install and configure fcli; manage sessions; use SpEL queries; build custom fcli actions

Supported AI assistants: JetBrains AI Assistant (IDE 2025.1+), GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and any assistant that supports the Agent Skills standard.

Example prompts that activate the skills:

  • "Find all critical SQL Injection vulnerabilities in the payment-service release" → fortify-fod
  • "Fix the authentication bypass issue in UserService.java" → fortify-remediate
  • "Show me the data flow for this XSS finding and suggest a fix" → fortify-ssc
  • "Add Fortify SAST scanning to my GitHub Actions workflow" → fortify-cicd-integration
  • "Create a new release in Fortify and list available entitlements" → fortify-create-app + fortify-fod

MCP Server Integration

For assistants that support the Model Context Protocol, the plugin also manages the fcli MCP server, which exposes Fortify capabilities as a structured set of typed MCP tools. While the Fortify Agent Skills described above use `fcli` directly as a CLI tool, the MCP server is a complementary option for assistants or workflows that prefer a programmatic tool interface.

  • Exposes fcli product modules (SSC, FoD, ScanCentral SAST) as typed MCP tools accessible to any MCP-compatible AI agent
  • Automatically configures Copilot's MCP server settings in `~/.config/github-copilot/intellij/mcp.json` (Linux/macOS) or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\github-copilot\intellij\mcp.json` (Windows)
  • Provides direct vulnerability query tools — get_vulnerabilities() and search_app() — for LLM-driven security insights
  • The plugin handles all MCP server lifecycle management — start, stop, and configuration
  • Requires fcli 3.21 or later for full AI feature support

Streamlined Sidebar Workflow

A step-by-step guided workflow in the tool window sidebar:

  • Settings — Configure Fortify platform (FoD, SSC, ScanCentral), server URLs, and fcli binary path
  • Authentication — Connect with PAT, username/password, or client credentials
  • Application Selection — Browse and select application versions/releases for scanning
  • Vulnerability Scanning — Trigger SAST (local), SC SAST (remote), and SCA (open-source) scans with real-time progress
  • Results Review — View, filter, and audit security findings with bulk operations support
  • Remediation — Apply Aviator-powered code fixes with inline diff preview

Key Capabilities

  • Issue List — View, filter, group, and search security findings with configurable filter sets
  • Issue Details — Inspect vulnerability details including traces, recommendations, and history
  • Bulk Auditing — Update audit fields on multiple issues simultaneously
  • Auto-Login — Automatic session restoration on IDE startup
  • fcli Integration — Full JSON-RPC 2.0 communication with Fortify CLI for all backend operations

Requirements

Fortify CLI (fcli) v3.21 or later — The plugin uses fcli as its underlying engine to interact with Fortify products. fcli must be installed and accessible on your system PATH. See fcli Installation for setup instructions. The plugin can automatically install the latest version of fcli on machines with internet access. fcli v3.21 or later is required for AI Agent Integration features. If you are using this plugin with IntelliJ IDEA, install IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.0 or later — The plugin is designed for the latest IntelliJ IDEA versions. Works with IntelliJ IDEA Community and Ultimate editions. JetBrains AI Assistant (for bundled Fortify Skills) is available in IDE.

Getting Started

  1. Install fcli — Follow the fcli installation guide to set up Fortify CLI on your machine.
  2. Open Settings — Navigate to Tools > Fortify Code Security > Settings.
  3. Configure Platform — Select your Fortify platform (Fortify on Demand or SSC).
  4. Authenticate — Provide your credentials to connect to your Fortify instance.
  5. Select Application — Browse available applications and select the version/release to scan.
  6. Trigger Scan — Start a SAST (local), SC SAST (remote), and SCA (open-source) scan directly from the IDE sidebar.
  7. Review Results — View vulnerabilities and audit findings.
  8. Auto-Remediate — Apply Fortify Remediation Aviator suggestions.

Feedback & Support

  • Plugin Documentation: JetBrains Plugin Marketplace
  • Fortify Code Security Documentation: Fortify Code Security
  • Fortify on Demand Documentation: Fortify on Demand
  • Fortify SSC & ScanCentral SAST Documentation: Fortify Software Security Center
  • fcli Documentation: Fortify CLI (fcli) v3
  • GitHub Repository: github.com/fortify/fcli
  • OpenText Support: Contact your OpenText Customer Manager or visit the Fortify Support Portal

idea-plugin.name: GitLab CI Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Static syntax and structural checks for .gitlab-ci.yml — catch mistakes before running a real pipeline, not after.

Flags jobs referencing a stage: that isn't one of the pipeline's stages (the declared stages: list, or GitLab's defaults when there is none), jobs missing script:/ trigger:/extends:, malformed rules: entries using an unrecognized key, jobs combining only:/ except: with rules: (GitLab rejects that job: they can't be used together), and duplicate job names.

Also catches the pipeline errors GitLab otherwise only reports when you push: a job whose needs: or dependencies: point at a job in a later stage, a need listed twice, a circular extends:, and an extends: chain deeper than GitLab's 10 levels -- with GitLab's own wording, and never guessing about jobs or stages that come from an include:. Files with CI/CD inputs are checked on the pipeline after their spec: header.

100% local by default — every static check runs against the file already open in the editor, never a live GitLab API. Live pipeline status is opt-in: configure a GitLab instance and Personal Access Token in Settings to see a "GitLab CI" tool window with real pipelines and jobs for the project's detected remote. Skip that setup and the plugin makes zero network calls, exactly as before.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no popups.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Spring Config Drift Inspector
idea-plugin.description:
Catch broken environment configuration before it reaches production. This plugin compares every application*.yml, application*.properties, .env, and docker-compose*.yml file across your profiles and reports what a code review alone tends to miss.

What it finds

  • Missing keys — set in some environments, silently absent from others, with default-profile inheritance handled correctly. Comparisons stay scoped within one config system (Spring / .env / Compose), so a Spring-only key is never reported missing from an .env-only profile. The Key Matrix marks those cells as ~ (not applicable)
  • Shape drift — the same key is a number in one environment and a string, list, or nested object in another — including a scalar in one profile versus a list of objects in another
  • Exposed secrets — passwords, tokens, API keys, private keys, and credentials embedded in URLs. Values are masked the moment they are detected and are never stored, logged, or written to a report. Correctly externalized values (${DB_PASSWORD}, or postgresql://${DB_USER}:${DB_PASSWORD}@…) are left alone; only what is actually committed (including non-blank placeholder defaults) is flagged
  • Unresolved placeholders — ${DB_HOST} references with no default and nothing in the project to supply them
  • Metadata contract violations — cross-checked against spring-configuration-metadata.json and, when present, your own @ConfigurationProperties classes (Java and Kotlin) for keys declared but never set, set but never declared, and simple type mismatches

Relaxed binding is understood, so driver-class-name, driverClassName, and DRIVER_CLASS_NAME count as one property rather than three. Profiles that only override a handful of keys are recognised as partial overlays within each config system instead of being reported as incomplete environments; that judgement can be overridden per profile in Settings | Tools | Config Drift.

Every finding jumps to the exact key in the exact file. Inline highlights and the tool window refresh automatically a couple of seconds after you save a config file — or after a config file or folder is moved, renamed, or deleted. Results export as Markdown for a pull request or JSON for a CI gate.

Scope

This is static comparison plus a lightweight metadata contract check — it does not reimplement the Spring Binder (nested properties inside a list/map of a custom type aren't modeled, only the container itself), resolve SpEL, Vault, or Config Server values, read your real environment variables, or modify your files. @ConfigurationProperties reading is a syntactic PSI walk, not semantic type resolution — for Kotlin classes specifically, this means a nested property is only followed into a type declared in the same file.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.2.1

  • New: headless config-drift CLI on GitHub Releases for CI gates (check --fail-on error|warning|never, exit codes 0/1/2)
  • New: optional repo file .config-drift.yml for shared CLI defaults (fail-on, path, profiles.complete / profiles.overlay); explicit CLI flags still win. IDE Settings remain separate
  • New: CLI --format sarif for GitHub Code Scanning, and --no-matrix for shorter Markdown suitable for sticky PR comments
  • New: sample GitHub Action that posts a sticky Markdown report on the PR and uploads SARIF (see docs/examples/github-action-config-drift.yml)
  • Analysis engine split into :core / :cli / IntelliJ plugin modules; IDE behaviour unchanged for drift findings, matrix, and suppressions

0.2.0

  • New: .env files are compared across profiles alongside application*.yml/.properties — including missing-key, shape-drift, and secret detection. Profiles follow the dotenv convention (.env, .env.production, .env.production.local)
  • New: docker-compose.yml / compose.yml support — each service's environment: block is checked, keyed per service (web.DB_HOST vs worker.DB_HOST). Profiles follow the filename; env_file: references are not followed. Compose ${VAR:-default} defaults are understood alongside Spring's ${VAR:default}
  • New: comparisons are scoped per config system (Spring / .env / Compose), so a Spring-only key is never reported missing from an .env-only profile; the Key Matrix uses ~ for not-applicable cells
  • New: metadata contract checks also read project @ConfigurationProperties classes (Java and Kotlin), not only spring-configuration-metadata.json. Kotlin uses a syntactic PSI walk — nested types are only followed when declared in the same file. Depends on the bundled Java and Kotlin plugins
  • Secret detection also recognises underscore-separated key names (DB_PASSWORD, API_KEY)
  • Fixed Key Matrix cells wrongly showing inherited (^) across config systems
  • Fixed scalar-vs-list-of-object shape conflicts when YAML flattens indexed children as app.items[0].name
  • Fixed secret false positives on correctly externalized JDBC URLs such as postgresql://${DB_USER}:${DB_PASSWORD}@…
  • Fixed automatic re-analysis when a folder containing config files is moved, renamed, or deleted
  • Fixed partial-overlay detection to judge peers per config system
  • Fixed Kotlin cross-file nested types producing spurious declared-but-never-set INFO findings when only nested children are set

0.1.1

  • Fixed a race where dismissing a finding while an automatic re-analysis was in flight could make the dismissed finding silently reappear
  • Fixed a performance issue where every VFS change event in the IDE (not just config file changes) triggered a virtual file resolution, needlessly on the EDT
  • Fixed a caching bug where a metadata file that failed to read once could stay incorrectly cached as empty until its next unrelated change
  • Fixed a potential crash in the Key Matrix tool window when the profile set changes
  • Config file discovery order is now deterministic across runs
  • The Copy Report toolbar buttons now show a brief confirmation when the report is copied to the clipboard
  • "Analyze Spring Config Drift" is now also available by right-clicking an application*.yml/.properties file, in the Project view or the editor
  • A partial-overlay finding's Location column now names the Settings page it jumps to, instead of showing "—" as if the row led nowhere

0.1.0

  • First release: cross-profile comparison of YAML and properties configuration
  • Missing key, shape drift, secret exposure, unresolved placeholder, and metadata contract detection
  • Findings and key-matrix tool window with jump-to-source
  • Markdown and JSON report export
  • Partial-overlay profile detection, overridable in Settings | Tools | Config Drift

idea-plugin.name: Speedbump
idea-plugin.description:
Speedbump finds performance problems in Java code by static analysis. It walks the code's PSI tree and highlights performance anti-patterns directly in the editor — no need to run, benchmark or profile the program.

What you get

  • 104 inspections, all enabled by default and grouped under Settings → Editor → Inspections → Speedbump, where each one can be toggled or given a different severity.
  • Findings appear as warnings while you type, with an explanation of why the pattern is slow.
  • 24 of the 104 inspections ship a quick-fix (Alt+Enter) that rewrites the code for you — for example, turning string concatenation in a loop into a StringBuilder. The remaining inspections report the problem and explain the recommended change, which is often too context-dependent to apply mechanically.
  • Purely static analysis: fast, deterministic, and runnable over a whole project via Analyze → Inspect Code or in CI.

What it covers

  • Strings and text (16) — concatenation in loops, redundant String constructors and toString calls, StringBuffer used single-threaded, case-insensitive comparison via toLowerCase.
  • Collections and maps (21) — missing initial capacity, indexed access of a LinkedList, keySet iteration followed by get, containsKey before get, manual copy loops, EnumMap and EnumSet opportunities.
  • Boxing and numerics (12) — autoboxing in loops, boxed accumulators, new Integer(...) instead of valueOf, new BigDecimal(double), Math.pow for small exponents.
  • Loops (10) — loop-invariant calls, size() and length recomputed in the condition, nested loop membership tests, busy-wait loops.
  • Streams and Optional (12) — stream().count() instead of size(), boxed streams where IntStream fits, filter().findFirst().isPresent(), parallelStream() used without a measured benefit.
  • Regular expressions (6) — Pattern.compile inside a method or loop, String.matches with a constant regex, replaceAll with a literal pattern.
  • I/O and logging (10) — unbuffered streams, byte-by-byte reads, resources not opened in try-with-resources, System.out.println and file reopening inside loops, expensive logging arguments evaluated without a level check.
  • Concurrency (7) — a new Thread per task, synchronizing on a String or boxed value, ThreadLocal.set without remove, check-then-act on a ConcurrentMap, compound operations on volatile fields.
  • Reflection, exceptions, date/time and allocation (10) — reflective lookups on repeated paths, exceptions used for control flow, shared SimpleDateFormat, Calendar.getInstance(), object allocation inside loops, and mappers such as ObjectMapper rebuilt on every call.

Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2 or newer. Java only — other JVM languages are not analysed.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0 — four new inspections, now 104 in total.

  • Mapper or parser factory created per call — ObjectMapper, Gson, JAXBContext.newInstance() and the javax.xml and validation factories built inside a method body instead of once. Field initializers, constructors, @Bean/@Provides/@Produces/@Singleton methods and assignments to fields are not reported.
  • Expensive log argument without a level check — a debug or trace argument that is concatenated, formatted, collected or serialized with no isDebugEnabled() / isTraceEnabled() guard. Ships a quick-fix that wraps the statement in the matching check.
  • Expensive work fed into logging without a level check — serialization whose result exists only to feed a fluent log.atInfo() builder, computed before the level is consulted.
  • String concatenation passed into a recursive call — a prefix copied and re-allocated at every level of a traversal; carry a StringBuilder instead.
  • Charset.forName, Calendar.getInstance(), formatter creation, Matcher creation, reflective lookups and system property lookups are now also reported inside per-element lambdas (forEach, map, filter, …) and directly recursive methods, not only inside loops. Inspection settings are preserved.

1.0.0 — first public release.

  • 100 Java performance inspections, all enabled by default and grouped under Settings → Editor → Inspections → Speedbump: strings and text (15), collections and maps (21), boxing and numerics (12), loops (10), streams and Optional (12), regular expressions (6), I/O (8), concurrency (7), and reflection, exceptions, date/time and allocation (9).
  • Quick-fixes for 23 of the inspections — press Alt+Enter to rewrite the flagged code, for example turning string concatenation in a loop into a StringBuilder.
  • Descriptions for every inspection, shown in the inspection settings panel: what is detected, why it is slow, and the recommended replacement.
  • Dedicated colour attributes with Default and Darcula scheme entries, so the highlighting of performance findings can be restyled independently.
  • Works with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2 and newer.

idea-plugin.name: Coroutine Leak Detector
idea-plugin.description:
Coroutine Leak Detector analyzes Kotlin code in Android projects to catch common coroutine and Flow lifecycle mistakes before they cause memory leaks or crashes in production.

Currently detects:

  • GlobalScope misuse — coroutines launched with GlobalScope are never automatically cancelled and can leak.
  • Unsafe Flow collection — collecting a Flow without repeatOnLifecycle or flowWithLifecycle can run outside the intended lifecycle.

Each detection comes with a clear explanation and, where possible, a quick fix to guide the migration.

idea-plugin.name: SageMath Core
idea-plugin.description: First-class SageMath language, runtime, type-intelligence, completion, and documentation support for PyCharm.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 1.7.8 — Fixes IllegalAccessError on PyCharm 2026.2 (split plugin layout): the sugar parser called the Python parser's protected parseSimpleStatement across class loaders, which JVM access control rejects; it now uses the public parseStatement (a superset that falls through to the same method for non-compound statements), so .sage parsing works again.
  • 1.7.7 — Mirrors the Sage preparser's numeric-literal conversion at the assignment boundary: the sage command wraps every integer literal as `Integer(...)` and every float as `RealNumber(...)` (verified against `sage.repl.preparse`: `x = 5` → `x = Integer(5)`), so `ct = 2432...` in a .sage file is a Sage Integer at runtime — and now the target is typed accordingly, which is what lets `ct.nth_root(3)` complete. This is a general preparse-semantics rule (no function whitelist — the interim getReturnType patch was removed: type knowledge lives in the stub data layer, which stubgen 0.8.3 extended to pure-Python modules). Literals in other positions keep their Python types: a PSI identifier's text must come from the document buffer, so the wrapping cannot be reproduced in the parse tree without rewriting the file.
  • 1.7.6 — The implicit sage.all namespace now completes in .sage files: typing an unqualified name (RR, Mod, ...) offers the whole injected namespace with a "sage.all" tail. PyCharm's own importable-name completion only scans real .py modules (it excludes .pyi stubs), so it happened to offer CC/QQ/ZZ (declared in the cc.py bridge file and the pure-Python rational_field.py / integer_mod_ring.py) while RR and Mod — declared only in the generated .pyi stubs — never appeared. The plugin now fills the namespace itself, straight from the stub data layer (sage/all.pyi's __all__ plus its top-level declarations), inserting the bare name without an import (sage injects the namespace at runtime). Also fixes the type chain behind those names: from-import aliases (`from sage.interfaces.ecm import ECM as ECM` — most of all.pyi) are now followed to their real declaration (through the name indexes — the import element's own reference resolves to nothing from inside the stub tree), because PyCharm's type engine cannot derive a type from an import element itself: `ecm = ECM()` was left untyped and `ecm.` completed nothing without an explicit sage.all import. Completion entries now also carry a fixed "sage.all" tail text and callable names (functions, classes, factories like ZZ/QQ/RR/CC, symbolic functions) insert `()` with the caret inside — the `_Type_*` factory attributes are followed through the name indexes (with a `_with_category` fallback for the runtime-only subclass names) instead of relying on the type engine, and `getAnnotationValue()` is read as the annotation text string that this platform actually returns. `for q in prime_divisors(p - 1)` chains type correctly once the companion stubgen 0.8.3 stubs (pure-Python modules included) are installed.
  • 1.7.5 — Typing a quote character in .sage files now inserts the pair ("", '' or triple-quoted) with the caret inside, exactly like .py files: the quoteHandler extension point resolves handlers by the language at the caret (the Sage dialect) without falling back to base languages, so Python's own quote handler never applied to .sage files; a Sage-registered handler now inherits its behavior.
  • 1.7.4 — The implicit sage.all namespace now resolves sage.all module declarations FIRST (top-level attributes and from-import aliases like `N` = numerical_approx), before the global name indexes — single-letter names previously collided with unrelated sage modules and produced wrong call signatures ("unexpected argument" on N(1)).
  • 1.7.3 — Locate the sage.all stub module through the function index (GF anchor) instead of PyModuleNameIndex, which does not reliably index .pyi stub modules; ZZ/QQ/RR/CC/SR now resolve without the explicit import.
  • 1.7.2 — Fix a regression in the implicit sage.all namespace: commenting out `from sage.all import *` in a .sage file no longer leaves GF/ZZ/... flagged as unresolved references (the explicit-import gate is now PSI-based, so a commented-out import does not count).
  • 1.7.1 — The New-menu entry text for the Sage file template is now localized through the createFromTemplateActionReplacer pipeline: "Sage 文件" on a zh-CN IDE, "Sage File" otherwise.
  • 1.7.0 — "New → SageMath → Sage File" in the project view: create a fresh .sage file from the right-click New menu (file template with a hint that ^ is power / ^^ is XOR and sage.all is implicit).
  • 1.6.6 — The settings-preview descriptions of the Sage postfix templates are now in Chinese (matching the IDE language): every call-wrap key plus the .b2i/.i2b conversions.
  • 1.6.5 — Fix the settings page "Resource not found" error: every call-wrap postfix template now ships its own description.html (the preview panel resolves it as a static per-class resource and never consults the template's getDescription() method), so clicking .ZZ/.CC/... no longer logs a SEVERE error.
  • 1.6.4 — The new-template editor's condition list is trimmed to the Sage-accurate set: string / list / dict / set / tuple / non-None plus the ready-made sage.all class conditions (Integer, Rational, RealNumber, ComplexNumber, FinitePolyExtElement, Polynomial, Matrix, FreeModuleElement) and the class chooser. Python's number/iterable/boolean/exception categories are not offered — they misjudge sage types (sage numbers don't inherit builtins int/float/complex and sage containers don't inherit abc.Iterable).
  • 1.6.3 — Fix the .b2i/.i2b expansions (the selected expression is now substituted instead of the literal word "expr"); the settings preview of the call-wrap family no longer shows an extra dot in the after state (per-key preview resources); double-clicking a Sage template now opens the edit (rename) dialog like Python's built-ins; the new-template editor offers a Sage-apt condition set (expression kinds plus ready-made sage.all class conditions).
  • 1.6.2 — Postfix Completion settings: the Sage templates now appear under their own top-level "SageMathPostfix" group (registered under a Python-family meta-language) instead of being nested under Python, and the "+" button can create new Sage postfix templates (same editor as Python's, with expression-type conditions; created templates apply in .sage files only).
  • 1.6.1 — Fix the Sage postfix completion popup: SageFile now reports the Sage file type (getFileType() override, mirroring the platform's PyiFile pattern), so the postfix-applicability copy file is created as a SageFile and the .ZZ/.CC/... set appears in .sage files. The .b2i/.i2b keys now carry the platform-required leading dot (.b2i/.i2b), fixing both their popup entries and expansion.
  • 1.6.0 — Full caret lexical remapping to Sage preparse semantics: ^ parses as power (e^254 now follows the __pow__ type chain), ^= as power assignment, ^^ as bitwise XOR and ^^= as XOR assignment — all while the on-screen text never changes. The misused-^ inspection now targets these remapped forms and its ^= quick fix writes ^^= directly. The postfix provider now returns only the Sage template set; Python's built-in postfix templates are collected automatically through the base-language chain.
  • 1.5.0 — Sage postfix completion: .ZZ/.QQ/.RR/.CC/.SR/.Integer/.N/.factor/.show/.vector/.matrix, plus CTF number theory (.euler_phi, .carmichael_lambda, .divisors, .number_of_divisors, .prime_factors, .squarefree_part, .next_prime, .random_prime, .primitive_root, .factorial, .numerator, .denominator, .continued_fraction, .cyclotomic_polynomial, .sage_eval) and bytes/int conversion (.b2i, .i2b); Python's built-in postfix set stays available. New inspection: flags ^ / ^= in unambiguous bytes contexts (Sage power vs Python XOR) with a quick fix to ^^. The Sage lexer now merges the ^^ pair into one XOR token, so the correct Sage XOR spelling no longer shows a parser error.
  • 1.4.1 — Fix PsiInvalidElementAccessException on PyCharm 2026.2: stale stub-index elements are re-validated and never dereferenced through a dropped AST node.
  • 1.4.0 — Supports the whole PyCharm 2026 release year (261–263); GitHub Actions CI builds the plugin and attaches tagged releases.
  • 1.3.2 — The project tree shows the Sage icon for .sage files (file PSI override).

idea-plugin.name: Nullify
idea-plugin.description:
Read your Java code the way it was meant to be read. Nullify folds noisy annotations and wildcards into clean ?/!/out/in syntax — without changing a single line of your source.

See it in action

Type @Nullable String, and it folds to String? right before your eyes. Hover or Ctrl+click the folded text, and it still jumps to the declaration. It's just a view — your source never changes.

Why Nullify?

Java's annotations are powerful, but they come with a lot of noise. A single field can pile on a wall of text:

@NotNull
@Unmodifiable
private final Map<@NotNull String, @Nullable List<@NotNull Token>> cache;

With Nullify, that reads as:

@Unmodifiable
private final Map!<String!, List?<Token!>> cache;

Same code. Same behavior. Only the noise is gone.

Folding is a view, not a rewrite — the source file stays exactly as you wrote it, so your diffs, CI, and teammates' tools all see the same Java as always.

Why you'll love it:

  • Reads like Kotlin. ? and !, out and in, clean array syntax — the compact style you already know, applied to your Java.
  • One style for the whole type system. Nullity markers, wildcards, arrays & varargs, var inference, qualified types, intersection casts — all fold into one consistent, familiar look.
  • Finds annotations wherever Java hides them. On the type, on the declaration, on the class, on the whole package — no matter which of the four spots a nullability annotation lives in, Nullify resolves it correctly.
  • Nothing breaks. Navigation, completion, and other plugins keep working on folded code. Folded placeholders even keep non-nullity annotations like @Value("${app.name}") and can still jump to what they point at.
  • Catches annotation chaos. A built-in inspection flags duplicated and mixed-library nullability annotations, with one-click fixes.
  • Your editor, your rules. Turn each kind of folding on or off, register your own annotations, and choose the style that fits your team.

Features

1. Nullity at a glance — Foo? / Bar!

@Nullable Foo → Foo?, @NotNull Bar → Bar!. Nullify understands annotations wherever Java puts them — on the type, the declaration, the class, or the whole package — and gets every position right.

2. Variance that reads itself — out / in

? extends Foo → out Foo, ? super @Nullable Bar → in Bar? — the same variance words Kotlin uses, so generic signatures finally read the way they mean.

3. Arrays & varargs, normalized — Array?<String!> / Vararg?<Object?>

Arrays and varargs fold into clean generic syntax — Array?<String!>, Vararg?<Object?> — with every dimension's annotation placed exactly where it belongs. Nothing is flattened, nothing is misattributed.

4. Navigation never breaks

Folding should never cost you navigation. Ctrl+click any part of a folded placeholder — the type, a type argument, the ?/! marker, even a preserved annotation's value literal — and you land exactly where the IDE would have taken you before folding.

5. Catch annotation chaos

Nullify ships the Inconsistent Nullability Annotation inspection: it spots duplicated or mixed-library nullability annotations (@javax.Nonnull vs @org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull, @NotNullByDefault vs @ParametersAreNonnullByDefault, …) and offers one-click quick fixes — remove the duplicate, or align it with the file's / project's standard annotation. An Aggressive analysis mode (on by default) keeps the whole file's warnings up to date as you type; switch to Prudence mode to re-analyze only the edited region when large files need snappier feedback.

6. Your rules, your defaults

Under Settings → Editor → Nullify you control everything:

  • Toggle nullity and wildcard folding independently, and pick Kotlin-style marker placement.
  • Register your own @Nullable / @NotNull annotations — Nullify understands them just like the built-ins.
  • Configure class/package/project-level nullability defaults (@NotNullByDefault, @ParametersAreNonnullByDefault, …).
  • Built-in support for the popular libraries: JetBrains, JSpecify, Spring, AndroidX, Eclipse JDT, Checker Framework, FindBugs/SpotBugs, and more.
  • Choose the symbol for unbounded wildcards — ? or *.
  • FQCN inputs with code completion, and an interface that speaks your IDE's language (English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, French, and German).
  • Show or hide the nullability reason hint above collapsed folds — its look (including color) is themed through the editor color scheme.

7. Reasons that stay with you

When Nullify collapses @Nullable("some reason") into String?, the reason doesn't vanish — it reappears as a hint right above the folded code: "This is nullable because "some reason"." It appears only while the fold is collapsed, resolves constant reasons too (@Nullable(REASON)), and follows your editor's colors.

Long reasons stay out of your way: a hint that exceeds the inline length collapses to a truncated one-liner — "This is nullable because "returns null when no entry mat…"." — and expands to the full multi-line text when you click the hint, click the fold arrow beside it, or press the expand/collapse shortcut. The threshold is adaptive by default, scaling with your editor's font size.

The hint is a first-class editor citizen: its Reason hint attribute under Settings → Editor → Color Scheme → Nullify themes foreground, background, and effects like any editor text, its font size can be nudged relative to the code font, and a leading prefix — none, *, •, §, your own symbol, or Nullify's gutter icon — sets it apart at a glance. Everything down to the whole feature is tunable under Settings → Editor → Nullify → Folding Behavior.

8. The compact view, automatically

As you could see from above, Nullify folds collapse by themselves the moment the project finishes its analysis — and keep folding live while you type (final @NotNull var foo = "" becomes final String! foo = "" as soon as the initializer is written). Folds you expanded manually stay expanded, and the whole behavior can be switched off under Settings → Editor → Nullify → Folding Behavior.

9. Comments become reasons

Documenting why something can be null is good practice — retyping it into the annotation is not. When a @Nullable/@NotNull that supports a reason sits next to a comment (on the line above, trailing the annotation, or closing the declaration line), Alt+Enter offers Migrate comment to annotation reason: the comment's text becomes the annotation's reason — @Nullable("Returns null when no entry matches") — and the comment is removed. The intention never highlights anything by itself, and Javadoc or reason-less annotations are left untouched.

10. Nullability Javadoc, generated

Documenting nullability belongs in the Javadoc — writing the sentence by hand does not. When a nullability-annotated element's Javadoc does not document it yet — a method parameter without its @param tag, a return type without @return, a thrown type without @throws, a type parameter without its @param <T> tag, or a field/class without any Javadoc at all — Alt+Enter offers Append nullability Javadoc: the kind-adaptive sentence (@param key a String which is nullable) is appended, or a /** … */ comment created around it, with the reason clause selected and the caret right after because : type a reason to replace it in one stroke, or press Backspace to drop the clause and keep a complete sentence. The sentence is English by default; under Settings → Editor → Nullify it can follow the IDE language or one of the fixed Deutsch / Français / 日本語 / 简体中文 modes.

What gets folded

A quick tour of the folding you'll see every day — including the less obvious spots:

Java you writeWhat Nullify shows
@Nullable FooFoo?
@NotNull BarBar!
@Nullable Foo<@NotNull Bar>Foo?<Bar!>
? extends Fooout Foo
? super Barin Bar
@NotNull String[]Array<String!>
Object @Nullable ...Vararg?<Object>
@Nullable Foo @NotNull []Array!<Foo?>
? extends @Nullable Fooout Foo?
@NotNull String @Nullable [] @NotNull []Array?<Array!<String!>>
@Nullable var name = ...String? (inferred type)
@ConfigValue("${app.name}") @NotNull String@ConfigValue("${app.name}") String!
(Serializable & @NotNull Consumer<...>)Serializable & Consumer!<in String!>
@Nullable final var foo = ...final String? foo (modifier kept)

Nullify can even take such a complex type:

@NotNull List<
    ? extends @Nullable Supplier<
        Map<
            ? extends @NotNull CharSequence,
            @Nullable Consumer<? super CharSequence>
            >
        >
    > @NotNull [] list;

// Folds to `Array!<List!<out Supplier?<Map<out CharSequence!, Consumer?<in CharSequence>>>>>`.

Installation

From the JetBrains Marketplace: Settings → Plugins → Marketplace → search "Nullify" → Install.

From disk: Settings → Plugins → ⚙️ → Install Plugin from Disk… and select the downloaded .zip.

After installation, restart your IDE and open any Java file. Folding is on by default — just start reading.

Compatibility

  • IDEs: IntelliJ IDEA 2025.3.4+ (Ultimate & Community) and compatible JetBrains IDEs.
  • Language: Java.
  • License: Proprietary.

Feedback & Roadmap

Found a bug? Want a feature? Nullify tracks everything transparently:

  • Issues & Feature Proposals — Tracking Document Site | Report Site
  • Changelog
  • Rate & Review — your review on the Marketplace makes a real difference
  • Contact — Kurv Cygnus

Made with ☕ and a healthy impatience for annotation noise.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Custom Javadoc sentence templates (NL-F23): The doc-language option under Settings → Editor → Nullify now offers Custom...: write your own sentence template for Append nullability Javadoc using ${head}, ${article}, ${type_of_target}, ${nullability_of_target}, ${select_start}, ${select_end} and ${carpet_position}. ${article} is optional; the rest are required. ${select_start}/${select_end} delimit the reason clause that is inserted selected (the closing period stays outside it), and ${carpet_position} marks the caret right after "because ". The field pre-fills with the built-in English template; an invalid template (missing or unknown placeholders, misordered markers) is rejected with an explanation.

idea-plugin.name: Flow Lens
idea-plugin.description:
Flow Lens turns a selected function into an explorable map of what runs next. Put the caret in a method, run Analyze Flow, and read the execution path forward from there. Every step leads back to the source.

It is a reading tool for unfamiliar code, debugging, review, and onboarding. It is not a repository-wide analyzer and not a runtime tracer: it follows explicit calls in the source, within a depth and node budget you control, and marks every place it stopped rather than trailing off.

What it shows

  • Real evaluation order. save(convert(load())) reads as load, then convert, then save — not as the order the text is written in. Chained calls follow the receiver chain; arguments evaluate left to right.
  • Control flow as structure. Conditions, switches, loops, and try blocks are drawn as containers with labelled branches, and the sequence resumes after them instead of hanging off one branch.
  • Uncertainty, stated rather than hidden. Every call carries a resolution status and a dispatch confidence. A virtual call that may be overridden at runtime says so; an interface call with no single responsible continuation stops rather than guessing — and you can choose which implementation to follow, with the card still reporting the confidence it actually has.
  • Asynchronous timing. A lambda, a Kotlin trailing lambda, or a Go closure handed to a call becomes a step of its own with a body you can open, and it says when it runs: in place, concurrently, as a goroutine, deferred — or that the timing could not be determined, which is stated rather than left for you to assume.
  • Your code, or everything. Repetitive runs of library calls collapse into one card by default, and a setting can hide calls to code outside the project entirely — with the map saying how many it removed, so an absence never reads as "nothing was called".
  • Somewhere to work from. Pin the functions you keep returning to, save a flow together with the limits it was analyzed at, re-open recent ones, and export any flow as Markdown or as a Mermaid diagram for a review or an issue.

Languages: Java, Kotlin, and Go (Go requires the JetBrains Go plugin). One flow may cross Java/Kotlin boundaries, because the analyzer is chosen per resolved target rather than once for the whole run.

Where it runs: Flow Lens needs an IDE with Java support. It is developed and verified against IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate; other JetBrains IDEs may work but are not verified targets.

Local-first: no AI service, no server, no network calls. Nothing you analyze leaves your machine, and the logs hold counts and timings rather than your source.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0 — Hide external calls.

  • A new setting — Hide calls to code outside the project, off by default — removes library and built-in calls that were not entered from the map entirely, so a complex flow reads as your own code. Hidden calls cost no node budget, which goes to your functions instead.
  • A call handed a lambda or function literal keeps its card, so your own body stays where it belongs; unresolved calls always stay.
  • The removal is disclosed rather than silent: the status area and both exports say how many calls were hidden.

1.0.0 — First release.

  • No new capability, and that is the point: the feature set is settled, and 1.0 is about the one thing Flow Lens does being dependable. From a selected function, it maps execution forward and shows the uncertainty and the analysis boundaries rather than hiding them.
  • Everything below shipped during development and is listed so you can see what the plugin grew from.

0.5.0 — Asynchronous semantics.

  • A body handed to a call — a lambda, a Kotlin trailing lambda, a Go closure — is no longer invisible. It appears as its own step, with its own frame you can open, named after the call it was given to.
  • Each one says when it runs, in words: in place, concurrently, as a goroutine, deferred — or that the timing could not be determined. Flow Lens states an unknown timing rather than letting position imply an answer, and the status area counts the ones it could not justify.
  • Go parity: go func() { … }() and defer func() { … }() bodies are now visible.

0.4.0 — Ambiguity and sharing.

  • An interface or abstract call is no longer a dead end: Flow Lens lists the implementations the project contains and follows the one you choose. The call still reports the dispatch confidence it actually has — a choice is not a proof — and says whose body it is showing.
  • Export a flow as Markdown or as a Mermaid flowchart, carrying the same uncertainty the canvas shows, so a map can go into a review or an issue.

0.3.0 — Developer workflow.

  • Flow Pins: mark a function and it stands out in every flow that reaches it, across restarts.
  • Saved Flows: keep an entry point with the limits it was analyzed at, and re-run it later exactly as it was.
  • Recent analyses: the last ten entry points, one click away.
  • Analyze from Here: promote the selected call's target to the new root.
  • A running analysis now names the callable it is working on and shows how much of the node budget is spent; a finished one summarizes why its map stops where it does, and each count leads to the card.

0.2.0 — Control flow on the map.

  • Branches, multi-way branches, loops, and exception handling are now part of the map: a structure is one container with labelled sections, and the sequence visibly resumes after it.
  • Java if/switch/loops/try, Kotlin if/when/loops/try, and Go if/switch/select/loops, plus return and throw as terminal markers.
  • A repeated call appears once inside its loop container instead of being duplicated outside it.
  • The "control flow simplified" disclosure now appears only for control flow that is genuinely not represented, such as a short-circuit operand or a break, rather than on every branch.

0.1.0 — Multi-language method flow and Flow Canvas.

  • Analyze a Java, Kotlin, or Go function into an explorable flow map; analysis crosses Java/Kotlin boundaries per resolved target.
  • Evaluation-order call extraction for nested, chained, and argument calls; call sites stay distinct from target symbols.
  • Resolution and dispatch classification: project, external, unresolved, built-in; exact, declared target, ambiguous, unknown.
  • Go goroutine and defer semantics preserved; compiler-generated declarations are never followed as authored code.
  • Progressive local-first canvas with nested frame expansion, cycle, depth-limit and node-limit markers, project-boundary crossings, selection details, and target / call-site navigation.
  • Bounded cancellable analysis off the EDT, with indexing wait and stale-source handling; project-scoped settings; English and Japanese UI.

idea-plugin.name: FlywayGuard
idea-plugin.description:
FlywayGuard is a sentinel for Flyway migration scripts in IntelliJ IDEA - it detects and blocks Flyway version conflicts before commit, push, and merge.

FlywayGuard —— Flyway 迁移脚本哨兵

在提交与推送前拦截 Flyway 版本化迁移脚本的违规操作，把版本冲突解决在 push 之前，避免流水线/项目启动时报错：禁止修改或删除已推送的脚本、禁止版本号重复、禁止新增版本乱序（低于项目内或上游最高版本）。提供工具窗口实时标红（重复 / 乱序 / 已推送被改）、修改已推送脚本时的实时警示与文件状态图标（合规绿箭头 / 非法警示）、merge 后冲突通知。纯 IDE 级行为检测与拦截，不向用户仓库写入任何代码。仅 git 仓库项目生效。

FlywayGuard

Blocks Flyway versioned-migration mistakes before commit and push, so the pipeline never fails at startup: no modifying or deleting already-pushed scripts, no duplicate versions, and no out-of-order versions (below the highest project or pushed version). The tool window highlights anomalies in real time (duplicates / out-of-order / pushed scripts modified), editing an already-pushed script triggers a real-time warning with file status icons (green arrow for valid / warning for invalid), and conflicts are notified after merges. Pure IDE-level detection and interception — no code is implanted into your repository. Only active in git repositories.

idea-plugin.name: Flaky Test Linter
idea-plugin.description:
Flaky Test Linter — lint your tests for the flakiness SAST ignores

SonarQube, Semgrep and CodeQL lint your production code; your test suite is the blind spot. This plugin statically flags the deterministic flakiness anti-patterns — anchored to the empirical flaky-test taxonomy (Luo et al., FSE 2014). Offline, no network.

  • Fixed sleep in a test (Thread.sleep, delay, browser.pause, page.waitForTimeout, numeric cy.wait) — Async Wait is the #1 empirical flaky cause; use an explicit wait on a condition.
  • Test with no assertion — a test with no oracle silently protects nothing; a delegation guard keeps verify*/assert*/should* helper and Kotest x shouldBe y tests quiet.
  • Brittle XPath locator — index (//div[2]), position()/last(), or absolute paths break on any layout change; attribute locators are left alone.
  • Unbounded blocking wait — latch.await() / thread.join() / sem.acquire() with no timeout can hang until the CI job times out.

Each language loads only where the IDE supports it: Java and Kotlin in IntelliJ IDEA / Android Studio, JS/TS in WebStorm / IDEA Ultimate — the plugin installs in any JetBrains IDE. More rules and a headless CI mode (SARIF + baseline that fails only on new flake) are on the roadmap.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.5.0

  • Pro — new rule (K1, Concurrency): flags async work started in a test — executor.submit, CompletableFuture.runAsync, a coroutine launch/async, or a thread { } — that is never awaited or synchronized, so assertions can race the background task. Precision-first: it abstains if the method awaits/joins/gets the result at all. Java & Kotlin.

1.4.0

  • Pro — new rule (N1, Real network call in a test): flags a real network endpoint reached from a test — raw Socket/ServerSocket, url.openConnection(), DNS, or JS fetch/axios/node http — which depends on an external service being up. Java, Kotlin & JS/TS.

1.3.0

  • Pro — new rule (O1, Test Order Dependency): flags a call that mutates global/process state (System.setProperty, Locale.setDefault, TimeZone.setDefault, System.setOut) from inside a test body — it leaks into later tests. Java & Kotlin.

1.2.0

  • Double-click (or press Enter on) a finding in the Flakiness Report to jump straight to that line in the editor.
  • The tool window now shows a distinct stripe icon.

1.1.0

  • Now Freemium. The four existing inspections (fixed sleep, test with no assertion, brittle XPath locator, unbounded blocking wait) and the headless CI mode (SARIF + baseline) stay free and unchanged.
  • Pro — Flakiness Report tool window: scan the whole project's test sources for a test-hygiene score (% of test methods with zero flakiness findings), a filterable findings table, and HTML/JSON export.
  • Pro — two new rules: wall-clock dependency (T1, Luo "Time") and unseeded randomness (R1, Luo "Randomness") for Java, Kotlin and JS/TS.
  • A free 30-day trial of Pro is available from this page.

1.0.0

  • First release: four flakiness inspections — fixed sleep, test with no assertion, brittle XPath locator, and unbounded blocking wait — for Java, Kotlin and JS/TS, from one shared, precision-first rules engine (anchored to the Luo et al. FSE 2014 flaky-test taxonomy).

idea-plugin.name: Lattency
idea-plugin.description:
See where Java code leaves the process.

Lattency adds gutter markers for database, HTTP, messaging, and file I/O. It follows calls through project code, so you can see whether a method eventually leaves the process without walking the call chain by hand.

  • Distinct icons for database, HTTP, messaging, file, and generic I/O.
  • Dimmed icons distinguish transitive I/O from direct I/O.
  • Tooltips explain the complete sink chain, with click-through navigation.
  • Zero configuration for common Java and Spring APIs, including Spring Data, JDBC, REST clients, Kafka, Pub/Sub, JMS, RabbitMQ, and file APIs.
  • A committed lattency.yml can add project-specific sinks, exclusions, and a custom propagation depth.

Private by design: the analysis is entirely static. Lattency does not run your application, make network requests, or collect telemetry.

Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2025.2 or newer. Java only; Kotlin is not supported.

Documentation · Report an issue · Source code
idea-plugin.change-notes:

idea-plugin.name: Module Boundary Leak Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on an import of an internal package (project convention: a .internal. segment in the package path) from a DIFFERENT Gradle/Maven module than the one that declares it -- hidden architecture coupling that, in large monorepos/microservices, precedes cascading-deployment incidents: a module's "private" internals change and break an undeclared consumer that should never have had access.

Resolves each import via real PSI reference resolution (not a global index lookup) combined with real platform module resolution -- the module graph IntelliJ already imported from your real Gradle/Maven project, not a second hand-rolled parser of build files. Confirmed gap: the bundled Package Checker analyzes CVEs of declared dependencies, not internal module architecture; no Marketplace plugin dedicated to this found.

Stated honestly: v0.1 is Java only (Kotlin's import PSI is a separate hierarchy, out of scope for this version) and works against a single multi-module Gradle OR Maven project (not both mixed in the same analysis); the "internal" convention must be a literal .internal. package segment -- never inferred from a javadoc/comment.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Deadlock Lock-Order Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Builds a real lock acquisition-order graph from synchronized blocks/methods inside a single Java class, and flags a gutter warning on every site that closes a CYCLE in that graph -- the classic static-deadlock signal: one method acquires lock A then, while still holding it, acquires lock B; another method in the same class acquires B then A. If two threads hit those two methods at the same time, each can end up holding one lock while waiting forever for the other.

A real mechanism, not a text pattern -- this walks the actual PSI tree to find genuine lexical nesting of synchronized sites, builds a directed graph keyed by the lock expression text, and runs a real DFS cycle search over it (the textbook approach from MIT/ECOOP 2005 "Static Deadlock Detection for Java Libraries"). IntelliJ's own thread dumps only show a deadlock AFTER it happens at runtime; no Marketplace plugin found does static lock-order cycle detection ahead of time.

v0.2: cross-method edges. A lock acquired not by direct textual nesting but through a call to ANOTHER method of the same class -- synchronized(a) { helper(); } where helper() itself acquires lock b (directly, or transitively through its own calls) -- is now followed too, with real-cycle-safe memoization so a genuine call cycle between methods never hangs or crashes.

v0.3: cross-CLASS edges through an injected collaborator. A call like synchronized(a) { collaborator.helper(); }, where collaborator is a field/parameter of the caller's class, is now followed into the collaborator's own lock graph -- the most common real-production shape (a service calling into another injected service). An interface/abstract collaborator type is followed only when exactly ONE class in the same module implements it; the chain is bounded to 3 collaborator classes deep, an explicit documented cost bound.

Stated honestly: lock identity is matched by exact expression text (lockA and this.lockA are treated as different locks). Java only; ReentrantLock/java.util.concurrent locks and Kotlin's synchronized(){} are not yet covered.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Integer-Overflow-on-Widening Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on an int * int/int + int expression assigned/passed directly to a long-typed destination (a local variable's initializer, an assignment, a method parameter, or a method return) with no widening cast on either operand -- CWE-190, Integer Overflow or Wraparound. The operation happens in 32-bit int arithmetic FIRST, silently truncating the result (often to a negative value) before the already-wrong value is widened to long.

Integer overflow analysis for Java has few dedicated tooling options in general; this narrow, syntactically unambiguous form (a direct widening assignment with no intermediate cast) has no dedicated Marketplace plugin found.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only the exact shape int OP int assigned directly to a long destination -- never analyzes longer expression chains, and never multiplication/addition of more than two operands.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Retry Without Backoff+Jitter Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on a retry mechanism with a FIXED interval between attempts instead of exponential backoff + jitter: a manual for/while retry loop that Thread.sleep(constant)s in its catch, Spring @Retryable with no real exponential @Backoff, or Resilience4j's RetryConfig built with a fixed .waitDuration(...) and no .intervalFunction(...).

The "thundering herd" anti-pattern -- synchronized retries from multiple instances of a service saturate the downstream exactly at the same instant, documented in distributed-systems literature (AWS Architecture Blog, Google SRE Book) as a real cause of cascading availability incidents. JOptimize (Marketplace, confirmed) flags only the ABSENCE of any retry on an HTTP call -- this is a deeper granularity: the QUALITY of a retry mechanism that already exists.

Stated honestly: v0.1 covers Spring Retry and Resilience4j (known declarative forms) plus the manual for/while + catch + Thread.sleep(constant) pattern -- never analyzes a fully custom retry implementation with none of these recognizable signals.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

Fixed

  • Review/star CTA now links to this plugin's own Marketplace reviews page instead of the vendor's generic plugin list.

idea-plugin.name: Kafka Premature Offset Commit Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on a Kafka consumer poll-loop (while (true) { ... poll(...) ... }) that dispatches asynchronous work (ExecutorService.submit(...), CompletableFuture.runAsync(...)/ .supplyAsync(...)) without waiting for it to finish (.get()/.join()/ .awaitTermination()) BEFORE the consumer commits offsets -- either explicitly (commitSync()/ commitAsync() called right there regardless of the async work's real completion) or implicitly (no manual commit at all, relying on Kafka's own default enable.auto.commit=true, which commits on the next poll() cycle regardless of whether the dispatched work finished).

If the consumer crashes between the commit and the real completion of that work, the message is lost silently -- no error, no retry, nothing visible. Extensively documented as a real, common Kafka consumer bug (Medium, Conduktor, official offset-management guides); no Marketplace plugin found dedicated to this.

Correlates three independent signals in the same loop body -- async dispatch alone is fine if the loop waits for it; a commit call alone is fine if nothing async was dispatched; no explicit commit only matters because it means the risky auto-commit default is in play.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only the official org.apache.kafka:kafka-clients client with the standard poll-loop shape -- never covers Kafka Streams or wrapped messaging frameworks (Spring Kafka's @KafkaListener is out of scope, a future extension).

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

Fixed

idea-plugin.name: Exception-Escape Chain Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on a catch (Exception e) (the broad type, not a narrower specific exception) that silently swallows -- no rethrow, no logging -- a specific CHECKED exception that a call inside its try block can actually throw, directly or transitively through a bounded same-class call chain. A real business exception (e.g. PaymentDeclinedException) caught this way leaves the system in an inconsistent state with no trace to diagnose the real incident.

"Exception Catcher" (Marketplace) solves the opposite problem (where is X caught); no plugin found that computes the real escape set through a call chain.

Stated honestly: chain depth is bounded to a fixed constant (never unlimited); only follows calls to methods of the SAME class -- a call to another class (a further narrowing from the original design, which also considered same-module calls) or an external library is treated as unknown and cuts the chain there, never inferred.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

idea-plugin.name: Cache-Invalidation Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Warning on a .save(...) call inside a method whose class also has a hand-rolled Map-backed cache field (populated by a computeIfAbsent/manual containsKey+put "get-or-compute" pattern), when that method never touches the cache field -- stale data served after a real update, a silent inconsistency between what's written and what's read.

No Marketplace plugin found dedicated to hand-rolled cache invalidation gaps -- outside the @Cacheable ecosystem, which already has its own declarative invalidation mechanism.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only a hand-rolled cache with Map as the backing structure inside a single class -- never covers @Cacheable/Caffeine/Redis as an external cache. "The same data source" is inferred heuristically (the mutator method never mentions the cache field's name at all) -- a real risk of false positives if that heuristic is loose, an honestly-acknowledged limit.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

idea-plugin.name: Kafka Topic Feedback-Loop Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Flags a Spring Kafka @KafkaListener method whose OWN transitive call graph (same class, or one injected collaborator, UNBOUNDED depth, cycle-protected -- not a fixed hop limit) reaches a .send(...) back to the SAME topic it consumes -- a real self-feeding/"poison pill" loop that can saturate an entire consumer group under load, documented as a real anti-pattern in Confluent's own guides on avoiding cyclic topic dependencies.

Never just "a producer and a consumer of the same topic exist somewhere in the project" -- that alone proves nothing; the real path back, resolved via a genuine whole-project call graph, is what this plugin confirms.

Stated honestly: v0.1 only Spring Kafka's @KafkaListener (consumer side) and KafkaTemplate.send(...)/ KafkaProducer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(...)) (producer side), string-literal topic names only; a manual KafkaConsumer.subscribe(...) poll-loop consumer is out of scope (a different angle already covered by this catalog's own Kafka Premature Offset Commit Companion).

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.

idea-plugin.name: Log Injection Companion
idea-plugin.description:
Flags an unsanitized logging call reachable from an HTTP endpoint parameter -- CWE-117 (Log Injection): an attacker can inject a CRLF sequence to forge fake log entries, hiding a real attack trail or misleading whoever reviews the logs later (SEI CERT IDS03-J, "Do not log unsanitized user input").

Built on a REAL whole-project interprocedural taint analysis -- the base technique real dataflow frameworks use: the actual project call graph, condensed into strongly connected components via Tarjan's algorithm (handling recursion/mutual recursion correctly), with taint summaries computed per method to a real FIXED POINT, not a bounded-depth approximation. The hardest algorithmic technique in this catalog.

Stated honestly: AWS CodeGuru Reviewer has a dedicated log injection detector, but it's CI/batch, not an inline IDE inspection. Qodana's own taint analysis covers OWASP categories A01/A03/A07/A08/A10 -- Log Injection (A09, Security Logging Failures) is NOT among them, and Qodana taint analysis requires a paid Ultimate Plus license regardless (not Community Edition). No dedicated Marketplace plugin found for this exact angle.

Free. No license nags, no telemetry, no network calls.
