idea-plugin.name: Azure DevOps Community
idea-plugin.description:
Azure DevOps is a plugin to enable working with Git and TFVC repositories on Azure DevOps Services or Team Foundation Server (TFS) 2015+.
GitHub | Issues | Discussions | Changelog

Features
  • Supports authenticating with Azure DevOps Services and TFS 2015+ to work with source code in Git and TFVC repositories.
  • Checkout code from Git and TFVC repositories on Azure DevOps Services and TFS 2015+.
  • Git specific features:
    • Import IntelliJ projects into Git repositories on Azure DevOps Services and TFS 2015+.
    • Create pull requests and view your active pull requests.
    • Create a new branch and associate it with the work item you are working on.
    • Quickly browse to file history or commit details on the web from the IDE.
  • TFVC specific features:
    • Execute all basic version control actions such as add, delete, rename, move, etc.
    • View local changes and history for your files.
    • Lock and unlock files and directories.
    • Add labels to files and directories.
    • Create, view, manage, and edit a workspace.
    • Supports using a TFS proxy.
  • View work items based on queries and select one or more work items to associate with your commits or checkins.
  • Check the build status of your repository and queue a new build if desired.
  • Supports proxy settings configured in the IDE's System Settings section.
  • Edit cached project information through configuration management.


This is a community fork of the unmaintained Microsoft plugin, updated for the 2026.1 platform.
Compatible with IntelliJ-based IDEs (including Rider) versions 2026.1 and later

End User License Agreement & Privacy Policy
By installing this plugin, you agree to our end user license terms and privacy policy. For information about our privacy policy, please view the Microsoft Privacy Statement
Note: When using the TFVC support, this plugin will pass your Team Foundation credentials securely to the TF command line tool. That tool is installed separately and it is up to the user to verify that it is in a secure location on disk and has not been tampered with.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 2.0.9:
    • Opening a project with very deep directories (for example a Chrome for Testing bundle under bin/Debug) no longer floods the IDE with one "TF205022: The following path contains more than the allowed 259 characters" error per directory. The TFS SDK rejects local paths longer than 259 characters on every OS, so such directories are now treated as not under TFVC. Any other TFVC client failure during VCS root detection is logged as a warning instead of being reported as a plugin error.
    • The Work Items tab of a TFVC project no longer fails with "getTeamProjectReference() is null" when the collection has more than 100 team projects. The team project was looked up only in the first page of the server's project list, so the work item list and the query drop-down stayed empty; it is now requested by name, with a fallback that goes through every page. This also fixes "Compare with Latest Repository Version" for such projects. If the project still cannot be found, the tab names the missing team project instead of showing a NullPointerException.
  • 2.0.8: Maintenance release with no behavior changes. The full automated test suite (960 tests) is restored after the move from PowerMock to Mockito 5 and now runs on every change and before each release. The remaining compiler warnings are cleared.
  • 2.0.7:
    • TFVC checkout handles an existing server workspace properly. A TFVC workspace is named after the target folder and lives on the server, so deleting the local folder does not remove it and a second checkout into the same name used to fail. Now checkout shows a dialog that names the workspace and offers a "Fix Workspace on Server" button to delete it and retry (OK leaves it untouched). Cancelling the "Edit the workspace before getting sources" dialog no longer leaves an orphaned workspace behind, and a failed workspace creation reports an error instead of the progress bar quietly disappearing.
    • The context menu in the Pull Requests and Work Items tabs renders correctly again. On the current platform the old Swing menu showed the entries collapsed on top of each other, without hover highlight and effectively unclickable; it now goes through the platform popup factory. Right-clicking a row also selects it, and "Create Branch" in the Work Items tab no longer throws when nothing is selected.
    • The TFVC "Create Branch" dialog checks the target path. It must be a server path starting with "$/" (for example $/TeamProject/NewBranch). A bare name previously reached the tf client and failed with a confusing "First free argument must be a server path" error; the dialog now keeps Create disabled and explains what is expected.
    • Under the hood: the Git and TFVC checkout providers use the current VcsCloneComponent API instead of the removed doCheckout, and java.util.Observable/Observer plus the remaining deprecated platform and JDK calls are replaced (the Plugin Verifier is down to three overrides that have to stay while 2026.1 is supported). No behavior change from these. Also added a small plain-JVM unit test set that builds and runs without the legacy test suite.
  • 2.0.6: Removed the non-working help ("?") button from the Manage Workspaces dialog. Replaced another batch of deprecated platform API calls with their current equivalents. No behavior changes.
  • 2.0.5: Reworked the Feedback button — it now links to the plugin's JetBrains Marketplace reviews, GitHub Issues, and GitHub Discussions instead of the old, non-functional Microsoft feedback dialog. Replaced a first batch of deprecated platform API calls. No behavior changes.
  • 2.0.4: The credentials prompt now opens on top of the Settings dialog and is modal to it. Cancelling "Update credentials" no longer stores an empty credential or breaks TFVC change detection. Removed the last internal API usage.
  • 2.0.3: Replaced most platform APIs scheduled for removal so the plugin keeps working on 2026.2 and later. Proxy settings are now read through the current platform proxy API.
  • 2.0.2: Replaced all internal and override-only API usages flagged by the Plugin Verifier (Marketplace compliance).
  • 2.0.1: Renamed to "Azure DevOps Community", enabled signed publishing, and improved TFVC check-in error messages.
  • 2.0.0: Revived fork. Migrated to the IntelliJ Platform 2026.1 (works in Rider 2026.1+); updated the rd protocol and the TFVC reactive backend to run on JDK 21.

idea-plugin.name: Git Local Review
idea-plugin.description:
Review your changes like a pull request — before it exists.

Open a virtual pull request over any diff range — a comparison between any two refs (A...B, same as a GitHub PR when B is HEAD), the staging area, or the working tree — and track per-file reviewed state with GitHub-style viewed checks in a dedicated tool window. Reviewed state survives commits, is invalidated automatically when a file changes again, and is kept per diff range in your local workspace.

idea-plugin.name: Branchive
idea-plugin.description:
Branchive

Version control for teams that work with large binary assets, backed by the Branchive server-side fork of Epic's Lore VCS.

This plugin registers Branchive as a first-class VCS in every IntelliJ-platform IDE (IntelliJ IDEA, Rider, CLion, PyCharm, WebStorm, …). It wraps the lore command-line client to drive the core version-control loop directly from the IDE:
  • file-status coloring and the Local Changes view
  • commit, revert (discard local edits)
  • diff against the current revision
  • branch create / switch / merge, and first-class Push / Pull (Sync)
  • merge-conflict resolution — keep Mine (Ours) or Theirs per file, then complete or abort
  • Perforce-style lock-on-edit (a Lore lock is acquired when you start editing a file)
Branchive Cloud sign-in (browser-based PKCE) is available from Tools → Branchive Cloud; when signed in, the plugin authenticates the lore CLI as you for Branchive Cloud pushes/pulls. Self-hosted and local workspaces continue to operate against the ambient-authenticated lore workspace.

Implements Branchive IDE Integrations Contract v2.0.0.

idea-plugin.name: Sapling SCM Integration
idea-plugin.description:
Sapling SCM (sl) integration for JetBrains IDEs. Brings first-class version-control support to Sapling working copies, which the bundled Git integration cannot operate on.

Native VCS provider for .sl-mode repositories:

  • Changes view, side-by-side diff, and revert against committed content
  • Per-file history and per-line blame / annotate
  • A repository Log tab with commit graph and bookmarks as refs
  • A 3-way merge dialog for resolving conflicts
  • Actions for pull, push, goto, uncommit, shelve/unshelve, and bookmarks

Embedded Interactive Smartlog (ISL) — Sapling's own web UI hosted in a tool window, wired to the IDE: click a file in ISL to open it in the editor, theme-synced to the IDE, with commit and amend performed in ISL (matching Sapling's no-staging-area model).

Everything works by invoking the sl command-line tool as a subprocess; the plugin embeds no Sapling source code and requires the Sapling CLI to be installed.

Unofficial, independent project. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Meta. "Sapling" is a trademark of Meta Platforms, Inc., used here only to describe the software this plugin integrates with.
idea-plugin.change-notes: 0.1.0 — Initial release: native Sapling VCS provider (changes, diff, revert, history, blame, log, 3-way merge) plus the embedded ISL tool window with IDE bridge and theme sync.

idea-plugin.name: Forget-to-Stage-Me-Not
idea-plugin.description: Forget-to-Stage-Me-Not is a plugin that shows a warning each time you try to git commit from the UI and you have unstaged changes. Useful for developers coming from IDEs (like Visual Studio) where this case is handled explicitly.

idea-plugin.name: Git Profiles
idea-plugin.description: Manage git identity profiles (user.name and user.email). Store profiles once, then apply any of them as the global git identity or assign one per git repository in every project.

idea-plugin.name: GitFocus
idea-plugin.description:
New in recent releases

  • A tool window for your worktrees and windows. The GitFocus button on the left stripe lists, under Active windows, every open IDE window, then under Other every worktree — closed — where GitFocus is switched on or whose branch has a filter designated for it, plus the remaining worktrees of this window's repository, so a checkout not yet using GitFocus is one click away. Both sections group by repository, each under its own label. Rows read name [branch] with directory and chip color; double-click focuses the window or opens the worktree in a new one, the X on an open row closes that window, and the right-click menu shows, closes or opens it.
  • Branch filters are edited on their branch. A filter designated for a branch takes hand edits to its sources only while that branch is checked out; anywhere else the editing rows are grayed out, while switching, renaming, re-designating and Reset Filter keep working. The branch popup lists every named filter, even one created in another repository — picking it resets it and makes it yours.
  • Switch windows by keyboard. Alt+Shift+W (or GitFocus → Show Worktrees) opens the worktrees tool window with every open IDE window under Active windows, grouped by repository and read as name [branch] with its chip color. It opens with this window's row selected, so the cursor starts where you are; arrows move, typing filters, and the X at the end of a row closes that window. The chord toggles the tab the way the IDE's own Alt+<digit> tool-window shortcuts do.
  • Branch and color in the Window menu. The project rows at the bottom of the IDE's Window menu now read name [branch] and carry the window's chip color, so same-named worktrees are tellable apart before you switch.
  • Diff across several commits. A file's Show Diff menu now offers All Commits when two or more filter commits touched the file, and Select Range… from three — a two-handle slider picks the first and last commit to compare.
  • A filter per branch. Right-click a branch → Use GitFocus Filter for This Branch…: the filter is named after the branch, fills with the commits that branch owns, and switches itself on whenever you check the branch out. Switch branches and the view follows.

GitFocus hides what you are not working on. Pick a few commits (or directories and files), and the Project view shows only the files that belong to them. Once GitFocus is enabled, your local changes and open tabs stay visible too — each behind its own switch.

How it works

  • Filters. A filter is a list of commits, directories, and files. The files changed by those commits become the base of what you see. You get one Default Filter plus three named filters, so you can keep one view per task or branch and just switch between them.
  • A filter per branch. Give a branch one of your filters and it becomes that branch's view: named after the branch, filled with the commits the branch owns, and switched on whenever you check that branch out — off again when you move away. Set it up by right-clicking the branch, on any branch, not only the current one. Correct its sources by hand on that branch; from other branches the filter can be switched, renamed, re-designated or reset, but not edited.
  • Look without committing to it. Temporarily Show Children opens a filtered directory so you can see what is inside. The extra rows are gray italic, change nothing, and are gone as soon as you clear them — or add the ones you wanted to a filter and keep them.
  • Hiding never blocks navigation. Go to Definition landing on something hidden puts it on the tree first — the file or package, plus every folder above it — so Ctrl+click behaves the way it does without GitFocus. Do it by hand with GitFocus: Show in Project View in the editor's right-click menu, or switch the automatic part off in Settings.
  • Extra context, one switch each. Show the files your visible files import (one hop). Show sibling files and directories, so you see what else lives in the same package or folder. Show root files and top-level directories to reach the rest of the project. Choose which local changes stay visible: all changed files, workspace only, staged only, or none — and whether open tabs stay shown.
  • Capture your working set. Add all currently changed (or staged) files to a filter with one click, so the view survives the commit.
  • Per-file diffs from the tree. Right-click a visible file → Show Diff: its local changes (current vs staged, staged vs HEAD) and each filter commit that touched it. When several commits did, All Commits spans them all in one diff and Select Range… lets a two-handle slider pick which first and last commit to compare.
  • Scope and colors. A "GitFocus" scope matches exactly what is visible — usable in Find in Files and File Colors.
  • Tell windows apart. The main toolbar (new UI) shows the open directory name as a colored chip — click it to pick a fixed color, or end the directory name in a color name or palette number (web-blue, myrepo-3) and it gets that color by itself. The IDE's Window menu lists each project as name [branch] in the same color. The GitFocus tool window on the left stripe — Alt+Shift+W, or GFW in Find Action — lists every open window under Active windows, then every worktree where GitFocus is on or whose branch has a filter plus this repository's other worktrees, all grouped by repository. Arrows move, Enter switches or opens, typing filters.
  • It follows your task. GitFocus joins the IDE's own Tools → Tasks & Contexts, so opening a task restores the view you were using with it.
  • Starting over. Per filter, Clear Sources empties its entries and Reset Filter returns it to defaults; Settings → Reset All Filters and Settings… resets everything at once.

Where the controls are

Right-click in the Project view or in the Git log and open the GitFocus menu — that is where you act on what you selected: add it to a filter, look inside it, run its tests. The GitFocus button in the Project view header holds the display switches, the capture actions and the Filters menu. Branch filters are set up by right-clicking a branch. Every switch also appears in Find Action (double-press Shift, type "git focus") and can get a keyboard shortcut in Settings → Keymap.

Use case 1: focus on a few commits

  1. Open the Git log (Alt+9 / ⌘9).
  2. Ctrl-click the two or three commits you care about.
  3. Right-click → GitFocus → Set as Default Filter.
  4. Turn on GitFocus → Enable GitFocus — it is off after installation.
  5. The Project view now shows only the files those commits touched, plus your local changes and open tabs.

Use case 2: see a bit more around the focused files

All display switches live in the Project view header button and in the actions menu (double-Shift):

  1. Show Direct Imports — also show files imported by the visible ones (Java, Kotlin, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Go, Ruby, Rust — whatever your IDE supports).
  2. Show Sibling Files / Show Sibling Directories — see what else lives next to your files.
  3. Show Root Files / Show Root Directories — reach the rest of the project, for example to add more folders to a filter.

Use case 3: two branches, two views

  1. On branch feature-a: select its commits in the Git log, right-click → GitFocus → Add to Filter → Filter 1.
  2. GitFocus → Filters → Filter 1 → Set Name… — call it "feature-a".
  3. Check out the other branch and put its commits into Filter 2 the same way; name it "bugfix-b".
  4. Switch views any time with Filters → pick one → Use Only This. Nothing to rebuild after a checkout.

Use case 4: run only the visible tests

  1. Focus on the commits or directories you are working on, so the test tree shows only the classes that matter.
  2. Right-click the test directory in the Project view → Run Focused Tests (or Debug Focused Tests).
  3. Only the visible test classes run — not every test class that happens to live in that directory (Java and Kotlin).

Works in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, GoLand, RubyMine, and RustRover (2024.2+). The UI is available in English, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean — the IDE's display language selects the locale. Polish and Russian translations are also included and used when the IDE runs under those locales.

Not compatible with Rider, Android Studio, DataGrip, and DataSpell: these IDEs replace or bypass the Project view that GitFocus filters. Installing the zip there is refused at startup with the IDE's standard "conflicting module" notice.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.21.3

  • Fixed: compatibility with the latest IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 EAP builds, where the bundled Tasks & Contexts plugin was renamed. Opening a task there restores the GitFocus filter again.

0.21.2

  • Fixed: compatibility with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3, where Tasks & Contexts moved into its own bundled plugin. Opening a task there restores the GitFocus filter, as in earlier IDE versions.

0.21.1

  • Fixed: in the GitFocus tool window a branch that fit its row could still be cut by one character (…ain (main)) on some font sizes.

0.21.0

  • Every worktree of a project in the GitFocus tool window. Once GitFocus is used in one checkout of a repository — or one of them is an open window — the tool window lists all of that repository's worktrees, not only the ones already using GitFocus.
  • Branch-first rows. Each row now leads with the branch and shows the worktree's directory name dim at the right edge; the full path moved into the row's tooltip.
  • Rows fit the tool window. No more sideways scrolling: each row is fitted to the visible width by itself. A directory name short of room is cut in the middle, and a very long branch loses its middle / segments first, so the end of the name stays readable.

0.20.0

  • Changed lines highlighted in the editor. Two new switches in the GitFocus popup (the Project view header button), both off by default: Highlight Lines Changed by Commits tints the whole row of every line your filters' commits added or modified — per file, from just before the oldest of those commits to the newest — and Highlight Locally Modified Lines tints every row that differs from the last commit. The rows follow the code while you type, and an edited commit row turns into a local one.
  • Gutter stripe and scrollbar mark. Every highlighted range also gets a coloured stripe beside the line numbers and a thin mark on the scrollbar, so the change stays visible where another plugin paints its own row background.
  • Your colours. Settings ▸ Editor ▸ Color Scheme ▸ GitFocus: row background and stripe colour for both kinds of rows, with defaults for light and dark themes.

0.19.1

  • Alt+Shift+W starts on this window. The worktrees tab now opens with the (this window) row selected — every time, also when the tab was already visible with the focus in the editor — so the arrows always start from where you are. It used to preselect the window after this one.

0.19.0

  • The worktrees tab is the window switcher. It now opens with Active windows — every open IDE window, this one included, whatever its GitFocus state — and Other below it: the closed worktrees that were listed before. A window whose project has no git repository at all is listed by itself at the end of the first section, so no open window can be missing from the list.
  • Grouped by repository. Both sections list each repository under its own label with its worktrees indented beneath it, main checkout first, so same-named branches in different repositories are never confusable.
  • Close a window from its row. Every row under Active windows ends in an X that closes that window (File → Close Project semantics).
  • Alt+Shift+W opens the tab. The separate Switch Project Window… popup is gone: its shortcut now opens the worktrees tab, selecting the window after this one, so Alt+Shift+W then Enter still jumps to the next window. The chord toggles the tab like the IDE's own Alt+<digit> tool-window shortcuts, and Find Action still finds it under Switch Project Window, GFW or WT.

0.18.1

  • No more "Synchronous execution on EDT" error. Designating a filter for a branch, editing a filter's sources, Reset All and Load Settings all consult the repository identity, and doing so right after a project opened — before the identity cache had warmed — ran git on the UI thread, which the IDE reports as an error. Those operations now finish in the background when the cache is cold; the menus catch up a moment later.

0.18.0

  • Parent checkouts in the worktrees window. Every repository that shows a worktree row also shows its main checkout, marked "(main)", so the parent of the listed worktrees is always one double-click away. The second block is now captioned Other.
  • Faster way in. Typing GFW or WT in Find Action (double-Shift or Ctrl+Shift+A) opens the GitFocus worktrees tab.

0.17.0

  • A tool window for your worktrees. The GitFocus button on the left stripe lists git worktrees in two blocks: Using GitFocus — every worktree, open or not, of any known repository where GitFocus is switched on or whose checked-out branch has a named filter designated for it — and the remaining worktrees of this window's repository. Rows read name [branch] with directory and chip color, a green dot marks an open window, and "(this window)" marks this one. Double-click or Enter focuses the window or opens the worktree in a new one; right-click offers Show Window, Close Window or Open; typing filters; Refresh picks up worktrees added outside the IDE. Known repositories are the open windows and the IDE's recent projects; closed checkouts are read from their own workspace settings.
  • Close windows from the switch popup. Every row of Switch Project Window… (Alt+Shift+W) ends in an X that closes that window the way File → Close Project does; the popup stays open for the next one.

0.16.0

  • Branch filters are edited on their branch. A filter designated for a branch takes hand edits to its sources — adding, setting, removing or clearing entries, and the per-entry rows — only while that branch is checked out in its repository. From any other branch, a second worktree or a detached HEAD those rows are grayed out; the filter can still be switched on and off, renamed, re-designated and reset. Designating a branch, and the commit scan that follows, work from anywhere as before.
  • Reset Filter works on a filter created in another repository. Its row in the Filters menu now opens; every item but Reset Filter is grayed out. Resetting frees the slot at once — unowned and empty, for any window to claim.
  • The branch popup lists every named filter. Use GitFocus Filter for This Branch… also offers filters created in another repository, labelled with the branch they serve. Picking one asks for confirmation, resets it (its sources cannot come along), designates it for your branch and runs the commit scan.
  • Fix: filters of one repository no longer read as "created in another repository" on some branches. A repository was recognized by the root commit of the checked out branch only, so a branch with a different root — an orphan branch, or one cut before another history was merged in — made every filter look foreign. Every root commit of the repository now counts.
  • Switch Project Window… (Alt+Shift+W). A popup listing every open IDE window as name [branch] with the window's chip color. Arrow keys move, Enter (or a click) switches, Esc or the title-bar X closes, typing filters. The row after the current window is preselected, so Alt+Shift+W then Enter jumps to the next window. Also in the GitFocus menu above Settings; the shortcut is reassignable in Settings → Keymap. Rows show the folder on the left and the branch on the right, so branches line up whatever the folder names.
  • Window menu rows show branch and color. The project rows at the bottom of the IDE's Window menu now read name [branch] and carry a square in the window's chip color. They follow branch checkouts, chip color picks and window opens/closes. A window whose repo-name chip is hidden keeps a plain row. The current window's row shows its square in the highlighted frame the IDE uses for checked rows with icons.

0.15.0

  • Show Diff across several commits. When a file was changed by two or more of the filters' commits, its Show Diff menu now offers All Commits — one diff spanning from before the oldest commit to the newest. With three or more, Select Range… opens a two-handle slider to pick the first and last commit of the span to compare.
  • Both rows compare file content between two points in history, so changes from in-between commits are included even when those commits are not in the filters.

0.14.0

  • The window chip color can follow the folder name. While the repo-name chip is set to Automatic, a directory name that ends in a color name or a palette number now gets exactly that color: web-blue, repo-deep-purple, myrepo-3 (numbers 1–16, counted in the chip popup's order). The ending must be separated by -, _, . or a space; any other name keeps the usual automatic color, and a color you picked by hand always wins.
  • If a folder name happens to end in such a token (for example a clone named project-2), its automatic chip color changes after this update. Click the chip and pick a color to pin the one you prefer.

0.13.0

  • Named filters are now shared. A named filter is defined once and every project window sees it — including every worktree and clone of the same repository. Deleting a worktree no longer loses the filters, or the branch designations, you built in it.
  • Filters belong to their repository. Each named filter remembers which repository it was created in (recognized by the repository's first commit — works offline, across worktrees and clones). In projects of a different repository it is listed grayed out as created in another repository and cannot be enabled; entries can only be added from the owning repository.
  • On/off stays yours per project. Sharing covers the definition — name, sources, branch designation. Which filters are switched on remains per project window, so two worktrees on different branches keep different views. Branch auto-enable keeps working per window.
  • Designating the current branch applies at once. Use GitFocus Filter for This Branch… on the branch you are standing on now enables the filter immediately instead of waiting for the next checkout.
  • Reset All is local. Reset All Filters and Settings… now resets only the current project's own settings; shared named filters survive. Delete a shared filter per filter (Reset Filter), which affects every project.
  • Named filters saved by earlier versions inside a single project are not migrated: recreate the ones you use and they become shared. The default filter is untouched.

0.12.0

  • Branch filters. Right-click a branch → Use GitFocus Filter for This Branch… and pick the filter that is that branch's view. The filter is renamed @branch: <branch>, fills with the commits the branch owns (you choose which from a checklist), and switches itself on when you check that branch out — and off again when you leave. Works on branches you are not on. Each filter can opt out via Auto-Enable When Branch Matches.
  • Temporarily Show Children. Right-click a filtered directory to look inside it without switching GitFocus off. Filtered-out children appear in gray italic and change nothing — Clear All Temporarily Shown puts them back, and Add Selection to Default Filter keeps the ones you want.
  • Navigation still works. Ctrl+click a symbol or an import whose file or package GitFocus is hiding and it now appears in the tree, with the folders above it — the jump the IDE was already making simply lands instead of quietly finding nothing. GitFocus: Show in Project View (editor right-click) does the same by hand, and Settings → Show Navigation Targets turns it off.
  • Tasks & Contexts. Opening a task under Tools → Tasks & Contexts restores what the Project view was filtered to, alongside the tabs and breakpoints the IDE already restores.
  • Ignore Non-Branch Filters. One switch leaves every filter without a branch out of the view, so a branch's view stands alone. Nothing is disabled, so switching it back off restores everything exactly.
  • Reset. Per filter, Clear Sources empties its entries while Reset Filter returns the whole filter to defaults; Settings → Reset All Filters and Settings… does the lot.
  • The Filters menu now lists every filter, empty ones marked (empty), and named filters start switched off. The display switches moved out of the right-click menu into the GitFocus button in the Project view header, which was getting crowded.

0.11.0

  • GitFocus now starts disabled: after installation nothing is hidden until you switch on GitFocus → Enable GitFocus. After this update, previously enabled projects need that switch turned on once again — filters and settings are preserved.
  • Run Focused Tests: right-click a directory → GitFocus → run or debug only the test classes the filtered tree shows; uses Gradle or the JUnit runner to match the IDE's "Run tests using" setting.
  • Plugin page refreshed: recent features listed up top and a new "run only the visible tests" use case.

0.10.0

  • Repo-name chip: the main toolbar (new UI) shows the open directory name on a colored background — tell IDE windows apart at a glance; click to pick a fixed color; can be switched off in the GitFocus Settings submenu.

0.9.0

  • The Project view header button now opens the full menu: display switches, the capture actions, and Filters.
  • The GitFocus context-menu entry shows the plugin icon.
  • Enabled filters are marked with a check icon in the Filters list, and every filter menu starts with an Enabled switch.
  • Choose which local changes stay visible — all, workspace only, staged only, or none — and toggle open-tab visibility.
  • Show Diff: per-file diff menu — current vs staged, staged vs HEAD, and each filter commit's own change to the file.

0.8.0

  • Localized UI: Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean — the IDE's display language selects the locale.
  • Direct-import following for eight languages: Java, Kotlin, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Go, Ruby, and Rust.
  • Every switch reachable from Find Action (double-Shift), assignable in Keymap, and behind a Project view header button.
  • Modernized VCS log APIs; verified compatible from 2024.2 through 2026.2.
  • Excluded IDEs where the Project view filtering cannot apply: Rider, Android Studio, DataGrip, DataSpell.

idea-plugin.name: GitButler for IDE
idea-plugin.description:
Adds GitButler virtual-branch support to the IDE: commit to virtual branches straight from the IntelliJ commit window, and browse your GitButler workspace in a dedicated tool window — unassigned changes, applied branches, their commits and the files each commit changed, with diff navigation, pull, push, unapply, rename/uncommit and drag-and-drop amend built in. New virtual branches can be created from the tool window or named straight from the commit window. The native Git branch menu gains a GitButler submenu to apply or unapply a branch.

This is an unofficial plugin and is not affiliated with or endorsed by GitButler. The GitButler mark is used under its CC0-1.0 brand assets (github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler-brand-assets).

idea-plugin.name: Git Branch Notes
idea-plugin.description:
Displays local Git branch notes next to local and remote branch names in IntelliJ IDEA.
  • Annotates local and remote branches in the Git Log branch dashboard.
  • Lets you add, edit, and delete notes from native single-branch action menus.
  • Copies a remote note once when creating a new local tracking branch.
  • Copies a local note once when Push creates a remote branch with an exact source mapping.
  • Optionally shows the current local branch and its note in the status bar.
  • Stores all notes locally in the repository's Git configuration.
No external service or project file is required.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Adds locally stored notes for remote branches.
  • Adds native branch actions for creating, editing, and deleting notes.
  • Copies remote notes to newly created local tracking branches without overwriting local notes.
  • Copies local notes to remote branches created by IntelliJ IDEA Push without overwriting remote notes.
  • Makes the optional status-bar widget disabled by default.

idea-plugin.name: IssueHub
idea-plugin.description:
IssueHub brings your GitHub issues into the IDE. Browse and open issues for the current repository from a dedicated tool window, without leaving your editor.

  • Lists issues for the GitHub repository detected from your project's Git remote
  • Shows issue number, title, labels, and assignee
  • Search issue titles and bodies, and filter by state, author, assignee, labels or milestone
  • Sort by creation date, last update or comment count
  • Opens an issue as an editor tab, full width and splittable next to your code, with the description rendered in the IDE's own styling
  • Reads the whole thread in that tab: comments alongside closes, reopens, label, assignee and milestone changes, title edits, and references from other issues and commits
  • Keeps the issue's assignees, labels, projects (with the fields each board tracks, such as status, size, estimate and dates), milestone, and the pull requests and branches opened for it in a sidebar beside the thread, the way GitHub's own issue page does
  • Jumps to the issue on GitHub whenever you need the browser
  • Keeps accounts under Settings | Tools | IssueHub: paste a token and have it checked against the server before it is saved, or adopt a GitHub account your IDE is already signed in with, on github.com or on an Enterprise host
  • Stores every token in the IDE's secure credential store, never in plain text
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • GitHub Enterprise repositories are detected from the project's git remote, as long as an account is set up for that server. SSH, HTTPS and ssh:// remotes with a port are all recognised.
  • Settings | Tools | IssueHub | Repository names the repository a project reads issues from, for when the git remote points elsewhere, such as a fork whose issues live upstream. It takes owner/name, host/owner/name for an Enterprise server, or a pasted repository URL, and is kept per project without being shared through version control. When no repository is detected, the tool window links straight to it.

Changed

  • Each repository is read with the account on its own server, so a github.com project and an Enterprise one use their own tokens. Before, every project used whichever GitHub account was added first.
  • When GitHub won't serve the issue list without an account, the tool window says so and links straight to the accounts page instead of showing a raw error. A private repository opened with no account set up asks for one, and a saved token that GitHub now refuses, expired or revoked, is called out as such. The list reloads when you come back from the accounts page.

idea-plugin.name: GitLab Sync & Smart Cleanup
idea-plugin.description:
Sync a GitLab fork with its parent repository and clean up local branches — without manually configuring an upstream remote.

  • Pull / Rebase / Hard Reset the current branch onto the default branch of the parent (non-forked) repository — the parent is resolved automatically via the GitLab API.
  • Delete Merged Local Branches — finds and deletes branches already merged (including squash-merge) into master and/or the parent's master, or whose upstream was removed on the server.
  • Optional automatic check for stale branches and divergence from the parent on project open.
  • Import TLS certificates for Gradle sources and the GitLab host (origin) into the JDK cacerts — for corporate TLS proxy setups.

Синхронизация форка GitLab-репозитория с его родителем и уборка локальных веток — без ручной настройки upstream-remote'а.

  • Pull / Rebase / Hard Reset текущей ветки на default-ветку родительского (не форкнутого) репозитория — родитель находится автоматически через GitLab API.
  • Delete Merged Local Branches — находит и удаляет ветки, уже влитые (включая squash-merge) в master и/или в родительский master, либо с удалённым на сервере upstream.
  • Опциональная автоматическая проверка лишних веток и отставания от родителя при открытии проекта.
  • Импорт TLS-сертификатов источников Gradle и GitLab-хоста (origin) в cacerts JDK — для случаев с корпоративным TLS-прокси.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed a deprecated/internal API usage flagged by the Plugin Verifier in the "About Plugin" action.

Исправлено использование устаревшего/внутреннего API, на которое указывал Plugin Verifier, в действии «About Plugin».

idea-plugin.name: Got
idea-plugin.description:
Native version control support for Game of Trees (got) in the IDE.
  • Detects .got/ work trees automatically
  • File status, native diff, and modified-lines gutter
  • Commit and rollback from the Commit tool window
  • File history and Update Project (got update / got fetch)
  • Send action (got send) and a Settings panel for the got binary path
See the README for details on how each feature maps to the underlying got command.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Clone repositories over ssh:// from the native Clone Repository dialog ("Got" in the Version control dropdown)
  • GOT_AUTHOR now falls back to git config's user.name/ user.email when a repo doesn't define its own author

idea-plugin.name: SVN Integration for TortoiseSVN
idea-plugin.description: Bridges JetBrains IDE context menus to the installed TortoiseSVN client on Windows. Supports Project View, editor popups, editor tabs, and Rider File System/Solution Explorer.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.3.3

  • Fixed multi-directory TortoiseSVN commands treating selected directories as files.
  • Path files now use TortoiseSVN's required UTF-16LE, no-BOM, LF-only format so directory Commit and Update recurse correctly.
  • Added pre-launch path-file validation to prevent malformed selections from reaching TortoiseSVN.

0.3.2

  • Added 23 TortoiseSVN commands to Project View, editor, and editor-tab context menus.
  • Added native Rider File System and Solution Explorer context-menu integration, including Unreal projects.
  • Added the TortoiseSVN Files tool window for selecting open files and running batch Update or Commit.
  • Added compact filename/path rows, double-click-to-open, and a complete TortoiseSVN context menu in the tool window.
  • Added automatic and configurable TortoiseProc.exe discovery.
  • Kept the integration independent from the JetBrains Subversion plugin and IDE VCS mappings.

idea-plugin.name: AOne GitLab Connect
idea-plugin.description:
Professional GitLab integration for self-hosted and cloud instances developed by AOne Consultancy. Supports GitLab versions 13.x to 19.x. Features:

  • Merge Request List & Details
  • Pipeline Status Monitoring
  • Open File in GitLab Web UI
idea-plugin.change-notes: Initial beta release of GitLab integration.

idea-plugin.name: Git Chrono
idea-plugin.description: Pick any date and time for your commit. The native Commit button updates to Commit on [Selected Date and Time] the moment you select a date, and reverts to normal when no date is set.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Pick a custom commit date and time from the Git Commit tool window; the Commit button reflects the selected date/time before you commit.
  • After a successful commit, HEAD is automatically amended so the commit and author date match what you picked.
  • Toolbar icon changes to indicate a backdated or future-dated commit, with a clear indicator when a custom date is active.

idea-plugin.name: Git Identity Guard
idea-plugin.description:
English

Git Identity Guard prevents an unintended Git name or email address from being recorded in commits to your GitHub repositories.

The plugin uses the GitHub accounts already configured in IntelliJ IDEA and protects repositories whose GitHub.com remote owner matches one of those accounts.

  • Resolves and caches the GitHub no-reply email for each configured account.
  • Checks the effective user.name and user.email when a project opens, when repository remotes change, and before a commit.
  • Offers one-click actions to apply the privacy identity or ignore a repository.
  • Writes only repository-local Git configuration and only after explicit confirmation.
  • Provides English and Simplified Chinese user interfaces based on the IDE language.

Privacy: Identity comparisons happen locally. GitHub API requests reuse credentials managed by IntelliJ IDEA, and the plugin contains no telemetry.

Current scope: GitHub.com repositories owned by a configured personal account. GitHub Enterprise Server, organization-owned repositories, and SSH host aliases are not currently protected.

简体中文

Git Identity Guard 用于防止错误的 Git 用户名或邮箱被写入 GitHub 仓库的提交记录。

插件直接使用 IntelliJ IDEA 中已配置的 GitHub 账号，并保护 GitHub.com Remote owner 与其中某个账号匹配的仓库。

  • 获取并缓存每个账号的 GitHub no-reply 隐私邮箱。
  • 在项目打开、仓库 Remote 变化及 Commit 前检查最终生效的 user.name 和 user.email。
  • 提供一键应用隐私身份或忽略仓库的操作。
  • 只有在用户明确确认后才写入仓库级 Git 配置。
  • 根据 IDE 语言提供英文或简体中文界面。

隐私说明：所有身份比对均在本地完成。GitHub API 请求复用 IntelliJ IDEA 管理的凭据，插件不包含遥测功能。

当前范围：仅保护已配置个人账号名下的 GitHub.com 仓库；暂不保护 GitHub Enterprise Server、组织名下的仓库和使用 SSH 主机别名的 Remote。

Documentation / 文档与源码

idea-plugin.name: PR Insights
idea-plugin.description:
PR Insights

Review GitHub Pull Requests Without Leaving IntelliJ

Read comments, reply to discussions, resolve threads, browse open pull requests, checkout pull requests locally, and jump directly to the relevant code — without switching back and forth between IntelliJ and GitHub. PR Insights is an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that brings GitHub pull request reviews directly into your IDE.

Install from JetBrains Marketplace →     View on GitHub →

Why PR Insights?

Reviewing a pull request often means switching between your IDE to work with the code and GitHub to read and respond to review comments.

PR Insights brings these workflows together so you can stay focused on your code while keeping up with your pull request discussions.

Go beyond reviewing the diff. Checkout a pull request locally, run the application, verify the changes, and leave review comments based on what you actually see and experience.

Features

Live Comment Feed

View pull request comments and review threads directly inside IntelliJ. Updates appear automatically without requiring a manual refresh.

Reply and Resolve

Read discussions, reply to comments, and resolve or reopen threads without opening GitHub in a browser.

Jump Directly to Code

Click a comment's file or line reference to open the relevant location directly in the IntelliJ editor.

Browse All Open Pull Requests

View all open pull requests in your repository, not just the pull request associated with your current branch.

Checkout Pull Requests Locally

Checkout any open pull request directly from IntelliJ and review the changes in your local environment.

Run the application, test the changes, explore the implementation, and verify the behavior before leaving your review comments.

Pull Request Notifications

Optionally receive notifications when a pull request you're watching gets a new commit, comment, or review decision.

GitHub Authentication

Use the GitHub account already connected to IntelliJ when available, with support for a personal access token when needed.

Light and Dark Themes

Choose between system, light, or dark themes to match your preferred workflow.

How It Works

  1. Install PR Insights from the JetBrains Marketplace.
  2. Open a Git repository with a GitHub remote in IntelliJ IDEA.
  3. Open the PR Insights tool window.
  4. Browse and select an open pull request.
  5. Checkout the pull request locally to inspect and run the changes.
  6. Review the implementation and verify the behavior in your local environment.
  7. Read, reply to, and resolve discussions directly from your IDE.

Installation

  1. Open IntelliJ IDEA → Settings → Plugins.
  2. Search for PR Insights in the Marketplace.
  3. Click Install.
  4. Restart IntelliJ IDEA if prompted.
  5. Open a Git repository with a GitHub remote and start reviewing your pull requests.

Open Source

PR Insights is open source and developed openly on GitHub.

View Source Code on GitHub →

Get PR Insights

Bring GitHub pull request reviews closer to the code you're already working on.

Install PR Insights from the JetBrains Marketplace →

License: MIT

idea-plugin.name: Bulk Merge Requests
idea-plugin.description:
Creates merge requests for all open projects in a single dialog.

Pick the source and target branch per repository, following the layout of the IDE's own Push dialog, and confirm once. One merge request is created per selected repository. A repository that fails never stops the others: every result is reported together, with direct links to what was created and a clear reason for what was not, and the failed ones can be retried in one click.

Built for workspaces with many repositories: filter the table, set a source or target branch across all of them at once, and override it per repository where needed.

Supported hosts: GitLab, GitHub, Gitea and Forgejo, each on their hosted service as well as on your own server. Access tokens are stored in the IDE password safe.

idea-plugin.name: git review workflow
idea-plugin.description:
Walk a PR in order, then edit and run it — not just read the diff.

git review stages the entire pull request into your working tree as uncommitted changes. Reviewing it is then ordinary local work: jump to a definition, follow a call, run the tests, fix what you find. When you are done, your fixes are extracted onto a branch of their own — the author's commits stay exactly as they were.

The tool window keeps your place in it:

  • The reading order the author wrote, one file at a time, each with the reason that change is there — instead of an alphabetical list of files you have to reassemble in your head.
  • The whole range when there is no reading order: open one diff, or all of them at once.
  • Pause and come back. A review survives switching branches; your edits are held until you finish it.

Requires the git review command-line tool: npm install -g git-review-workflow (Homebrew, a Windows installer and a no-Node one-liner).
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • A CLI failure the panel cannot parse now keeps the CLI's own explanation. Instead of replacing useful stderr with the parser's generic complaint about unreadable porcelain, the panel shows the detail the command supplied; the parser message remains the fallback when there is no CLI detail.
  • The current branch refreshes after review-changing actions. Starting, finishing, undoing, and other mutations now refresh the IDE repository before the panel refreshes, so the branch shown by Source Control and the review state agree immediately.
  • Choosing a base branch lists each branch once. The current branch could be added again when it was already among the candidates, making one destination look like two different choices. The picker now presents one row per branch.
  • Finish and undo cleanup copy now names the exact tradeoff. The confirmation says your edits stay on their destination branch while Keep edits & remove Undo removes the option to undo this finish; the pending-finish banner says the edits are staged for that branch, must be committed before switching branches, and can still be undone.

Visualize Git branches, tags, merges, and repository topology as an interactive revision graph inside JetBrains IDEs.

Revision Graph helps you understand how long-lived branches, releases, tags, and merges relate without expanding every commit in Git Log.

Features:

  • Explore local and remote branches, tags, HEAD, and merge relationships
  • See upstream Ahead/Behind status without duplicate reference labels
  • Trace how two selected revisions diverged from their common visible ancestor
  • Filter loaded history and visible reference categories independently
  • Compare revisions, switch branches, create branches or tags, and open focused Git Log views through the IDE's bundled Git integration
  • Navigate large graphs with search, pan, zoom, Fit to Canvas, and Center HEAD
  • Use English or Simplified Chinese UI on light and dark IDE themes

Revision Graph has no analytics, telemetry, advertising, or external service. Repository history is read locally using the configured Git executable.

idea-plugin.name: Git Flow GUI
idea-plugin.description:
Git Flow GUI — the branching model, without the CLI.

A maintained graphical front end for the Git Flow branching model, working in every JetBrains IDE.

No git-flow installation required. The long-abandoned Git Flow plugins shell out to the git-flow CLI and fall over with "Gitflow is not installed", "git: 'flow' is not a git command", or "Unsupported Git Flow Version". Git Flow GUI drives plain git through the IDE's own integration, so it works wherever git does.

And it works with the CLI, in both directions. Import adopts the branch names, prefixes and tag prefix from a repository that git flow init already configured. Init writes those same keys back, so a repository you set up here works for a teammate on the command line, or on another plugin, who never installs this one.

Features

  • Initialise or adopt — set a repository up for Git Flow, writing the configuration under the same keys the git flow CLI uses, so your teammates' CLI and other plugins agree with you. Already have a repo set up elsewhere? Import its configuration instead. It works both ways on purpose.
  • Set a repository up, or adopt one — Init writes the standard git-flow configuration keys into .git/config, and Import reads them back. Configuration travels with the repository, not with this plugin, so a teammate on the CLI or on a different plugin is never locked out.
  • Start branches — feature, bugfix, release, hotfix and support branches off the correct base branch, with the resulting branch name shown before you commit to it.
  • Finish properly — releases and hotfixes merge into main, get tagged, and are also merged back into develop, so the two never silently diverge. The confirmation spells out every step before anything happens.
  • Never lose track of a half-finished flow — if a step fails part-way, you are told exactly which steps already landed and that nothing was rolled back, instead of a bare error that leaves you guessing what happened to your work.
  • Stay up to date — bring a flow branch in line with the branch it came from by merging or rebasing, your choice, with the trade-off spelled out.
  • Switch and clean up — jump to any flow branch, including one that exists only on a remote (a local tracking branch is created for you), and delete branches you're done with, locally or on the remote too.
  • Publish — push a flow branch and set its upstream in one action.
  • Start a branch from an issue — pick a ticket and get the correctly named branch. Built on the IDE's own Task Management, so every tracker it supports works here — GitHub, GitLab, Jira, YouTrack, Redmine, Trac and the rest — using the credentials you have already set up. Nothing extra to configure.
  • Several git roots? — pick which repository the actions apply to. No more guessing which root a release just merged into.
  • Branch tree — every flow branch grouped by kind, the one you're on marked, and the ones that exist only on a remote shown too. Double-click to switch.
  • A nudge, not a nanny — warns before you commit straight onto main or develop, which is the easiest way to drift out of the model by accident. Warns; never blocks.
  • See every git command — the tool window logs each command the plugin runs and git's own output, so an automated four-step merge is never a black box.
  • Status bar — the flow branch you're on, always visible, with every action one click away.
  • Everything in one tool window — which flow branch you're on and what exists, with every action in the same place. Nothing is buried in a menu, and only the actions that make sense right now are enabled.
  • Configurable — branch names, prefixes, tag prefix, fast-forward, delete and push behaviour, per project. Open it straight from the tool window, or find it at Settings → Version Control → Git Flow.
  • Safe by default — refuses to run on a dirty working tree or mid-merge, checks that merge targets and tags are usable before anything irreversible starts, validates branch names before calling git, and explains merge conflicts instead of dumping stderr.

By Veryation.

Website  ·  Support
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Multi-repository projects could act on the wrong repository. Every action resolved its repository through the first git root the platform happened to list, so in a project with several roots a release could be merged into the wrong one. Actions now use the selected repository, the tool window grows a picker when there is more than one root, and the choice is remembered by path.
  • A failed Finish no longer looks like lost work. Finishing runs several irreversible steps in a row; if one failed partway, the old message said what broke but not where the repository had been left. Failures now list the steps that did land and state plainly that nothing was rolled back — deliberately, since unwinding a merge you may have started resolving is more dangerous than leaving it.
  • Three failure states are refused before anything irreversible starts, instead of midway through: a merge already in progress, a merge target branch that does not exist (the main-vs-master misconfiguration, which otherwise merged a release into nothing), and a version tag that is already taken (which otherwise landed the merge, then failed).
  • Merge-conflict messages now point at git merge --abort for anyone who would rather back out than resolve.
  • Commit and Stash are only offered where they help. The "uncommitted changes" warning put those two links on every refusal, including ones they cannot fix — and git stash fails outright on a repository mid-merge, so following the advice produced a second error.
  • Notification text no longer runs past the end of the balloon. Messages were written as though for a dialog; the balloon cuts off after about three lines, which was hiding the command that resolves the problem. The important sentence now comes first — after a part-finished release, where the repository actually is leads, and the error follows.

Added

  • Initialize Git Flow in a repository — writes the standard git-flow configuration keys into .git/config, so a repository set up here also works with the git-flow CLI, with other Git Flow plugins, and for a teammate who never installs this one. Combined with the existing import, configuration now flows in both directions.
  • Sync — bring a flow branch up to date with its base branch, choosing merge or rebase with the trade-off spelled out. Rebase is offered first as the right default for unshared work, never assumed, because rewriting published history is the one mistake here that costs someone else real work.
  • Checkout, including branches that exist only on the remote — a local tracking branch is created, which is what picking up a teammate's branch actually means.
  • Delete — keeps git's safe -d. If the branch holds commits that are not merged into develop or main it says so before asking you to confirm, and offers to discard them as a deliberate second choice rather than refusing outright or forcing quietly. Removing the remote copy is a decision each time, offered only when a remote copy exists, and never the default button.
  • Branch tree in the tool window, replacing the "3 feature, 1 release" summary. It shows which branches exist, which one you are on, and which are remote-only. Double-click to switch, or right-click for the actions that apply to that branch — Switch and Delete on one you are not on, Finish, Publish and Update on the one you are.
  • Command log, on its own tab — every git command the plugin runs on your behalf, visible. Finishing a flow is several commands deep, and a failure should not leave you guessing what ran. Probe commands are excluded so a healthy repository does not fill the log with normal negative answers.
  • Status bar widget showing the current flow branch without opening the tool window. Hides itself entirely in projects without git.
  • Commit guard — warns before a commit lands directly on your main or develop branch, checking every root being committed to. It warns and never blocks: there are good reasons to commit on main, and Cancel returns you to the commit dialog with your message intact.
  • A tool window you can actually use in a narrow panel. Per-repository setup — Initialize, Import config and Settings — sits in the title-bar menu rather than taking five rows, buttons are sized to their labels instead of stretching, and Refresh is in both the title bar and the panel so it cannot vanish when the header runs out of room.
  • Start a branch from an issue in your IDE's task tracker, keeping the issue id in the branch name. Built on the IDE's own Task Management, so every tracker it already supports works — Jira, YouTrack, GitHub, GitLab, Trac, Asana and the rest — using credentials the IDE already stores. The plugin ships no tracker connectors of its own.

idea-plugin.name: Ticket Prefixer
idea-plugin.description:
Adds a button to the commit toolbar that writes the ticket number from your current Git branch into the commit message — when you press it, not before.

That timing is the point. Assistants like Copilot replace the entire contents of the commit message field when they generate a message, so a ticket number that was inserted automatically when the commit dialog opened is gone by the time you commit. Here you let the assistant write first and press the button afterwards: nothing touches the field again, and the ticket survives.

The ticket is found by a regular expression you control, so any branch scheme works — PROJ-4711, bare digits, or a convention of your own. Presets for Jira keys and for numeric ids fill that in for you if you would rather not write one. A template controls where the number lands: #{ticket}: {message} prepends, {message} (#{ticket}) appends. If the message already opens with the ticket in some other format — which is what a generated one tends to do — that reference is rewritten into your template instead of a second one being added.

The insertion is a normal undoable edit and keeps the caret where it was.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Renamed from TicketStamp to Ticket Prefixer. This is a normal update: your branch pattern, your message template and any keyboard shortcut you assigned to the button all carry over. Only the name changes — in the plugin list, in the settings page and on the notifications.

New: preset buttons on the settings page for Jira keys and for numeric ids. The numeric preset is the shipped default; the Jira one reads PROJ-1234 whole, where the numeric pattern would have kept only the 1234. Both just fill the two fields, which stay editable.

New: when the commit message already opens with the ticket in a different format, which is what an AI-generated message tends to produce, that reference is rewritten into your configured template instead of a second one being added in front of it. A mention further inside the text is left untouched.

idea-plugin.name: Git Emoji Lint
idea-plugin.description:
Git Emoji Lint adds emoji prefix templates to the Git commit message editor. Pick a template from the Commit tool window toolbar to generate a feat✨: style prefix, making your commit history more readable and consistent.

📚 中文说明

在 Commit 工具窗口提供工具栏按钮，选择模板后自动生成 feat✨: 格式的 commit 前缀，让提交记录更直观、更规范。

  • 可视化设置页面：Settings → Tools → Git Emoji Lint
    • 自定义格式模板：支持 ${'$'}{emoji}、${'$'}{type}、${'$'}{name}、${'$'}{description} 四种占位符，自由组合出你想要的任何前缀格式。
    • 模板列表增删改：表格中 emoji、type、name、description 四列均可直接编辑，支持添加新模板、删除不用的模板。

📋 默认模板

emoji type name description

🚀 perf 提高性能/优化 优化

🔧 chore 日常维护 杂项
🧩 deps 修改依赖版本 依赖
🔁 revert 还原之前的提交 回滚
🧪 test 增加测试代码 测试
📦 file 添加新文件 新文件
📌 tag 发布版本/添加标签 书签

⚙️ ci Action持续集成相关修改 持续集成
🙈 git 添加或修改.gitignore文件 不可见
🎉 init 初次提交/初始化项目 初始化

默认格式模板为 ${'$'}{type}${'$'}{emoji}: ，即生成 feat✨: 样式的前缀。所有模板及格式均可在设置页面自由修改。

idea-plugin.name: Workforest
idea-plugin.description:
Git worktree forest management from the IDE, driven by the workforest command line tool. Linux and macOS only (x64 and arm64): workforest has no Windows build, and the plugin cannot do anything without it.

Your repo has one working directory; your AI agents want five. Workforest gives every feature - and every agent - its own disposable git worktree in a predictable location, set up by the project's own symlinks and setup scripts, so parallel work on the same repo never collides.

  • Create Worktree: pick a local or remote branch, or name a new one; the worktree is created, set up, and opened as a project in a new window.
  • Open Worktree: switch to any worktree of the forest — in a new window, this window, or ask.
  • Checkout Worktree: collapse a worktree back into the main checkout.
  • Delete Worktree: remove one, optionally with its branch.
  • Lock / Unlock Worktree: keep one from being deleted, checked out, or pruned. Prune Stale Worktrees: drop the records of worktrees whose directory is gone.
  • Run Script / Stop Script: a scripts entry of the project config, in a new terminal tab of the chosen worktree.
  • Show the merged configuration, scaffold the project or local config, open a terminal in a worktree, copy its path.
  • A Workforest tool window: the project's scripts, and the main checkout with the worktrees (most recently opened first, uncommitted changes marked) — with tooltips, inline buttons, and context menus — plus the current worktree on the status bar.
The workforest CLI ships with the plugin and is the copy it runs, so nothing else is needed. Where this build carries no executable — a platform workforest runs on but ships no frozen build for — install it (uv tool install workforest, Homebrew, or the AUR) and the plugin picks it up from PATH.

Workforest is free, open source, and built by one person in the open. If it saved you a context switch today, please rate it five stars here and star the repository on GitHub.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.8.0

Locked and stale worktrees are understood everywhere, and a config with an unknown key no longer stops the tool.

  • A worktree whose directory is gone — deleted by hand, or on a drive that is not mounted — no longer breaks wf list, delete, checkout and the editor clients. list shows it as stale; open and checkout refuse it and name the fix instead of failing inside git.
  • wf prune removes the records of stale worktrees, naming each one; -n/--dry-run only names them. wf delete NAME on a stale worktree removes its record and leaves any files still there in place.
  • wf lock NAME [--reason TEXT] and wf unlock NAME: delete, checkout and prune refuse a locked worktree until it is unlocked. --force still means "discard uncommitted changes" and never overrides a lock; a locked worktree opens as usual.
  • list --json gains locked and prunable, and dirty is null for a stale worktree. list --porcelain has six columns instead of four: the lock and the stale reason follow dirty.
  • Both editor clients mark locked and stale worktrees, offer Lock, Unlock and Prune, show Unlock in place of Delete on a locked worktree, and leave a stale one only the actions that need no directory. A refresh that fails keeps the last listing on screen.
  • An unknown key in a config file — at the top level, in the make section, or in a script — is ignored with a warning instead of being an error, so a config written for a newer release still loads. A wrong value for a known key is an error as before.
  • Shell completion offers only the worktrees a command can act on for lock and unlock, and prints no warnings. Re-run eval "$(workforest shell-init)" (or restart the shell) to pick up the new completions.

0.7.0

Makefile targets are scripts without being configured.

  • wf make TARGET runs any target of the worktree's GNUmakefile, makefile, or Makefile with everything wf run gives a configured script: extra arguments, -b and a log file, the process group and terminal handling, exit status, records, exclusive preemption, and cleanup. A target runs under the name make:TARGET, so it never shadows the scripts map; wf stop --make TARGET stops it again.
  • The new make config section says which targets are offered by name — in shell completion and in the editors' script lists — through hidden, hide_scripts, show_scripts, and exclusive_scripts. Hiding is about what is offered, not what may run: a hidden target still runs when named. Targets are read out of the makefile rather than from make, so listing them never evaluates a $(shell ...).
  • Both editor clients list the makefile targets alongside the scripts, badged make, and run and stop them the same way.

0.6.1

  • The VS Code extension is published to Open VSX as well as the Visual Studio Marketplace, so VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf and the other forks install it from the registry they use.
  • On the Visual Studio Marketplace the extension is workforest-vscode, shown as Workforest for VS Code — the plain name is held there by another publisher. On Open VSX it stays workforest.

idea-plugin.name: Git Merge Into Plus
idea-plugin.description:
Merges the current branch into a target branch of your choice and automatically switches back to the current branch when the operation finishes.

Features:

  • Official Plugin Branding: Modern SVG plugin icons for light and dark IDE themes.
  • Git Branches Popup & Context Menu Integration: Seamlessly accessible directly from the IDE status bar branch widget, New UI main toolbar Git widget, and branch context menus with intelligent pre-selection.
  • Multi-Target Branch Merge: Select multiple target branches simultaneously using Cmd/Ctrl+Click or Shift+Click to merge into multiple targets sequentially with conflict abort and safe return to the original branch.
  • Searchable Branch Picker: Quickly filter and pick target branches, with the list returning to the top after opening, filtering, switching repositories, or updating favorites.
  • Real-Time Branch Counter: Live badge displaying branch totals, favorite stars, and dynamic match counts as you filter.
  • Favorites Pinned to Top: Star frequently merged branches with vibrant golden stars; pinned at the top of the list.
  • Pre-Merge Divergence Intelligence: Real-time status calculating commits to merge (ahead), branch divergence (behind), fast-forward possibility, and an unambiguous Up to date badge.
  • On-Demand Remote Sync: Merge and push first; optionally synchronize the target from remote and retry once only when push is rejected because the remote branch has newer commits (enabled by default with instant memory).
  • Target Branch Commit Preview: Instant preview of the latest commit (hash, author, date, subject) on any selected target branch.
  • Custom Merge Commit Message: Specify an optional custom commit message when --no-ff is enabled; falls back to Git standard message if left blank.
  • Dialog Resizing Memory & Spacious Layout: Automatically remembers customized window dimensions across invocations and IDE sessions, with an expanded default width.
  • Prompt Post-Merge IDE Status Refresh: Immediately updates Git repository references, working tree files, and VCS change statuses upon completion so the status bar and toolbar widgets reflect changes without delay.
  • Smart Memory: Remembers the last merged target branch for each repository.
  • Persistent Options: Remembers your --no-ff, push, and on-demand remote sync preferences across invocations.
  • Safe Checkout-Back: Automatically switches back to your original branch after merge, even if an error or conflict occurs.
  • VCS Operations Popup Integration: Directly accessible from the IDE's built-in VCS Operations Popup (Alt+` / Ctrl+V).
  • Quick Shortcuts & Menu Icon: Accessible via Git → Merge Into... with official Git merge icon or shortcut (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M / Cmd+Opt+Shift+M).

  • On-Demand Target Sync: Skip pre-merge pulls; synchronize and retry once only after a push is rejected due to remote updates, with automatic abort on synchronization conflicts.
  • Local-Only IDE Refresh: Refresh repository, files, and VCS status after returning to the original branch without fetching or pulling branches.

  • Remote Sync Enabled by Default & Instant Persistence: Update target branch from remote before merging is now enabled by default and immediately remembers your toggled preferences.

0.1.6

  • Pre-Merge Divergence Intelligence: Real-time check displaying incoming commits to merge (ahead), divergence metrics (behind), and an unambiguous Up to date status indicator.
  • Pre-Merge Remote Target Synchronization: Added option to automatically fast-forward the target branch from its remote tracking branch before merging.

0.1.5

  • Custom Merge Commit Message: Added an optional commit message input field activated when --no-ff is checked, supporting custom formats or falling back to Git defaults.
  • Real-Time Branch Counter & Fast Filter: Displays real-time branch and star counts in the search bar, updating dynamically as you filter.

0.1.4

  • Official Plugin Branding: Added official pluginIcon.svg and pluginIcon_dark.svg for the IDE Plugin Manager and JetBrains Marketplace.

0.1.3

  • Target Branch Commit Preview: Displays real-time preview of the latest commit on the selected branch before merging.

idea-plugin.name: Graft
idea-plugin.description:
Graft lets an MCP client such as Claude Code attach a git worktree to the current JetBrains IDE window and detach it again, the two things the IDE only offers through the mouse: File | Open | Attach and Remove from Project View.

What it adds

  • attach_worktree attaches a directory as an additional module of the open project. A directory without .idea gets one, named after the directory. It refuses up front, with an explanation, when a copied .idea would make the IDE fail with "Module name already exists", or when the directory is outside a trusted location.
  • detach_worktree removes an attached module and the dependency the primary module holds on it, and can delete the worktree's own .idea folder so the next worktree with that name does not collide.
  • list_attached_worktrees lists the modules in the window with their paths, linked-worktree status, checked-out branch, and owning repository.

How it works

Graft has no server, port, or configuration of its own. It contributes its tools through the bundled MCP Server plugin's own extension point, com.intellij.mcpServer.mcpToolset, so they appear in the same tool list as the IDE's built-in tools, follow the same allow list under Settings | Tools | MCP Server | Exposed Tools, and work from any client already connected to the IDE. Under the tools it calls the platform code behind the menu actions: the ProjectAttachProcessor the Open dialog uses for attach, and the module model's modifiable API for detach. Nothing is written to disk that the equivalent menu action would not write.

The workflow it is built for

The main checkout stays open in one window. An agent creates a worktree per ticket, attaches it, works in it, and detaches it when the branch merges:

Start issue 42: create a worktree off origin/main at ~/src/.worktrees/myapp/issue-42-login-form,
attach it to the myapp window, and run yarn install in it.
Issue 42 merged. Detach its worktree and delete the .idea it left, remove the worktree, and delete the branch.

Detach before git worktree remove: the IDE drops the module and VCS mapping cleanly, and the directory is empty afterwards. Every tool accepts the MCP Server's projectPath argument to pick the window when several projects are open.

Requirements

A JetBrains IDE from 2026.2 (build 262) or newer with the bundled MCP Server plugin enabled, and an MCP client connected to it. Restart the client after installing so it picks up the new tools.

Source code · Issue tracker · Changelog

idea-plugin.name: Changelog Pilot
idea-plugin.description:
Turn a bounded local Git commit range into a reviewable Markdown changelog.

Changelog Pilot reads local Git history, groups common Conventional Commit types and scopes, highlights breaking changes, preserves non-conventional commits under Other, and produces an escaped Markdown preview that can be copied for review.

Processing is local and read-only. Changelog Pilot does not publish releases, create tags, change commits, modify repository files, use AI, require an account, collect telemetry, or make network requests.

  • Grouping by common Conventional Commit type and scope.
  • Dedicated breaking-change section.
  • Reviewable Markdown preview and copy action.
  • 500-commit safety cap and 15-second process limit.

idea-plugin.name: Source Link for Azure DevOps
idea-plugin.description:
Open files, folders and repositories in Azure DevOps (Azure Repos) directly from the IDE, or copy the link to the clipboard.

Features

  • Open in Azure DevOps: opens the file, folder or repository in your default browser.
  • Copy Azure DevOps Link: copies the same URL to the clipboard.
  • Branch-aware: uses the upstream branch when available, the local branch otherwise, or the commit in detached HEAD.
  • Highlights the selected lines (or the caret line) when invoked from the editor.
  • Works with HTTPS and SSH remotes: dev.azure.com, visualstudio.com and Azure DevOps Server.
  • Credentials embedded in remote URLs (user name, PAT) are never included in the link.

Getting Started

  1. Open a project whose git remote points to Azure DevOps.
  2. Right-click a file, folder or editor tab and choose Azure DevOps > Open in Azure DevOps or Copy Azure DevOps Link. The same actions are available in the Tools menu.
  3. Optional: adjust the preferred remote and other options in Settings > Tools > Source Link for Azure DevOps.

idea-plugin.name: Diff Notes
idea-plugin.description:
Capture private review notes directly from code editors and native text diff views.

Diff Notes helps you collect line-specific feedback while reviewing local changes, without posting unfinished comments to GitHub, GitLab, or another service.

Review without breaking focus

  • Add a private note from the editor or diff context menu.
  • Keep up to 500 notes per project, with up to 2,000 characters per note.
  • Reopen the reviewed location from the Diff Notes tool window.
  • Copy a Markdown report grouped by file when the review is ready.
  • Use contextual line anchors that follow common insertions above reviewed code.

Local by design

Notes and line context stay in the IDE's local project workspace state. Diff Notes does not edit source files, create repository files, post comments, collect telemetry, require an account, or use the network.

If the target code changes and an exact contextual match is no longer available, Diff Notes falls back to the original stored line instead of making a weak guess. Always verify feedback before sharing it.
