  • ⚠️ Time-consuming
  • ⚠️ Difficult to standardize
  • ⚠️ Hard to scale in growing codebases

3TG accelerates your workflow by:

  • ✅ Generating structured TypeScript test foundations
  • ✅ Supporting React functional components (.tsx)
  • ✅ Reducing manual Jest / Vitest boilerplate
  • ✅ Enforcing consistent test architecture
  • ✅ Improving onboarding for new developers
  • ✅ Supporting scalable fullstack testing workflows

If you use TypeScript, React, Jest, or Vitest, 3TG upgrades your test generation process instantly.

🔥 What Makes 3TG Different?

Most IntelliJ test generators create empty shells.

3TG generates behavior-focused test foundations.

  • Analyzes exported TypeScript functions
  • Supports React functional components
  • Generates structured test blocks aligned with behavior
  • Creates manual mock files
  • Supports functional requirements files
  • Merges configuration intelligently
  • Integrates natively into IntelliJ with its own Explorer panel
  • Operates via Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) intelligence

This is not scaffolding. This is structured test acceleration.

Without 3TG With 3TG
Writing repetitive Jest boilerplate Structured, behavior-aligned test foundations
Inconsistent test structures Consistent architecture across projects
Weak template-based generation Configurable test rules
Slow developer onboarding Faster onboarding
No standardization across teams Scalable fullstack test automation

🧠 How It Works

  1. Install the extension
  2. Create a free account at 3tg.dev
  3. Enable the extension using your client ID
  4. Open a `.ts` or `.tsx` file

That’s it.

You can generate tests from:

Go from file → structured test foundation in seconds.

3TG generates structured unit test foundations aligned with function behavior — so you focus on business logic, not boilerplate.

🧑‍💻 Developer Experience

Settings

🔑 Activation (Free Plan Available)

3TG operates as Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS).

  2. Get your client ID
  3. Open the 3TG Support panel

No heavy onboarding. No complex setup.

❓ FAQ

Does 3TG replace Jest or Vitest?

No. 3TG generates structured test foundations that integrate with your existing Jest or Vitest setup.

idea-plugin.name: Samurai Test Runner

GoLand integration for the Samurai scoped testing framework.

Samurai is a Go testing framework with path isolation: you define a test tree using a single s.Test() method, the framework discovers all leaf paths, then runs each one independently with fresh local variables. Parallel by default, zero dependencies, bring your own assertions.

  • Click test results in the tree to navigate back to source
  • Pass/fail status indicators in the gutter after test runs

Requires github.com/zerosixty/samurai in your Go module.

idea-plugin.name: SpecBinder (Beta)
idea-plugin.description:
Gherkin (.feature and .specb file) language support for IntelliJ-based IDEs.

Features

  • Run configurations — gutter run icons on Feature/Rule/Scenario keywords to run tests directly
  • Navigation: Gherkin → Java — Ctrl/Cmd+Click from Gherkin elements and individual steps to their corresponding generated test classes, methods, and call sites
  • Navigation: Java → Gherkin — Ctrl/Cmd+Click from generated test methods and step call sites back to the originating elements in the feature file
  • Auto-recompile — automatically recompiles related SpecBinder marker classes when feature files are saved
  • Code completion — auto-complete Gherkin keywords and step text
  • Find Usages — find Gherkin step usages from Java step methods
  • Rename refactoring — use the IDE's standard Rename to update step patterns across Java code and feature files in one step
  • Syntax highlighting — full Gherkin syntax support aligned with SpecBinder conventions, including inline step parameter highlighting without requiring any backing Java code
  • Structure view — navigate Feature/Rule/Scenario/Step outline
  • Code folding — collapse Feature, Rule, Scenario, Background, and Examples blocks
  • Formatting — Reformat Code with standard 2-space Gherkin indentation and automatic table column alignment
  • Color settings — customize colors for individual Gherkin elements via Settings > Editor > Color Scheme > SpecBinder
  • Spell checking — detects misspelled words in step text, titles, descriptions, comments, and doc strings
  • Zero dependencies — no third-party plugin dependencies for better compatibility across IDE versions
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2026.19.0 - 2026-10-05

Added

  • The Execution Report now shows a Background step's data table or doc string under each scenario's copy of the step, the same way a scenario's own steps show theirs; each copied row links back to the matching row of the Background.
  • A Feature or Background title, a description line, a tag line or a Background step that you have just edited stops being linked in the Test Code pane until the class is generated again — the Java beside it was written from the old words — while the lines around it stay linked.
  • With the caret in the Test Code pane on the comment the generated class writes above a step's call, the step it repeats is framed in the spec — and each repeated table row frames its row; the comment above an Examples block's values frames that Examples line, and each tag inside a block of several tags frames the spec line that tag was written on. A caret on the step or tag line itself still frames only its call or annotation.
  • In the Project view, a spec that has not run yet — or has changed since its run — now shows its own icon: a small play triangle in the green of the IDE's run button, in place of the right chevron, and folders containing such a spec show a green ▹. The grey icon now means only that a scenario was aborted, so a spec waiting to be run is no longer mistaken for one that stopped short.
  • A Refresh SpecBinder Status action in the Project view's context menu brings spec file icons and folder chevrons up to date on demand. Chosen on a spec file it reads that spec's latest results again; chosen on a folder it does the same for every spec file beneath it. It is offered while either the spec file icons or the folder chevrons are turned on.
  • With the caret in the Test Code pane, a step method used in several places now frames the use nearest the spec editor's caret, or the one after it when two are as near. A step's call or step method always frames the step itself, never a row of its table or a line of its doc string.
  • The Test Code pane now links a Scenario Outline's Examples to the parameterised test they became: each Examples keyword is framed against its own source annotation, and each row of the table against the same row in that annotation's list of values.
  • The Test Code pane now links a step's data table and doc string line by line: each table row is framed against the line that builds it in the generated class, and each line of a doc string against the same line of the text block it became.
  • The Test Code pane now links a Background to the set-up method it was generated as, and a tag line to the tag annotation it became on the generated class or method.
  • The Test Code pane now links each Rule to the nested class it was generated as: with the caret on a Rule's title, the title is framed against that class's declaration.
  • The Test Code pane now links each line of a Feature's, a Rule's, a Scenario's or a Background's description to the same line of it in the generated class, in either direction — whether the description was written as Javadoc, the default, or as a @Description annotation. A Scenario Outline's description links the same way, and each line of an Examples block's description links to the same line of the comment above that block's values.
  • A spec file's icon in the Project view, and the chevron on its folder, now show the results of the last test run made in the IDE when no SpecBinder execution report is on disk, as the spec's gutter already did. The icon updates once the run finishes, and a scenario that has not run since it was added or changed keeps the file at no result.
  • The test methods of a class SpecBinder generates as abstract now show the result of the last run in the gutter, as any other JUnit test does. The run goes through the class that extends it, so the icons were left as plain run buttons before; a Rule's group shows the worst result beneath it, and where several classes extend the same generated class, a failure in any of them shows.
  • The colour of the lines linked across the split view can now be set separately for light and dark IDE themes. The Split view settings page has a picker for each, and the highlight follows whichever theme the IDE is using, so it can stay readable against a dark background without washing out on a light one.
  • The Execution Report now carries a tab per run, each named after the test class that made it and marked with how that run came out. A spec run by more than one class keeps a set of results per class, so the tabs are how you move between them; the pane opens on the most recent run and comes back to whichever one you left it on
  • Failed steps are now marked in the gutter, and their inline error panel opened, for runs made without the SpecBinder execution reporter too. With no report on disk the plugin reads what the IDE itself recorded for the last run: which step failed, its message, the whole stack trace while the IDE still holds that run's output, and the Expected / Actual values when the failure carried them — with the same Approve and Show diff buttons a reported failure offers.
  • The status icons the gutter and the spec file's toolbar wear can now be picked between two sets on the Execution results settings page: JUnit-style circles, modelled on the badges the IDE shows beside JUnit tests and used unless another set is picked, or SpecBinder chevrons, which match the spec file's own icon in the Project view. Each set is shown with its own icons beside its name, so the choice is made against the icons themselves, with a line under each saying when it reads better.
  • A file shown in the Test Code pane now carries the IDE's own notices above it — the warning that a generated source will be overwritten among them — set off from the code the way they are in the file's own editor tab.
  • The Split view settings page now shows the buttons a spec file's editor puts in its top-right corner: what each of the three view buttons puts on screen, and the button each tab adds to that row once it is turned on.
  • Inline doc-string previews can now be turned off. A switch on the Editor settings page decides whether an HTML, SVG or image doc string can be shown as a picture below its text; with it off no preview icon is offered and those doc strings read as plain text.
  • Each tab on the Test Code pane now carries the IDE's own icon for its file, so a class, an interface and an abstract class are told apart at a glance.
  • The Test Code pane no longer scrolls in step with the spec, and its synchronize-scrolling toggle has gone with it — following the caret already brings the right method up. The Execution Report keeps its own synchronised scrolling.
  • The Test Code pane no longer marks the method a step resolved to with a highlighted line; the frames on both sides already say which pair belongs together. The Step Implementation tool window keeps its mark.
  • The Test Code pane's own controls now keep their place however narrow the pane is, and a file tab that no longer fits is reached from the chevron at the end of the row.
  • An Example you have just edited stops being linked to its generated method, while the Examples around it stay linked — the method came from wording that has since changed, so the link would point at the wrong place. It goes as you type and comes back once the spec matches the generated class again.
  • The Test Code pane now frames the spec line you are on against the Java it pairs with, and the two scroll together. A generated class pairs at every level the spec has, while a hand-written test or a shared base pairs steps with the methods that implement them. Each view carries its own toggles, so turning the frames off while reading results leaves them on while reading code.
  • The Test Code pane can follow the caret. A toggle on its banner, off until turned on, opens whichever class implements the step you are reading and scrolls to that method, so moving down a spec shows each step's code as you reach it.
  • Each tab a spec file can show beside it now has a switch of its own on the Split view settings page — one for the Execution Report, one for Test Code. Turning a tab off takes its button away rather than leaving a view that could only ever be empty, and with every tab off spec files open in the platform's standard text editor. Test Code is on out of the box; the Execution Report stays off until turned on, and a choice made in an earlier build is carried over.
  • The pane beside a spec file can now hold a second document, Test Code: the Java the spec compiles to and is wired by, opened with a button of its own. It offers one tab per class behind the spec, each the IDE's own editor, so highlighting, completion and refactoring work there exactly as they would in the file's own tab. A spec with nothing generated for it yet says so rather than showing an empty pane.
  • The Execution Report now has a button of its own in the top-right of the spec file's tab, saying what the right-hand pane is showing while the view-mode buttons go on deciding whether it is open. Clicking it while the spec file is on its own opens the pane beside it, and each file remembers the document it was last left showing.
  • Failed steps are now marked down the Execution Report's scrollbar, one mark each, so a long report shows how many failures it holds and where they are without being scrolled through. Hovering a mark names the step.
  • SpecBinder's settings can now be found from the Settings search box. Typing "SpecBinder", or the name of an option on one of its pages, brings up the matching page, along with the plugin's inspections and colour entries.
  • The wording a user story is written with is now coloured apart from the rest of a Feature's title and description — who it is for, what they want and why — each with its own colour under Settings > Editor > Color Scheme > Gherkin, so a story's role, capability and benefit can be told apart at a glance or left looking alike. Only a Feature's own title and description are read this way.
  • A step suggestion now says when the step wants a doc string or a data table, and picking it lays the block out for you: empty doc-string fences, or a table headed with the step's own column names, indented below the step with the caret waiting in place.
  • Step suggestions now spell the pronoun as "I" rather than "i", the way a spec file spells it. Only the pronoun standing alone is changed.
  • The Run icon beside an Examples row now runs just that row, so re-checking one row leaves the other rows' results alone. Under Gradle a row still runs the whole outline, whose test filter cannot name a single row.
  • A vertical rule now marks the boundary between a spec file and the pane beside it, matching the line the IDE draws between any two editors it puts side by side.

Changed

  • The Reload link on the Execution Report's banner now sits straight after the run's time instead of at the far right of the banner, so it reads together with the time it offers to replace.
  • In the split view, a divider now separates the tabs at the top right of the Execution Report and the Test Code pane from the buttons beside them. It is drawn like the divider between the IDE's own view buttons, so the run or class names no longer read as more buttons.
  • Text matched by a stripPatterns entry is now plum in the light scheme and pink plum in Darcula, while the two markers of a stripBetweenPatterns range keep vermilion and salmon. The two strip text in different ways, so they now look different out of the box rather than only once you choose colours for them yourself.
  • The Execution Report no longer links a scenario whose steps have changed since the run — reworded, given a different table, or run after a Background step that has changed — since its rows were recorded from steps the spec no longer has. A Scenario Outline whose template has changed links to nothing either, and an Examples row whose values have changed stops linking to the example run with its old values, while the other rows stay linked. Extra spacing between words does not count as a change. A scenario added since the run, or one the spec has since dropped, links to nothing either, while the scenarios around it stay linked.
  • The Execution Report now links line by line. A Feature, Rule or Scenario title is framed against its heading in the report alone, each description line against the same line of the description the report shows, and a step with a data table or doc string against its own step row, with each table row and doc-string line framed against the same row or line beneath it — in either direction. A Scenario Outline's title, description and template steps link the same way, each to its own line of the template the report rebuilds. A blank line, a comment or a tag, which the report leaves out, is no longer framed against the nearest line above it, and the lines after it still find their own rows.
  • The scenario counts on a spec file's toolbar now follow an edit as soon as you pause typing, without waiting for the file to be saved, so they always agree with the gutter icons beside them. A scenario you change — by typing, or by approving a failed step's actual value — moves to not executed in both at once. The Project view still updates its icons when the file is saved.
  • In the Test Code pane, a step is now framed against the line declaring the method that implements it, rather than the whole method, when a hand-written test class is shown.
  • In the Test Code pane, a Scenario's title is now framed against the line declaring its generated test method rather than the Scenario and the whole method being framed as one block, matching how a Feature and a Rule are linked; the steps inside a Scenario keep their own links to their calls.
  • On the Split view settings page, the light- and dark-theme pickers for the linked-ranges colour now sit side by side on one line, under a bold "Linked-ranges colour" heading.
  • The legend for the agent status badges on the Agent integration settings page now shows each badge on a spec file's icon, with the diamond between the chevrons as it appears in the Project view, rather than the diamond on its own.
  • The Run and Debug entries offered from a spec file's gutter now name the Feature, Rule or Scenario by its title in the spec, rather than by the generated test class or method (scenario_2, CartFeatureTest$Rule_1). A row of an Examples table is named after its outline with the row's number. Where two parts of one spec share a title, the name also carries the line it starts on, so each keeps a run configuration of its own. Run configurations saved before this change are renamed the first time the gutter reuses them, unless they were given a name by hand.
  • The explanations on the SpecBinder settings pages have been reworded to name what they refer to rather than address the reader or point back with "it" and "its". On the Split view page, each tab's option now opens with a line saying what that tab shows, the preview of its toolbar button comes before the note about where that button appears, and the Execution Report's extra-data options open with a short paragraph explaining the inline panels they control.
  • The time a run finished has moved off the toolbar into a banner over the Execution Report itself. A spec run by more than one test class has a time apiece, so the banner belongs to the run on screen and changes with the tab you pick. The Reload link that offers a newer run sits there too, and Alt+clicking the banner still opens the run's JSON report file.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: A spec's execution results are now found by following the spec to the test classes that run it, matching how SpecBinder names each report after the class rather than the spec file. A spec run by more than one test class keeps a set of results for each instead of the last run replacing the others, and the gutter, Project view and toolbar follow the most recent run. Results written by an older SpecBinder are no longer found and are replaced on the next run
  • When the Execution Report pane has no rows to show because something went wrong, what went wrong is now shown under the message in the pane itself rather than offered only on hover. A report that could not be read names the parser's reason and the file to fix; a pane that could not be built names its reason. Long text wraps to the width of the pane instead of running off its edge.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: Execution results are now read from the execution report whenever one exists for a spec file, and from the IDE's own last-test-run state when none does — there is nothing to turn on, and the option that decided it is gone. A spec file with no report yet shows the IDE's own run and status icons rather than reading as not executed.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: A step recorded as failed now always carries its error icon, and clicking it always opens the inline error panel; the option that turned both off is gone. The panel's own options — the Expected / Actual previews and the project-code stack-trace frames — now stand on their own instead of being greyed out until that option was on.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: One Show Expected / Actual previews option now covers the HTML, image and SVG previews in the inline error panel, replacing the three per-kind options. If you had turned all three off, the previews stay off; otherwise they are on, as before.
  • The project-code stack-trace frames' font style and colour now sit together on one row under a single heading on the Execution results settings page, since they shape the same lines.
  • The Failed-step error panel section of the Execution results settings page now shows the failed-step icons within its explanation, level with the words around them, rather than on a line of their own, and lists its options as project-code frames, then Expected / Actual previews.
  • The colour setting for the bar down the side of the published-entries panels is now called "Published test reporter entries bar colour". The colour it sets is unchanged.
  • The status counts above a spec file now count each row of a Scenario Outline's Examples table as a scenario of its own, since the rows are what actually run and what the gutter marks one by one. A partly-run outline no longer reads as fully passed, and clicking a count steps onto the individual row rather than the heading above it.
  • Execution results now tell apart how a scenario went wrong, the way the IDE's own test results do. A scenario whose assertion did not hold is marked failed in amber, one stopped by any other exception is marked error in red, and one that aborted is marked aborted in grey. A scenario with no current result — never run, skipped, or changed since its run — shows the IDE's run icon. Both icon sets follow the same meanings, a Rule or Feature shows the worst result beneath it (error, then failed, then aborted), and hovering the icon names the step it stopped at, with the exception for an error.
  • The status counts above a spec file now have one count per result — passed, error, failed, aborted and not executed — in that order, each stepping through only its own scenarios. The run tabs over the Execution Report are marked with the worst result of their run.
  • The Execution Report pane now draws its status icons in the icon set picked on the Execution results settings page, as the gutter and the toolbar do.
  • Spec file icons and folder chevrons in the Project view now show an error in red apart from a failed assertion in amber. A spec with nothing to report — not yet run, changed since the run, aborted, or with no generated test class — shows a single grey marker.
  • The icon beside a failed step now says how the step went wrong, matching the icon of the scenario it belongs to: amber with a cross for an assertion that did not hold, red with an exclamation mark for any other exception, and the grey aborted mark for a step that aborted. The bar down the side of its inline error panel, and its mark on the scrollbar, take the same colour. Results the IDE recorded without the SpecBinder execution reporter tell an assertion failure from an error the same way, and a step that aborted its scenario now carries the aborted mark too while the IDE still holds that run's output.
  • Everything that acts on the pane beside a spec file has moved onto the toolbar over that pane, and the notice strips those controls used to sit on are gone. Each half of the row is as wide as the pane under it, so dragging the divider narrower crowds only that side — what no longer fits is reached from a chevron at the end of that half. The panes gained the height the strips were using.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The toolbar above a spec file can no longer be turned off, and the option that turned it off has gone from the Editor settings page: everything the row carries, including the tabs beside the spec, is reached from it and nowhere else. A recognized spec file therefore always opens in SpecBinder's editor; with every tab turned off it opens on its own.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The frames that pair a spec line with the line it matches are now one setting for the pane rather than one per tab, so the toggle reads the same whichever tab is on screen. If you had the frames off for one tab and on for the other, they are on for both now.
  • A Test Code file tab whose class comes from a compiled dependency now carries a mark on its icon, so a tab that will open decompiled code says so before it is clicked.
  • Where there is no report time to show, the toolbar now says so in a short label — "No execution report", "Report unreadable", "Cannot display" — with the full explanation and the cause on hover.
  • The Project view settings page now leads with File structure, and the Execution status options follow below the divider. Each option's explanation now reads as regular text, and the plain spec file icon is shown beside the note on what the files look like with status icons turned off. The options, and their defaults, are unchanged.
  • The heavier-chevrons option no longer carries a legend row or a hint of its own. Selecting it redraws the chevrons already previewed above it, so the page shows what the option does as it is used rather than describing it twice.
  • The options for the published JUnit TestReporter entries — the entries themselves, their Playwright traces and the colour of their bar — have moved to the Split view page, nested under the switch for the Execution Report, and are greyed out while it is off. What each option does, and its default, are unchanged.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: Folding doc strings when a spec file opens is now one option rather than seven per content type. It starts off, so a spec file opens with every doc string expanded until it is turned on.
  • The Execution Report switch on the Split view settings page now says where the report comes from: it is written during a run by the SpecBinder Execution Reporter, a JUnit 5 extension shipped separately that has to be added as a test dependency. Turning the switch on used to be the only instruction on the page, leaving a tab that stays empty until a run records something.
  • The two dropdowns on the General settings page explain themselves more briefly, keeping the per-option lines and dropping the paragraph above them. The spell-checking hint now also says where spelling is not checked: tags, outline parameter names, and the cells of data tables and Examples tables.
  • The two options that colour the project tree by the last run's result have moved from Execution results to the Project view page, under a new Execution status section. What they do, and their defaults, are unchanged.
  • The settings for what a spec file can show beside it now have a page of their own, Split view, sitting after Editor: a switch for each tab, and the colour of the ranges linked across the divider. Execution results now covers only what a report drives.
  • The option that shows a spec file's Feature, Rule, Scenario, Background and Example elements in the Project view tree now has a page of its own, Project view, rather than sitting among the options about how spec files are treated on disk. The option, its default and what it does are unchanged.
  • The first page under Settings > Tools > SpecBinder is now called General rather than File handling. Its place in the tree and everything on it are unchanged.
  • The button that launches an AI agent for a spec file has moved to the far right of the spec file's toolbar, behind a divider, so it sits apart from the controls that act on the spec file itself. The divider is only drawn while the button is there.
  • The Execution Report's controls have all moved onto its notice strip, and the report's own toolbar is gone. Synchronised scrolling and linked-range highlighting appear only while the report is beside the spec file, since neither means anything when the report is on its own.
  • The colour of the linked ranges is now set in Settings > Tools > SpecBinder > Execution results instead of from a dropdown on the toolbar button, which is a plain on/off toggle now. Changing the colour still recolours every open spec file straight away.
  • The button that shows published reporter entries has moved from the Execution Report's toolbar onto its notice strip, beside the line-numbers toggle, since both act on what the report shows rather than on the run it describes. Nothing about the entries themselves changes.
  • The spec file keeps its line numbers on the left when the Execution Report is beside it. They used to move across to face the report, which left the traffic-light tick above the scrollbar flickering between the two top corners.
  • The toolbar is a single row across the top of the tab again, carrying only what acts on the spec file, and it is hidden while the Execution Report is showing on its own. Everything that acts on the report lives on that view's own notice strip instead.
  • When an execution report was last updated is shown on a notice strip at the top of the Execution Report view, beside the results it describes. Once a newer report is written, a Reload link appears next to the time.
  • Misspelled words in a spec file now have a colour of their own, under "Other > typo" in Settings > Editor > Color Scheme > Gherkin. They are a red dotted underline out of the box, in place of the green wave every language shares — which all but disappeared under a Feature, Rule or Scenario title coloured green itself — and can be recoloured without touching how typos look in any other language. The words that are checked, the suggestions offered on one, and adding a word to the dictionary are all unchanged.
  • The three revision-markup entries under Settings > Editor > Color Scheme > Gherkin now sit with the typo entry under an "Other" heading, and are named after the options they come from. The colours themselves are unchanged, and a colour already set against one of them is kept.
  • The preview on the Gherkin colour settings page now includes revision markup, so selecting a strip-pattern entry has something to scroll to and blink.
  • A parameter in a step suggestion is now written in quotes, as "{item}" rather than {item}. The quotes are what a spec file reads a parameter by, so a suggestion that left them out wrote a step its step method no longer answered to.
  • Each step suggestion now reads as the step text, with the class or interface holding the step method shown to the right of it. The method name and the icon beside the text are gone, so the suggestion is exactly what will be written into the spec file.
  • The colour chooser opened from a panel's "Panel bar colour" swatch now previews the colour on the open panels as you pick it, so it can be judged against the panels themselves. Cancelling puts back the colour that was in use before.
  • The inline error panel's display options now live in Settings > Tools > SpecBinder > Execution results, nested under the switch that offers the panel. Applying a change redraws any error panel that is already open.
  • The colour of the bar down the left edge of image, HTML and SVG doc-string previews is now set in Settings > Tools > SpecBinder > Editor, under "Doc-string previews". Applying a new colour redraws any preview that is already open.
  • ⚠️ BREAKING: Published reporter entries and Playwright trace panels now open only in the Execution Report view, no longer under the steps of the spec file you are editing. The button that shows them is offered only while that view is on screen.
  • The colour of the bar down the left edge of published-entries and Playwright trace panels is now set in Settings > Tools > SpecBinder > Execution results, instead of from the toolbar button's dropdown, which is gone. Applying a new colour redraws the panels that are already open.
  • When an execution report was last updated is now shown at the top of the Execution Report view itself rather than at the right end of the spec file's toolbar. The date is labelled, so it no longer has to be read as a bare time out of context, and the Auto-reload checkbox and Reload link sit beside it.
  • The status lozenges and gutter icons beside a spec file now move to the newest execution report on their own as soon as a run writes one. Auto-reload governs only what the Execution Report view renders, so with it off the view stays on the run you were reading and says "Showing an earlier run" until Reload is clicked.
  • An Execution Report with no report in it is now empty all the way across. It kept an editor's gutter so the pane had a visible edge; the rule down the divider gives it one, so the gutter is gone.
  • An Execution Report with nothing to show now says why across the middle of the pane, the way the Test Code view says it has no test code, instead of in small type on the toolbar. It distinguishes a spec that was never run from a report that could not be read and from one that could not be displayed, with the cause on hover. The toolbar now carries only the time a report was last updated.

Fixed

  • The Execution Report pane now fills each Scenario Outline Example's steps with that row's values instead of showing the <placeholder> names, and colours each filled-in value like a step parameter.
  • With the Test Code pane following the caret, putting the caret on a description line now frames that line and its line of the Javadoc, and the pane scrolls to that Javadoc line. Before, the frames jumped to the Feature title and the class declaration, because the pane scrolling itself was read as if you had clicked into it.
  • A test run started while the IDE was still indexing — common right after a build — is no longer treated as one the plugin did not see: editing a scenario afterwards now shows it as not executed instead of keeping its old result. Spec file icons and folder chevrons in the Project view also catch up as soon as indexing finishes, rather than staying at a status worked out while it was still running.
  • The Run icon beside an Examples row now runs just that row even after the whole spec has been run, and its menu offers that row's own run. Before, it reused the spec's run configuration and ran every scenario, and the menu offered to run the whole spec. A row of an outline generated as an abstract class now runs through the class that extends it.
  • Running an Examples row of a Scenario Outline from the Run tool window now runs just that row, and running the outline's own node runs all its rows. Before, both failed to start, with JUnit reporting that the selected test could not be resolved.
  • Folder chevrons in the Project view now update after a save, a finished run or a build when they are turned on without the spec file icons. Before, they kept their first status until the IDE was restarted.
  • Opening an Examples row of a Scenario Outline from the Run tool window now goes to that row's line in its Examples table. Before, every row opened the Scenario Outline line.
  • With no execution report on disk, each Examples row of a Scenario Outline now shows its own result in the gutter, and the outline shows the worst of its rows. Before, every row showed only a run icon and the outline showed whichever row happened to run last, so a failing row could leave the outline marked passed. The toolbar counts each row too, and a row added or changed since the run shows as not executed.
  • A spec file's icon in the Project view now changes as soon as its status is refreshed — after a save, a finished run, a build or Refresh SpecBinder Status. Before, the folder chevron above it could already show the new result while the file kept its old icon, and an open editor tab could keep its old icon too.
  • With no execution report on disk, a scenario that has passed no longer shows the run icon as if it had been changed since its run when another module in the project generates a test class of the same name from different content. Its Rule and Feature no longer show the run icon on its account either.
  • With no execution report on disk, a Feature or Rule now shows as not executed in the gutter when one of its scenarios has not been run since it was added or renamed, instead of showing the passed result of the earlier run. A failure or error elsewhere in it still shows first.
  • Running a scenario from its gutter icon now runs that scenario when another scenario in the spec has the same title. The IDE used to pick up the run configuration of the first such scenario and offer to run it instead.
  • Double-clicking a failed or aborted scenario in the Run tool window now opens its line in the spec file, as it already did for a passed one, rather than the line in the generated Java test code where it stopped. Rerun Failed Tests keeps working for those scenarios.
  • Double-clicking the top node of a run of one test class in the Run tool window now opens the Feature line of its spec file, like every node beneath it, rather than the Java test class.
  • With no execution report on disk, a scenario edited since it was last run from the IDE now shows as not executed in the gutter and the count lozenges, instead of keeping the result recorded for its old wording; putting the wording back restores that result. The failed-step icon of such a scenario goes too, along with its inline error panel if it was open, and the icon comes back once the wording is put back. Results from runs made before this version, outside the IDE, or of test classes generated without scenario hashes keep showing as before.
  • A failed run made without the SpecBinder execution reporter now marks the failed step, and opens its inline error panel, for specs generated as an abstract class too, not only for those generated as a concrete one. The step can be found for as long as the IDE keeps that run's output. A failed comparison of Expected and Actual values now also shows its whole stack trace in that panel, not just its top line.
  • The button that highlights matching lines no longer shows while the pane beside the spec has nothing to link to — an Execution Report with no report loaded, or Test Code for a spec with nothing generated yet. The follow-caret toggle likewise stays hidden until Test Code has a class to show. Both appear once there is something in the pane.
  • Moving the caret or switching focus in a spec file shown beside its Execution Report or Test Code no longer holds up the editor while the plugin searches the project for what the line pairs with. The search now runs in the background, so the linked-range frame can appear a moment later, and the IDE no longer fills its error log with slow-operation reports that eventually stopped it reporting errors at all.
  • A colour picker on the settings pages no longer goes blank when the option it belongs to is turned off. It keeps showing the chosen colour, faded and with its code greyed out, so you can still see which colour is set while it cannot be changed.
  • The visual diff viewer's Clear highlight link now shows the not-allowed pointer while it is unavailable, as the dimmed wording already implied. The shape was asked for but never reached the screen, because the link stopped responding to the pointer at the same time.
  • The visual diff viewer's Clear highlight link now tells a screen reader it is available once it becomes clickable. It went on reporting itself as unavailable after the first difference was highlighted, so it was announced as dimmed while it could be used.
  • Collapsing a Scenario or a Rule now hides the error icons of the failed steps it hides. Until now the icon of a failure on the block's very last line stayed behind, drawn against the collapsed heading row, so whether a folded block kept showing an error came down to which of its steps had failed
  • A spec implemented by more than one test class can now be run. Running it asks which of them to run and launches that one, instead of reporting "No tests were found" — the run was targeting the generated class the tests extend, which cannot be run on its own. Dismissing the question runs nothing.
  • Running a spec now runs it, in projects where two modules hold spec files of the same name. The Run icon found the right generated class but then looked up the runnable test class by name across the whole project, landing in whichever module came first — so the run either tested a different module or reported "No tests were found". The status icons and counts read from the same lookup, so they could show a sibling module's results too.
  • The Test Code pane no longer throws when the class it is showing is rebuilt underneath it. Running a build while a spec file is open replaces the generated source, and the pane went on holding the file the build had already discarded — reporting an invalid-file error on the next caret move. It now waits for the replacement instead
  • The Execution Report pane no longer fails to display with an "Integer.intValue()" error for a spec holding a Scenario Outline. It happened when an example row recorded in the report could not be matched to a row of the Examples table in the editor and the run had recorded no line numbers — the pane gave up entirely instead of simply leaving that row unlinked
  • The Execution Report pane no longer shows a blank first row while there is no report to show. Beneath the banner saying there is no report, the pane is now simply empty, rather than drawing a line and a cursor that read as a run with an empty result.
  • The toggles on the Execution Report's banner are no longer offered while there is no report, since each of them changes how rows that are not on screen would read. They come back with the report.
  • The dropdown that picks which file extensions SpecBinder recognizes no longer cuts its own text short — ".feature and .specb" was drawn as ".feature...d .specb".
  • In the Execution Report, the rows of a recorded Rule now point back at the Rule that actually ran them. Once a Rule had been added or removed since the run, clicking a row highlighted whichever Rule had taken that position in the spec file, and the wrong Rule's background steps were inlined under the scenario.
  • A Rule left holding no scenarios now reads as not executed, and so does the Feature above it. Such a Rule is still run as a unit of its own, so a file could report as fully passed while one of the units under it had never run.
  • Adding, removing or retitling a Rule no longer costs every Rule below it the results of its last run. A recorded result is now recognised by the steps the scenario ran, wherever it has ended up in the file, so a scenario keeps its result when it moves between Rules and only genuinely new or edited scenarios read as not executed.
  • Everything that connects a spec file to its generated test code now goes quiet, instead of reporting an internal error, when the IDE cannot resolve Java for the project. The gutter Run icons, the toolbar's run button, navigation, step completion, Find Usages and the report's failure panels simply offer nothing, the way they do for a spec with nothing generated for it, and all of it comes back on its own once the project resolves again.
  • A spec file now opens even when the IDE cannot work out the Java version the project is written in, rather than leaving no way to read or edit the spec until the project itself is fixed. Should the results pane fail for any other reason, it is left empty and says so instead of taking the spec file with it.
  • Analysing a spec file no longer reports an internal error when indexing begins while the file is being checked. Typos, and the fixes offered on them, are unchanged.
  • Opening a spec file no longer reports an internal error on newer IDE versions. The editor's view buttons themselves are unchanged.
  • Find Usages on a step method, and renaming one, now stay within the module the generated test class belongs to. In a project whose modules keep their specs under the same relative path, they could list — or rewrite — steps belonging to another module's spec.
  • The Run menu offered by a scenario's gutter icon no longer writes an empty pair of brackets after the name: it reads "Run 'scenario_1'". What the entries do is unchanged.
  • A run started from a test method that carries no display name is now named after the method alone, without the empty pair of brackets that used to follow it. A method that does carry a display name is named by it, as before.
  • The Run icon beside an Examples row now appears whether or not gutter icons are driven by the execution report, and whether or not that row has ever run. The row naming the columns still carries none, since it stands for nothing to run.
  • Running a single Rule, or a single scenario inside one, no longer runs the same-numbered Rule in every other spec file of that package. The same correction applies when the failed tests of an earlier run are re-run.
  • The keyword suggestion list now opens under the first character of the keyword being written, wherever the line is indented to, instead of drifting further right the more you type. Picking a suggestion replaces the characters written so far rather than adding the keyword after them.
  • The step suggestion list now opens under the first character of the step text, wherever the caret stands within it, instead of being thrown left by the length of the whole step. Only the text written up to the caret decides where the list opens and what the suggestions are matched against.
  • Ctrl/Cmd+Click in a generated test class now opens the spec file of that class's own module, instead of a same-named spec in whichever module happened to be searched first. The same applies to Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Click on a step method call and to the spec file the debugger highlights while stepping through a test.
  • The Run icon in a spec file now runs the tests generated for that file's own module. Where several modules each hold a spec of the same name, clicking a Feature keyword quietly ran a neighbouring module's tests, while clicking a Rule, a scenario or an Examples row offered nothing at all. The gutter status icons and the toolbar counts read the same way.
  • Step completion no longer offers steps from unrelated spec files. Only the generated class belonging to the open file, in the same module, contributes suggestions, so the list is limited to the steps the tests for that file can actually call.
  • Ctrl/Cmd+Click from a spec file now goes straight to the generated test class of that file's own module, instead of offering a list of identically named classes, one per module, to pick from. Navigation from a step behaves the same way.
  • Revision markup is now highlighted when the strip patterns are shared as constants rather than written out as string literals in each marker class. The editor used to behave as though no patterns were configured — markup painted as ordinary spec text, no navigation, Find Usages, completion or rename from a marked-up step, and recorded run status not matching — while the build stripped the markers correctly.
  • Re-running a single scenario no longer strips the status from every other scenario in the file. Each scenario keeps the result of its own last run, including scenarios inside a Rule and scenarios that have moved.
  • A result recorded for one scenario could be shown against a different scenario that happened to have identical steps. The scenario that actually ran now gets its result, and the other reads as not executed.
  • After re-running a single scenario, clicking a status lozenge on the editor toolbar could jump to the wrong scenario. Each scenario is now counted and navigated to from its own result.
  • In the split editor, clicking a scenario's row in the Execution Report pane could highlight and scroll to a different scenario after a single-scenario re-run. Highlighting and scroll-sync now follow the right one.
  • A spec file's icon in the Project view could show as passed when only part of the file had run. It now reads not executed until every scenario has a result of its own.
  • Undoing an edit brings a scenario's recorded status back, instead of leaving it not executed until the next run.
  • An Examples row edited since the run now reads as not executed, the same as a row that never ran, instead of showing the plain run icon.
  • A scenario wrapped in removal markup no longer holds its whole file at not executed. SpecBinder generates nothing for such a scenario, so no run could ever clear it — leaving a grey Feature line, a grey file and folder in the Project view, and a not-executed lozenge nothing could shift. Only the scenarios SpecBinder actually generates now count towards the status above them and towards the toolbar counts; the removed scenario still shows as not executed on its own line.
  • The time shown in the editor toolbar's report section no longer claims more than it can. A report can hold results from several runs, so it now reads as when the report was last updated rather than when it was generated.
  • An Examples row of a Scenario Outline could show the result of a neighbouring row. Each row is now matched to its result by its own values, so re-running one row leaves the others alone and reordering the table carries every row's status with it.
  • A scenario headed Example: or Scenario Template: is no longer invisible to the features that pair it with its generated test. Its gutter Run icon opened an empty "Nothing here" popup, its recorded status was blank in the gutter and on the toolbar, Find Usages left out its steps, and navigation from a step method call would not open it.
  • One panel that cannot be reopened no longer costs you the others: a panel that fails to come back is skipped and the rest are reopened as usual.
  • The plugin no longer installs its "Auto-select terminal tab" hook when the bundled Terminal plugin is turned off.
  • The IDE's warning over a generated class now looks the same in the Test Code view as it does in an ordinary editor tab. It was drawn without the framing the current theme gives it, and sat on a grey the editor never uses, so it read as a fainter, unfamiliar strip beside the one the same file gets in a normal tab.
  • The selected file tab in the Test Code view now takes the colour the IDE gives a selected editor tab. It was reading only the look-and-feel's value and showing grey, ignoring the colour scheme's own answer, which is what an editor tab uses first.
  • The Test Code view no longer stays empty for a spec opened while the IDE is still indexing. Java cannot be resolved from a half-built index, and that answer was kept for the rest of the session; the view now asks again as soon as indexing finishes. The gutter Run icon and the status counts were held the same way.
  • Resting the cursor on a step implementation no longer paints stray highlights over unrelated code in the Java file. The marks the editor puts on the symbol under the cursor now fall only where that symbol occurs in the file being read; the spec steps a step method stands behind are still listed by Find Usages.
  • The editor no longer freezes while the Test Code pane works out which classes carry a spec, or while the Execution Report is scrolled. That work now happens in the background, so the pane fills a moment after it is asked for rather than holding the IDE still until it can — most noticeably just after a project finishes indexing, where it could stall repeatedly.
  • Switching between the Test Code pane's file tabs no longer shows the file unfolded for a moment before its imports and other folded sections collapse. Each file keeps its editor now, so coming back to a tab also returns to where you had scrolled to and to any sections you had opened by hand.
  • The selected file tab in the Test Code pane, and the selected run tab over the Execution Report, now wear the same colour the IDE gives the selected editor tab above them, instead of the grey a pressed toolbar button wears.
  • The file and run tabs over the right-hand pane now line up with the toggle buttons beside them, and carry the same spacing between one another as those buttons do. They stood a little high and ran into each other with no gap at all.
  • The last tab over the right-hand pane is no longer clipped, with the space before the buttons beside it swallowed, when the pane is widened until a hidden tab reappears. The row was working out how many tabs fit before their icons had been drawn, so it measured each tab narrower than it turned out to be and fitted one more than there was room for.

Removed

  • The "Allow folding Rules" option is gone from the Editor settings page. A Rule that spans several lines can now always be folded, in the spec editor and in the Execution Report alike, and the "Rules" choice under "Fold on open" is always available.

  • The "Don't wrap long lines in spec files" option is gone from the Editor settings page. Spec files never wrap long lines, so the columns of a wide data table always stay lined up; a long line scrolls sideways instead, in the spec editor and in the Execution Report alike.

  • The "Error panel bar colour" setting is gone from the Execution results settings page. A failed step's error panel bar now takes the colour of the step's own icon.

  • The option that turned Playwright traces on and off. A step's recorded trace now always opens as an expandable trace panel beneath that step in the Execution Report, since a trace only ever reaches the report because a run was set up to record one.

  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The Store the agent session id in the spec file option is gone from the Agent integration settings page, and a launched session's id is never written into a spec file. Each spec's agent sessions are now remembered only by the IDE, in a file alongside the project's other IDE settings, so launching an agent leaves your specs exactly as you wrote them and a read-only spec launches without complaint. If you had the option on, those sessions are not carried over — the # claude-session: lines already in your specs are now ordinary comments that nothing reads, and you can delete them at your leisure. Renaming or moving a spec in the IDE still keeps its sessions.

  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The Auto-Enable Remote Control (Claude Code only) item is gone from the Launch AI agent button's dropdown, and sessions started from the button no longer ask for remote control. Turn it on from within the session instead, the way you would in any terminal.

  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The Auto-reload checkbox is gone, and with it the automatic adoption of a newer execution report. A report is now only ever loaded when you ask for it, through the Reload link beside the time, so the results you are reading stay put until you choose to move on.

  • ⚠️ BREAKING: The editor no longer reports an unusable revision-markup pattern of its own accord, and the plugin's inspection for it is gone from Settings > Editor > Inspections. Building the project already reports both an invalid pattern and a marked range missing one of its ends, in the same place and with the same detail. How a spec file is coloured while a pattern is unusable is unchanged.

  • The error-panels button on the spec file's editor toolbar, and its dropdown, are gone. Open or close a failed step's error panel from the red icon beside the step; in split view, each pane's icon opens the panel in that pane only. The dropdown's options moved to the Execution results settings page.

  • The "Show Previews" button on the spec file's editor toolbar, and its dropdown, are gone. Open or close a doc string's preview from the preview icon beside its opening fence; in split view, each pane's icon opens the preview in that pane only. The preview bar colour moved to the Editor settings page.

idea-plugin.name: Pest Typed
idea-plugin.description:
Deep type intelligence for PestPHP's expectation API in PHPStorm.

Without this plugin, PHPStorm loses type information after the first -> on expect(). Property access, method chaining, and closure parameters all show as mixed.

Features

  • Type resolution through full expect() chains and HigherOrderExpectation
  • Closure parameter inference for scoped(), each(), and sequence()
  • Inlay hints for closure parameters showing inferred types
  • Impossible assertion inspection — warns when an assertion can never pass
  • Custom expectation support via expect()->extend() with optional @pest-type narrowing
  • SPX profile runner action for running Pest tests with profiling enabled

Type Resolution Through Chains

Pest Typed tracks types through the full expect() chain:

Closure Parameter Inference

Closure parameters in scoped(), each(), and sequence() are inferred as Expectation<TValue> with the correct generic type:

  • scoped() — receives the current value type
  • each() / sequence() — extracts the element type from arrays (LineItem[] -> LineItem) and collections (Collection<int, LineItem> -> LineItem)

Impossible Assertion Inspection

Flags assertion methods that will always fail at runtime:

// Warning: 'Order' is never a string
expect($order)->toBeString();

// Warning: 'int' is never a string
expect($order)->total->toBeString();

// OK — negation suppresses warning
expect($order)->not->toBeString();

Custom Expectations

Custom expectations registered via expect()->extend() are automatically indexed and supported in chains:

expect()->extend('toBeShipped', fn () => $this
  ->toBeInstanceOf(Order::class)
  ->status->toBe('shipped'));

// works — TValue preserved
expect($order)
  ->toBeShipped()
  ->total
  ->toBeGreaterThan(0);

To enable type narrowing for a custom expectation, add a @pest-type annotation:

/** @pest-type Order */
expect()->extend('toBeShipped', fn () => $this
  ->toBeInstanceOf(Order::class)
  ->status->toBe('shipped'));


expect($model)
  // narrows $model to Order
  ->toBeShipped()
  // ->total resolves as int
  ->total->toBeInt();

Without @pest-type, the original type is preserved (no narrowing). The annotation only applies to the immediately following extend() call.

Known Limitations

Factory mixed Type

PHPStorm can lose track of generic types on complex factory chains (e.g., with ->for(), ->has()), falling back to mixed. The plugin intercepts expect() and resolves the argument types directly, but PHPStorm's own mixed will still appear alongside them in the tooltip. To get rid of it:

  1. Start with toBeInstanceOf() to narrow the type:
expect($order)
  ->toBeInstanceOf(Order::class)
  ->id->toBeInt()
  ->status->toBeString();
  1. Add a @var annotation to the variable:
/** @var Order $order */
$order = Order::factory()->for(Team::factory())->create();

expect($order)
  ->id->toBeInt()
  ->status->toBeString();

Method Name Collision

If the expect() value defines a method with the same name as a Pest assertion (e.g., toBeString()), PHPStorm may navigate to that method instead of Pest's.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Support for PhpStorm 2026.2 and 2026.3. The plugin no longer declares an upper IDE bound, so it stays installable in future PhpStorm releases.

Fixed

  • Custom expectations registered with expect()->extend() inside a closure passed to another method call are now found. Indexing previously stopped at the enclosing call, so those expectations were missing from completion and type narrowing. The index rebuilds on first launch after updating.

Changed

  • Updated the build toolchain: Gradle 9.7.1, Kotlin 2.4.20 and IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.18.1.

idea-plugin.name: Http Server
idea-plugin.description:
Run a real HTTP server directly inside your IDE — no extra tools, no boilerplate, no containers.

Http Server lets you define routes, responses, headers, status codes, and latency using a simple .server file format. Hit run and your local API is live in seconds.

Why developers use it

  • Simulate a REST API — mock any endpoint your frontend or mobile app needs, without waiting for a real backend
  • Reproduce exact scenarios — craft the precise error codes, payloads, and latency your system will face in production
  • Prototype backends fast — validate your API contract before writing a single line of server-side code
  • Test edge cases reliably — return 500s, timeouts, empty responses, or malformed bodies on demand
  • Develop offline — keep working when the real API is unavailable, down, or rate-limited
  • Unblock parallel teams — frontend and backend can work simultaneously with an agreed contract expressed in a .server file

What you get

  • Start a local server directly from the IDE run button
  • Define routes with an HTTP-like syntax (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
  • Path parameters (/users/:id) and wildcard routes out of the box
  • Configure response status codes, headers, and artificial latency per route
  • Generate realistic random data on every request — {{ $random.name.fullName }}, {{ $random.internet.uuid }}, {{ $random.commerce.price }}, and 60+ other variables across 14 namespaces
  • Echo request data in responses — request.params.id, request.query.page, request.body.field, and ...request.body spread
  • Serve static files with the @file directive
  • Compose multiple .server files with RUN
  • Syntax highlighting, code folding, and autocomplete for .server files
  • Zero external dependencies or setup — it just works
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2026.2

  • Random data variables — use {{ $random.namespace.method() }} to generate realistic names, emails, UUIDs, prices, dates, booleans, and more on every request (14 namespaces, 60+ methods, range arguments supported)
  • Dynamic response variables — echo path parameters (request.params.id), query strings (request.query.page), and request body fields (request.body.email) directly in the response body
  • Body spread operator — use ...request.body to merge the entire request payload into the mock response, ideal for create/update endpoints
  • Mock API templates — ready-to-use examples for auth, users, products, and orders accessible from the Examples action
  • Syntax highlighting and autocomplete for {{ $random.* }} expressions with inline validation

2026.1

  • Static file serving with the @file directive — serve JSON, HTML, PDF, or any file directly from disk
  • Multi-file composition with RUN ./other.server
  • Wildcard routes and path parameters (/users/:id)
  • Artificial latency per route with the Delay header

idea-plugin.name: Gopher Glide
idea-plugin.description:
Gopher Glide (gg) is a modern, zero-scripting API traffic simulation and performance benchmarking CLI built in Go — a lightweight alternative to tools like k6, Gatling, or Locust that runs straight from standard .http files. No agents, no servers to stand up, no boilerplate code.

This plugin brings gg's traffic-simulation workflow directly into the IDE:
  • One-click runs — execute a traffic simulation, or scaffold a new run config, straight from any .http file or .gg.yaml config via gutter icons or the right-click menu, with a built-in profile picker (smoke, load, stress, soak, spike) for zero-config runs.
  • Native run dashboard — a dedicated "Gopher Glide" tool window shows a live stage timeline, RPS chart, error rate, and latency percentiles while a simulation runs — no terminal TUI involved.
  • Native snapshot workflow — a master-detail Snapshot View and Diff, with an inferred JSON schema tree (real type icons, presence %, stability), a status-code distribution chart, and profile-aware comparisons that warn when two snapshots aren't apples-to-apples. The diff view shows a full schema diff (added/removed/changed fields) alongside delta-formatted endpoint metrics. Run gg snap assert to gate regressions, and prune old snapshots by ID, tag, or age — entirely inside the tool window, no terminal involved.
  • One-click CI workflow generator — scaffold a ready-to-run GitHub Actions workflow that snaps a headless run, asserts it against your main-branch baseline, and posts the result as a PR comment.
  • Schema-validated config — JSON Schema completion and validation for .gg.yaml files, covering stages, snapshot tuning, and built-in profiles.
  • Zero manual setup — the plugin downloads and manages the gg binary for you, with update checks and diagnostics built into Settings → Gopher Glide.
Learn more and read the full docs at gopherglide.dev.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
A completely overhauled Snapshot View and Diff experience
This release is a full visual and functional rework of the native Snap dialogs, bringing them to parity with (and beyond) what gg's terminal TUI shows:
  • Snapshot View — a rich metadata header (date, requests, peak RPS, profile, config hash, sampling rate) above an endpoint table with a live-updating detail pane: an inferred JSON schema tree (with real type icons, and object/array/string/number distinctions) and a status-code distribution chart, including a synthetic "connection errors" bucket for failures that never received an HTTP status.
  • Snapshot Diff — the compare view gets the same treatment, plus a comparative Baseline/Target header, a mismatch warning banner when the two snapshots used different profiles or configs, and a full schema diff (added/removed/changed fields, colored consistently with the rest of the diff table) alongside a side-by-side status distribution comparison.
  • Delta-first diff formatting — endpoint and schema diff cells now show the current value with a ▲/▼ delta instead of a cluttered "before → after" pair, with NEW/GONE/CHANGED tags for added, removed, and modified fields.
  • Search and column chooser on both endpoint tables — filter rows live, and show/hide columns (Max Payload, P50/P99, etc.) with your choice remembered across restarts.
  • Profile-aware comparisons — snapshots now record which load profile generated them, surfaced in both dialogs and used to detect apples-to-oranges comparisons; legacy snapshots without a profile fall back to comparing config hashes.
  • Fixed a handful of longstanding bugs

idea-plugin.change-notes:
⚠️ Breaking changes

  • Snapshot bundle format bumped to v2. The plugin now refuses to load bundles whose manifest.json declares a version other than 2. If you see a warning banner inside the Page Mirror tool window after upgrading, regenerate your snapshots with playwright-snapshot-saver ≥ 0.7.0 — run npx playwright test in your project and the v2 bundles will replace the v1 ones. See docs/migration-v1-to-v2.md for the full migration guide.

Added

  • Outdated-bundle banner in the Page Mirror tool window. When the snapshot scanner finds bundle directories whose manifest version is unsupported, the tool window renders an actionable banner above the snapshot iframe with a link to the migration guide. The banner disappears automatically after you regenerate the bundles.
  • Strict v2 snapshot bundle support. The plugin reads CSS sidecars from resources/<sha1>.css and inlines them into the HTML before handing it to the JCEF srcdoc iframe, so resources/ references resolve correctly without a base URL.
  • Screenshots are now read from resources/screenshot.png or resources/screenshot.webp (was top-level in v1).

Fixed

  • Snapshots no longer scroll into empty space below and right of the rendered page when the iframe is scaled to fit the tool window width.
  • Snapshots taller than the capture viewport (e.g. dashboards) are no longer clipped at 720 px — the iframe grows to the document's full rendered height.
  • Switching focus to an already-open editor tab now reloads the matching snapshot. Previously the tool window stayed on whichever snapshot was loaded when the tab was first opened.

idea-plugin.name: Kensa
idea-plugin.description:
IntelliJ plugin for the Kensa testing framework.

Kensa is a Java/Kotlin testing library that captures expressive, human-readable test reports as HTML. This plugin brings those reports closer to your IDE.

Features

  • Gutter icons — pass/fail indicators appear next to @Test and @ParameterizedTest methods and their containing classes, updated automatically as tests run.
  • Click to open — click any gutter icon to open the corresponding Kensa HTML report in your browser, navigating directly to that test or class.
  • CI report support — configure a CI report URL template in Settings → Tools → Kensa to open remote reports when no local report is available, or choose between local and CI from a popup.
  • Console hyperlinks — the Kensa Output : marker in test console output becomes a clickable link that opens the report directly.
  • Live notifications — a balloon notification fires when a new report is written, with an Open Report action.

For an overview of what Kensa is and why it exists, see the introductory blog post.

Requirements

Kensa must be configured in your project. See the Kensa documentation and the Kensa GitHub repository for setup instructions.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Right-click a gutter icon to open the CI report. Left-click still opens the local report in a single click; when a CI report URL template is configured (Settings → Tools → Kensa), the gutter icon's right-click menu now offers "Open Local Report" and "Open CI Report", and its tooltip advertises the CI option. Previously the local/CI chooser lived only on the Alt+Enter intention menu, which devs rarely discovered, so a configured CI template appeared to do nothing — the gutter always jumped straight to the local report. KensaGutterLineMarkerProvider supplies the chooser through the gutter renderer's getPopupMenuActions(), so the fast local path is unchanged.

Changed

  • The plugin no longer declares dependencies on the JUnit, Gradle, and Maven plugins. None of their APIs were used (the test-run listener uses the platform's SM test runner, and location URLs are string-parsed), but the declarations meant the Kensa plugin silently refused to load for anyone who had disabled the bundled Maven or Gradle plugin. Only the platform and Java module dependencies remain.

Fixed

  • Reopening a project in the same IDE session no longer loses all Kensa results until a report is rewritten. The index loader was an application-wide singleton whose "skip unchanged files" mtime gate outlived the project, so the reopened project's (empty) results cache was never repopulated — gutter icons and the status bar stayed blank. The loader is now a project-scoped service, so its state dies with the project; this also fixes two windows open on the same directory sharing one gate.
  • indices.json reads and JSON parsing no longer run on the UI thread. VFS change events are delivered on the EDT inside a write action, and the listener parsed report files inline there — a UI freeze proportional to report size on every test run. The listener (KensaVfsListener) now only filters paths inline and hands file IO, parsing, and stale-entry pruning to a single-threaded background executor, preserving event order.
  • Gutter icon popup no longer risks PsiInvalidElementAccessException. The popup-menu callback is invoked speculatively during highlighting, by which time the marker's PSI element may have been invalidated; the provider now captures the project and target up front and never dereferences the element from callbacks.
  • High idle CPU. KensaOutputFileWatcherStartupActivity polled for new reports by walking the entire project tree (including build/, .git, node_modules) every 5 seconds, forever — continuous filesystem I/O even when the IDE was idle. The walk existed because reports written by terminal/external test runs land under an excluded build/ dir that VFS never reports. It is replaced by three bounded layers: (1) a native file-watch (addRootToWatch) on each discovered report dir, so changes to known reports surface instantly with no polling; (2) a 3-second targeted probe of only the build/output dirs — read from the module model's excluded roots (Gradle build, Maven target) — checking the fixed report shape (<buildDir>/<reportDir>/indices.json or …/sources/<id>/indices.json) so brand-new reports appear quickly without ever walking a build dir's contents; (3) a 60-second pruned safety walk for reports in unconventional locations, which also refreshes the build-root set and prunes stale entries. Idle CPU drops to near zero while a terminal test run still updates gutter icons within ~3 seconds (instantly for already-known reports). Site-mode bundles (build/<site>/sources/<id>/) are handled across all three layers.

idea-plugin.name: QA CoPilot
idea-plugin.description:
QA CoPilot — AI-powered API test generation for Spring Boot

QA CoPilot scans your open Spring Boot / Spring MVC project, builds a structured API contract, and generates a complete Cucumber + Rest Assured test framework — all without leaving the IDE.

Key Features

  • One-click generation — toolbar button, Tools menu, project/editor context menu
  • Dedicated Tool Window — last-run summary, output path, and one-click test execution
  • AI-powered scenarios — OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, and local LLM support
  • Business requirements ingestion — feed a .txt, .md, .pdf, or .docx doc to align scenarios with product intent
  • Domain-organised Gherkin — one .feature file per domain, derived from controller paths
  • Incremental mode — only regenerates scenarios for changed or new endpoints
  • Custom Run Configurations — QA CoPilot tests run config type with dry-run and live-API modes
  • Rich HTML report — executive summary, per-scenario URL / params / body, expected vs actual status + body with match indicators
  • Full Settings UI — configure everything under Settings → Tools → QA CoPilot

How It Works

  1. Open any Spring Boot or Spring MVC project in IntelliJ IDEA.
  2. Click Generate QA Tests in the toolbar (or Tools menu, or the QA CoPilot tool window).
  3. QA CoPilot scans all @RestController / @Controller classes, fingerprints endpoints, and writes a standalone Gradle test project to your configured output folder.
  4. Run the tests with Dry Run (no server needed) or Live API mode directly from the tool window.
  5. Open the generated HTML report for a professional API test summary.

Generated Output

  • Gherkin feature files — one per domain under src/test/resources/features/
  • api-contract.json — machine-readable endpoint contract
  • Rest Assured step definitions with shared and domain-specific steps
  • Standalone Gradle project — runs independently with ./gradlew test
  • Gradle test report + QA CoPilot HTML API report

Privacy & Data

  • When Generator = ai is selected, endpoint names and (optionally) your requirements document are sent to the configured AI provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, or a local server) to generate Gherkin scenarios. No data is sent in template mode.
  • AI API keys and auth tokens are stored in the OS keychain via IntelliJ PasswordSafe — never written to workspace.xml.
  • No telemetry or analytics are collected by this plugin.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2024.1 or later (Community or Ultimate)
  • JDK 17 or later
  • Spring Boot or Spring MVC project (Java)
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.1.2

  • Updated plugin metadata for the 0.1.2 release
  • Refined Marketplace-facing functionality details so users can better understand key capabilities and workflows before installing/updating
  • Improved release communication for easier awareness of what is new in QA CoPilot

0.1.1

  • Fixed ConnectException in JetBrains Runtime by switching all AI HTTP clients from java.net.http.HttpClient to HttpURLConnection, which correctly uses IntelliJ's configured proxy and SSL trust store
  • Fixed AI requests being routed to localhost when the provider was previously set to Local LLM — base URL is now ignored for OpenAI and Anthropic regardless of saved settings
  • Improved error messages for network connectivity failures with actionable guidance on proxy and firewall configuration
  • Eliminated template fallback on AI chunk omission — missing endpoints are now retried individually with the AI provider instead of silently falling back to template scenarios

0.1.0 — Initial Release

  • Tool window with Generate, Dry Run, and Live API run buttons
  • Full Settings UI: General, AI Provider, Business Requirements, Test Execution
  • Custom QA CoPilot tests run configuration type
  • Incremental scenario and parse caching
  • Multi-provider AI support: OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, local LLM
