idea-plugin.name: Deju Trace
idea-plugin.description:
Deju Trace follows a single targeted live API call through a running Java web app and paints the executed source line/branch coverage back into the editor like JUnit coverage, but for one real request.
  • Green: line fully executed
  • Yellow: decision point where only some branches were taken
  • Red: a line inside an entered method that never executed
Place a "deju point" on a controller/entry method, hit the endpoint, and see the code traces. Keeps the last 5 executions and exports a self-contained HTML report: a call tree in exact execution order, syntax-highlighted source, and the SQL each line issued. Entities, DTOs and generated builders can be folded out of it, so the report shows the code you are actually debugging.

The report opens on Where the time goes: one stacked bar splitting the whole run into the queries that cost the most, your own code, and the time nothing in the report accounts for — so "was it the database or was it us" is answered before you pick a tab.

Works against a JVM you launch from the IDE, one in a Docker container, or one on another machine.

Getting started
  1. Open Settings → Tools → Deju Trace and set Includes to your application's packages, for example com.example. Without this the agent instruments nothing.
  2. Press Copy agent VM option and paste it into your application's VM options. If the IDE launches your app, tick Auto-attach instead and skip this step.
  3. Start your application. Open the Deju tool window and press Connect.
  4. Click the gutter icon next to a controller method to place a deju point, then press Track.
  5. Hit the endpoint. Show paints the executed lines in the editor; Export writes the HTML report.
If it isn't working
  • "nothing is listening on that port" — the app was not started with the agent attached, or the port does not match. Re-copy the VM option and restart the app.
  • "the token does not match" — your -javaagent flag needs token=dejutoken.
  • "the port is unreachable" — running in Docker? Tick Traced JVM runs in a container or on another machine, re-copy the VM option (it adds bind=0.0.0.0) and publish the port.
  • Tracking started, but no run appears. Either the trace point does not exactly match a real method, or Includes does not cover its package, or you changed Includes without restarting the app — the -javaagent line is read once, at JVM start.
  • The report shows line numbers but no code. The source in the IDE does not match the running build. Point Source roots at the matching source.
  • "Recorded by agent X, but the plugin is Y" — restart your traced app after updating the plugin. A JVM keeps the agent it started with.
  • The report is huge or slow. Exclude entities and DTOs under Excluded types, or narrow Includes.
  • The report says "capped", or a large "Unrecorded" share. The run made more calls than the recording cap allows and the rest were dropped. Raise Recording cap (calls) in Settings, re-copy the VM option if your app is in a container, and restart it. A large untracked slice on a run that was not capped is the other case: that code is outside Includes, so no cap can reach it — widen Includes instead.
  • Clicking a line number does nothing. Those are jetbrains:// links and need JetBrains Toolbox installed. Use Copy path instead.
The companion agent is attached by you via -javaagent. It listens on loopback only by default; reaching it from a container or another host takes an explicit bind=. The connection token is a fixed value, dejutoken, so a hand-written agent flag never has to be kept in step with the IDE. It is published here and is therefore not a secret: what keeps the control socket private is the default loopback binding, so open it up only on a machine and network you trust. No variable values are captured. SQL statement text is recorded so queries appear in the call tree, but bound parameters are never read and stay as ? placeholders. There is no telemetry.

What Deju records… in Settings shows every file the plugin has written, what each one holds, and what is never captured. Clear Deju data… removes all of it, and uninstalling from a running IDE does the same.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2.7.0: where the run's time actually went, a callee's cost on the line that called it, and a recording cap you can raise

  • New: "Where the time goes" — one stacked bar at the top of the report, above the tabs. It splits the whole run into the queries that cost the most (grouped by statement, biggest six named), your own code, and untracked: time no recorded line or query explains, which is almost always code outside Includes. The segments always add up to the run, and each one reads out its time and share on hover, with its percentage and name drawn inside the segment itself.
  • New: the timing gutter charges a call back to the line that made it. A line's own time stops when it calls something, which is the right measurement but means the line costing you half the request reads as 0.2% — the half second was only visible after opening the callee and finding a number in there. Such a line now shows ↳ 30% [12 ms]: the arrow marks the figure as what the line called, not what it kept. It appears only when the call cost more than the line's own work, so a line calling a trivial getter still reports its own time, and the tooltip carries both figures plus what was called.
  • New: the recording cap is a setting. Settings → Tools → Deju Trace → Recording cap (calls), 1,000 to 10,000,000, default the 200,000 it has always been. Raise it when a report says capped or shows a large Unrecorded share — that share is the work that happened after the cap tripped. It costs roughly 28 bytes a call in the traced application's heap. Runs the IDE launches pick it up immediately; anything else gets it through the new maxCalls= argument in Copy agent VM option, and has to be restarted.
  • Capped reports now name the number. The warning used to say "the agent's cap", which told you nothing you could act on; it now says which cap was in force and where to change it.
  • Jumping to a called method is now a click. In the report's IDE view, a line that called something carries a small ↳ Class.method chip: one plain click opens that method, wherever its class lives. It replaces a bare ↷ glyph that named no destination and only opened under Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+click — which still works, for anyone used to it.
  • The Call Tree opens with every frame's source showing. 2.6.0 made each frame's lines a separate src toggle and left them off, which meant a tree of thirteen frames needed thirteen clicks before any code appeared. They are on by default now; Collapse all puts the structure-only view back in one click.
  • Fixed: "Expand all" broke the Call Tree. A folded run of identical queries is marked as SQL but stands for many calls and carries none of them, and the row-identity cache read a field off the one it did not have. The rebuild threw and the tree was left empty until the page was reloaded. Present since folding was added.

2.6.0: a call tree you can read at a glance, an IDE-style file view, and per-operand branch coloring

  • Call Tree shows the full call structure by default. Nothing is collapsed automatically any more — the caret is the only way to fold a call away. Each frame's own source lines are now a separate src toggle you click independently, off by default except on the trace root, so opening a call no longer also dumps every line of code underneath it. A hint above the tree explains what each click does.
  • New: a sticky breadcrumb above the Call Tree tracks which call you're scrolled into, so a deeply nested trace never leaves you unsure where you are.
  • Files is now IDE view. Instead of every file stacked one after another, a sidebar lists them by class name (no package) and position, and the main pane shows one file's full source at a time, opening on the trace point's own file by default.
  • New: Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+click a call in IDE view to jump straight to the method it calls into — the same "go to declaration" a real IDE gives you.
  • New: compound conditions are colored per operand. isA && isB used to paint the whole line yellow the moment the two disagreed. Each plain boolean operand now shows green when it was true, red when it was false, and a muted underline when a short-circuit skipped it or it varied across a loop — so you can see which half actually failed. A comparison like x > 5 can't be colored this way safely and still shows as a single yellow line.
  • Fixed: clicking a line in the Call Tree to reveal its source jumped the page. Rebuilding the tree used to forget every row's real height and re-guess it; row heights now persist across a rebuild, so the scroll position holds.

2.5.0: a minimap for the Flow Chart, and callers for the Flame Graph

  • New: Minimap. A corner overview of the whole Flow Chart, with a box marking what's on screen — click or drag it to jump straight to any part of a large diagram instead of scrolling to find it.
  • New: Callers of… on the Flame Graph. Pick a frame and see every call site that reaches it, merged by caller and stacked upward from it — a sandwich view for "what's calling this expensive thing everywhere", rather than only being able to read a single call path top to bottom.

2.4.1: a redesigned Flow Chart, a clearer Call Tree, and accurate line timing

  • Flow Chart redesigned. Each box is now three centered rows — class, method, and its time and share of the run — drawn with a soft gradient and shadow. Connectors are curves instead of elbows, and no longer bunch or cross where several arrows meet the same box.
  • New: Flow Chart boxes group by package. Adjacent boxes that share a Java package now sit on a soft colour-coded backdrop with a label, so a run through several layers of the same feature reads as one block instead of a row of identical-looking boxes.
  • New: Sort: by layer on the Flow Chart reorders each row by a guessed architectural layer — controller, service, repository/DAO, then SQL — instead of call order.
  • Flame Graph frames now show their time and share directly on the frame once it's wide enough to hold them, not only in the tooltip.
  • Call Tree decluttered. Indent guide lines mark nesting depth, and a frame's own total now reads bolder than the lines beneath it, so the call hierarchy and what's a total versus a self time are both easier to tell apart at a glance.
  • Fixed: Show's per-line time in the editor. Its font is smaller, and the time and share now read together as e.g. 12% [8.4 ms] instead of two crowded numbers — the report's Call Tree and Files line time now show the same format.
  • Fixed: Show didn't navigate to the method, only the top of the file. Opening a file from Show now lands on the exact line the traced method starts at.
  • Fixed: a max open files of 0 opened every file instead of none. Zero now means paint the coverage colour without opening any tabs at all — the "just show me the colour" case the setting exists for.
  • Fixed: recursive calls' timing was inflated. A self-recursive method double- (or worse-) counted its own time, once for the outer call and again for each nested call inside it; only the outermost call's span is banked now.
  • Clarified: what a line's timing figure covers. A line's self time and a method's total are summed across every call to that line or method anywhere in the run, not scoped to the one call they're shown under — tooltips throughout the report and the editor gutter now say so, rather than leaving a loop's line looking like it cost more than the frame containing it.
  • New: Includes can be left blank. With Auto-attach on, a run with no Includes configured now guesses a starting package from the run configuration's own main class — exact for a typical Spring Boot app, since its main class already sits at the root of what it component-scans — instead of silently instrumenting nothing until the field is filled in by hand.

2.4.0: a flowchart, a flame graph, and findings that read like a report

  • Renamed for clarity: API Flow is now Flow Chart, and it is the default view when the Flow tab opens.
  • Flow Chart, Flame Graph and Steps are now tabs of their own, not toggle buttons sharing a toolbar with everything else, so switching between them reads the way switching the report's other tabs already does.
  • New: each Flow Chart box shows its share of the run. Every step is the same size regardless of how long it took; a percentage now says which ones actually mattered.
  • Fixed: the Flow Chart's Play marker now rides the actual line into the next box instead of cutting a straight line through whatever sat between them, and a loop that hit the same call many times in a row now animates as one step marked with its count instead of idling through every repeat.
  • Flame Graph redrawn in the classic style — a warm, independently randomised colour per frame, a pale background wash, and no time ruler, the way Brendan Gregg's original reads. Searching now highlights matches in place and shows the percentage of the run they cover, instead of hiding everything else.
  • Fixed: the Flame Graph zoom box stopped reflecting the zoom actually applied and always read back "100"; it now shows the real value.
  • Findings are grouped by severity and collapsible, and a query inside one is now syntax-highlighted the same way it is everywhere else in the report.
  • New: Merge repeats in the Flame Graph. Every call that arrived by the same route through the code now becomes one frame, as wide as the time all of them took together, with the count in its tooltip — a loop of thousands of calls reads as a handful of frames instead of a wall of slivers. Turn it off when the question is what order things happened in.
  • Fixed: Save SVG on the Flame Graph threw and wrote nothing, broken by this release's own background wash; the export now falls back to a flat colour.
  • New: a user guide. docs/user-guide.md walks through setup for a local JVM and for a container, with a troubleshooting table built from the errors the plugin and agent actually print.

2.3.0: a flowchart with a start and an end

  • New: API Flow can run top to bottom. A button beside API Flow switches the diagram from left-to-right to a traditional top-down flowchart. A level with many siblings wraps onto more rows instead of stretching the diagram sideways, the same crowding fix the left-to-right layout already had.
  • New: Start and End. Every API Flow diagram, in either layout, now brackets the run with where it began and where every branch of it stopped.
  • New: Play leaves numbered footprints. Each step gets a number the first time the marker reaches it, in the order it reached them, so a paused or finished run still shows what happened when without replaying it.
  • New: play slower. The speed dropdown's presets stopped at 0.5×; a Custom… option now adds a slider down to a twentieth of that, for a first watch of an unfamiliar run.
  • New: Breakdown's name column resizes. Drag the handle next to it, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to see more of a long file or package path. The width is remembered next time.
  • New: copy a class or method name. Each Breakdown row has a copy button beside its name — the class alone grouped By file, class and method together grouped By method.

2.2.0: CPU time, comparing runs, and a flame graph that stays flat

  • New: CPU time. The summary bar now shows how much CPU this thread actually burned during the call, beside the wall-clock duration, so a slow request that was mostly waiting reads differently from one that was mostly computing.
  • New: Diff… compares any two recorded runs — duration, CPU and call-count deltas, the methods whose own time moved the most, and which lines' coverage changed. Useful before/after a fix.
  • New: Copy as Markdown puts a plain-text summary of a run — duration, CPU split, duplicate-query check, coverage count — on the clipboard, for pasting into a PR, an issue or a chat message.
  • New: Pin a run to protect it from being overwritten once every history slot has been used; Rename… gives it a name of your own instead of the auto-generated one; the history list now has a search box to filter by either.
  • New: history capacity is a setting, 1–25 instead of a fixed 5, in Settings → Tools → Deju Trace.
  • New: Breakdown can group by method as well as by file, for when one file's time really belongs to just one of its methods.
  • Fixed: the flame graph's horizontal scrollbar. A loop calling the same thing a thousand times used to draw a thousand boxes; identical repeats now fold into one, marked with their count, the way Glowroot's does.
  • New: tabs sit beside the trace point, in one row instead of two, so switching views no longer means hunting a second bar for what you were looking at.
  • Timeline's line/SQL/step controls moved beside the step name instead of the row's far edge, and clicking the name now opens them too.
  • Fixed: SQL was still getting cut short, both in the agent's own recording cap and in the flame diagram's inline preview. Both are gone; every view now shows the complete statement.
  • Renamed for clarity: Code Trace is now Call Tree, Graph is now Breakdown, and Flow Graph is now Flame Graph, in both the report and the Export dialog.

2.1.1: make the report yours, and see every call

  • New: build the report the way you want it. When you export, pick which tabs go in, which columns show, which tab it opens on, and light or dark.
  • New: change your mind later. Whoever opens the report can rearrange it from the Customize button, without exporting again. Press g.
  • Percentages, not just times. Show puts the share of the run beside each line's time in the editor, and in the report's Code Trace hovering a time tells you the same thing — so you can see what a line cost without doing the sums.
  • Past runs now show the date, not just the time, and the name is short — OrderController#place instead of the whole package.
  • Clicking a step in the Timeline highlights where it lands in the Code Trace, so you can see which row it took you to.
  • Fixed: the flame graph was hiding calls. Narrow ones were drawn on top of each other, so you could not see or hover them. Every call now gets its own space.
  • New: pick a minimum box width. Set it big enough and every single call in the run gets a readable name, however small it was.
  • Fixed: blurry, wrong-sized text. Labels were too small, and went fuzzy if your browser was zoomed out.
  • New: the report says how much of the run it missed. If the recording hit its limit, it now tells you the percentage instead of just saying "capped".
  • Hovering a call shows what it cost overall — how many times it ran, the total, the slowest one, and how much was its own code.
  • New: Save SVG. A sharp image at any zoom, and it never gets cut off the way a large PNG did.

2.1.0: the report tells you where to look

  • Action needed: the token is now always dejutoken. If you start your app with a hand-written -javaagent flag, change token= to dejutoken and restart it. Or copy the VM option again from Settings.
  • Fixed: Code Trace showed only the first screenful. Everything below it was blank, however far you scrolled. Any run longer than about 30 steps was affected. Scrolling now works.
  • New: a Findings tab. It reads the run for you and says what stands out: the same query run in a loop, one query eating the request, the method that really spent the time, calls repeated far more often than you would expect. Each one links to the step it came from.
  • New: a Timeline tab. One bar per step, in the order they ran. The solid part is time the step spent in its own code, the faint part is time inside what it called, so you can tell a slow method from one that merely called something slow.
  • Search now finds a class or a method. Typing a name used to match only the code lines, never the calls themselves.
  • Group repeats folds every repeat of the same call into one row, so a loop that ran two hundred times takes one line instead of two hundred.
  • Copy a step, or link to it. Each step has a copy button, and the address bar follows where you are, so you can send someone a link that opens on the same step.
  • Reports are much smaller. A big report is now packed inside the file and unpacked when you open it: 6.8 MB becomes under 900 KB. Small reports are unchanged. Very old browsers cannot open the packed ones.
  • Excluded types works by package too, and double-clicking a class opens it in the editor, at the method the run went through.
  • The Flow Graph and Timeline now hide your excluded types too, like the Code Trace already did. Before, they drew every class whatever you had excluded. Show excluded puts them back.
  • Show opens one file, the traced method's own, instead of five. The rest are still coloured, and you can jump to any of them from Excluded types.
  • Also fixed: Full now really shows every call; the counts add up; the date reads as a normal local date; your light/dark choice is remembered; j and k no longer break; the file picker means the same thing in both views; and reports print.

2.0.3: reports that open at any size

  • A large report used to be unopenable. Every recorded call became a table row before anything appeared, so a 200,000-call trace never finished loading. The Tree and Files views now render only what is on screen: the same trace opens in about half a second and holds a few dozen rows in the page instead of millions.
  • Fixed: the Flow Graph went blank on any sizeable run. It sized its canvas to the whole diagram, and a browser silently stops drawing past 65535 pixels, which is roughly 1,300 steps on a retina display. It now draws only the visible region, so length no longer has a limit.
  • Exported reports are around five times smaller. The call list is written as columns with the repeated class names and statements held in tables once each, rather than as one object per call re-spelling every key. A run that produced a 30 MB file now produces about 6 MB, with nothing left out. Reports exported by earlier versions still open.
  • Fixed: the Excluded rows control did nothing, or vanished. It disappeared entirely from reports exported with the source of excluded types omitted, which still show the “N excluded calls” rows, and it stayed lit but inert whenever a search or filter had already removed those rows. It now reflects what is actually on screen.
  • Fixed: Suggest, All and None in Excluded types did nothing. Each set the selection and then immediately overwrote it with the state of the checkboxes it had not yet updated.
  • Excluded types lists classes in execution order and numbers them, so the dialog reads in the same order as the editor tabs and the report.
  • Flow Chart is now Flow Graph, follows the Files picker like the Tree does, and starts with Group repeats off. Its canvas is created when the tab is first opened rather than shipped in every export.
  • Fixed the tool window opening with its rows stretched far taller than their contents until the panel was resized, a settings page that clipped controls with no scrollbar to reach them, and a horizontal scrollbar across What Deju records….

2.0.2: the agent ships as its own release asset

  • Fixed: the standalone agent jar was never built. Every release now produces deju-agent-<version>.jar alongside the plugin zip. The task that makes it existed but was wired to nothing, so it only ran if you invoked it by name, and the versioned asset was missing from the release.
  • This is what a containerised JVM downloads. A setup script pins DEJU_VERSION and fetches that file, so the agent in the container always matches the plugin in the IDE; without the version in the name, a cached copy survives a bump and surfaces much later as a protocol mismatch. The copy bundled in the plugin keeps its fixed deju-agent.jar name and is byte-identical to the published one.

2.0.1: three ways to read one request

  • The report is now three tabs. Code Trace is everything the report already did, unchanged. Graph and Flow Chart are new, and neither is built until you open it, so the file still opens instantly and a reader who only wants the trace pays nothing for the rest.
  • Graph ranks files by the time they actually cost, their own code plus the SQL they issued, each query charged to the method that issued it. Self time on its own hides the database entirely, and totals double-count every caller up the stack, so neither answers "which file is slow" by itself. Include SQL switches between the two readings.
  • N+1 detection. A file that issues the same statement more than once carries a ×N badge with the statement and its total cost, and the run's worst offender is named at the top of the tab. Matching ignores whitespace and case, so the same query built two ways still groups.
  • Flow Chart draws the call tree on a canvas, top to bottom in execution order. Click a step to fold its calls away; a run of identical sibling calls collapses into one box marked ×5, which is usually what an N+1 looks like from the side. Queries are laid out on their clause lines in the box itself rather than trimmed to a hover.
  • Flame layout. Switch the diagram from nesting to time: box width is duration, with a time ruler across the top, click-to-zoom into any frame and a breadcrumb back out. Zoom stretches the time axis and not the text, so zooming out to compare shapes keeps the labels readable. Save PNG exports it.
  • Frames are coloured by owning class from a fixed palette checked for colour-blind separation against both themes, so two classes never share a hue and the narrow slivers stay tellable apart. Queries keep the SQL orange throughout.
  • Chrome moved out of the toolbar. Theme and help are icon buttons in the top-right corner, the code filter sits in the stats row at full height, and the "showing N of M" count now rides with the trace point.
  • Internal: replaced the deprecated platform comment component, so the plugin now reports zero deprecated API usages on 2024.1 through 2024.3.

1.3.0: reading the tree without the noise

  • Filter calls by time, three ways. The call filter offered only "at least this long". It now also does less than and between, with presets for each, and Custom… lets you pick the comparison and type the bounds (750us, 1.5 ms, 2s). Between-ranges are half-open, so the presets tile without a call landing in two of them.
  • Hide SQL, or the excluded-call summaries. Two toolbar toggles for reading control flow on its own: SQL hides every query and folded query run, Excluded rows hides the "… N excluded calls" summaries.
  • Long queries are trimmed to three lines with Show full query to open them, so a trace with thirty statements is still a call tree rather than a wall of SQL.
  • Show opens 5 files rather than 10. Every recorded file is still painted, so opening one by hand shows its coverage immediately; the limit only governs how many tabs appear unasked. Configurable as before.
  • Total time reads in the unit you think in. It was always milliseconds, so a slow request showed "94812 ms". It now carries the larger unit alongside once it reaches one: 94812 ms (1m 34s).
  • Step numbers are numbered badges instead of "#1", and the report header carries a Code Traces chip.
  • Fixed: the Files view hid the top of every method section. A stray overflow on the file card made it the nearest scroll container, which stopped the sticky file header positioning against the page and left it sitting on top of the method heading below it.
  • Fixed: the custom time-filter field appeared on load instead of waiting for Custom… to be chosen.

1.2.0: SQL in the trace, and a report you can actually read

  • Docker without a port-forwarding sidecar. The agent takes a new bind= argument, so a containerised JVM can expose its control socket the same way the JVM's own debugger does: bind=0.0.0.0 plus a published port, and the IDE connects straight to it. The default is still loopback-only, and the agent refuses to listen on any other address unless a token is set. Tick Traced JVM runs in a container or on another machine in Settings and Copy agent VM option fills the argument in for you.
  • SQL queries appear in the call tree, at the line that issued them, with their own timing. Statement text only; bound parameters are never read and stay as ? placeholders, and nothing is captured unless a trace is armed. Statements are formatted onto clause lines and syntax-coloured, long ones are trimmed to three lines with an expand control, and a toolbar toggle hides SQL entirely for reading control flow on its own.
  • Java syntax highlighting in the exported report, in both light and dark themes (keywords, strings, comments, annotations and types), instead of the flat monochrome the report used to show.
  • The report has been redesigned around the platform's own look: system typography, a monospace face that matches the IDE editor, hairline borders, a translucent toolbar that stays put while you scroll, and a segmented control in place of the old buttons. Light and dark are both first-class.
  • Smaller reports. The embedded logo was a 1024×1024 image shown at 28 pixels and carried twice, costing ~149 KB in every file; it is now sized for the job. Export also offers an Essential mode that leaves excluded types' source out of the document rather than shipping it and hiding it.
  • The Files picker now works in the Tree view too, so a trace can be stripped down to one layer, and long class names are no longer truncated.
  • Excluded types. A single request touches dozens of entities, DTOs and generated builders that are not what you are debugging. The report's new Essential view folds them into one "… N excluded calls" row at the call site, keeping the count and total time visible; Full still shows every recorded frame. A call is only folded when everything underneath it is also excluded, so a getter that triggers a lazy load stays on screen with the query it caused.
  • Choose the types under Settings → Tools → Deju Trace: case-insensitive globs by class name (*dto, *entity) or by package (*.dto.*), plus your own. Per-class exclusions… overrides any pattern for one class, in either direction. Nested classes follow their outer class, so excluding a response wrapper also excludes the builder generated inside it. Stored per project; the recording itself is never filtered.
  • Show opens 5 files instead of all of them, in execution order, the traced method's own file first. Every recorded file is still painted, so opening one of the others later shows its coverage and timings immediately. The limit is configurable (0 = no limit) and what was not opened is named in a notification.
  • Run configurations repair themselves. A -javaagent path pinned to a previous build stops the JVM from starting at all once the plugin updates. Fix run configurations rewrites the path in place, preserving your port/token/includes arguments and leaving any non-Deju agent untouched; Refresh agent on disk re-extracts the bundled jar.
  • The plugin now reports which agent build is actually loaded in the traced JVM and warns when it is older than the installed plugin, the usual cause of a report missing newer features, since a -javaagent is fixed at process start and needs the application restarted.
  • You can see, and delete, everything Deju keeps. What Deju records… in Settings lists every file the plugin has written, what is in it, its size, and what is never captured, with a button to open each location. Clear Deju data… removes the lot: recorded runs, exclusion rules, connection settings and the extracted agent, naming anything it could not delete rather than reporting success. Uninstalling from the Plugins page of a running IDE clears the same data.
  • The connection token is generated per installation. It used to ship as a fixed string in the plugin source, which is not a secret, and it is the only thing guarding the agent socket once bind= opens it beyond loopback.
  • Recorded runs no longer risk reaching a commit. They live under .idea/ and contain executed SQL statement text, so the directory now carries its own .gitignore instead of relying on yours.
  • Fixed: Copy agent VM option handed out a path that broke on the next update. It named the version-stamped jar, which is renamed and deleted whenever the plugin updates, so a flag pasted into a compose file, a Gradle build or an env var would fail at JVM start with "Error opening zip file or JAR manifest missing". It now gives the fixed-name path, which stays valid across updates.
  • Fixed: the tool window forced a horizontal scrollbar when docked at its usual width. Its controls wrapped onto new rows but still reported their width as if they were on one line, so the panel always claimed to be wider than the dock.

1.1.0: the HTML report becomes a call tree

  • New default view: Tree. Every method invocation in exact execution order, each numbered with the step it ran at, with each method's own lines interleaved with the calls it made, placed at the line that made them. A trace now reads top to bottom.
  • Per-call inclusive timing, a hot path highlight that follows the slowest chain, and a minimum-time filter. Neither ever reorders the tree.
  • Runs of identical sibling calls fold automatically, so an N+1 query loop no longer floods the page. Click to expand; order is preserved.
  • Files view: lines are grouped into named method sections; file headers stick to the top and carry line, unexecuted and timing counts; long reports open collapsed so they read as an index.
  • Click any line number to open it in the IDE (requires JetBrains Toolbox), with Copy path as a fallback.
  • Keyboard navigation throughout; press ? for the full list.
  • Fixed: "API order" sorted by hash-set iteration order instead of the order classes were actually entered, making it effectively arbitrary.
  • Fixed: "Slowest first" ranked by inclusive time, which always favoured whatever sat highest on the call stack. Self time and total time are now separate options: self time finds the method actually doing the slow work.
  • Unchanged guarantees: no variable capture, no telemetry, and no network calls or remote resources in the exported report.

0.1.0: initial MVP, line/branch coverage for one targeted call, last-5 history, and HTML export.

idea-plugin.name: Liquibase Sudarshan - SQL & Data Validator
idea-plugin.description:
Catch Liquibase, PostgreSQL and Oracle errors before they reach the database. Liquibase Sudarshan validates Liquibase formatted SQL scripts against your repository's DDL schema right inside the editor — no SQL is ever executed during validation.

  • Staging/temp-table datatype and length mismatches against the real target table
  • INSERT value validation: VARCHAR length, numeric ranges, DECIMAL precision/scale, BOOLEAN, DATE, TIMESTAMP, UUID
  • NULL values in NOT NULL columns, missing mandatory columns
  • MERGE source/target table and column-mapping validation
  • Duplicate primary-key/unique values in static datasets, unused staging columns
  • Changeset metadata, header/attribute typo detection and rollback checks
  • Country-specific static dataset validation against the global schema
  • Quick fixes (Alt+Enter), pre-commit and pre-push validation, repository-wide validation report with navigation
  • Optional read-only database dry run: pending changesets, live precondition checks, foreign keys, INSERT/UPDATE data preview (PostgreSQL and Oracle)
  • Bitbucket pull-request review (Cloud and Server/Data Center): validate only the PR's changed lines and optionally post inline review comments

Release execution simulation (Simulate Release…): validates the exact ordered country/environment run your CI/CD pipeline (e.g. Jenkins) would execute:

  • Six stages in order: global DDL → static datasets → country datasets → update scripts → environment-specific SQL (never for PROD)
  • Sequential schema build-up: tables or foreign-key targets used before their DDL runs, duplicate definitions, ALTER before CREATE
  • Cross-file checks: duplicate changeset ids, unique-key INSERT collisions
  • Per-environment policy guardrails: destructive SQL needs an --approved-destructive <ticket> marker, PROD requires rollbacks
  • One optional .liquibase-sudarshan.yml configures the IDE, the bundled headless CLI and your pipeline identically — a release that passes validation does not fail in SIT/UAT/PROD
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.4.3 — No deprecated platform APIs on current IDEs. The JetBrains verifier reported 9 deprecated-API usages against IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 EAP; it now reports none on 2026.1, 2026.2 and 2026.3, while the 2021.2 floor is unchanged. Read actions, credential-store keys, tree speed search and the settings-applied highlighting restart now use APIs that exist, undeprecated, on every supported build. No functional changes.
0.4.2 — Memory fixes. Three things kept memory for the whole IDE session and no longer do. (1) The per-file cache stored each file's complete parsed syntax tree alongside its findings, although only the findings are ever read — up to 128 full ASTs per project; it now keeps findings only. (2) The tool window's report listener was never deregistered, so every recreated tool window left a dead Swing panel — and the report's file references — reachable; listeners are now tied to the content's lifetime. (3) JDBC drivers self-register with java.sql.DriverManager, a JDK-global static that pinned the driver's class loader and, through it, the whole plugin class loader — so each plugin update stranded the previous copy of the plugin plus the ~7 MB Oracle driver permanently. The plugin never uses DriverManager, so the registration is now undone immediately and driver class loaders are closed on unload.
0.4.1 — Unsaved edits are now validated. The repository report, the database dry run and the pre-commit check read the file from disk, so a file edited but not yet saved was validated in its PREVIOUS state and reported "0 errors" while the editor already underlined the problem. All three now read the editor's buffer, like the inspection always did. Also: a keyword broken by a stray space (INS ERT INTO …) is reported as exactly one error naming the whole span — "'INSERT' is split by a space" — with a one-click fix, instead of the generic unknown-keyword message.
0.4.0 — Supported IDE floor drops from 2022.3 to 2021.2: the plugin now ships Java 11 bytecode (2021.2–2022.1 run JetBrains Runtime 11 and cannot load Java 17 class files) and avoids the two APIs that blocked it — ActionUpdateThread (2022.2+) and ContentFactory.getInstance() (2022.3+). Every feature works on every supported version; only the optional integrations vary, and those depend on which plugins the IDE has (VCS for pre-commit, Git for pre-push, the database plugin for SQL-language gutter markers), not on its version. Verified with the JetBrains Plugin Verifier against ten builds: 2021.2, 2021.3, 2022.1, 2022.2, 2022.3, 2023.1, 2023.2, 2023.3, 2024.2 and 2025.1. 2021.1 is not supported — it bundles Kotlin stdlib 1.4, which lacks lowercase(), Char.code and the kotlin.io.path API.
0.3.4 — Release Dry Run… (country + SIT/UAT/PROD picker) is removed. The dry run against the configured datasource stays: right-click a file or folder and choose Dry Run Against Database, or let it run automatically inside Validate Liquibase Repository and the pre-commit/pre-push checks — same read-only execution plan, data preview and live precondition checks, no environment to pick.
0.3.3 — A declared endDelimiter is now verified against the body: if the delimiter (e.g. '/') never appears, Liquibase cannot split the statements — ERROR for multi-statement bodies (they are sent as one and the release fails), warning for single-statement bodies ("terminate with '/'"). Strict rule, applies in the editor, CI/Jenkins gate and Bitbucket PR review.
0.3.2 — Four new rules from the Liquibase formatted-SQL practice guides: a PL/SQL object (package/procedure/function/trigger/type) without endDelimiter is a strict ERROR (Liquibase splits the block on every inner ';' and the deployment fails); CREATE OR REPLACE without runOnChange:true warns (a later edit fails with a checksum error); non-staging DDL mixed with DML in one changeset warns (DDL auto-commits — a later failure leaves the database half-changed); changesets without --comment get a weak warning. The last three are checkboxes under Validation rules.
0.3.1 — Catches the real-world ORA-00933 shape: a missing ';' before COMMIT/ROLLBACK is now detected as a strict ERROR (the database receives "DELETE … COMMIT" as one statement and the deployment fails). New rules from the Liquibase formatted-SQL reference: explicit COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside a changeset warns (Liquibase manages the transaction; configurable), statements before the first --changeset warn (Liquibase never executes them), and a rollback containing only COMMIT warns (use '--rollback empty' instead).
0.3.0 — Validation now mirrors real execution: a missing statement delimiter (';') is an ERROR — Liquibase would send both statements to the database as one and the release would fail right there — instead of a warning. Syntax/delimiter and DDL/schema checks are strictly enforced and cannot be switched off; every other rule is a checkbox under Settings | Tools | Liquibase Sudarshan | Validation rules. The same strict rules apply everywhere: editor, repository report, release simulation/dry run, CLI/CI and Bitbucket PR review.
0.2.5 — Release Dry Run gains a Table differences tab covering EVERY table on either side: NEW (created by this release), database-only (drift), match, or different — with column-level deltas (type, nullability, missing/extra columns), the live row count per table, and this release's data impact (inserts/updates/same/conflicts/skips).
0.2.4 — Bitbucket review simplified per user feedback: no branch scanning or PR auto-detection — paste the PR link and exactly that PR is reviewed. The connection stays remembered (token in the IDE credential store, auto-filled per Bitbucket host, including when pasting a URL for a different host).
0.2.3 — Oracle datasource fix: the schema field's old default 'public' (a PostgreSQL notion) made Oracle connections show 0 tables and miss DATABASECHANGELOG. The default is now empty, and on Oracle a leftover 'public' is treated as unset (PUBLIC is a reserved role and can never own tables) — so existing settings heal themselves.
0.2.2 — Bitbucket review is now connected end to end: the open PR is auto-detected from the checked-out branch's Bitbucket remote (Detect Open PR), the token is remembered in the IDE credential store after the first use, and when a datasource is configured the review also runs the read-only dry run and shows, for every table the PR touches, whether it already exists in the connected database and its row count.
0.2.1 — Compatibility widened: now installs on IntelliJ IDEA 2022.3 and every newer version (was 2023.2+; builds before 2022.2 run on Java 11 and cannot load modern plugins). Verified with the JetBrains Plugin Verifier against 2022.3, 2023.2, 2024.2 and 2025.1. Also fixes a progress-indicator exception during repository validation on 2024.2+.
0.2.0 — Release Dry Run…: pick a country, environment and server and compare — strictly read-only — the data the branch would write against the data in the live database, per column (INSERT / UPDATE with diffs / SAME / CONFLICT); changesets already in DATABASECHANGELOG from previous releases are shown as SKIP and never re-execute. Review Bitbucket PR… (and CLI --bitbucket-pr): fetch a pull request's diff from Bitbucket Cloud or Server/Data Center, validate only its changed lines, and optionally post the review to the PR as inline comments plus a summary. Also: parser robustness fix (malformed VALUES rows could hang the editor) and 100% enforced line coverage of the validation core.
0.1.1 — Marketplace listing polish: point-based description; no functional changes.
0.1.0 — Release execution simulation: Tools | Liquibase Sudarshan | Simulate Release… (and CLI --simulate --country=CC --env=ENV) validates the exact ordered country/environment run Jenkins would execute — sequential schema build-up (tables or FK targets used before their DDL runs, duplicate definitions), cross-file checks (duplicate changeset ids, unique-key collisions), and per-environment policy guardrails (destructive SQL needs an --approved-destructive <ticket> marker, PROD requires rollbacks, PROD never gets environment SQL). Configurable via a repository-root .liquibase-sudarshan.yml; ships a Jenkinsfile gate template.
0.0.2 — Performance and size release: plugin download is ~20x smaller (JDBC drivers are no longer bundled — they load from the classpath, a custom JAR, or a one-click SHA-256-verified download from Maven Central); per-file validation results are cached so unchanged files re-highlight instantly; editing data files no longer invalidates the schema cache (only DDL changes do); lexer fast-path optimizations.
0.0.1 — Initial public release: editor inspections with quick fixes for Liquibase SQL (datatypes, lengths, NULLs, MERGE mappings, duplicates, delimiters, changeset header/attribute typos), pre-commit and pre-push validation, read-only database dry run for PostgreSQL and Oracle (execution plan, INSERT/UPDATE data preview, live precondition checks), datasource tool window with DATABASECHANGELOG browser, and a headless CLI for CI/VS Code. IntelliJ IDEA 2023.2+ (Community and Ultimate), no upper version bound.

idea-plugin.name: Logs - Large Log Viewer
idea-plugin.description:
Open the log file your IDE gives up on.

Logs opens a one gigabyte log file in about five milliseconds and shows you the first screen straight away. The file is never loaded into memory, so opening it does not depend on how big it is, and the IDE does not freeze while it works.

Reading

  • Any size. Reading is done from the disk as you scroll, one block at a time. A one gigabyte file of six million lines was opened, scrolled end to end, searched and filtered on an ordinary laptop, and the index that makes that possible costs about one megabyte of memory for that file.
  • It reopens where you left it. Close the IDE on line 4,999,993 of a gigabyte and that is the line you come back to.
  • Colour by log level. ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG and TRACE, plus SEVERE, FATAL, FINEST and Android's E/ form, read out of plain text, JSON and logfmt lines. A stack trace takes the colour of the message above it, so the whole failure reads as one thing.
  • Filter to the lines you want. Tick the levels to keep, type text to require, or both. On the gigabyte file, filtering six million lines down to the 1,204,544 ERROR lines takes about four seconds, and results appear as the scan runs rather than after it. The gutter keeps the real line numbers from the file, so a filtered line 33 is still line 33 when you talk to a colleague about it.
  • Find without decoding the file. The search runs over the bytes on disk, so it costs the same on a gigabyte as on a small file. Next, previous, match case, and every hit on screen highlighted.
  • Go to a line with the IDE's own Ctrl+G, straight to line five million.
  • Follow the file as it is written, and stay at the end. The file is not locked while you do, so whatever is writing the log can still rotate, rename or truncate it.
  • Select and copy by dragging, shift-clicking, double-clicking a word or triple-clicking a line, with Ctrl+A for all of it. Select more than one copy can hold and it tells you exactly how much it copied instead of quietly truncating.

A log file is still a file, so you can change it

  • Edit a line in place. Press F2 or Enter on a line, and it becomes an editable field. What you type replaces the line. Redacting a password out of a log you are about to attach to a ticket takes two keystrokes.
  • Delete lines. Select them and press Delete. They are struck through and dimmed until you save, and every other line keeps its real number from the file.
  • Add a note. Ctrl+Enter puts a new line under the one you are on, marked with a + in the gutter, so you can write down what you worked out next to the evidence for it.
  • Undo and redo, with Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z. An entry on the undo stack is an action, not a line, so cutting forty thousand lines of startup noise is one Ctrl+Z to put back.
  • Save with Ctrl+S, and only your changes are written. Every untouched byte is copied through as a byte and never decoded and re-encoded, so mixed line endings, a byte order mark and any invalid character already in the file survive exactly as they were. A log holds whatever some process wrote, and redacting one password is not a reason to rewrite the rest of somebody's evidence. An edited gigabyte is written back in about four seconds.
  • Nothing is thrown away silently. Closing a tab with unsaved changes asks Save or Discard; closing the project asks Save, Discard or Cancel, and Cancel really cancels.
  • A log that is read-only on disk stays read-only here, and says so rather than letting you spend ten minutes redacting a file it cannot write.

Configuration you can find, in a screen that explains itself

Settings, then Editor, then Logs. Every level has a colour for light themes and a colour for dark ones, with a live preview drawn by the same code the viewer uses, and a change reaches an open gigabyte file the moment you press OK. No IDE restart, no XML file, no regular expressions to get right before anything is coloured at all.

What it deliberately does not do

Logs does not touch the console output of a process running inside your IDE. That is a different job, several free plugins do it well, and this one stays out of their way. It registers for .log files and their rotated forms such as app.log.1 and app.log.2026-07-25, and nothing else, so it cannot take over a file you wanted opened somewhere else.

Works everywhere JetBrains does. Logs depends only on the platform, so it installs in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, GoLand, Rider, RubyMine, CLion, DataGrip, RustRover and Android Studio, Community editions included.

Pricing, stated plainly

  • $19 per year for a personal licence.
  • $49 per year for a commercial licence.
  • 30-day free trial with everything unlocked. No feature is held back during the trial.
  • There is no free tier. After the trial, Logs needs a licence. Saying so here rather than letting you find out later is the whole point.

If all you need is colour on a small log file, there are free plugins that do that, and you do not need this one. This one exists for the file that is too big for them.

Known limits, stated up front

  • Find and filter read the file on disk. Your unsaved edits are drawn on screen and are written when you save, but until you save, a search or a filter is looking at what is on disk. Save first if you want to search your own changes.
  • Editing is by the line, not by a caret. You replace a line, delete lines, or add a note. There is no free-roaming text caret across the file: that is what makes a six million line file editable at all, and your IDE's ordinary editor is still one click away on the strip at the bottom of the tab for the small files where a caret is what you want.
  • Find is plain text, not regular expressions, and there is no match counter. Case-insensitive matching folds ASCII letters, which covers level names, class names and stack frames but not accented text.
  • A selection is made with the mouse. Shift with the arrow keys does not extend it yet.
  • Some deliberate ceilings, all of which say so on screen rather than failing quietly: one delete covers at most 100,000 lines, a filter shows at most the first 2,000,000 matching lines, one copy holds at most 8 MB, and a single line is displayed up to 64 KB.
  • UTF-16 files are refused with a clear message rather than shown as nonsense. A byte-wise scan cannot split UTF-16 lines correctly, and PowerShell transcripts are the common case, so this is named rather than hidden.
  • Compressed logs (.log.gz) and files that are not on the local disk are not opened.
  • Updating the plugin needs an IDE restart to take effect.

These are on the roadmap. Compatibility with new IDE releases comes first: this plugin is built to keep working when JetBrains ships, and that is treated as a feature, not as maintenance.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2026.1.1

Adds a licensing screen with a direct link to start the free 30-day trial or enter a licence, so licensing can be handled without leaving the editor. Wording and punctuation polish throughout. No functional changes.

2026.1.0 - first release

Opens large log files without loading them into memory: a gigabyte file opens in milliseconds and reopens where you left it. Colouring by log level with a settings screen that applies changes without an IDE restart. Filtering by level and by text, keeping the file's real line numbers. Find over the bytes on disk, Go to Line, following a file as it is written, and selection and copy with an honest cap. Editing a log file in place: replace a line, delete lines, add a note, undo and redo, and a save that copies every untouched byte through unchanged.

idea-plugin.name: LogGlass
idea-plugin.description:
Open huge log files instantly, without freezing your IDE and without making the file read-only.

  • Streams instead of loading. A multi-gigabyte log opens in seconds because only the line offsets are indexed; lines are read from disk as you scroll.
  • Never blocks the UI. Indexing and filtering run on background threads with a cancellable progress bar.
  • Leaves your files alone. LogGlass opens a separate viewer. It never marks the underlying file read-only and never modifies it.
  • Level highlighting and instant filtering for ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG and TRACE.
idea-plugin.change-notes:

  • First release.
  • Open any file in the LogGlass viewer from the project tree or editor context menu.
  • Streaming line index so large logs open without loading the file into memory.
  • Filter by text and by severity level.

idea-plugin.name: JSONL Lens: JSON Lines / NDJSON Viewer
idea-plugin.description:
A million-line .jsonl file should be something you can just open. JSONL Lens opens it in place: records are indexed in the background and read on demand, so the first page shows before the index finishes and memory stays low whatever the file size.

The viewer is free and stays free. Pro is a subscription for this plugin: USD 1.90 a month or USD 19 a year for individual use. For organizations it is, per user, USD 3.90 a month or USD 39 a year.

The record-per-line file every pipeline emits opens in an IDE tab, and Pro writes the page or the matches back out as a Parquet table.

JSONL, JSON Lines and NDJSON are one format under three names, and this is a viewer for all of them. Every .jsonl / .ndjson file gets a JSONL Lens editor tab alongside the regular editor, including files far beyond the IDE's large file limit.

The free tier is permanent.

Free - the full JSONL viewer, for files of any size:

  • Any size: streaming line index, cancellable, with progress; browse records while indexing runs
  • Find in file: full-text search across every record (Ctrl+F), case toggle, next/previous jump between matching records, highlighted hits in the record view, and a matches-only mode that pages through just the hits, built on the same streaming scan, so it works on multi-gigabyte files
  • Record browser: paginated table with raw line and pretty-printed JSON views, jump to record number
  • Grid view: records as rows, fields as columns, with the column set derived from a sample of the file
  • Schema stats: field names, types, null/missing rates, min/max/avg for numerics, distinct value counts and approximate token counts, computed on a clearly labeled sample (first 1000 + 1000 random records)
  • Compressed files: .jsonl.gz / .ndjson.gz open transparently (decompressed to a temporary file, cleaned up when the tab closes)
  • Malformed input: malformed lines, blank lines, CRLF endings and oversized records are handled and reported, and the file still opens

The browser pages to the last line of the file, with no record cap. In the grid view a nested object is flattened into dot-path columns, so meta.source becomes a column of its own, and a value that is itself an object or an array shows as one-line JSON in its cell. It runs on 2024.2 and newer with no upper build, and every release is checked across that whole range before it ships, Community, Ultimate and the newest preview build among them. Only .jsonl, .ndjson, .ldjson and .jsonlines files are claimed, with their .gz forms, never plain .json, and the text editor stays the tab that opens first for a file it can show. A file too large for it opens on the JSONL Lens tab first.

Pro - optional paid tier, for working with the data:

  • Filter queries: keep only the records where fields match, for example lang == "en" && score >= 0.5, scanned across the whole file, then browse just the matches
  • Export: write the current page, search matches or filter matches out to a new .jsonl, CSV or Parquet file; in the Parquet file nested values land as JSON text columns
  • Full-file stats: run the schema stats over every record, exact rather than sampled

Each Lens plugin comes with its own free 30-day Pro trial. A year of continuous subscription earns JetBrains' perpetual fallback license: the version available when that year started stays yours for good, including its fixes.

It is built for machine learning and data engineering work: training data, eval sets, model outputs, exports and logs.

Part of the Lens family, eight viewers built on one engine; JSONL Lens, Log Lens and Parquet Lens share one filter query language in Pro. Log Lens reads multi-gigabyte service logs the same way, with level chips and follow mode. Parquet Lens does it for Parquet, Arrow, and Feather datasets. Those two export to JSONL from their Pro tiers, as do SQLite Lens, DuckDB Lens and XLSX Lens, so their output opens here as a browsable grid. Export as Parquet from Pro and, when Parquet Lens is installed, one click on the finished-export balloon opens the file there.

The guides and the overview of all eight viewers are at twilightventures.dev. Write to support@twilightventures.dev about anything to do with the plugin or a purchase, suggestions included; for a bug, name the version and the rough size of the file, or use the issue reporter at the end of the Help menu, which opens a prefilled new issue in your browser for you to read before you post.

Runs entirely locally: the plugin makes no network calls and handles no credentials, and Pro license state is read from the IDE's own licensing system.

What it does not do:

  • No editing by design: your file is never modified; a Pro export writes a new file and leaves the original alone.
  • Not a formatter or linter: malformed lines are reported and shown as they are, not rewritten.
  • Filter queries are field predicates, not SQL: no joins, no aggregations.

If JSONL Lens helps you, a short review tells us what to work on next.
