idea-plugin.name: ADB Pro
idea-plugin.description:
ADB Pro — Android Build, AAB, Signing, R8, Release, and CI/CD Toolkit

ADB Pro is an Android Studio and IntelliJ IDEA plugin for developers who want the Android release workflow inside the IDE instead of scattered across Gradle commands, bundletool scripts, signing utilities, lint reports, dependency commands, and CI templates.

It helps teams prepare Android apps for real distribution: build variants, inspect AAB/APK artifacts, verify signing identity, run release readiness checks, generate R8/ProGuard rules, analyze bundle size, manage dependencies, run lint, configure CI/CD, and set up new projects from one tool window.

Release Readiness for real artifacts

Release Readiness checks both local and remote AAB artifacts before upload or promotion. It records artifact SHA-256, extracts signing certificate SHA-1 and SHA-256, lets you classify certificates as production upload, Play app signing, debug, staging, or internal test identities, and remembers remote scan results from configured repositories.

The checklist is designed to catch quiet release mistakes that normal builds can miss: debug builds, debuggable manifests, missing or unexpected signing certificates, test or staging environment markers, cleartext traffic, test domains, hardcoded API keys, target SDK deadlines, versionCode problems, privacy permission concerns, missing icons, test files in the bundle, oversized artifacts, R8/ProGuard configuration gaps, and persistence or reflection models that may be broken by minification.

AAB, APK, signing, and installation tools

  • AAB Tools: Convert Android App Bundles to APK sets, install AABs to devices, manage bundletool automatically, scan configured remote repositories, and cache remote AAB artifacts for inspection.
  • Signing Tools: Sign APKs, run zipalign, verify signatures, inspect signing metadata, and manage keystore-based release workflows.
  • Bundle Inspector: Analyze AAB/APK contents, compare size across versions, track size history, identify large files, detect redundant resources, and review WebP conversion opportunities.
  • Device Manager: Discover ADB devices, monitor connection state, and select target devices quickly for install and build workflows.

Build, quality, and optimization workflow

  • Build Tools: Run Gradle builds, select variants, execute batch builds, inspect build output, and keep build history.
  • R8 Assistant: Generate ProGuard/R8 keep rules from dependency templates, scan reflection usage, inspect mapping files, deobfuscate stack traces, and reduce minification risk.
  • Resource Obfuscation: Configure AabResGuard visually with obfuscation dictionaries and release-oriented resource shrinking workflows.
  • Lint Tools: Run Android Lint tasks, load XML/HTML reports, show parsed issues by severity, filter findings, and manage lint baselines.
  • Dependency Health: Analyze dependency trees, detect conflicts, duplicates, downgrades, deprecated libraries, unused version catalog entries, and hardcoded dependency versions.
  • Build Performance: Review Gradle configuration health, build performance indicators, and optimization suggestions.

Project setup and automation

  • Quick Setup: Configure Android channels, SDK dependencies, version properties, signing config, R8 rules, ResGuard, CI/CD files, and project defaults with automatic backup and undo support.
  • CI/CD Tools: Generate pipeline configuration for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Gitee Go, and Android release automation workflows.
  • Web Navigation: Open curated Android developer resources for repositories, official documentation, backend services, testing, analytics, CI/CD, app stores, and optimization tools.
  • Logs: Review local ADB Pro operation logs and diagnostics from inside the tool window.
  • Dashboard: See project health, version and SDK information, quick actions, recent activity, and release-oriented status summaries.

Local-first workflow

ADB Pro stores analysis data, logs, scan history, and configuration locally in the IDE or project workspace. It does not automatically upload your source code, signing files, AABs, APKs, or analysis reports.

Compatibility

Works with Android Studio and IntelliJ IDEA 2022.3+. Requires Java 17 and an Android Gradle project with a Gradle wrapper for build-related actions.

idea-plugin.name: Kt-Typealias-Ts
idea-plugin.description:
Enhances Kotlin's typealias by enforcing strict compile-time type safety.

This plugin prevents accidental mixing of distinct typealiases that share the same underlying type (e.g., preventing assigning a UserId to an OrderId, even if both are strings).

Features:

  • Assignment Safety — Prevents cross-assignment between distinct typealiases
  • Function Call Validation — Enforces strict argument matching
  • Return Type Enforcement — Validates return expressions
  • Equality/Comparison Warnings — Flags comparisons between distinct aliases
  • Lambda Return Checking — Validates lambda body return types
  • When/If Branch Checking — Ensures all branches match expected alias
  • Property Delegation — Checks by lazy and delegate providers
  • Generic Type Alias Support — Recursive type argument checking
  • Nullable Alias Handling — Proper UserId? vs ProductId? detection
  • Quick-Fix Actions — IDE suggestions to fix mismatches
  • Opt-in Mode — Only check @TypeSafe annotated aliases
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • EqualityChecker: Warns when comparing values of different typealiases (==, !=, ===, !==).
  • LambdaReturnChecker: Validates lambda body implicit and explicit return types against expected type context.
  • BranchExpressionChecker: Ensures all when/if branches yield consistent typealiases when used as value expressions.
  • DelegationChecker: Checks by lazy { ... } and delegate providers for typealias consistency.
  • Nullable alias handling: Properly unwraps nullability so UserId? vs ProductId? is still detected as a mismatch.
  • Generic/collection alias support: Recursive type argument checking (e.g., List<UserId> vs List<ProductId>).
  • Quick-fix actions: IDE suggestions including "Change variable type", "Suppress for statement", and "Wrap with type alias".
  • @TypeSafe annotation: Opt-in mode where only annotated typealiases are inspected.
  • Settings panel: Configurable inspection mode and per-checker enable/disable toggles (Settings > Tools > Typealias Safety).
  • DiagnosticMessages utility: Enhanced error messages that include expanded type information.
  • Opt-in filter: shouldInspectAlias() respects settings mode and annotation presence.

Changed

  • AliasInfo model now includes isNullable and typeArguments fields for richer type representation.
  • isTypealiasMismatch() now recursively checks type arguments for generic alias mismatches.
  • All checkers now produce enhanced diagnostic messages via DiagnosticMessages utility.
  • All checkers respect the opt-in annotation filter via shouldInspectAlias().
  • TypealiasSafetyInspection now routes to all new checkers with settings-based enable/disable support.
  • Plugin description updated to reflect all new capabilities.
  • plugin.xml registers applicationService and applicationConfigurable for settings.

idea-plugin.name: CatalogLens
idea-plugin.description:
Makes Gradle version catalogs (libs.versions.toml) navigable, and shows what they actually resolve to.
  • Ctrl/Cmd-click any [libraries] entry to open its Maven Central or MvnRepository page.
  • Gutter icons on [versions] entries open upstream release notes inline in a tool window (GitHub releases and developer.android.com changelogs), with one-click "use this version" pinning.
  • Sort catalog groups A→Z — a floating editor icon opens a diff preview; tick exactly the groups you want sorted, then apply or cancel. Blank lines and comments delimit groups and stay in place.
  • Resolved-version inlay hints when a dependency resolves to a version other than the one declared, a "Why this version?" insight that explains the selection, and a catalog-vs-resolved delta — all in the "CatalogLens Resolved" tool window. (Requires the bundled Gradle plugin.)
  • Alt+Enter on any entry to copy its Gradle dependency declaration to the clipboard.
Catalog links are built locally — no network access just to edit.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 0.7.7: the Releases tool window now renders Markdown changelogs as well. A link to a repository's CHANGELOG.md — OkHttp, Retrofit, Coil, Moshi, Picasso, desugar_jdk_libs, the Facebook Android SDK — opens inline with the same per-version cards you already get for GitHub Releases and developer.android.com: the entry matching your catalog is marked "current", and every other one offers a one-click "Use this version" that pins it into libs.versions.toml. Which heading starts a release is worked out per file, so Keep a Changelog (## [3.6.2] - September 4, 2026), ## Version 5.5.0 and underlined Version 2.1.5 *(2018-03-07)* all split correctly while ### Added subsections stay inside the release they belong to. Reference-style links are resolved into real links and their definition block is dropped, so the notes read cleanly, and the file is fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com — no GitHub API rate limit, and repository renames keep working. Fixed: developer.android.com pages no longer show an empty "Version 1.3 — No release notes" card with a meaningless "Use 1.3" button. Those headings only group a release series (DataStore, Room, Media3, Compose, Navigation and most other AndroidX pages), so they are now dropped, or kept as a plain divider with no version to pin when they carry a compatibility note of their own; a stable release that groups its own pre-releases keeps both its notes and its pin. Also fixed: the "Open in browser" link no longer draws a focus ring when the tool window opens, _2026-08-16_-style dates now render as emphasis instead of raw underscores, and a page that loads but holds no recognisable version notes now says exactly that instead of blaming your connection. Bundled artifact map refreshed: OkHttp and Retrofit have moved to the lysine-dev organisation and Square's old hosted changelog is gone, so both now point at the live repositories. Added Navigation3, ProfileInstaller, Baseline Profile, LocalBroadcastManager, the Facebook Android SDK and the Koin compiler plugin, plus per-library group prefixes for Compose animation, compiler, foundation, material, material3 and runtime so those resolve to their own release notes instead of the umbrella Compose page.
  • 0.7.5: new "Resolved Dependencies" surface — see what your version catalog actually resolves to, not just what it declares. End-of-line inlay hints in libs.versions.toml show the resolved version whenever it differs from the declared one. Click a hint (or right-click an entry → "Why this version?") to resolve the artifact through Gradle and see why that version was selected — selection reasons, the requested-by chain, and one-click re-resolution in another configuration — in a new "CatalogLens Resolved" tool window. Capture a resolved baseline, then "Compute Resolved Delta" to diff the catalog against it: what you changed, transitive ripples, catalog pins a transitive overrode, and rejected/excluded artifacts. Plus a new Alt+Enter intention on any [libraries], [bundles] or [plugins] entry to copy its Gradle dependency declaration — implementation(libs.…) / alias(libs.plugins.…) — to the clipboard. Requires the bundled Gradle plugin.
  • 0.6.0: changelogs now open inline in a new "CatalogLens Releases" tool window instead of the browser. GitHub release pages are fetched via the REST API (tag, date, formatted notes, clickable links; cached 30 minutes for the unauthenticated rate limit) and developer.android.com pages (androidx, AGP, Play Core, …) are parsed and rendered the same way, split into per-version cards. The viewer knows your catalog version: the matching entry is marked "current", and every other version shows a "Use this version" link that pins it straight into libs.versions.toml (undoable). Theme-aware colors, selectable headers, soft-wrapping. Pages that can't be parsed fall back to the browser. Also expanded the bundled artifact map with many more AndroidX and third-party release links.
  • 0.5.4: expanded bundled artifact map — added changelog links for Paparazzi, detekt, ktlint, Turbine, Dokka, ML Kit, OpenTelemetry, mockk, Mockito, Hamcrest, assertk, Compose Hot Reload, koin-annotations, flow-preferences, JWTDecode, compose-stable-marker, and others; new group-prefix fallbacks for GMS, Google Maps, ZXing, Salesforce Marketing Cloud, and more.
  • 0.5.3: sort preview now lists each unsorted group with a checkbox — pick exactly which groups to sort, with a live diff preview. Safer apply: keeps caret and scroll position, aborts if the document changed underneath, dialog size is remembered. Quoted keys now sort by their unquoted name.
  • 0.5.2: sort preview result pane editable — revert individual hunks before applying.
  • 0.5.1: maintenance release — links always open in the system browser.
  • 0.5.0: new editor action — sort catalog entries A→Z within each group (blank lines, comments and table headers act as delimiters and stay in place), with a diff preview where individual changes can be reverted before applying. Available from a floating editor icon and the editor context menu.
  • 0.4.0: Maven Central links open the Versions tab directly; maven.google.com links open the artifact's full version list (no stale pre-selected version).
  • 0.3.0: Google-Maven-only artifacts (androidx, com.android, Firebase, GMS, ML Kit, …) now link to maven.google.com instead of a dead Maven Central page.
  • 0.2.0: per-file cached catalog index (faster highlighting on large catalogs), long-form [plugins] entries now resolved, settings UI fixes (table editing no longer interrupted, robust bindings), global settings now roam via Settings Sync.
  • 0.1.0: artifact links on [libraries] entries, upstream changelog gutter icons on [versions] entries, bundled artifact map with project/global overrides.

idea-plugin.name: LogPose
idea-plugin.description:
LogPose — see what your Android app is actually doing, right in the IDE

LogPose turns your app's runtime behaviour into a clean, structured timeline inside a tool window — network, pushes, database, background work and feature flags — and lets you mock any response straight back to the device. No proxy, no certificates, no adb logcat | grep: a one-line OkHttp interceptor emits each exchange and the plugin reassembles it.

Your coding agent can read the running app

LogPose exposes the live capture over MCP, so Claude Code — or any MCP client — reads the running app and you just ask: "what failed in the last 2 minutes?", "which worker ran 20 times on startup?", or "mock /v1/orders to return a 500 so I can see the error UI." Real traffic, not a log line you pasted. Click ⚡ Connect Coding Agent to copy the command; it serves on the IDE's built-in web server, localhost only, authenticated with a per-project token that also selects which project's capture to read.

  • Read — list_events, get_event, get_trace, find_failures, session_summary
  • Follow one id — get_related returns every event carrying a business id (order_id 21053953) as a timeline, across traces and including rows with no trace at all; list_correlation_keys says which keys this project uses
  • Diagnose — query_hotspots, worker_history, config_changes: "what's making this screen slow?", "did SyncWorker retry?", "what flag changed before this broke?"
  • Change what the app receives — create_mock, set_mock_enabled, delete_mock, list_mocks, plus list_scenarios / load_scenario / save_scenario for whole bottled sessions, so an agent can reproduce a state and verify its own fix without you driving the UI
  • Start a flow and wait for the result — inject_fcm delivers a synthetic push into the running app and await_event blocks until what it triggered arrives: trigger → await → assert, with no polling
  • Response bodies can be withheld while still exposing request shape, statuses and timings

Capture

  • One row per HTTP exchange — request and response together, never interleaved, never cut off by logcat's ~4 KB line limit
  • Firebase Cloud Messaging pushes and token refreshes appear inline in the same timeline, so you can read push → API call → UI as one story
  • Database, background work and remote config — Room queries show their operation and table, a WorkManager request occupies one row that updates as it runs and badges its retries, and a remote-config activation reports exactly which flags changed with before → after values
  • Your own events — LogPose.event("UserDao.insert") { … } puts any subsystem on the same timeline; events carry their own presentation, so they render with no plugin update
  • Duplicate detection flags repeated calls and likely double-submits

Inspect

  • Collapsible JSON trees plus a real IDE JSON editor (folding, line numbers) in Raw mode
  • One-click filters: URL search and type toggles (NET / FCM / DB / WORK / CONF / ANLY / APP) always on the bar, with method, status, hide-noise and duplicates-only a click away in the Filters popover — every active choice echoes as a removable chip
  • Copy as cURL, copy JSON or a response body, find within a body
  • Multi-select rows and copy the call sequence as plain text — ideal for bug reports
  • First-class multipart upload (S3 / GCS) metadata instead of raw bytes

Mock & replay

  • Right-click any captured request → Mock this endpoint and serve a response without touching backend or app code
  • Replace the whole body, or merge your JSON into the real response: override one field, add keys, and let everything else stay backend-generated
  • Edit the response field by field — fold what you don't need, tick exactly what to override, and see the original value beside your change
  • Inject latency, timeouts and connection failures, cap how many times a rule serves, and match paths with * wildcards
  • Narrow a rule to requests carrying particular query parameters, headers or body text, and serve a different response per hit — a 500 then a 200 tests retry logic in one rule
  • Rules sync to the device over adb, report live hit counts, and clear themselves when you stop capturing — mocked rows are badged, so the timeline never lies about what the app actually received
  • Save a rule set, or a whole recorded session, as a committable scenario file and load it to put the app in a known state offline

Drive

  • Inject a push — most mobile journeys start with one, so LogPose delivers a synthetic FCM data message into the running app in-process (no Play services, no network). Re-send a captured push verbatim, or compose a new one
  • Trace waterfall — read a whole flow on one time axis: what the push set off, what overlapped, what is still running, and what took the longest
  • Correlation keys — group that flow by the id you actually know (order_id 21053953) rather than a trace hash. The key names a value; the value is matched anywhere in an event, so the group spans traces and reaches rows that carry none. Paste an id from a ticket with Find by value…

Requires the logpose-android interceptor in your debug/staging build (a zero-overhead no-op ships for release). Mocking needs logpose-android 1.2.1+; database, worker, config and app events need 1.4.0+; push injection and the new mock matchers/steps need 1.7.0+, and 1.7.1+ collapses an injected push and the app's own re-log of it into a single row. Correlation keys need no library support at all — they read the payloads you already emit. Works in IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio, light and dark.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• Each kind's row says the useful thing. A wall of repeated polling collapses to one line with an ×N pill, the median duration and an occurrence ‹ n/N › stepper in the detail (it breaks on any non-2xx — a failed poll always stands alone). DB rows lead with the verb and the table, with the full statement greyed behind them, and BEGIN/END ceremony folds into a single muted transaction ✓ · 4 statements · 128ms row. Worker rows state their state with shape and semantics — ✓ succeeded, ● running with a live count-up, ✕ failed, an outlined RETRY ×N — and surface the tag that tells one DataSyncWorker from another. Analytics rows drop the · ANALYTICS echo and put the screen in the fact column.
  • A systematic visual pass — one axis owns hue. Amber used to mean PUT, 4xx, db, warning, timeout and pending-sync at once. Now kind keeps the seven hues (row glyph, TYPE chip, detail pill, waterfall bars — nowhere else), status carries only semantics (2xx/3xx neutral, amber = warning, red = failure), method drops colour entirely and encodes read-vs-write by weight, and anything LogPose itself caused (MOCK, INJ) is the only solid accent fill in a row.
  • Rows reclaimed 46–92px each — FCM and structured rows no longer reserve empty method/status columns for a grid only HTTP uses. The hover ⧉ cURL and ⇉ flow affordances became real buttons that stay visible on the selected row instead of hiding until you hover.
  • The filter bar earns its space — search, type chips and the count stay; method, status, hide-noise and duplicates moved into a Filters popover with a badge, and every active choice echoes as a removable chip on a second row. That row is also where two previously silent behaviours finally explain themselves: "status filter → showing HTTP only" and "db hidden by default". Below ~440px the type chips collapse to glyphs.
  • "Filtered to nothing" is its own state — it names the count and the filter actually narrowing the list, and offers a loosener picked by measuring which one would reveal the most events, instead of showing the setup guide to someone who already has 218 events captured.
  • The waterfall got its first design pass — axis labels below the canvas, durations right-aligned in a fixed column, lanes sharing the list's selection model, and open spans pulsing on a smooth ease. (It also fixed a real bug: span bars were painting at 27% alpha instead of 70%.)
  • Group a flow by the id you actually know — define your app's correlation keys (order_id, trip_id) in the filter bar's ⋯ → Correlation keys…, seeded with suggestions found in the capture, and every entry point reads order_id 21053953 instead of a trace hash. The key only names a value; the value does the matching — anywhere in an event's url, bodies, FCM data, db args or sections — so a group spans several traces and reaches the GET /order/21053953/ that carries no trace at all. The scan parses JSON nested inside string values (an FCM data["body"]), and matching is delimiter-bounded with a 4-character floor, so 2105 never matches 21053953. Keys are per project; LogPose ships none of its own, and a suggestion groups nothing until you tick it.
  • Open a flow from anywhere — a row's menu leads with Show waterfall — order_id 21053953 and Filter by order_id 21053953 (trace actions still there, now labelled as traces); the hover band that shows ⧉ cURL also shows a ⇉ flow glyph that opens the row's best grouping in one click; the waterfall header states what it grouped by and offers a switcher between order_id / trip_id / trace; and a key filter appears as a removable chip. Find by value… needs no row at all: paste an id from a ticket or a backend log and it tells you how many events carry it before you commit.
  • Two new MCP tools (21 total) — get_related returns everything carrying one business id in get_trace's shape (by key + value, by a bare pasted value, or by event_id), and list_correlation_keys reports the configured vocabulary plus inert suggestions. get_trace now explains an empty result — an app that mints its own trace for a push, or an HTTP client not built with LogPose.traceCalls(...), is the usual reason — and points at get_related.
  • An injected push is one row again — the app's own FirebaseMessagingService re-logging a push LogPose injected used to add an unmarked twin beside it. With logpose-android ≥ 1.7.1 both emissions share the message id, so they collapse into one row that stays marked INJ. Note the consequence: the surviving row carries the app's trace rather than the injection's, which is one more reason to group these by key.
  • Start a flow, don't just watch it — right-click any captured push → Re-send this push, or Compose push… for a new one: LogPose delivers it into the running app in-process, no Play services and no network. Register LogPose.onPushInject { } in app init (or keep a FirebaseMessagingService in the manifest and LogPose finds it reflectively). Injected pushes appear as ordinary FCM rows marked INJ, and the device reports which tier consumed it. Simulates foreground data-message delivery — not the system notification tray. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.7.0.
  • Scenarios — save the current mocks, or snapshot the whole session, into a committable .logpose/scenarios/<name>.json, then load it to put the app in a known state offline. A snapshot builds one rule per endpoint from the latest real response, skips (and counts) endpoints with no completed response, and never re-serves LogPose's own mocked rows as if the backend had said them. Scenario files contain captured bodies — review before committing.
  • Trace waterfall — a new detail card lays a whole trace on one time axis: a lane per event, spans as bars, point events as dots, in-flight spans drawn out to now, with the event count, wall span and slowest event in the header. Open it from a row's context menu (Show waterfall) or by clicking the trace chip on any detail card; click a lane to jump to its row.
  • Richer mocks — an Only when… section matches on query parameters, headers and a request-body substring, and a Then respond… step list serves a different response per hit (500 then 200 tests retry logic in one rule). Body matching fails closed, so a body the device can't buffer goes to the network rather than being mocked on a guess. Rules using these are withheld from a device on an older library instead of being pushed and silently ignored. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.7.0.
  • Five new MCP tools (19 total) — await_event blocks until the event you're waiting for arrives, so an agent's loop becomes trigger → await → assert instead of polling list_events; inject_fcm sends or replays a push and returns the trace it delivered inside; list_scenarios / load_scenario / save_scenario expose the scenario files. create_mock gains match_query, match_headers, match_body_contains and responses.
  • The mocks strip tells the truth about sync — pushed revision vs the one the device acknowledged, so pending and failed read as pending and failed; a broadcast adb refused is caught (am prints errors and still exits 0); an ack that never arrives raises a notification instead of hijacking the detail pane; and the device's active rule count now surfaces the reinstall-reset case. "Loaded" is not "live", and the strip finally says which.
  • No-op parity is now enforced — the release stub had drifted (it was missing LogPoseInterceptor(config, emitter), so a custom sink compiled in debug and failed in release). Fixed, and a reflection parity test in the library build fails on the next drift.
  • Headless capture export for CI — with logpose-android ≥ 1.6.0 and LogPoseConfig(exportEnabled = true), scripts/export-capture.sh dumps the whole capture as NDJSON over adb, so a pipeline can assert on the wire with no IDE/MCP session. create_mock now warns when a timeout/ connection_failure has latency_ms = 0 (it throws instantly, testing the failure path, not an in-flight window), and a mocked request shows an in-flight row while its latency plays out. push-mocks.sh --verify reads the device ack back to confirm rules actually applied.
  • Async HTTP rows can join a trace — wrap a flow in LogPose.withTrace { } or traceContext() and, with the client set up via LogPose.traceCalls(...), the request's row lands in the same get_trace group as the flow's other events — even across a viewModelScope.launch. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.5.7.
  • Honest mock hit counts — list_mocks now reports served, counted from the captured mocked responses in the buffer, instead of the device counter that read 0 while a rule was demonstrably serving. create_mock's warning names the real precondition (restart the app so it announces itself to this capture). Ambient trace now also covers the FCM row itself, and LogPose.continueTrace { } carries a trace across a viewModelScope.launch — both need logpose-android ≥ 1.5.6.
  • Reliability & test-orchestration — capture now reports whether it's running (and auto-reattaches after an adb drop, so it no longer dies silently on a reinstall); create_mock warns loudly when no device is synced; a new clear_capture tool and a scripts/push-mocks.sh make the mocked tier runnable in CI; chatty analytics/DB feeds are capped so they can't evict the events you care about; and stale mocks are pruned on a new app run. Ambient trace scope LogPose.withTrace { } needs logpose-android ≥ 1.5.5.
  • Typed rows & detail — every row leads with a colour-coded type glyph (one hue per kind); non-network rows keep the method/status columns clear so the centre lines up, and the type is stated once instead of as a doubled, truncated pill. TYPE filter chips are lit in the matching hue, and the detail pane renders flat key/value data as a table.
  • Analytics on the timeline — LogPose.logAnalytics(...) puts every analytics event next to the API call and screen that fired it, with an ANLY filter chip. A new analytics_events MCP tool verifies event contracts and returns the observed screen-to-screen flow. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.5.4.
  • Quick mock diff — a diff button on each mock row opens the original captured response beside what the rule serves, without opening the editor first.
  • Replayed workers — WorkManager replays finished work from earlier runs to a fresh observer, which used to look like it ran again this session (why a worker could read as "20 runs on startup"). Those are now marked with a muted replayed badge, and worker_history splits "ran this session" from replays. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.5.3.
  • 1.7.1 — the coding-agent docs now lead with example prompts ("what failed in the last 2 minutes?", "mock /v1/orders to return a 500") so it's obvious what to ask. No behaviour change.
  • Sessions — a capture that spans an app restart is no longer reported as one timeline. Each run is reported separately, with its own span and counts, and list_events can be scoped to one run. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.5.0.
  • Wider redaction by default — credential headers beyond Authorization (API-KEY, X-Auth-Token, vendor tokens matched by name) are masked before anything leaves the device. Update logpose-android to pick this up.
  • Summaries you can act on — session_summary now returns the ids behind every failure and duplicate burst instead of bare counts, identical failures collapse into one entry with a count, and kinds that never fired report zero rather than going missing.
  • Database, background work and remote config on the timeline — the three things every Android app has, now first-class alongside HTTP and FCM. Room queries show their operation and table (users · SELECT id FROM users), a WorkManager request occupies one row that updates as it runs and badges its retries, and a remote-config activation reports exactly which flags changed, with before → after values. New DB / WORK / CONF filter chips, and MCP tools for "what's making this screen slow?", "did SyncWorker retry?" and "what flag changed before this broke?". Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.4.0.
  • Your coding agent can read the running app — LogPose now exposes the live capture over MCP, so Claude Code (or any MCP client) can answer "what did the app actually request, and why did it fail?" from real traffic instead of a pasted log line — and can create a mock to reproduce or unblock a state. Click ⚡ Connect Coding Agent to copy the command. Served on the IDE's built-in web server, localhost only, authenticated with a per-project token.
  • Log anything, not just HTTP — LogPose.event("UserDao.insert") { … } puts your own subsystems on the same timeline: database queries, background jobs, analytics, feature flags, navigation. Events carry their own presentation, so they render with no plugin update. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.4.0; older versions keep working unchanged.
  • New look — a redesigned brand mark (a prompt that points north), native IDE context menus, and a roomier, better-organised mock editor.
  • Field-by-field mock editing — edit a captured response as a tree: fold what you don't need, edit any value in place, and in merge mode tick exactly the fields to override (a changed value shows the original beside it). Add new keys, drop to raw text, or hit Compare with original for a side-by-side diff of what the app will actually receive.
  • Merge (patch) mocks — keep the real backend response and deep-merge your JSON on top: override one field, add keys, leave the rest untouched. Merging now recurses into arrays by index, so you can change a field inside data[0] without replacing the array. Needs logpose-android ≥ 1.2.1.
  • Mock & replay — right-click a captured request → "Mock this endpoint…" to serve a response back to the app instead of hitting the network: edit status/body/headers, add latency, or simulate a timeout / connection failure. Rules live in a Mocks strip (toggle, edit, delete, hit counts), persist per project, and mocked rows carry a purple MOCK pill. Requires logpose-android ≥ 1.1.0 on the device.
  • FCM push messages in the timeline — Firebase Cloud Messaging pushes and token refreshes now appear inline alongside HTTP traffic, tagged FCM with a NOTIF/DATA/TOKEN badge. Selecting one shows the notification, metadata, and the data payload as a JSON tree. A new TYPE filter (NET/FCM) narrows the stream. Feed events from your FirebaseMessagingService via the new LogPose.logFcmMessage / logFcmToken library API.
  • Failed requests now show why — instead of an opaque "(failed)", the Response and Overview cards display the captured exception (connection reset, timeout, cleartext-not-permitted, …) so the failure is diagnosable.
  • Duplicate-call detection — repeated identical requests fired in a quick burst are flagged with a DUP ×N tag; overlapping non-idempotent calls (double-submits) are highlighted in red, with a warning in the overview and a "Dupes" filter to isolate them.
  • Raw JSON now colors keys vs. values (matching the tree), shows line numbers, and pre-collapses deeply-nested nodes on large payloads.
  • Response headers are hidden by default behind a "Headers" toggle (request headers stay shown) — no more CSP noise drowning the body.
  • Light-theme support (adapts to the IDE theme)
  • Raw JSON mode is now a real editor with code folding
  • One-click filter bar (method/status toggles, Hide-noise switch)
  • Find in request/response, server trace-id in the overview
  • Multi-select rows and copy the call sequence as a plain-text timeline
  • Helpful empty state

idea-plugin.name: Compose Optimizer

idea-plugin.name: StringSmith - Android Strings Toolkit
idea-plugin.description:
StringSmith turns strings.xml management from a chore into a smooth workflow. Extract hardcoded literals with context-aware replacement, rename keys and update every reference in one undoable action, copy resources across locales, and flag duplicate or dead entries — all without leaving the editor. Works in Android and Kotlin / Compose Multiplatform projects, in both K1 and K2 modes.

Getting started: put the caret on a hardcoded string and press Ctrl+Alt+X (or Alt+Enter → Extract to strings.xml). Pick a key — done.

Extract

  • Context-aware replacement: stringResource in Composables, getString in Activity/Fragment/View, R.string in other Kotlin, @string/ in XML layouts
  • Kotlin Multiplatform / Compose Multiplatform: stringResource(Res.string.key) with auto-imported generated Res (package auto-detected, overridable in settings)
  • Auto-import for Compose stringResource with sorted imports
  • Duplicate-value detection during extract — reuse an existing key instead of adding a copy
  • Multi-locale propagation across values-* folders
  • Kotlin template expressions extracted as format args ("Hello $name" → %1$s + argument)
  • Quick-fix intention on hardcoded literals (Alt+Enter)
  • Quick Extract — skips the dialog when the target is unambiguous (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+X)
  • Batch Extract — extract every string in a file in one pass, with colour-coded per-row status and a one-click Fix collisions action (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+B)
  • Key suggestions romanize Greek/Cyrillic and strip Latin accents (Καλημέρα → kalimera)
  • @Preview composables excluded by default (configurable)

Edit

  • Rename a string key and edit its default + per-locale values in one undoable step (Ctrl+Alt+E or Alt+Enter)
  • Renames every R.string.key, Res.string.key, and @string/key reference, scoped to the declaring module and its dependents — and reports how many were updated

Duplicate

  • Copy a resource to a new key across res/values/strings.xml and every values-* locale in one undoable step (Ctrl+Alt+D or Alt+Enter)
  • Reuses each locale's existing translation; untranslated locales are skipped, not filled with the default
  • Optionally redirects the reference under the caret to the new key

Navigate

  • Alt+Click on a <string name="…"> entry in strings.xml lists every usage of the key (R.string.key, Res.string.key, @string/key) and jumps there — or shows a picker with a code snippet and File.kt:line when there is more than one. Works in Android and Compose Multiplatform.
  • Ctrl+Click jumps to the same key in the other values-* locale files. On Android this is the IDE's native gesture; StringSmith adds it for Compose Multiplatform, where it is missing.
  • Generated Res accessors are excluded; matches on the same line collapse to one entry

Inspect

  • Hardcoded string highlight (opt-in)
  • Duplicate value in strings.xml (same text, different keys)
  • Unused string resource (no reference anywhere)
  • Format-string mismatch across locales — a locale whose %s/%d arguments don't match the default entry (crashes at runtime); covers Compose Multiplatform, which Android Lint doesn't check

Settings: key prefix and naming convention, replacement style per context, locale defaults, format-arg detection, inspection toggles, exclusion patterns, custom Composable wrapper names, and a live key preview.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Changed

  • Find usages moved to Alt+Click. Listing every place a <string name="…"> key is referenced is now bound to Alt+Click (and the editor right-click menu) instead of Ctrl+Click, freeing Ctrl+Click for locale navigation (below). Works the same in Android and Compose Multiplatform.

Added

  • Ctrl+Click between locales in Compose Multiplatform. Ctrl+Click on a <string name="…"> entry now jumps to the same key in the other values-*/strings.xml files. Android Studio already provides this for res/values; StringSmith adds it for composeResources, where the IDE had no equivalent.

idea-plugin.name: Firebase Co-Pilot Build Uploader
idea-plugin.description:
Firebase Co-Pilot: Build Uploader — The all-in-one Firebase App Distribution tool for Android developers.

Build, sign, and distribute your Android app to Firebase App Distribution without ever leaving Android Studio. The plugin handles everything: flavor detection, APK assembly, release signing, upload, release notes, and tester-group distribution — all from a single tool window.

✦ Core Features
  • Auto Flavor Detection — Scans build.gradle / build.gradle.kts for productFlavors (both Groovy and KTS DSLs). Falls back to a firebasecopilot-flavors.json file when Gradle parsing is not possible.
  • Build Type Selection — Supports Debug, Release, and any custom build types defined in your project.
  • One-Click Build & Deploy — Runs ./gradlew :app:assembleFLAVORBUILDTYPE, locates the generated APK, and uploads it to Firebase — all in a single click.
  • Build Only Mode — Assemble an APK locally without uploading.
  • Firebase Auth via Service Account — Authenticates using a Service Account JSON file. No manual token management or CLI setup required.
  • Release Notes — Choose from saved templates or write custom notes. Notes are attached to the Firebase release automatically.
  • Tester Group Distribution — Reads groups from the firebaseAppDistribution { } block in your build.gradle and distributes the release to those groups automatically after upload.
  • Live Build Log — Streams Gradle output directly in the tool window panel.
  • Persistent Settings — Remembers your last App ID, service account path, and up to 20 saved release note templates across IDE restarts.
  • Recent Deployments History — Tracks the last 10 deployments with timestamps, flavors, build types, and Firebase Console links.
  • Auto Project Sync — Re-scans flavors and build types automatically whenever Gradle syncs, keeping the UI always up to date.
✦ Signing Configuration (New in v2.0)
  • Release Signing Warning — Detects missing signing config when "release" build type is selected and prompts you to configure it before building.
  • Signing Config Wizard — Generate a signingConfigs block and inject it into build.gradle / build.gradle.kts automatically.
  • Create New Keystore — Generate a brand-new .jks / .p12 keystore via keytool with a guided form (alias, passwords, certificate DN, validity period) — no terminal required.
  • Use Existing Keystore — Point to an existing keystore file and the plugin writes keystore.properties and injects the Gradle signing block for you.
  • Secure by Default — Credentials are stored in keystore.properties (never hardcoded in build.gradle) and the plugin automatically adds keystore files and property files to .gitignore.
  • Supports Groovy & KTS — Signing config injection works for both build.gradle (Groovy) and build.gradle.kts (Kotlin Script).
✦ How to open
Build → Firebase Co-Pilot: Build Uploader or press Alt+Shift+B. The panel docks to the right sidebar.

✦ Requirements
  • Android Studio (Hedgehog or later recommended)
  • A Firebase project with App Distribution enabled
  • A Service Account JSON with the Firebase App Distribution Admin IAM role
idea-plugin.change-notes:
2.0.1 — Platform compatibility & security hardening
  • Fix: JetBrains Marketplace compatibility warnings — Migrated away from deprecated IntelliJ Platform APIs scheduled for removal in Android Studio 2025.x / 2026.x (file chooser, Gradle sync listener, and project refresh APIs).
  • Fix: Dependency vulnerabilities — Upgraded Google Auth Library and pinned transitive dependencies to resolve CVE-2023-2976 (Guava) and WS-2019-0379 (Apache Commons Codec).
  • Improvement: Compile SDK — Plugin is now built against Android Studio 2025.1 Platform APIs for forward compatibility with current IDE releases.
  • No functional changes — Build, deploy, signing wizard, keystore creation, and Firebase upload behavior are unchanged from v2.0.0.
2.0.0 — Signed APK & Signing Configuration Support
  • New: Release Signing Wizard — Detects missing signing config when the "release" build type is selected and shows a clickable inline warning. Opens a guided dialog to apply signing configuration directly from the panel.
  • New: Create Keystore dialog — Generate a new .jks / .p12 keystore via keytool without leaving Android Studio. Supports full certificate DN, custom alias, separate key/store passwords, and configurable validity period.
  • New: Gradle signing config injection — Automatically writes keystore.properties and injects a signingConfigs block into build.gradle or build.gradle.kts. Safe to re-apply — replaces any previously injected block.
  • New: Auto .gitignore update — Keystore files and property files are added to .gitignore automatically to prevent accidental credential commits.
  • New: Tester group auto-distribution — Reads groups from the firebaseAppDistribution { } block and distributes releases to those groups after every upload.
  • Fix: Duplicate APK from wrong flavor — APK discovery is now scoped strictly to the selected flavor + build type directory; stale APKs from other flavors are never used.
  • Fix: Gradle abort on missing Firebase task — The -x appDistributionUpload exclusion flag is now only passed when the Firebase Gradle plugin is actually present, preventing "Task not found" errors on plain projects.
  • Fix: Correct Firebase Console URL — The console link now uses the URL returned directly by the Firebase API instead of a reconstructed one.
  • Improvement: Auto-refresh on Gradle sync — Flavor and build type combos update automatically after every Gradle sync without requiring a manual refresh.
1.0.0 — Initial release
  • Auto flavor detection from build.gradle / build.gradle.kts
  • Build type selection with flavor combos
  • One-click Build & Deploy to Firebase App Distribution
  • Service Account JSON authentication
  • Release notes templates with persistent history
  • Live Gradle build log in the tool window

idea-plugin.name: KMP Expect/Actual Tracker
idea-plugin.description: A project-wide coverage dashboard for Kotlin Multiplatform expect/actual declarations. Lists every expect and shows which targets supply an actual, flagging incomplete declarations. Includes an editor inspection with actual-stub generation, coverage gutter icons, and HTML/CSV export.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • MissingActualInspection — expect declarations missing an actual on one or more platforms are now flagged directly in the editor with a warning, using the same project-wide scan as the tool window. Toggle/severity under Settings → Editor → Inspections → Kotlin Multiplatform.
  • Generate 'actual' stub quick fix — the inspection offers a fix per missing platform that creates a TODO-bodied actual stub in the platform's source set, in the same package and file name as the expect. Handles functions, properties, classes/objects, interfaces, and enums.
  • Coverage gutter icons — expect declarations get a coverage-aware line marker (green = all platforms covered, red = something missing) that navigates to the actual implementations.
  • Coverage statistics bar — the tool window now shows a summary line ("42 expects · 36 complete (86%) · 6 incomplete") with a per-platform breakdown tooltip.
  • Group-by modes — group the coverage tree by package, by module, or by missing platform ("what do I need to write to ship the iOS target?"), with per-group coverage badges.
  • Platform filter — scope the whole tree to a single platform; combined with the incomplete-only toggle it shows exactly what's missing on that target.
  • Export report — save the coverage matrix as a standalone HTML page or CSV file from the tool window toolbar.
  • Right-click context menu — Jump to Source and Copy Qualified Name on tree rows.
  • Reveal in Expect/Actual Tracker — editor context-menu action that selects the expect under the caret in the tool window.
  • Settings page (Settings → Tools → KMP Expect/Actual Tracker) — custom excluded path patterns, auto-refresh debounce interval, and a toggle for treating src/main as Android.
  • Persistent view state — the incomplete-only toggle, group-by mode, and platform filter survive IDE restarts.
  • Unit tests + CI — tests for the coverage model, statistics, report generators, platform detection heuristics, scanner, and stub generator; the Build workflow now runs on pushes to main and on pull requests.

Changed

  • Coverage cache invalidation now happens project-wide on any Kotlin PSI change (not just while the tool window is open), keeping the inspection and gutter icons fresh.

idea-plugin.name: TAO LogExt

TAO LogExt is a highly customizable Android LogCat viewer plugin for Android Studio designed to provide a more readable, performance-optimized, and AI-powered logging experience.

  • Custom Coloring: Fully customizable foreground and background colors for every log level.

  • Tags Preset: Save/load tags presets. Preset history for quick change.
  • Source Navigation: Clickable links for FileName.kt:Line patterns.

idea-plugin.name: Termanager
idea-plugin.description:
Termanager

Easily manage and run project-specific terminal commands! Using the tool window on the right panel of your project, you can store your frequently used commands and run them in the root directory of your project with a single click.

Features:

  • Project-Based Persistence: Each project saves its own list of commands independently.
  • Rich CRUD Support: Add new commands, edit, or delete existing ones.
  • Embedded Console (ConsoleView): Track command output in real-time in a colored console view.
  • Concurrency Lock and Debounce: Security lock and click filter to prevent running multiple commands simultaneously.
  • IDE Progress Integration: View running commands in the IDE's bottom right "Background Tasks" progress bar, and cancel them if desired.

How to Use?

  1. After installation, click the Termanager panel on the right edge of the IDE.
  2. On the first launch, 6 default Gradle commands (Clean, Build, etc.) will be loaded automatically.
  3. To add a new command, press the + (Add) button on the top bar, and fill in the Title and Command fields.
  4. Double-click a command in the list, or select the command and click the Run button on the top bar to trigger it in the project's root directory.
  5. Observe outputs in real-time through the ConsoleView in the bottom panel while the command is running.
  6. If you want to interrupt a running command, press the Cancel button on the IDE's bottom right progress bar to stop the execution.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Fixed

  • Fixed the Stop button not actually terminating running commands and Scrcpy sessions; the whole process tree is now killed instead of only the wrapping shell process.
  • Removed usage of a scheduled-for-removal platform API by adding explicit ActionUpdateThread overrides to all custom actions.

Changed

  • Redesigned the Scrcpy Settings dialog using IntelliJ's modern Kotlin UI DSL, grouped into Video, Window, Behavior, Audio & Input, Recording, and Advanced sections.
  • Reworked the Scrcpy device list into theme-aware, rounded cards with color-coded running/stopped status.
  • Added many more Scrcpy CLI options (fullscreen, read-only, orientation, crop, render driver, start-app, UHID mouse/gamepad, forward-all-clicks, legacy-paste, clipboard auto-sync, disable-screensaver) plus a free-text "Extra Arguments" field.

idea-plugin.name: ComposeLens
idea-plugin.description:
ComposeLens is a performance analysis tool for Jetpack Compose, built for Android TV and mobile. Right-click inside any @Composable function and get a complete picture of its performance risk — static analysis across the full call tree, live recomposition counts from a real device, and GPU overdraw measurement with screenshots — all without leaving Android Studio.

Designed for production codebases. Tested on Demo App on TV — a multi-module Compose app spanning 74+ composables, two git repos, and a real Android TV device.


What it does

🔬 Static Analysis — full call tree, not just the function you click

The analyzer walks the real PSI call graph from your caret position, resolving cross-file and cross-module references, and runs five independent checks on every composable it reaches:

  • Unstable parameters — raw List<T>, Map, Set, Array as parameters prevent Compose from skipping recomposition. Flags them and suggests ImmutableList or @Stable wrappers. Skips parameters already typed as kotlinx.collections.immutable types — no false positives.
  • Missing list keys — items() and itemsIndexed() without a key = { } parameter force Compose to recompose every item on any list change. Caught in production: ChannelTabsList, OTPKeyboardView, BundlingRecommendPlansRow.
  • Unmemoized computation — Regex(), filter(), sortedBy(), map(), groupBy() running unwrapped in a composable body re-execute on every recomposition. Caught in production: two bare Regex() calls and a sortedBy() in StyledPlanText. Does not flag trivial literal-collection chains like listOf(1,2,3).map { }.
  • Inline data-layer construction — UserRepository().getUser() constructs a new object on every recomposition. Only flags constructor-then-chain patterns; stored references like viewModel.load() are never flagged.
  • GPU overdraw risk — chained .background().background(), mixing background() with drawBehind { } on the same element, and backgrounds inside lazy-list item scopes. Caught in production: OTTDialogBackground (background + drawBehind on same composable), BundlingMoreDetailsScreen and ChannelTabDetail (lazy-item backgrounds on an Android TV screen).

📊 Risk Scoring & Report

Every composable in the scanned tree gets a weighted risk score (HIGH finding = 3pts, MEDIUM = 1pt). The HTML/PDF report lists all findings by composable, shows the score ranking, and includes exact file paths and line numbers. Open in browser → Cmd+P → Save as PDF for pull request reviews.

Real output: 74 composables scanned, 7 HIGH findings, 29 MEDIUM findings, 4 overdraw risks — all with file paths pointing into the real source tree across two modules (iptv-home and airtel-unified-sdk).

📸 Runtime Overdraw Capture — GPU screenshot analysis

Enables Android's built-in GPU overdraw visualization on the device, takes a screenshot via adb exec-out screencap, and bucket-scores every pixel by overdraw depth:

  • True color = 1× draw (no overdraw)
  • 🔵 Blue = 2× draws (acceptable)
  • 🟢 Green = 3× draws (investigate)
  • 🔴 Light red = 4× draws (problematic)
  • 🔴 Dark red = 5×+ draws (fix urgently)

Produces a weighted overdraw score and cross-references pixel measurements with static OVERDRAW_* findings from the same composable. Overdraw visualization is always disabled after capture — the device is never left in debug mode.

Real output: 4 captures across BundlingDetailsDialog, BundlingMoreDetailsScreen, CustomiseServicesScreen, and UpgradeDTHPostPaidPlansScreen — each with full pixel breakdown, HWUI layer data, and correlated static findings — embedded directly in the final HTML report.

⚡ Live Recomposition Counting

Injects SideEffect { println("RECOMP_...") } into every composable in the call tree, commits the changes as a git checkpoint (so they can always be reverted safely), runs the app on device, then reads logcat and counts recompositions per composable. Results are cross-referenced with static findings to distinguish confirmed hotspots (high counts + findings) from hidden hotspots (high counts, no static findings).

Git safety: per-repo checkpoint commits with hook-skipping, canonical-path-aware multi-repo support, and atomic rollback if any repo's checkpoint fails.


Menu actions — right-click inside any @Composable

All actions appear under ComposeLens in the editor right-click menu. Place your caret inside a @Composable function body before right-clicking.

🔬 Analyze Composable Performance

Runs all five static checks across the full composable call tree rooted at the function your caret is in. Walks cross-file and cross-module PSI references, stops at library boundaries, and caps at 150 composables. Opens an inline Markdown report with every finding — check ID, severity, file path, line number, and a specific fix suggestion. Also computes a weighted risk score per composable (HIGH = 3pts, MEDIUM = 1pt) and shows a ranking so you know where to start.

When to use: first action to run on any new screen or before a pull request.

🎨 Analyze Overdraw Risks

Focused version of the above — runs only the three GPU overdraw checks across the call tree and opens a dedicated overdraw report. Faster than the full analysis when you already know performance is fine but want to specifically audit rendering cost.

Detects: chained .background().background() on the same element, mixing background() with drawBehind { }, and backgrounds inside lazy-list item scopes (on Android TV a 20-item list with per-item backgrounds = 20× fill-rate cost per frame).

When to use: after receiving jank reports on TV, or when auditing list-heavy screens.

📸 Capture Overdraw Screenshot

Two-step runtime overdraw measurement directly from a connected device or emulator:

  1. Run this action — ComposeLens auto-detects adb, lists connected devices, enables Android's GPU overdraw visualization (setprop debug.hwui.overdraw show_overdraw), and shows a confirmation with the color legend.
  2. Navigate to the screen you want to measure in your running app.
  3. Right-click → ComposeLens → Capture Overdraw Screenshot — the plugin takes a screenshot via adb exec-out screencap -p, immediately disables overdraw visualization (the device is never left in debug mode), bucket-scores every pixel by overdraw tier, and opens a combined report with the annotated screenshot embedded inline.

The report shows: weighted overdraw score (0.0 = perfect), pixel breakdown by tier, the screenshot with overdraw colors active, HWUI layer data, and any static OVERDRAW_* findings from the same composable cross-referenced side-by-side.

When to use: to confirm or rule out overdraw as the cause of jank on a specific screen.

⚡ Inject Recomposition Tracking

Instruments every composable in the call tree with a SideEffect { println("RECOMP_FunctionName_hash") } counter. Before injecting, commits any uncommitted tracked files as a git checkpoint (so your working tree stays clean and the injection is always safely reversible). Supports multiple git repos in the same scan — each gets its own checkpoint commit.

When to use: when static analysis found potential issues and you want to confirm which composables actually recompose at runtime, and how many times.

↩️ Revert Recomposition Tracking

Removes all injected SideEffect counters and restores the original source files. Uses two strategies: in-memory file snapshots captured at inject time (instant, session-scoped), and git soft-reset to the pre-inject SHA (durable, survives IDE restarts). If the IDE crashed mid-session, the git revert still works — run this action and the instrumented commits are unwound cleanly.

When to use: after you've finished measuring — always revert before committing or pushing.

▶️ Start Performance Capture

Prepares the device for a recomposition measurement session. Clears logcat so previous recomposition counts don't pollute the measurement. Optionally runs a Gradle install task (installDebug or custom) so the instrumented build is deployed automatically. Stores the device serial so subsequent actions use the same device without prompting.

When to use: immediately after injecting recomposition tracking and before launching the app through the screen you want to measure.

⏹ Stop Capture & Show Report

Reads the logcat dump from the connected device, counts how many times each RECOMP_* tag appeared, and opens a combined Markdown report. The report cross-references counts with static findings to surface two insight types:

  • Confirmed hotspot — high recomposition count AND static findings. Fix immediately.
  • Hidden hotspot — high recomposition count but no static findings. ComposeLens flagged something the static checks couldn't see (e.g. state being read in a parent scope).

When to use: after exercising the screen under test — scroll, interact, trigger the state changes you care about — then run this to capture the counts.

📄 Generate PR Report (HTML/PDF)

Generates a self-contained HTML file combining everything collected in the session: static findings table, risk score ranking chart, recomposition counts bar chart (top 15 composables), overdraw screenshot captures with pixel breakdowns, HWUI layer data, and the full findings list with file paths and line numbers. The HTML file is written to a temp path and opened in your default browser automatically.

To save as PDF: in the browser, press Cmd+P (macOS) or Ctrl+P (Windows/Linux) → set destination to "Save as PDF" → Save. The resulting PDF is suitable for attaching to pull requests or sharing with the team.

When to use: at the end of a full analysis session — after running static analysis, capturing overdraw screenshots, and measuring recomposition counts — to produce a single shareable document.

📋 Manage Reports

Opens a visual panel listing every report cached in the current session — Static Analysis, Recomposition Counts, and each Overdraw Capture run. Each entry shows the composable name, key metrics (finding counts, recomposition peak, overdraw grade and score, device, timestamp), and a Remove button that appears when you hover over the row.

Clicking Remove shows a confirmation dialog explaining exactly what will be excluded from the final PDF (e.g. "The overdraw screenshot, pixel distribution, and HWUI layer data for this capture will not appear"). Only that one entry is removed — the rest of the session stays intact. You can remove any combination of reports before generating the final PDF.

What is not touched: source files, git history, or checkpoint commits. Removing a report from the session does not undo the analysis or delete any files on disk.

When to use: before generating the PR report, to review what will be included and prune any captures that were taken on the wrong screen or are no longer relevant.


Typical workflow for a full report

  1. Open the Kotlin file containing the screen-level composable you want to audit.
  2. Place caret inside the @Composable function body.
  3. Right-click → ComposeLens → Analyze Composable Performance. Review findings inline.
  4. Right-click → ComposeLens → Inject Recomposition Tracking. Wait for git checkpoint.
  5. Right-click → ComposeLens → Start Performance Capture. App installs (or run it yourself).
  6. Exercise the screen — scroll, interact, trigger the states you care about.
  7. Right-click → ComposeLens → Stop Capture & Show Report. See recomposition counts.
  8. Right-click → ComposeLens → Capture Overdraw Screenshot. Navigate to the screen on device, then run the second part of the action to take the screenshot.
  9. Right-click → ComposeLens → Revert Recomposition Tracking. Source files restored.
  10. Right-click → ComposeLens → Generate PR Report (HTML/PDF). Browser opens the full report → Cmd+P → Save as PDF → attach to your pull request.
  11. Right-click → ComposeLens → Manage Reports. Review the list of cached reports, remove any that should not appear in the final PDF, then proceed.

Requirements

  • Android Studio Hedgehog (2023.1) or newer / IntelliJ IDEA with Kotlin plugin
  • Kotlin plugin (bundled in Android Studio)
  • For runtime features: adb on PATH or ANDROID_HOME set
  • For recomposition tracking: project must be in a git repository
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Initial release.

idea-plugin.name: IDE Desktop Pet Sprite
idea-plugin.description:
IDE Desktop Pet Sprite — A desktop floating pet that reacts to your IDE's state.

Show a always-on-top desktop companion while you work in IntelliJ IDEA or Android Studio. Gradle sync, indexing, build/compile, and run/debug each trigger a distinct animation and status badge; success and failure bring celebration or dejected expressions. Replaceable sprites — built-in original slime Gel by default.


GitHub | 中文文档 | Get Started | Privacy


Features

  • State-aware animations: Gradle sync, indexing, build/compile, run/debug, success, failure, and idle.
  • Always-on-top floating window — draggable, resizable (S / M / L), position remembered (multi-monitor safe).
  • Switch character: built-in Gel, local sprite upload (PNG / WebP / GIF), or online Petdex catalog.
  • Per-project character override with preview in settings.
  • Right-click menu: reset position, resize, switch character, temporarily hide, or permanently disable.
  • Transparent background; never steals editor focus.
  • Settings → Tools → Desktop Pet Sprite, or Tools → Desktop Pet Sprite Settings, or Search Everywhere for Desktop Pet / 桌宠.

State mapping

IDE eventPet state
Gradle syncThinking · Sync
IndexingLooking around · Index
Build / compileRunning · Build
Run / debugRunning (faster) · Run
SuccessJumping · Done ✓
FailureDejected · Error ✗
IdleIdle

When multiple activities overlap, priority is: run > build > sync > index > idle.


Compatibility

Requires IntelliJ Platform build 242+ (2024.2 or later). Works with IntelliJ IDEA, Android Studio, and other IntelliJ-based IDEs.



IDE Desktop Pet Sprite · 构建状态桌宠

在 Gradle Sync、建立索引、构建/编译、运行/调试 等不同状态下， 于桌面显示一只会随状态变化的悬浮宠物，并在成功 / 失败时给出表情反馈。 宠物素材可替换（默认内置原创史莱姆 Gel）。


功能

  • 同步 / 索引 / 构建 / 运行 / 成功 / 失败 / 待机 —— 各有不同动画与状态徽标
  • 悬浮窗置顶、可拖拽、可调大小（小/中/大），位置自动记忆（多屏安全）
  • 可切换形象：内置 Gel、本地上传精灵图（PNG / WebP / GIF）、在线形象库 Petdex；支持按项目设置不同形象
  • 右键菜单：重置位置 / 调整尺寸 / 切换形象 / 临时隐藏 / 永久关闭
  • 透明背景，不抢占编辑器焦点
  • Settings → Tools → Desktop Pet Sprite（桌面宠物），或 Tools → Desktop Pet Sprite 设置…，或双击 Shift 搜索「桌宠」

兼容版本

需要 IntelliJ Platform build 242+（2024.2 及以上）。适用于 IntelliJ IDEA、Android Studio 及其他基于 IntelliJ 的 IDE。


作者 anjiemo · Copyright © 2026 anjiemo · Apache License 2.0


Privacy · 隐私

No personal data is collected. Optional Petdex downloads contact petdex.dev over HTTPS only when you use that feature. By using this plugin, you consent to this data usage. See the Privacy Policy.

不收集个人数据；仅在使用 Petdex 在线形象库时经 HTTPS 访问 petdex.dev。 详见 隐私政策。
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 多项目身份区分：宠物顶部显示项目昵称/名称标签（聚焦或悬停时展示），支持自定义截断模式（中间省略 / 末尾省略）
  • 聚焦高亮动效：活跃项目窗口获焦时，宠物身后显示向外发散的波动光晕，以 30 FPS 流畅驱动
  • 设置页实时预览：修改配置时宠物外观 0 延时同步，取消时自动回滚
  • 使用单调时钟（System.nanoTime）驱动动效，免疫系统时钟调整
  • 缓存字体行高，消除 30 FPS 绘制循环中每帧 ~90 次 BufferedImage 分配导致的 GC 高压
  • 将形象加载（磁盘 I/O + 图片解码）移至后台线程，修复切换宠物时 IDE 卡住问题

idea-plugin.name: CMP Resource Viewer
idea-plugin.description:
CMP Resource Viewer brings drawable previews to Compose Multiplatform projects — the previews Android Studio's Resource Manager and editor skip, because composeResources/ isn't an Android res/ folder.

Resource grid tool window

  • Thumbnails of every drawable, SVG, Android vector XML, raster image (including WebP) and font under composeResources/, labeled with the full filename including extension.
  • Search by name or extension, group by type (Drawable / Font / Files), resize thumbnails, and toggle a checkerboard / light / dark backdrop so light-colored icons stay visible.
  • Auto-refreshes when resources change, plus a manual refresh button. Right-click for the usual file actions — Move, Rename, Copy, Safe Delete, Find Usages, Show in Explorer — plus Copy Value (Res.drawable.name).

Code / Split / Design editor

  • Open a vector .xml or .svg and get a live design preview alongside the source, updating as you edit.
  • Image-editor toolbar on the preview: transparency chessboard, pixel grid, zoom in/out, 1:1, fit to window, and open-in-external-editor.
  • Color pipette — hover the artwork for a live swatch + hex readout, click to copy the hex to the clipboard.
  • Info readout with the drawable's intrinsic size, format, and file size.

Pure-platform plugin — works in Android Studio and IntelliJ IDEA.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.1.0 — preview image-editor toolbar (chessboard, pixel grid, zoom/fit/1:1, open externally), color pipette (copy hex), and a size/format/file-size readout; tool-window refresh button; plus internal cleanup of deprecated platform APIs.

1.0.1 — first public release

  • Resource grid with thumbnails, search, group-by-type, size slider, background toggle, a refresh button, and a file context menu; labels and search include the file extension.
  • Live Code / Split / Design preview for vector XML and SVG, with an image-editor toolbar: chessboard, pixel grid, zoom controls, color pipette (copy hex on click), open-in-external-editor, and a size/format/file-size readout.
  • Renders SVG, Android vector drawables, raster, WebP, and font (ttf/otf) previews; thumbnails are cached.
  • Vector drawables support linear/radial/sweep gradients and clip-path, resolve @color/ references, and show a default tint for unresolved colors.

idea-plugin.name: Flutter Widget Wrapper
idea-plugin.description:
Context-aware Flutter widget wrappers in the Alt+Enter menu. Wrap a widget without moving code by hand, fixing indentation or rebuilding constructors.

Wrap the right way, in the right place

  • Built-in wrappers: Align, AnimatedSize, Expanded, Flexible, GestureDetector, InkWell, Opacity, Positioned, SafeArea, SingleChildScrollView, SliverPadding, SliverToBoxAdapter and Stack.
  • 24 optional presets: Consumer, BlocBuilder, ValueListenableBuilder, AnimatedBuilder, LayoutBuilder, Hero, Visibility, ClipRRect, Tooltip, Dismissible and more.
  • Only valid wrappers are offered: Expanded and Flexible for direct children of Row, Column or Flex, Positioned for direct children of Stack, and only sliver-aware wrappers inside sliver:/slivers:.
  • Tab-stops (with choices) jump to the values to edit right after wrapping, and enclosing const keywords are removed when a wrapper adds a closure.

Many ways to wrap

  • Alt+Enter, with a preview for every wrapper, or a single searchable Wrap with… popup.
  • Surround With (Ctrl+Alt+T / ⌥⌘T) and postfix templates: Text('a').opacity + Tab.
  • Wrap several selected siblings of a children: list at once.
  • Replace Widget with… swaps a wrapper for another one while keeping its child (e.g. Flexible → Expanded).

Your own wrappers

  • Create wrapper from Widget turns an existing widget into a reusable wrapper, including builders such as BlocBuilder, Consumer or StreamBuilder: the widget their builder: returns becomes the placeholder, and early returns are kept.
  • Dart editor with live preview and validation; import and export as JSON.
  • Share wrappers with your team through a .flutter-wrappers.json file in the project root.
  • Edit or hide any wrapper right from the Alt+Enter submenu.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
Added

  • Wrapping adds the imports the wrapper needs. Each wrapper lists them in imports (alternatives as a|b). They are inserted following directives_ordering, in the same undo step as the wrap. material.dart/cupertino.dart count as widgets.dart. Built-ins and presets declare theirs; unchanged copies of presets added earlier inherit them.
  • A hint warns when an added import's package is not in pubspec.yaml; between alternatives, the one in pubspec.yaml is preferred.
  • Create wrapper from Widget fills in the import of the widget's library (src/ files map to their public library, e.g. material.dart).
  • Wrapper editor: Imports field (accepts a pasted import '…';). Settings: option to turn auto-import off; the detail line shows each wrapper's imports.

idea-plugin.description:
Flutter and Dart tools for everyday work

Small tools that make Flutter and Dart work faster: smarter pubspec.yaml editing, package and code docs on hover, better navigation, and helpful inline hints.

Package management

Navigation

idea-plugin.name: Remote ADB Connector
idea-plugin.description:
Remote ADB Connector

Connect to Android devices attached to a remote Windows ADB server from your Linux Android Studio instance.

  • One-click connection to remote ADB servers
  • Automatic device discovery and TCP mode switching
  • Continuous monitoring with auto-reconnect
  • No shell scripts or manual CLI commands required
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.9

  • Throttled plugin logger UI updates to eliminate Swing Event Dispatch Thread (EDT) freezes during rapid logging
  • Isolated ADB stream reading to dedicated daemon thread pool to prevent ForkJoinPool starvation
  • Ensured child ADB processes are forcibly destroyed on cancellation/interruption to prevent process leaks
  • Fixed monitor executor shutdown race conditions by awaiting thread termination in Windows and Linux monitors

1.0.8

  • Fixed UI thread (EDT) freezes by offloading all connection teardown, monitor shutdowns, and process kills to background coroutines
  • Replaced blocking Thread.sleep calls with non-blocking, cancellable Kotlin coroutine delay calls
  • Added ADB process tracking and forcible cancellation on disconnect to prevent orphaned process leaks
  • Fixed state machine transition edge cases and auto-reconnect flow when all devices are lost

1.0.5

  • Added selective per-device connection options (WiFi and USB) in the Available Devices list
  • Implemented dynamic port forwarding for USB mode to support multiple concurrent USB connections without conflicts
  • Enabled continuous Windows server background monitoring alongside local Linux connection tracking

1.0.3

  • Added interactive "Help" button in the tool window showing setup commands for exposing the Windows ADB server
  • Updated documentation with network setup guides and visual mockups

1.0.2

  • Added light and dark themed plugin icons for Marketplace and IDE Plugin Manager

1.0.1

  • Initial release
  • Full connection workflow: discover, prepare, connect, monitor
  • Auto-reconnect on device disconnection
  • Persistent settings
  • Tool window with real-time status
  • Custom branding and icons for sidebar and plugin marketplace

idea-plugin.name: Specter Ghost-UI
idea-plugin.description:
The automated ghost-UI (skeleton screen) generator for Jetpack Compose.

Put the caret inside any @Composable function and press Ctrl+Alt+H (or right-click and choose Generate Specter UI). Specter clones the function into a standalone *Specter skeleton: structure and modifiers are preserved so the skeleton occupies exactly the same space as the real UI, while Text, Image, Icon and button leaves become shimmering SpecterBox bones with sizes inferred from text content and Material typography. Self-contained shimmer helpers and light/dark @Preview functions are added automatically.

Generated skeletons are plain Compose code with no runtime dependency. See the project README for the optional runtime SDK (auto bones for Compose and XML views).
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.1.1 - Declare K1 and K2 Kotlin plugin mode support.
0.1.0 - Initial release: Generate Specter UI action with Safe Mock generation, typography-aware bone sizing, shape recovery from clip/background modifiers, and synchronized shimmer helpers.

idea-plugin.name: Compose Hot Reload
idea-plugin.description:
Compose Hot Reload for Android

Apply hot reload to a running, debuggable Jetpack Compose app from Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA. The plugin includes the hotreload CLI, starts one watch session for the selected device, and reports its state in the status bar.

Get started

  1. Open Settings | Tools | Compose Hot Reload and select your project.
  2. Use Refresh discovery as a suggestion, then review and save an explicit configured profile with the app, variant, watched modules, target JDK, and device.
  3. Run the matching doctor and prepare flow so the CLI owns the installed debug APK baseline.
  4. Start from the status-bar widget or Tools | Start Hot Reload. Wait for Ready, save one Compose body edit, then use the same control to Stop.

Configured Gradle-plugin integration with a reviewed profile is the stable path. Zero-touch bootstrap and live literals are experimental. Use one API-30+ device and one watcher at a time.

Quickstart and source | IDE settings guide | AI-assisted setup guide
idea-plugin.change-notes:
• 0.2.0 — Defines configured Gradle-plugin integration with reviewed profiles as the stable onboarding path. Zero-touch and live literals remain experimental; public AI-assisted setup and recovery guidance is included.
  • 0.1.8 — Zero-touch now supports apps with a minSdk of 23. Hot reload remains enabled only on API 30+ devices; older devices safely skip the runtime.
  • 0.1.7 — Zero-touch now supports projects with Gradle composite builds (for example, an included build-logic build). The bundled bootstrap is inert in included builds and continues to instrument the selected root-build app modules.
  • 0.1.6 — Preflight now surfaces the real doctor output and a Report on GitHub action when the environment check can't run; auto-discovers the Android SDK (local.properties / ANDROID_HOME / platform default) for GUI-launched IDEs; expands ~ in path settings.
  • 0.1.5 — Added a pre-Start environment preflight: the plugin runs hotreload doctor before launching and, if the environment is not ready (missing Android SDK build-tools, no connected device, or the app is not running), shows an actionable notification with a Start anyway option instead of a raw CLI error. Also rebuilt against the 2026.1 IntelliJ platform and verified against the newest IDE builds.
  • 0.1.4 — Removed all use of internal IntelliJ plugin-descriptor APIs (every PluginManager descriptor lookup became @ApiStatus.Internal on 2026.2). The plugin version is now baked in at build time and the bundled CLI is located from the plugin's own jar; no behavior change. Fixes the Marketplace compatibility rejection.
  • 0.1.2 — Replaced an internal-platform API (PluginManagerCore.getPlugin) with PluginManager.getPluginByClass for resolving the bundled CLI; no behavior change. Plugin ID is now dev.hotreload.ide.
  • 0.1.1 — The hotreload CLI is now bundled inside the plugin. Install from disk (or the Marketplace) and hot-reload with no repo clone: leave the Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Compose Hot Reload ▸ CLI launcher field blank to use it. Requires the Android SDK (build-tools 36.0.0) on the machine.
