idea-plugin.name: ClawDEA
idea-plugin.description:
ClawDEA gives Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and any OpenAI-compatible model a self-maintaining understanding of your project. Its standout capability is a project wiki that stays in sync with your code, ships an orientation primer with every turn, and is ready to share across a team via git — so your AI assistant starts every conversation already knowing how your codebase works.

Bring your own model. Beyond Claude and Codex, ClawDEA can drive any OpenAI-compatible provider — a self-hosted model server, an internal gateway, or a third-party API — via an importable JSON profile (no plugin update needed). A tool-capable model gets the same full agentic chat as Claude and Codex: the whole MCP toolset, a Skill tool and an Agent tool for sub-agent dispatch, diff-gated edit review, and permission-gated shell access. The new Roles tab lets Chat, Wiki upkeep, and Completions each run on an independently chosen provider — run chat on Claude, wiki upkeep on a cheap OpenAI-compatible model, and completions on a third.

Most Claude plugins wrap the CLI in a chat window. ClawDEA goes further: a living knowledge layer plus JVM profiling as a diagnostic loop, on top of IDE-grade code navigation, edit review, and debugging. The result is an AI pair programmer that reasons from a maintained model of your project, profiles a slow test and proposes a source-level fix, and navigates by reference instead of regex.

See it in action: the README has a live demo of Claude autonomously debugging a Java application — setting breakpoints, stepping, inspecting variables, and mutating runtime state to verify hypotheses.

What makes ClawDEA different

  • A self-maintaining project wiki. A project-local wiki under .claude/wiki/ plus an auto-generated REPO_STATE.md. A commit-driven drift detector notices when a page's claims go stale, an orphan-subsystem detector flags whole new areas no page mentions at all, and a bundled wiki-author agent drafts the fix — with auto-update enabled it lands edits unattended. The primer ships with every turn so Claude starts each conversation oriented — no "let me explore the codebase first". The ask_wiki_librarian tool answers design questions in its own fresh context, citing pages and verifying against current source — and works no matter which provider you chat with, running on whichever backend the Wiki role (Roles tab) points at.
  • Team-ready knowledge sharing. Run /wiki-relocate docs/llm-wiki to commit the wiki path to .clawdea/config.json; teammates auto-discover the shared wiki on clone, with per-user vs team-shared drift state split automatically. Cross-repo navigation for monorepos via .clawdea-workspace.md and sibling-repo tools.
  • JVM profiling as a diagnostic loop. One-click profiling of tests and run configurations via JDK Flight Recorder. Claude analyzes CPU hotspots, allocation pressure, and memory leaks (.jfr and .hprof), then proposes source-level fixes. Entry points: /profile slash command, gutter icon on @Test methods, or imported recordings.
  • IDE-grade code navigation, debugging & edit review. IntelliJ's PSI index as MCP tools (find_usages, find_callers, find_implementations, find_supertypes, resolve_symbol and more — precise and complete, not grep), a 21-tool live debugger with breakpoint-ownership tracking, and diff-gated edit review. Coexists with IntelliJ's own bundled MCP server: enable it and ClawDEA drops the few overlapping tools, keeping everything the IDE has no equivalent for (the usage/caller/type-hierarchy graph, ownership-tracked debugging, diff-gated edits, profiling, and the knowledge layer). Detection is fail-open.

The rest of the toolkit

  • Native edit review. Each proposed change opens IntelliJ's diff dialog with Accept/Reject. A fallback coordinator catches built-in Edit/Write calls that bypass MCP and adds inline buttons with file revert, so Claude cannot silently overwrite your work.
  • Inline completions. Tab-completions powered by the Claude API, or an OpenAI-compatible profile once one is imported and a model selected, using editor context from the context engine.
  • Intention actions (Alt+Enter). Explain, Optimize, Generate Test, Security Check, Add Documentation, Refactor with Instructions, Ask Claude, Fix with Claude. Works with Claude or a selected OpenAI-compatible provider.
  • Chat panel. Streams responses with Markdown, tool-use cards, and clickable code references that navigate to source. Supports Auto, Plan, and Ask modes. @-mention for inline file and symbol picking, backed by IntelliJ's filename and short-name caches. Choose your backend: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or a verified-agentic OpenAI-compatible provider profile — all three run through the same MCP toolset (index, debugger, edit review, primer, skills), and the OpenAI-compatible agent loop additionally gets a Skill tool and an Agent tool for sub-agent dispatch.
  • Per-role providers (Roles tab). Chat, Wiki upkeep, and Completions each get an independent provider + model picker — point wiki authoring or completions at a different (e.g. cheaper) model than the one you chat with, without switching your whole setup.
  • Tool-call permissions. Three modes (Confirm all / Allow safe / Allow all), with honoring of Claude Code's permissions.allow / permissions.deny rules. Permission cards block the CLI inline until you decide.
  • Slash commands + Claude Code skills. Built-ins (/stop, /clear, /mode, /cost, /compact, /resume, /profile, /callers, /usages, /implementations, /supertypes, /note, /promote-to-wiki) plus Claude Code skills discovered at runtime.
  • Session resume. Pick up a previous session with conversation history replayed in the chat panel.
  • Auth flexibility. Claude via Anthropic API key, Claude subscription sign-in, AWS Bedrock, or Google Vertex; OpenAI via ChatGPT subscription sign-in or an OpenAI API key; any OpenAI-compatible provider via whatever credentials its imported profile declares — secrets live only in the IDE's PasswordSafe, never in a settings file or an exported profile.

Staying in sync with Claude Code

ClawDEA wraps the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess and runs a weekly drift-monitoring job that diffs claude --help, npm versions, and selected docs against a moving snapshot, plus a PR-time fixture-replay test over a recorded stream-json transcript. Upstream changes to the CLI get caught by CI, not by users.

Getting started

  1. Install the CLI: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
  2. Install this plugin.
  3. Open Settings → Tools → ClawDEA (Providers tab) and configure an Anthropic API key, sign in with a Claude subscription, configure AWS Bedrock / Google Vertex credentials, or import an OpenAI-compatible provider profile.
  4. Open the chat panel (Tools → Toggle ClawDEA Chat) and start coding.

Requirements

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1+
  • Java 21 on the IDE's JBR (bundled)
  • Claude Code CLI installed (and/or the OpenAI Codex CLI to chat with Codex; an OpenAI-compatible provider needs no CLI at all — just an imported profile)
  • Claude auth (Anthropic API key, subscription, AWS Bedrock, or Google Vertex) and/or OpenAI auth (ChatGPT subscription or OpenAI API key) and/or an OpenAI-compatible profile's own credentials

GitHub · User guide · Report an issue

ClawDEA is licensed under Apache 2.0. "Claude" and "Claude Code" are trademarks of Anthropic, PBC. "IntelliJ", "IntelliJ IDEA", and "JetBrains" are trademarks of JetBrains s.r.o. ClawDEA is an independent integration and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic or JetBrains.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
3.0.1

Claude turns finish correctly with current Claude Code

  • Fixed turns that stayed visually active after Claude finished. Claude Code 2.1.220 changed the field ordering of terminal stream-json events. ClawDEA now reads envelope fields only from the root JSON object, so multi-step and tool-using turns reliably leave the thinking state.
  • Preserved terminal result and error text regardless of field order. End-of-turn payloads are now extracted from the root event instead of relying on their position relative to the event type.

3.0.0

Bring your own model: full agentic chat on any OpenAI-compatible provider

The headline feature of this release: ClawDEA can now drive any OpenAI-compatible API — a self-hosted model server, an internal gateway, or a third-party provider — as a full agentic chat backend, on equal footing with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex.

  • Import a provider via a JSON profile — no plugin update needed. A profile declares the endpoint, model catalog, credential flow, and pricing for an OpenAI-compatible API. Preview and confirm before it’s trusted; plain HTTP is rejected outside localhost by default.
  • Full agentic chat, not just completions. A tool-capable model gets the whole MCP toolset (index, debugger, diff-gated edit review, primer, skills), a permission-gated shell, streamed reasoning in the collapsible Thinking block, and cancel-and-continue steering — the same experience as Claude and Codex.
  • Skill tool. An agentic OpenAI-compatible model can now invoke your Claude Code skills directly, shown as a compact “Using skill” chip instead of pasting the whole skill document into the chat.
  • Agent tool for sub-agent dispatch. The model can call an Agent tool to run a focused sub-agent, whose steps stream into the same collapsible sub-agent card you see with Claude. Skills that fan out into parallel work no longer stall on this backend.
  • Verify Tool Support. One click sends a harmless no-op probe function and reports whether a model can actually call tools — a real signal, never a guess, and never spends tokens unless you ask it to.
  • Context-window management. Configure a per-model context window in the profile; the agent loop compacts the conversation before a model overflows its window — with a conservative default when unset — so smaller models (e.g. 128K) stay coherent on long turns instead of degrading.
  • Loop-breaker. If a model gets stuck repeating the same failing tool call, ClawDEA now nudges it to change approach and stops the turn cleanly rather than spinning.
  • Credentials never leave PasswordSafe. A profile describes how to authenticate, never the credential itself; exported profiles come as a secrets-free template or a configured export that still carries zero secret values.
  • See the User Guide to use a profile, or the new profile-building guide to add a provider that isn’t supported yet.

Per-role providers — a tabbed Settings UI

  • Point Chat, Wiki, and Completions at different providers. The new Roles tab lets each of the three roles run on an independently chosen provider and model — chat on Claude, wiki upkeep on a cheap OpenAI-compatible model, completions on a third. A Reset defaults button recomputes smart defaults from whichever provider you’re authenticated with.
  • Settings is now tabbed: Providers / Roles / Permissions / Knowledge Layer / Profiling / Advanced, replacing the old flat panel.
  • The wiki-librarian works no matter which provider you chat with. Design questions now route through an ask_wiki_librarian tool that runs on whichever provider the Wiki role points at — Claude, Codex, or an OpenAI-compatible profile — instead of a Claude-only mechanism. This also fixes a Windows-only crash where the old mechanism could exceed a command-line length limit.

Wiki: orphan-subsystem detection

  • Catches whole new subsystems the wiki has never mentioned. The existing drift detectors only flag a page whose claims are contradicted by a change — they’re blind to a brand-new area dropped in with no page at all. A new detector clusters related classes and flags any cluster the wiki never mentions, closing that gap.

Fixes

  • A fresh chat now launches on your pinned model, not a fallback. Setting a default model on the Roles tab previously showed the right model in the dropdown but the CLI silently launched on its own default until you re-picked it manually.
  • Fixed a JCEF-related crash on some machines. A missing platform module declaration could crash the chat panel with NoClassDefFoundError the moment it opened, on IDEs where JCEF wasn’t already loaded by another plugin.
  • Settings apply no longer knocks an open chat onto a different provider. Changing any setting (even an unrelated one) could silently rebuild an open chat tab onto the global default provider. An open tab now always keeps its own provider and model; only new chats pick up a changed default.
  • Per-turn cost no longer over-reports. The cost chip summed the CLI’s cumulative session total on every turn instead of each turn’s marginal cost, inflating the running total.
  • A verified-agentic model is honored everywhere, not just in chat. Wiki authoring and drift detection previously ignored a model’s Verify Tool Support result and could refuse to start even after you’d confirmed the model could call tools.
  • Sub-agent panels stay readable during parallel work. Fixed a layout bug where a tall, actively-running sub-agent panel showed no scrollbar and clipped its own steps, and fixed parallel sub-agents leaking their steps into the main chat instead of staying in their own cards.
  • A stale code index no longer crashes symbol search. find_symbol now skips a momentarily-outdated index entry (e.g. right after an edit) instead of failing the whole lookup.

2.2.0

Chat with any OpenAI-compatible provider

  • Bring your own provider via an importable profile. Import a JSON profile in Settings → Tools → ClawDEA to chat with any OpenAI-compatible API. The profile defines the endpoint, model catalog, credential flow, and pricing — no provider-specific setup, and you preview and confirm every profile before it’s activated.
  • Full agentic chat, not just completions. When a model supports tool calls, the chat panel drives it as a real agent through ClawDEA’s MCP toolset — index/search, the live debugger, diff-gated edit review, the project primer, and your skills — plus a permission-gated shell. Tool calls surface the same Allow / Always allow / Deny card and native diff dialog as Claude and Codex.
  • Streamed reasoning. Models that emit reasoning show it live in the collapsible Thinking block above the answer.
  • Cancel-and-continue steering. Send a message while the model is working: ClawDEA folds in your guidance, keeps the valid text produced so far, and never runs a half-finished tool call.
  • Verify tool support before you rely on it. A Verify Tool Support button checks whether a model can actually call tools, on demand — so it never spends tokens behind your back. Models that can’t call tools stay in completion-only mode and can’t start an agentic chat.
  • Resume your conversations. OpenAI-compatible chats appear in /resume alongside Claude and Codex; resuming the same profile restores the full tool state.
  • Cost estimates from your rate card. The per-turn footer and Cost Control use the profile’s configured per-token pricing (input, output, cached, and reasoning) for a spend estimate scoped to that provider.
  • Credentials stay safe. Secrets live only in the IDE’s PasswordSafe — never in settings files or on disk — and exported profiles are always redacted.
  • Switching providers is always your call. ClawDEA never silently moves a conversation to a different provider on an error; carrying a conversation across providers asks first and clearly states that only message text transfers.

2.1.0

Codex, now on the app-server protocol

  • Streamed reasoning. When you chat with OpenAI Codex, the model’s reasoning now streams live into a collapsible Thinking block above the answer, then auto-collapses when the turn ends.
  • Real credits & rate limits. Cost Control now shows your actual remaining ChatGPT-subscription credits and rate-limit windows (reported by Codex’s app-server), reusing the same gauge as Claude — instead of a notional estimate.
  • Codex shell & patch approvals go through ClawDEA’s permission gate. Codex’s own shell commands and file patches now surface the same inline Allow / Always allow / Deny card as Claude’s tools, honor your permissions.allow/permissions.deny rules, and open the native diff dialog for edits.
  • Native interrupt & mid-turn steering. Esc interrupts a live Codex turn natively. And you can now steer mid-turn: send a message while Codex is working and it’s injected into the running turn (turn/steer) — the model folds in your guidance without restarting. (Claude has no steer primitive, so a mid-turn message queues for the next turn as before.)

Fixes

  • Switching provider mid-session no longer leaves the chat in a mixed state. Flipping between a Claude and an OpenAI provider now rebuilds the session on the correct backend, so the model dropdown, the assistant label, and the carried-over conversation all stay in sync — no more “Codex” label under a Claude model list, and your context is carried over.
  • Smoother IDE during reasoning-heavy turns. Streamed reasoning is now coalesced and throttled before it reaches the chat view, and the view scrolls instantly rather than animating per token — removing a source of UI sluggishness on long Codex turns.
  • The pause button now disappears when a turn ends. A stray trailing event could re-open the “Thinking” indicator after a response had finished, leaving its pause button stuck on screen; it now stays hidden once the turn is genuinely done.
  • Faster, quieter wake from sleep. When the machine wakes, only the visible chat tab rebuilds its view immediately; hidden tabs defer until you switch to them, avoiding a burst of simultaneous browser rebuilds.
  • Codex CLI is found when launched from Finder/Dock. ClawDEA now resolves the codex binary from your login shell’s PATH, so the subscription status card and chat work even when the IDE didn’t inherit your shell environment.

2.0.0

Chat with OpenAI Codex, not just Claude

  • OpenAI Codex is now a first-class chat backend. Pick OpenAI (ChatGPT subscription) or OpenAI API as your provider and the chat panel drives the codex CLI instead of claude — through the same ClawDEA MCP server, so Codex gets the full toolset: the IntelliJ index/search tools, the live debugger, diff-gated edit review (propose_edit/propose_write), the project primer, and your Claude Code skills. Switch backends from the model dropdown; ClawDEA routes to the right CLI automatically.
  • ChatGPT sign-in. Set the provider to OpenAI (ChatGPT subscription) and run /login (or use the settings card) to sign in with your ChatGPT account via codex login. An OpenAI API key is also supported.
  • Resume across backends. The session picker lists both Claude and Codex conversations (labeled by origin). Resuming a session started with the other backend replays the prior conversation as context so you can continue seamlessly; same-backend resume is native.
  • Codex-aware chrome. The assistant label, the “… is thinking” status, and the per-turn footer (model · effort · time) reflect whichever backend is active. The Cost Control card shows an honest notional estimate for the flat-rate ChatGPT subscription rather than a per-turn dollar bill.

Inline completions and intention actions remain Claude-only for now; OpenAI support is scoped to the chat panel.

1.9.1

The chat adapts when docked horizontally

  • Responsive layout for bottom/top docks. When the ClawDEA tool window is docked along the bottom or top edge (short and wide), the top and bottom control bars merge into a single compact row and the input shrinks, so the scarce height goes to the conversation. Docked left/right it keeps the full two-row layout, and it re-arranges automatically as you re-dock or drag the splitter.

Fixes

  • The activity hint no longer disappears on long conversations. On a long-running chat, a slow first response after a tool result could trip an internal watchdog that tore the turn down while the CLI was actually still working — leaving activity with no visible “Thinking” hint (with or without sub-agents). The turn now self-heals the moment output resumes, the watchdog is more patient before intervening, and a slow shell-environment probe can no longer fail a session resume or restart.
  • “Reset all-time” in Cost Control now clears everything. The reset button covers both estimated savings and measured knowledge upkeep, but it only cleared the estimate — leaving a stale upkeep figure and “Overall” total behind. It now clears both.

1.9.0

See whether ClawDEA is saving you money

  • Estimated Savings / Cost in the Cost Control panel. A new section estimates the net dollar effect of ClawDEA’s knowledge layer and IDE integration versus a standard Claude Code setup — the wiki librarian keeping exploration out of the main context, the IDE index replacing file reads — netted against what the layer costs to run (wiki/workspace upkeep and the per-turn primer). It shows this chat, this month, and all-time, each with a confidence range.
  • Honest by design. The estimate is a directional comparison against a baseline we don’t actually run, and it can go negative: a short, one-shot session may cost more than it saves, and the panel says so — the section title flips to “ClawDEA Estimated Cost” when the all-time net is negative. Estimated lines carry a ± range; measured costs do not.
  • Refines on resume. Live sessions show a conservative floor (per-subagent costs aren’t observable mid-stream); reopening a conversation reconstructs the full session from its transcript for a sharper estimate.
  • Knowledge upkeep moved. The standalone “Knowledge upkeep” card is now a line inside the new section, so its cost is netted in one place instead of shown separately.

Parallel sub-agents you can actually follow

  • Live sub-agent panels are pinned and stack. When Claude delegates to sub-agents, each one gets its own panel pinned to the bottom of the chat so it stays visible while it works — and when several run in parallel, their panels stack there instead of scrolling out of view. A panel only rejoins the normal conversation flow (collapsed to a one-line summary with its step count) once that sub-agent finishes.
  • No more output broken mid-phrase. Sub-agent reasoning no longer bleeds into the main answer: parallel sub-agent activity used to cut Claude’s reply off mid-sentence and could make the progress dots disappear while work was still going. The main reply now stays intact, and each panel shows a live “running · N steps” progress line.

Spend tokens on completions only when you ask

  • Manual completion hotkey. A new Trigger Inline Completion action (default Alt+\, ⌥\ on macOS) requests a suggestion on demand — it always works, even with automatic completions on. Rebind it in Settings → Keymap → “Trigger Inline Completion”.
  • Optional manual-only mode. Enable “Only request completions on hotkey” in Settings to suppress as-you-type completions entirely, so API tokens are spent only when you press the hotkey. Off by default — automatic completions are unchanged unless you opt in.

Fixes and polish

  • The activity hint stays put during long and parallel work. The pulsing “Thinking” dots no longer vanish mid-turn — they are re-asserted on each message and tool result and kept animating through long, quiet stretches, so a slow or parallel sub-agent run always shows that something is happening.
  • Chat view recovers after sleep or a display change. When the machine wakes from sleep or you (un)plug a monitor or move the window between displays, the chat could freeze or render at half resolution and never recover. ClawDEA now rebuilds the view automatically (and /refresh-view forces it), replaying the conversation into a fresh, responsive surface.
  • Cost Control numbers reconcile and always show. The savings section now adds up — estimated per-lever savings, measured upkeep, and a single “Overall” bottom line — and the all-projects, all-time aggregates show immediately on a brand-new chat instead of asking you to run a few turns first.
  • IDE index-tools savings are no longer stuck at $0.00. The first file read that the IDE index avoids is now priced at the full input rate (not the cache rate), so the estimated saving from index tools reflects the real cost avoided.

1.8.1

Windows: chat starts reliably again

  • Fixed: “The command line is too long” on Windows. With the wiki librarian enabled, the chat could fail to start on Windows — the helper subagents were passed to the Claude CLI as a long inline argument that exceeded the Windows command-line limit. ClawDEA now launches the CLI in a way that isn’t bound by that limit, so chat starts normally. macOS and Linux were unaffected.

1.8.0

See — and control — what each turn costs

  • Per-turn cost footer. Every completed turn now shows the model it ran on, the effort level, the elapsed time, and the cost — e.g. Opus 4.8 · effort high · 12.3s · $0.0421. The model and effort appear even under the “Default” selection, so you always know what actually ran.
  • Cost shown on subscription and Bedrock too. When your plan reports no per-turn dollar figure (subscription, and often Bedrock), the cost is computed from token usage with a per-model rate table, so the running total still moves.
  • Per-chat running total. Each chat tab tracks its own “chat” spend independently. Reopening a past conversation reconstructs its accumulated cost and shows it at the bottom, just like a live turn.
  • Cost Control panel. Click the cost chip to open a panel showing, per provider you’ve used: your subscription usage (spend limit or rate-limit windows, live from your Claude account), or your tracked Bedrock spend (this month and all-time). Below that: this chat’s cost, a by-model breakdown, and a Knowledge upkeep breakdown of what wiki and workspace creation/updates have cost. The daily-budget control lives in the panel footer and still color-codes the chip as you approach it.
  • Model selector labels the default. Once a Default-selection turn has run, the model dropdown’s “Default” entry shows what it resolved to — e.g. Default (Opus 4.8).

1.7.1

Wiki authoring that actually lands, and a tidier project footprint

  • Fixed: recorded wiki suggestions now get written. When the wiki librarian recorded a “missing concept” suggestion, the page could sit unwritten — the authoring pass ran on a slow periodic tick (or got wedged) and sometimes reported success without producing a file. Recording a suggestion now kicks off authoring immediately, the author has more time to finish, and a page is verified on disk before the suggestion is marked done.
  • No more leftover claude processes. Background claude -p helper processes are now tracked and cleaned up when the plugin unloads or the IDE quits, instead of lingering after you close the IDE.
  • Tidier project footprint. ClawDEA's own per-project files (the default-mode wiki and the generated repo-state summary) now live under .clawdea/ instead of .claude/, and existing projects are migrated automatically on startup — nothing to do by hand. The redundant SIBLINGS.md file is no longer written.

1.7.0

Sub-agents are now first-class in the chat

  • Sub-agents render as collapsible cards. When Claude dispatches a sub-agent (the Agent tool), its work now appears as a single card titled by what the sub-agent was asked to do, instead of the sub-agent's tool calls flooding the transcript. The card auto-expands while the sub-agent runs — so you can watch its steps stream in — then collapses to a one-line summary when it finishes. Click the header to expand it again; click any inner step to see that step's output.
  • Parallel sub-agents stay separate. When several sub-agents run at once, each gets its own card and its own steps — no more interleaved confusion.
  • Resumed sessions look right too. Reopening a past conversation reconstructs the sub-agent cards and the to-do checklist, rather than leaving a row of empty tool badges.

Keep Claude working toward a goal

  • /goal support. Set a completion condition with /goal <condition> and Claude keeps working across turns until a fast model judges it met — no need to prompt each step. A sticky goal banner shows the condition, how many turns it has run, and the evaluator's latest reason, updating after every turn; each evaluation also leaves a short inline note in the transcript.
  • Stop it any time. Click Clear in the banner (or run /goal clear / /goal stop) to halt a running goal immediately; the banner clears and a ✓ Goal achieved note appears when the condition is met on its own.

1.6.4

Wiki librarian no longer swallows its own answer

  • Fixed: the librarian sometimes came back empty. When the wiki librarian spotted a gap worth flagging for the next wiki refresh, its actual answer was getting dropped on the way back — you'd see only a terse “logged a suggestion” note instead of the explanation you asked for. The librarian now always returns its full answer, with the suggestion noted at the end.

1.6.3

Smarter by default

  • Baseline working defaults. ClawDEA now adds a small, always-on set of working defaults to Claude's instructions — stay surgical (don't refactor or reformat code you weren't asked to touch; surface worthwhile improvements as a separate suggestion instead of folding them in silently), prefer the simplest change that works, verify before claiming done, and ask only when a request is genuinely ambiguous and guessing wrong is costly. These are values, not a mandated procedure, and your project's CLAUDE.md and any installed workflow skills always take precedence — so they raise the floor without getting in the way of more capable tooling. Toggle them off any time via Settings → Tools → ClawDEA (“Inject baseline working defaults into system prompt”).
  • Tunable system prompts. ClawDEA's core system prompts (MCP tool routing, wiki-librarian routing, edit-review) and the new baseline defaults now live in editable resource files rather than compiled into the plugin, so the prompt text can evolve with model generations.

1.6.2

JetBrains MCP server coexistence

  • No more duplicate tool names. When IntelliJ's bundled MCP Server plugin is installed and its server is enabled, ClawDEA stops registering four tool names that collide with JetBrains' surface: search_text, find_files, resolve_symbol, and get_diagnostics. Claude Code now sees one tool per name; ClawDEA's unique tools (find_usages, find_callers, find_implementations, all debug_*, all propose_*, profiling, wiki, workspace) remain available.
  • Fail-open detection. ClawDEA reads JetBrains' setting via reflection. If the setting class is renamed or otherwise unreadable, ClawDEA logs a WARN and keeps its full surface registered, so the plugin stays useful even after future JetBrains internal changes.

1.6.1

Drift state no longer dirties the working tree

  • Rebase / merge no longer abort with "unstaged changes". The drift detector now skips rescan and dismiss while a git operation is in progress (GitRepository.state != NORMAL), so .wiki-state.json is never rewritten mid-rebase, mid-merge, mid-cherry-pick, or mid-revert.
  • Idle ticks no longer write to disk. lastSyncedCommit is now advanced only on the first-run baseline or when a rescan actually applies an event; routine ticks leave the field where it is. The team-shared .wiki-state.json stops appearing as a phantom modification after every commit, fetch, or branch switch.

1.6.0

Scala support

  • Scala in the index tools. find_symbol, find_usages, find_callers, find_implementations, find_supertypes, and resolve_symbol now work on Scala sources via a new ScalaLanguageSupport. Companion-class ambiguity is resolved with multiResolve, and import refs are resolved through the Scala plugin's own resolver so wildcard/aliased imports are followed correctly.
  • Optional Scala-plugin integration. When the IntelliJ Scala plugin is installed, ClawDEA loads clawdea-scala.xml and registers a ScalaPluginPsiBridge that powers find_related_types and a new Scala-specific MCP tool, find_implicit_definitions, listing implicit givens, val/def declarations, and extension blocks in a Scala file.

Build-tool adapter abstraction

  • Pluggable build tools. A new BuildTool interface and BuildToolRegistry let ClawDEA discover Gradle, Maven, sbt, and Mill projects uniformly. FileCollector and the diagnostics pipeline now route through this registry instead of hard-coded Gradle paths.
  • Maven, sbt, Mill. MavenBuildTool walks the module tree, dispatches Kotlin/Scala compile when the respective Maven plugins are present, and reads pom.xml via the new PomReader DOM helper. SbtBuildTool and MillBuildTool bring sbt and Mill projects into the same flow.
  • Per-language compile dispatch. Gradle now dispatches Scala to compileScala; BuildTool.compileCommandFor takes a LanguageSupport so each adapter picks the right task per language.

Diagnostics tier improvements

  • IntelliJ first, build-tool fallback. get_diagnostics now prefers IntelliJ inspections and the in-process CompilerManager over a build-tool subprocess. A new CompilerManagerDiagnostics helper turns the async compile API into a sync result. Tier 2 returns a clean "No diagnostics found." on empty inspection results instead of falling through.

UX polish & fixes

  • Edit-status badges now match the Auto-allowed style; the "Ask unlisted" approval mode gets a question-dialog icon in settings.
  • Chat: thinking indicator is force-repainted after hide so it never lingers as a ghost row.
  • Wiki: drift bookkeeping picks up legacy .drift-state.json at custom wiki paths; MCP errors are now logged with full context.
  • CLI: CliEventParser handles array-form tool_result content so structured tool outputs no longer render as empty.

1.5.0

Wiki team mode

  • Choose where the wiki lives. The new /wiki-relocate <repo-relative-path> slash command moves the wiki out of .claude/wiki/ into a path your team agrees on (e.g. docs/llm-wiki/) and writes .clawdea/config.json. Anyone who clones the repo automatically picks up the configured location — no setup needed. The relocate command shows an editable AskUserQuestion card with move/copy/none options so you can confirm before files are touched.
  • Per-user vs team-shared drift state. In team mode the wiki's drift bookkeeping splits into <wikiDir>/.wiki-state.json (committed: lastSyncedCommit, persistent suggestions) and .clawdea/wiki-state.local.json (gitignored: per-user dismissals, last scan, probe misses). Branch switching now correctly re-anchors drift detection without forgetting your personal dismissals.
  • Commit-anchored drift detection. CommitWikiDriftDetector now uses lastSyncedCommit..HEAD instead of a wall-clock window, so wiki drift survives rebases, force-pushes, and laptop downtime accurately.
  • Single source of truth for the wiki path. New WikiLocator project service routes every wiki-aware code path (MCP tools, drift, primer, suggestion writer, ChatPanel) through one resolver, with idempotent migration from the legacy .drift-state.json on first read in team mode.

/seed-wiki bootstraps both layers

  • One command to start. /seed-wiki now also creates CLAUDE.md from a scoped template if missing, and appends a "## Wiki" section linking to the wiki index when CLAUDE.md is present but the link is not. Bootstrap of CLAUDE.md and the wiki concept pages happens in a single turn.
  • Smart suggestions. When CLAUDE.md or the wiki index are missing, the chat surfaces an info block with a clickable /seed-wiki link instead of the generic /init nudge. The link runs the command for you with one click.

UX polish

  • Editable AskUserQuestion cards. Multi-choice prompts can now include an optional freeform text input, so commands like /wiki-relocate can offer "use this default path or type your own" without two round trips.
  • Per-kind drift icons. The drift banner, digest, and refresh prompts now show distinct icons per drift kind (code-rename, manifest-stale, wiki-suggestion, commit-drift) via the new DriftEventIcon helper.
  • Per-tool icons for wiki MCP tools. read_wiki_page, search_wiki, and edits inside the wiki directory now render with wiki-specific icons in the chat tool header.
  • Project tree refreshes after /wiki-relocate so moved/copied files show up immediately in the IDE.

1.4.3

Multiple-choice questions no longer get stuck after a long delay. When a multi-choice prompt sat open longer than the CLI's ~60 s permission round-trip cap (claude-code #50289), Claude finalised its turn as denied and would re-ask the same question on a follow-up "continue" instead of using your answer. Late answers are now re-injected as a synthetic user message so the conversation moves on with your selection; Skip likewise tells the model to proceed without an answer.

1.4.2

/resume now renders past sessions the way they actually looked. Resumed conversations were showing empty Write tools, edits as bare paths under the wrong "You" label, and AskUserQuestion / Task widgets rendered completely differently from the live stream. The replay path now shares a single rendering pipeline with the live event stream, so what you see when you resume matches what you saw the first time. (#7)

1.4.1

Auto-update wiki now actually edits the wiki. When you turn on "Auto-update wiki on drift", the wiki-author subagent now lands its proposed changes to disk in the background. Previously the subagent ran but its edits never reached your wiki because it was waiting for a diff-approval dialog that nobody could see.

  • Recording wiki suggestions ("missingConcept", "staleConcept", "incompleteConcept" via the librarian) is now reliable — previously failed silently for some inputs
  • The wiki-author runs in fully unattended mode, has access to the project's IntelliJ index tools (find_symbol, search_text, etc.), and inherits your auth (subscription / Bedrock / Vertex) just like the chat
  • Failures are now logged with enough context (exit code, stderr) to tell you why a wiki update didn't land instead of failing silently

1.4.0

Wiki knowledge layer

  • Agent-based wiki: replaced system-prompt-based wiki usage with specialized sub-agents wiki-librarian and wiki-author — slimmer system prompt, always-fresh findings (no long-session decay), supports larger wikis with better coverage on big projects
  • Wiki-librarian routing: Claude now consults the wiki-librarian subagent before answering project-understanding questions, grounding answers in synthesized concept pages with verified source citations
  • Wiki-author subagent: replaces the dream-based wiki maintenance system with a commit-driven drift detector that identifies stale wiki claims from git history, and a wiki-author subagent that rewrites affected pages
  • Drift banner suppression: with "Auto-update wiki" enabled, wiki-author events are handled silently without surfacing the drift banner; only truly unresolvable events remain visible

Permission UX

  • Multi-panel routing: permission cards now appear in the chat tab that triggered the tool call instead of whichever tab is focused, fixing wrong-tab approvals in multi-tab projects
  • Auto-allowed badge: the "⚡ Auto-allowed" marker now shows reliably on fast tool calls (it was racing with the HTTP signal on sub-second tools)
  • Compact permission card: removed redundant tool name and input echo since that info is already visible in the tool header above

1.3.6

  • Windows: CLI permission settings no longer crash the CLI — cmd.exe was stripping double-quotes from .cmd shim arguments, mangling the inline permission JSON; settings are now passed via a temp file
  • Windows: tool-call panels show just the filename for Read/Write/Edit actions, matching macOS behavior (was showing the full C:\\... path)

1.3.5

  • Windows: ClawDEA now finds the Claude CLI when IntelliJ is launched from the Start menu/Explorer — probes %APPDATA%\\npm, %LOCALAPPDATA%\\Volta\\bin, %USERPROFILE%\\.local\\bin, and C:\\Program Files\\nodejs. PowerShell shims are transparently redirected to the sibling .cmd
  • Windows: .cmd/.bat shims now launch correctly — the executability check no longer rejects them (Windows decides launchability via PATHEXT, not the executable bit)
  • Large system prompts no longer overflow the OS command-line limit — the appended system prompt is now written to a temp file and passed via --append-system-prompt-file, fixing crashes on Windows (32 KB limit) and risk on Linux (ARG_MAX) when the skill catalog or primer grows large
  • Release workflow now attaches the signed plugin zip to GitHub releases automatically

1.3.4

  • Compatibility fix for JetBrains Marketplace: profiling no longer uses an internal API flagged by Marketplace moderation

1.3.3

  • Refreshed plugin icons (Marketplace thumbnail + tool-window, light and dark)
  • First JetBrains Marketplace release

1.3.2

  • Knowledge-layer reasoning: path-aware wiki probe, invariant-first concept pages, correction capture
  • New find_symbol MCP tool — resolve class/method/field names to definition locations via the PSI index
  • Per-session tool-approval state fixed
  • Stronger tool-routing guidance steers Claude toward the index tools and away from filesystem grep for code symbols

1.2.0

  • JFR-backed profiling: CPU, allocations, memory leaks, .jfr/.hprof import, gutter icon on @Test methods

1.1.0

  • Hardened tool-permission UX and CLI session reliability
  • Drift monitoring for Claude Code CLI changes with weekly digest + PR-time fixture replay

1.0.0

  • Initial public release for IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1

Supported IDEs

idea-plugin.name: Blamely
idea-plugin.description:
Blamely attributes every line of code to AI or human — across inline completions, chat apply, and agent runs. The breakdown appears in the status bar as you work, survives branch switches, and attaches permanently to each commit via git notes.

All data stays on your machine. No account, no telemetry, no network access.

How it works

  1. Record. When an AI tool edits a file, its hook calls blamely record <tool>.
  2. Watch. The daemon also tails Cursor logs, Copilot transcripts, and filesystem activity.
  3. Attribute. On every commit, the global post-commit hook diffs the commit against stored edits and writes per-line attribution.
  4. Report. The IDE plugin reads those notes back into the status bar, tool window, and gutter.

After each commit

A clear AI vs Human bar prints in your terminal immediately after git commit:

AI 72% (18)  [████████████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░]  Human 28% (7)
  claude  12 lines  (claude-opus-4-6) — 4200 in / 890 out tok
  cursor   6 lines  (composer-1)      — 1100 in / 340 out tok

Status bar

The status bar widget shows live AI / Human metrics for the active file:

AI: 751 © 24 = 98%  |  Human: 12 © 3 = 2%  |  claude-opus-4-6

© = characters, = = lines. Click to open the full panel.

Changes tool window

The Blamely → Changes tab shows per-file AI / Human breakdown for all uncommitted work on the current branch, with a visual progress bar per file and a session summary at the bottom.

History tool window

The Blamely → History tab shows AI vs Human share across past commits — total lines, per-model breakdown, commit table with timing, and a segmented bar. Example:

482 AI lines · 40.2%  |  716 Human · 59.8%
18 commits · 44 files · Coding: 32m 17s · AI wait: 50s

#1  claude-opus-4-6  135 lines · 28.0% · 1 commit
#2  cursor-composer   82 lines · 17.0% · 3 commits

Example report.yml (attached to each commit)

scope: "this_commit"
generated_at: "2026-03-05T00:43:50Z"
branch: "main"
commit_hash: "3317ed295e"
commit_message: "[AI-assisted] feat: update analysis"

ai_sources:
  - claude
  - cursor

files:
  - path: "src/utils/parser.ts"
    source: "claude"
    model: "claude-opus-4-6"
    ai_lines_added: 22
    human_lines_added: 65
    percentage: "40.0%"

Requirements — Install the CLI first

macOS

curl -sSL https://blamely.ai/blamely-mac-install.sh | bash

Linux

curl -sSL https://blamely.ai/blamely-linux-install.sh | bash

Windows (PowerShell)

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "irm https://blamely.ai/blamely-windows-install.bat | iex"

Installers are idempotent — safe to re-run after adding a new AI tool. Verify:

blamely status    # daemon health + detected tools
blamely doctor    # full self-check

Full guide: blamely.ai

Features

  • Line-level blame — Gutter icons + tooltips (AI vs human per line)
  • Status bar widget — Live AI / Human chars, lines, percentage, active model
  • Changes tool window — Per-file breakdown for uncommitted work on current branch
  • History tool window — Per-model stats, commit table, timing across past commits
  • Git notes — report.yml on every commit via refs/notes/blamely
  • Pre-commit / pre-push hooks — Survive plugin upgrades via stable runner scripts
  • Branch-scoped sessions — State under .git/blamely/<branch>/
  • Actions — Generate Report, Show Blame, Install/Restore Hook, Show Commit Report, Push AI Notes
  • VS Code compatible — Same .git/blamely layout; both IDEs share attribution data
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.8.5

  • Editing very large files no longer freezes the IDE — a small change to a very large file could make the plugin use a huge amount of memory and bring the IDE to a halt. It now stays light however large the file is, and very large changes are attributed more accurately too.
  • Git worktrees are fully supported — if you work on several branches side by side in separate worktrees, each one now shows its own correct record of who wrote what.
  • Blamely now works with OpenCode — code written by OpenCode (V1 and V2) is now tracked and credited to it.
  • git push no longer waits for Blamely — sharing attribution with your team now happens in the background, and a push that fails no longer loses your in-progress attribution.
  • Commits are fast again in long-used repositories — tidying up old records could add tens of seconds to every commit, especially on Windows. It now takes a moment.
  • A new look — Blamely has a new logo.

1.8.2

  • Pasting no longer freezes the IDE — every paste of more than a few characters made Blamely run several git commands before the editor was allowed to respond, and a multi-cursor paste, or the automatic reformat that follows one, multiplied that by every insertion point. Blamely now gets the same information without running anything at all, and does the rest out of your way. Typing is lighter too: the plugin was copying the whole file three times on every keystroke, even when nothing needed those copies.
  • Branching before you commit no longer credits the AI's work to you — working on your main branch and creating a branch when it is time to commit (git checkout -b my-feature) quietly lost the entire session's AI attribution, and the commit reported every AI-written line as hand-written. It is now carried across the branch you made, and the gutter is right straight away rather than only after the commit.
  • Attribution reaches your remote again after the first clash — once a teammate's breakdown had arrived at the remote before yours, or your own rebase had rewritten yours, every send after that was refused in silence and your records stayed on your machine. Both sides are now brought together and sent.
  • Blamely now tells you when a project switches it off — a project that manages its own git hooks (Husky, lefthook, pre-commit) takes over the setting Blamely depends on, and Blamely then records nothing at all there. blamely doctor now reports it and tells you what to do.

1.8.1

  • Attribution written on a detached HEAD is no longer lost — while you were on a detached HEAD (during a rebase, or after checking out a commit directly), the IDE saved your in-progress attribution to a different folder than the one Blamely reads at commit time, so that work was credited to nobody. Both now agree.
  • Blamely uses far less CPU while you type — the plugin re-read your whole project's attribution on every keystroke, and ran git twice every three seconds just to notice commits, plus twice more each time it saved your in-progress attribution. Commits, branch switches and stashes are now noticed the moment git writes them — instantly instead of up to three seconds later — and the re-read happens when the data actually changes rather than while you're still typing.
  • Switching tabs is quick again — opening a file used to re-read attribution for the entire project. It now reads only the files you can see.
  • Leftover Blamely processes — when recording lines an AI tool had deleted, the plugin started a helper it never waited for and never limited, so a stuck one stayed running until you closed the IDE. They now give up after ten seconds, and no more than a few run at a time.

1.7.0

  • A setting for when the AI/Human breakdown doesn't show up — on very large projects, or slow and company-managed machines, Blamely could give up reading your history before it finished and leave the gutter and tool window empty. It now waits up to a minute instead of a few seconds, and you can raise that further under Settings → Tools → Blamely → Authorship CLI timeout.
  • The plugin ships fully readable — all code-scrambling was removed, so the published plugin is exactly the public source and your security team can verify what runs in your IDE.

1.6.9

  • Attribution survives cherry-pick, squash, and stash — reorganizing your history keeps the AI-vs-human credit on each line instead of resetting it to Human.
  • The gutter and tool window keep up with your work — Blamely now notices file and branch changes as they happen, so the AI/Human view refreshes on its own instead of lagging behind.
  • Same behaviour as the VS Code extension — attribution, the status bar, and the Changes and History views now match what the VS Code extension shows for the same project.

1.6.4

  • AI work no longer slips to "Human" — brand-new files an assistant creates (for example a generated package.json) are now credited to the assistant instead of falling back to Human.
  • Attribution survives history changes — amending, rebasing, or re-committing a change keeps its AI/human credit instead of resetting it to Human.
  • Lighter and faster with the editor open — background refreshes now run one at a time, so Blamely no longer piles up dozens of helper processes that competed for resources and slowed things down.
  • Just one background helper — only a single Blamely daemon runs at a time; duplicates exit instead of accumulating.
  • Quicker gutter on large repositories — per-file attribution now reads commit history in fewer steps, so the gutter fills in faster.

1.6.3

  • More accurate when AI and your edits mix — when an assistant rewrites a file you'd just edited by hand, your lines stay yours and only the assistant's lines are credited to it.
  • Works across your whole workspace — AI and human changes are now tracked in every Git repository in the workspace, not just the first one found.
  • New files show up right away — brand-new files appear in the gutter the moment you start writing, without staging them in Git first.
  • A friendly nudge for new projects — open a folder that isn't a Git repository yet and Blamely offers to set it up.
  • Clearer status bar — the AI and human summary now leads with the percentage.
  • A cleaner, consistent gutter — the AI and human markers share the same crisp sizing across VS Code and JetBrains.

1.6.0

  • Status bar count now matches the gutter — the AI/Human status bar widget previously summed every tracked file across the project and counted blank lines, while the gutter shows only the active file and skips blanks. The widget now reports the active file only, resolved exactly like the gutter (repo-relative path + live blank-line check), so the number equals the icons in front of you.

idea-plugin.name: Trans MD
idea-plugin.description:
Trans Md

Adds one-click translation to the JetBrains Markdown preview, powered by Google Translate.

Features

  • Translated Preview tab next to the standard Markdown preview — no separate window needed
  • Side-by-side source editor and translated preview in a single split panel
  • Translate and Refresh buttons added directly to the Markdown toolbar
  • Translates in chunks so large files work reliably
  • Preserves code blocks, inline code, URLs, front matter, and math blocks ($$) untranslated
  • Caches translation results per-session to avoid redundant API calls
  • API key stored securely in the OS keychain via the IDE credential store
  • Target language configurable from Settings → Tools → Trans Md

Requirements

  • Google Translate API key with the Cloud Translation API enabled

Trans Md

Google Translate 기반으로 JetBrains Markdown 미리보기에 원클릭 번역 기능을 추가합니다.

기능

  • 기본 Markdown 미리보기 옆에 번역 미리보기 탭 추가 — 별도 창 불필요
  • 소스 에디터와 번역 미리보기를 하나의 분할 패널에서 나란히 표시
  • Markdown 툴바에 번역(Translate) 및 새로고침(Refresh) 버튼 직접 추가
  • 대용량 파일도 안정적으로 처리하기 위해 청크 단위로 번역
  • 코드 블록, 인라인 코드, URL, 프런트 매터, 수식 블록($$)은 번역하지 않고 그대로 유지
  • 세션 내 번역 결과를 캐시하여 불필요한 API 호출 방지
  • API 키는 IDE 자격증명 저장소를 통해 OS 키체인에 안전하게 보관
  • Settings → Tools → Trans Md에서 대상 언어 설정 가능

요구사항

  • Cloud Translation API가 활성화된 Google Translate API 키

idea-plugin.name: Claude Token Monitor
idea-plugin.description:
Track your Claude API rate limits in real time - right from the IDE status bar. No more switching to the Anthropic console mid-session to check if you're about to hit a quota.

☕ Buy me a coffee - if this plugin saves you time, a small tip keeps development going!

What it does

Claude Token Monitor polls the Claude API in the background and displays your current token and request usage as a compact widget in the status bar. A single glance tells you how much of your quota is left and when it resets.

Key features

  • Live status bar widget - color-coded indicator updates automatically (green to orange to red as usage climbs)
  • Dual rolling-window tracking - monitors both the 5-hour and 7-day windows for Claude.ai Pro / OAuth accounts
  • Detailed hover popup - shows tokens used, requests remaining, percentage consumed, and exact reset times
  • API key & OAuth support - works with standard sk-ant-* keys and Claude.ai Pro OAuth tokens; one-click autofill from your local Claude CLI credentials
  • Configurable polling interval - 10 s to 3600 s, default 30 s
  • Zero external dependencies - lightweight, no third-party libraries
  • Multilingual UI - English, Ukrainian, and German

How it works

The plugin sends a minimal test request to the Claude API at a configurable interval and reads the rate-limit headers returned by Anthropic. It always selects the cheapest available model (Claude Haiku) for polling so overhead is negligible.

Configuration

Open Tools → Claude Token Monitor to enter your API key or OAuth token, set the refresh interval, and link directly to the Anthropic console.
